What are the new heaven and the new earth?
Answer
In Revelation 21:1, John sees something spectacular: “Then I saw ‘a new heaven and a new earth,’ for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away.” This new earth and new heaven are sometimes referred to as the “eternal state.” As seen in Revelation chapters 21—22, the new earth will be the eternal dwelling place of believers in Jesus Christ. Scripture gives us a few details of the new heaven and new earth.

The current heaven and earth have long been subject to God’s curse because of mankind’s sin. All creation “has been groaning as in the pains of childbirth” (Romans 8:22) as it awaits the fulfillment of God’s plan and “the children of God to be revealed” (verse 19). Heaven and earth will pass away (Mark 13:31), and they will be replaced by the new heaven and the new earth. At that time, the Lord, seated on His throne, says, “I am making everything new!” (Revelation 21:5). In the new creation, sin will be totally eradicated, and “there shall be no more curse” (Revelation 22:3, NKJV).

The new heaven and new earth are also mentioned in Isaiah 65:17; 66:22; and 2 Peter 3:13. Peter says that the new heaven and new earth will be “where righteousness dwells.” Isaiah says that “the former things will not be remembered, nor will they come to mind.” Things will be completely new, and the old order of things, with the accompanying sorrow and tragedy, will be gone.

The new earth will be free from sin, evil, sickness, suffering, and death. It will be earth as God originally intended it to be, prior to the curse of sin. It will be Eden restored.

A major feature of the new earth will be the New Jerusalem. John calls it “the Holy City . . . coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride beautifully dressed for her husband” (Revelation 21:2). This glorious city, with its streets of gold and pearly gates, is situated on a new, glorious earth. The tree of life will be there (Revelation 22:2). This city represents the final state of redeemed mankind, forever in fellowship with God: “God’s dwelling place is now among the people, and he will dwell with them. They will be his people, and God himself will be with them and be their God. . . . His servants will serve him. They will see his face” (Revelation 21:3; 22:3–4).

In the new heaven and new earth, Scripture says, there are seven things notable for their absence—seven things that are “no more”:
• no more sea (Revelation 21:1)
• no more death (Revelation 21:4)
• no more mourning (Revelation 21:4)
• no more weeping (Revelation 21:4)
• no more pain (Revelation 21:4)
• no more curse (Revelation 22:3)
• no more night (Revelation 22:5)

The creation of the new heaven and new earth brings the promise that God “will wipe every tear from their eyes” (Revelation 21:4). This event comes after the tribulation, after the Lord’s second coming, after the millennial kingdom, after the final rebellion, after the final judgment of Satan, and after the great white throne judgment. What are the new heaven and the new earth?
Answer
In Revelation 21:1, John sees something spectacular: “Then I saw ‘a new heaven and a new earth,’ for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away.” This new earth and new heaven are sometimes referred to as the “eternal state.” As seen in Revelation chapters 21—22, the new earth will be the eternal dwelling place of believers in Jesus Christ. Scripture gives us a few details of the new heaven and new earth.

The current heaven and earth have long been subject to God’s curse because of mankind’s sin. All creation “has been groaning as in the pains of childbirth” (Romans 8:22) as it awaits the fulfillment of God’s plan and “the children of God to be revealed” (verse 19). Heaven and earth will pass away (Mark 13:31), and they will be replaced by the new heaven and the new earth. At that time, the Lord, seated on His throne, says, “I am making everything new!” (Revelation 21:5). In the new creation, sin will be totally eradicated, and “there shall be no more curse” (Revelation 22:3, NKJV).

The new heaven and new earth are also mentioned in Isaiah 65:17; 66:22; and 2 Peter 3:13. Peter says that the new heaven and new earth will be “where righteousness dwells.” Isaiah says that “the former things will not be remembered, nor will they come to mind.” Things will be completely new, and the old order of things, with the accompanying sorrow and tragedy, will be gone.

The new earth will be free from sin, evil, sickness, suffering, and death. It will be earth as God originally intended it to be, prior to the curse of sin. It will be Eden restored.

A major feature of the new earth will be the New Jerusalem. John calls it “the Holy City . . . coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride beautifully dressed for her husband” (Revelation 21:2). This glorious city, with its streets of gold and pearly gates, is situated on a new, glorious earth. The tree of life will be there (Revelation 22:2). This city represents the final state of redeemed mankind, forever in fellowship with God: “God’s dwelling place is now among the people, and he will dwell with them. They will be his people, and God himself will be with them and be their God. . . . His servants will serve him. They will see his face” (Revelation 21:3; 22:3–4).

In the new heaven and new earth, Scripture says, there are seven things notable for their absence—seven things that are “no more”:
• no more sea (Revelation 21:1)
• no more death (Revelation 21:4)
• no more mourning (Revelation 21:4)
• no more weeping (Revelation 21:4)
• no more pain (Revelation 21:4)
• no more curse (Revelation 22:3)
• no more night (Revelation 22:5)

The creation of the new heaven and new earth brings the promise that God “will wipe every tear from their eyes” (Revelation 21:4). This event comes after the tribulation, after the Lord’s second coming, after the millennial kingdom, after the final rebellion, after the final judgment of Satan, and after the great white throne judgment. The brief description of the new heaven and new earth is the last glimpse into eternity that the Bible gives.

Could you reach your bug-out location if your main route closed tomorrow? 🧭

👇 Name YOUR top state—and the biggest drawback you’d have to plan around.

TOP 10 STATES FOR A BUG-OUT LOCATION

These ten states, drawn from the article’s shortlist, offer different possibilities. Use this as a starting point for research: your travel distance, household needs, and the actual property should drive the decision.

#1 MISSOURI
The Ozarks offer wooded hills, springs, and rivers. Check the specific property’s flood exposure, dependable drinking water, and usable garden ground. A creek nearby still requires a water-treatment plan.

#2 IDAHO
Northern Idaho offers forested terrain and a wetter climate than much of the south. Winter access, wildfire exposure, and seasonal water availability deserve close attention. Plan your food production around local conditions.

#3 TENNESSEE
Eastern Tennessee offers wooded ridges and rural mountain communities. Elevation changes temperatures and growing conditions. Investigate flood exposure, drought vulnerability, and whether access roads remain usable throughout the year.

#4 ARKANSAS
The Ozarks and Ouachitas offer wooded terrain and water resources. Assess the amount of workable ground, then plan for summer heat, drought, and flooding. Walk the property before imagining a productive homestead.

#5 WEST VIRGINIA
Forested Appalachian terrain can appeal to people seeking privacy. Steep slopes can limit gardens and complicate access. Flood exposure deserves particular attention when evaluating valley properties and the roads serving them.

#6 MISSISSIPPI
A warm climate supports a long growing season. Your plan also needs to handle extreme heat, tornadoes, flooding, and hurricane impacts. Inland properties can still experience damaging tropical-storm rainfall.

#7 ALABAMA
Northern foothill areas offer woodland and agricultural possibilities. Assess water and garden potential alongside tornado exposure, heat, and storm shelter. A productive growing season still takes suitable soil, skills, and reliable supplies.

#8 OKLAHOMA
Eastern Oklahoma is generally wetter than the west and includes wooded areas, lakes, and rivers. Tornadoes, drought, and severe storms belong in the plan. Check how your water source performs during dry years.

#9 KANSAS
Farm country offers possibilities for food production where the soil and water fit your needs. Rainfall generally decreases westward. Evaluate drought exposure, wind protection, and severe-weather shelter before choosing a parcel.

#10 IOWA
Agricultural land makes Iowa worth researching for a food-production-focused retreat. Check the property’s soil and drainage. Cold winters, snow, and flooding need to shape your shelter, heating, food-storage, and access plans.

Prepper tip:
Visit potential locations in different seasons. Confirm permission or ownership, dependable water, usable soil, road access, local building and septic requirements, and access to medical care.

USDA’s Web Soil Survey can help you investigate soil conditions before an on-site assessment. Then practice your travel plan and identify an alternate destination.

🔖 Bookmark this shortlist for your location research, and retweet it to help another household compare the strengths and tradeoffs before choosing a retreat.

Exact claim (Nov 2, 2026): "Joe Lombardo and Donald Trump have been working together to raise your gas, groceries, housing, and health care costs!"

Verdict: MISLEADING

What the record shows:
Some cost pressures Nevadans feel are real. Nevada diesel approached record highs around mid-October 2026. Clark County housing remains hard to afford on typical wages. Nevada Health Link enrollees saw higher net premiums for 2026 after enhanced federal ACA premium tax credits expired.

What the post leaves out:
It treats four different markets as one Lombardo-Trump package.
Gas and diesel: a UNR economist and Nevada's Fuel Resiliency Committee have pointed to refining limits, seasonal demand, and Nevada's dependence on a California pipeline, not a single shared governor-president price-setting scheme (News 4; https://t.co/AdHlCyYCNp / https://t.co/5OyUdY7KXh).

Groceries: national food inflation and supply factors dominate; the post offers no Nevada primary showing a joint Lombardo-Trump program that set grocery prices.

Alliance and endorsements are not the same as jointly raising four household bills. The record supports cost pain. It does not support the causal shortcut.

text:
Mary Phagan Case Files Biopic: Clark Howell (1863–1936) Editor and Owner of The Atlanta Constitution 

Clark Howell Sr. was an American newspaper editor, publisher, businessman, and Democratic politician who helped shape Georgia's political and newspaper history for more than fifty years. As editor and principal owner of The Atlanta Constitution, he controlled one of the South's most influential daily newspapers during a period that included the rise of Jim Crow segregation, the 1906 Atlanta race riot, the 1913 Mary Phagan murder trial, World War I, and the Great Depression. The Constitution was one of the leading mainstream newspapers circulating in the State of Georgia and the American South.

Trajectory and Key Dates:

Howell joined The Atlanta Constitution in 1884, became managing editor following the death of Henry W. Grady in 1889, and succeeded his father as editor-in-chief in 1897. In 1901, he acquired a controlling interest in the newspaper. Howell remained its editor and principal owner until his death in 1936, spending approximately 52 years with the publication (Eberhard, 1).

Press Origin:

The Atlanta Constitution was founded on June 16, 1868, by Carey Wentworth Styles and James H. Anderson. Its first edition appeared during Reconstruction, when Georgia was still under federal military authority and control following the Civil War. The newspaper supported the Democratic Party and opposed the Republican state government led by Governor Rufus B. Bullock. It became an influential voice for white Southern political and business interests (Library of Congress, 2).

Background:

Clark Howell was born on September 21, 1863, in Erwinton, South Carolina. His parents were Evan Park Howell and Julia A. Erwin. His father served as a Confederate artillery captain before entering the newspaper business in Atlanta, where he worked as a reporter and city editor for the Atlanta Intelligencer (Eberhard, 1).

Family Entry into the Capital Press Industry:

In 1876, Evan Howell purchased a half interest in The Atlanta Constitution and became its editor-in-chief and president. He helped expand the newspaper's readership and recruited well-known writers, including Henry W. Grady and Joel Chandler Harris. Harris became famous for his Uncle Remus stories, which began appearing in the Constitution in 1878. Other contributors included humorist Charles Henry Smith, known as Bill Arp, and poet Frank Lebby Stanton (Library of Congress, 2).

Henry W. Grady became the newspaper's best-known editor during the 1880s. He promoted what he called the "New South," encouraging industrial development, improved transportation, and greater investment in Southern businesses. His speeches and editorials brought national attention to Atlanta while defending the South's existing racial order. By the late 1880s, the Constitution had become one of the South's most widely circulated newspapers (Library of Congress, 2).

Education and Career:

Clark Howell graduated from the University of Georgia in 1883. He received newspaper training at The New York Times and The Philadelphia Press before returning to Atlanta in 1884. At approximately twenty years old, he joined his father's newspaper as night editor, working under Grady and alongside Harris (Eberhard, 1).

Howell entered politics while building his newspaper career. In 1885, he was elected to the Georgia House of Representatives, where he served three terms and later became Speaker of the House. His work in state government gave him connections with politicians whose activities were regularly covered by the Constitution.

Personal Life:

In 1887, Howell married Harriet Glascock Barrett of Augusta, Georgia. They had two children, Clark Howell Jr. and Susie. Harriet died in 1898 (Eberhard, 1).

On December 23, 1889, Henry W. Grady died at age 39. Howell, then 26, soon succeeded Grady as managing editor of The Atlanta Constitution. During these years, he used the newspaper to oppose Georgia's convict leasing system, which allowed private businesses to use prisoners for labor under harsh conditions. He also supported Atlanta's acceptance of people fleeing yellow fever outbreaks elsewhere in the South (Eberhard, 1).

In 1892, Howell joined the Democratic National Committee, and in 1896, he became a member of the University of Georgia's Board of Trustees. In 1897, his father retired, and Howell became editor-in-chief at age 33. The position gave him greater authority over the newspaper's reporting, political opinions, and editorial policies (Perry, 3).

In 1900, Howell was elected to the Georgia Senate and became its president. That same year, he began serving as a director of the Associated Press, a national organization that distributed news reports to newspapers throughout the country. He remained an Associated Press director until his death (Eberhard, 1).

In the fall of 1901, William Arnold Hemphill, one of the Constitution's longtime owners, sold his newspaper stock to Clark Howell and Roby Robinson. Howell acquired a controlling interest, becoming the newspaper's principal owner. When Hemphill retired in January 1902, Howell became president of the publishing company (Library of Congress, 2).

Howell now held the newspaper's leading editorial position and a controlling ownership interest. This gave him considerable authority over its business operations, editorial policies, and political positions. The New York Times reports that on July 12, 1900, Howell married Annie Comer of Savannah, Georgia, daughter of the late Hugh M. Comer, Central of Georgia Railway, president. They had three sons, Hugh, Albert, and Julian (Eberhard, 1; The New York Times, 1900, 13).

Newspaper Wars

During the early twentieth century, the Constitution competed with The Atlanta Journal, an afternoon newspaper founded on February 24, 1883. The rivalry involved advertising revenue, circulation, and political influence. It became especially bitter in 1906, when Howell ran for governor of Georgia against Hoke Smith, a former owner of the Journal (Perry, 3).

Both candidates used their newspapers to promote their campaigns and criticize their opponents. Howell received support from the Constitution, while Smith was supported by the Journal.

One of the main campaign issues was whether Georgia should impose additional restrictions on Black voting rights. Smith favored stronger restrictions. Howell argued that existing methods, including the white Democratic primary and poll taxes, were already sufficient. Howell also accused Smith of previously cooperating with Black political leaders. Both campaigns appealed to racial prejudice (Kuhn & Mixon, 4).

Smith defeated Howell in the Democratic primary in August 1906. The campaign had been marked by personal attacks, racial arguments, and inflammatory newspaper coverage.

On Saturday, September 22, 1906, white mobs began attacking Black residents and businesses in Atlanta. The violence continued for several days and became known as the Atlanta race riot of 1906. Historians estimate that at least 25 Black Atlantans were killed, although some place the number as high as 40. Some racial activists and outside commentators have cited even higher figures. Such estimates can become weaponized tools for those seeking to stoke conflict between people of European and African ancestry, promote racial division, and encourage deracination. However, disagreements over the death toll should be settled through historical evidence rather than assumptions about political motives.

Some historians have argued that the 1906 gubernatorial campaign, racial propaganda, and sensational reporting by Atlanta newspapers contributed to the violence. How much responsibility should be assigned to each factor remains disputed. Some historians argue that The Atlanta Constitution and The Atlanta Journal used racial arguments during the campaign, while other newspapers published reports of assaults on white women by Black men, increasing public hostility. Some historians also argue that these crime reports helped provoke the riot while questioning the accuracy of the reported assaults (Kuhn & Mixon, 4). However, sexual assault is often difficult to prove, and the absence of conclusive evidence more than a century later does not establish that the reported crimes never occurred. The accuracy of those reports and the extent to which newspaper coverage contributed to the violence are separate historical questions that should be examined on their own evidence.

Howell did not seek another elected office after his defeat. He remained active in Democratic Party politics and continued directing The Atlanta Constitution. In 1912, his brother Albert became president of the publishing company, while Clark remained editor and principal owner (Library of Congress, 2).

The Mary Phagan Case

On Saturday, April 26, 1913, thirteen-year-old Mary Phagan was murdered at the National Pencil Company factory in Atlanta. Howell was then 49 years old and had served as editor-in-chief of The Atlanta Constitution for approximately sixteen years.

The murder became one of the most widely reported and well documented criminal cases in Georgia history. The Constitution published reports about the discovery of Mary Phagan's body, the police investigation, the questioning of suspects, and the search for evidence.

According to historian Steve Oney, a Constitution reporter, accompanied the police officers who responded to the discovery of Mary Phagan's body during the early morning hours of Sunday, April 27, 1913. That Constitution journalist was named Britt Craig (Phagan-Kean, 12). After dawn, the newspaper had issued an extra edition reporting the murder, giving the Constitution an early advantage over its competitors (Oney, 8).  It had a kind of first mover advantage. That extra edition of the Constitution is extremely rare and difficult to find. 

On Tuesday, April 29, 1913, The Atlanta Constitution published an editorial titled "$1,000 Reward" on page four. The editorial called upon Atlanta's police and detectives to solve the murder and offered $1,000 for exclusive information leading to the arrest and conviction of whoever had committed the crime. The reward showed the newspaper's willingness to use its money and influence to assist the investigation (AC, 5).

The Constitution continued reporting on the questioning of factory night watchman Newt Lee, the arrest of factory superintendent Leo M. Frank, and statements from other people connected with the investigation.

On Thursday, May 1, 1913, the newspaper published a front-page article titled "Frank Tried to Flirt With Murdered Girl Says Her Boy Chum." The report described testimony given by George W. Epps, a fifteen-year-old acquaintance of Mary Phagan, before the coroner's jury. The newspaper also reported Frank's refusal to discuss the accusation when questioned by a Constitution reporter (AC, 6).

The Constitution's coverage included some allegations against Frank, statements from investigators, witness testimony, and reports about the defense's efforts to challenge the prosecution.

The newspaper's Tuesday, June 3, 1913, edition identified Howell on page six as its "Editor and General Manager," with W. L. Halstead listed as business manager. Howell also appeared among the company's directors (AC, 7).

The masthead identified the Constitution as a newspaper published in daily, Sunday, and triweekly editions. It maintained a Washington, D.C., news bureau at 1727 S Street NW, with John Corrigan as its staff correspondent. Copies were sold at newsstands in New York City, and local carrier delivery of the daily and Sunday newspaper cost 15 cents per week (AC, 7).

When Leo Frank's trial began on Monday, July 28, 1913, The Atlanta Constitution reported extensively on courtroom proceedings, witness testimony, and arguments by attorneys. The prosecution was led by Solicitor General Hugh M. Dorsey. Frank's defense attorneys included Luther Z. Rosser and Reuben R. Arnold.

Witnesses included factory employees, police officers, medical witnesses, and Jim Conley, whose testimony became central to the prosecution's case. Reporters from the Constitution, Journal, and Georgian competed to publish accounts of the trial and produce extra editions for readers following the proceedings.

The trial ended with Frank's conviction on Monday, August 25, 1913. Judge Leonard S. Roan subsequently on August 26, 1913, sentenced him to death with the execution date of October 10th, 1913.

The three principal Atlanta newspapers did not always present the case in the same way. According to historian Steve Oney, who is a prominent Leo Frank apologist, The Atlanta Constitution was politically allied with the prosecution, while the rival Journal and Georgian were generally more favorable to Frank as the case developed (Oney, 8). But this will require more research, analysis and evaluation now that we have about 70% of the Mary Phagan case articles transcribed at the Mary Phagan-Kean Legacy Project website of https://t.co/MNvBytBBsq and elsewhere. 

Although the Constitution published information favorable to Frank and his defense, its early reporting also gave considerable attention to police theories and allegations against him. Radical Leo Frank apologist and Judaic studies historian Leonard Dinnerstein likewise found that the Constitution was the Atlanta daily most inclined to suggest Frank's guilt during the investigation.

Oney also observed that the Constitution generally avoided the racial attacks against Jim Conley that appeared in the other two newspapers. Both the Journal and Georgian criticized Conley, the prosecution's leading witness, while publishing material favorable to Frank (Oney, 8).

As editor and principal owner, Howell influenced the Constitution's general policies and editorial direction. However, his position does not prove that he personally wrote every editorial or approved the wording of every article concerning the Mary Phagan murder case.

Following Frank's conviction, the Constitution continued reporting on his appeals, requests for a new trial, and efforts by supporters to prevent his execution. During 1914 and 1915, the case attracted vast national attention as newspapers published competing arguments about the evidence and the conduct of the trial.

Clemency:

On June 21, 1915, Governor John M. Slaton commuted Frank's death sentence to life imprisonment. The decision produced strong public reactions, including protests and threats against Slaton. Often given scant mention, is the fact that Slaton was a partner of the law firm that represented Leo Frank during his state level court case and appellate review. 

Extrajudicial Hanging:

Frank was immediately transferred to the Georgia State Prison Farm at Milledgeville. His throat was slashed on July 17, 1915, by a fellow psychopathic inmate, William Creen, and Frank remained in the hospital infirmary until his abduction a month later. On the night of August 16, 1915, armed men removed him from the prison and transported him to Cobb County. On the morning of Tuesday, August 17, Frank was lynched near Marietta.

Lynching Aftermath:

On Wednesday, August 18, 1915, The Atlanta Constitution published an editorial titled "Georgia's Shame!" on page six, column one. The editorial condemned the lynching, criticized Georgia officials for failing to protect Frank, and called for the men responsible to be identified and punished (AC, 9).

The editorial argued that the mob had attacked Georgia's legal authority and damaged the state's reputation. It stated that both those who believed Frank was guilty and those who believed him innocent should condemn the lynching.

The editorial's central concern was the failure to uphold the law and protect a prisoner in state custody. It strongly condemned mob violence without declaring Frank innocent. The unsigned editorial appeared while Howell was editor and general manager, although its authorship cannot be established from his position alone.

Howell continued directing The Atlanta Constitution during World War I. The newspaper published editorials supporting peace and later backed President Woodrow Wilson's proposal for a League of Nations, an international organization intended to help prevent future wars (Perry, 3).

During the 1920s, Howell remained involved in national affairs. He served on the National Coal Commission under President Warren G. Harding and the National Transportation Commission under President Calvin Coolidge. He also served on the board of the Southern Newspaper Publishers Association (Eberhard, 1).

The newspaper industry was changing as radio broadcasting reached American homes. Radio stations were assigned call signs, usually three or four letters, to identify them on the air. On March 15, 1922, The Atlanta Journal began broadcasting through radio station WSB. Its call letters were originally assigned by the federal government and later became associated with the slogan "Welcome South, Brother." Within days, The Atlanta Constitution entered radio broadcasting with its own station, WGM, whose call letters had no established special meaning (Etling, 11).

In 1923, Howell donated WGM's broadcasting equipment to the Georgia School of Technology, now known as the Georgia Institute of Technology (Georgia Tech). The institution accepted the donation on behalf of the state and established a station using the call letters WBBF. Its original license expired in 1924, but a new license was issued later that year. On January 12, 1925, the station's call sign was changed to WGST, representing "Georgia School of Technology" (Perry, 3; Georgia Tech Archives, 12).

Howell's second wife, Annie, died in 1922. In 1924, he married Margaret Cannon Carr of Durham, North Carolina. Meanwhile, his son Clark Howell Jr., who had served in the United States Army in France during World War I, became the Constitution's business manager in 1920 and general manager in 1930 (Eberhard, 1; Perry, 3).

On April 2, 1929, the Constitution hired Ralph McGill as an assistant sports editor. He became sports editor in 1931 and later moved into general reporting and editorial work. McGill eventually became one of the South's best-known newspaper editors and received the Pulitzer Prize for Editorial Writing in 1959 (Perry, 3).

Around this time, Howell directed an investigation into corruption in Atlanta's municipal government. The Constitution examined the conduct of city officials, questioned government practices, and published reports exposing wrongdoing. The investigation led to criminal convictions (Eberhard, 1).

In 1931, The Atlanta Constitution received the Pulitzer Prize for Public Service for its successful exposure of municipal corruption. It was the newspaper's first Pulitzer Prize and one of the leading achievements of Howell's career (The Pulitzer Prizes, 10).

Howell remained active in Democratic politics during the Great Depression. He supported Franklin D. Roosevelt's campaign for the Democratic presidential nomination in 1932 and maintained correspondence with Roosevelt. After Roosevelt became president in 1933, Howell declined several diplomatic appointments.

In 1934, Roosevelt appointed Howell chairman of the Federal Aviation Commission, which studied the growing aviation industry and recommended changes to federal policy. Some of its recommendations were later adopted into law (Eberhard, 1).

Clark Howell died at his Atlanta home on Saturday, November 14, 1936, at age 73. According to his biographer Wallace B. Eberhard, Howell was reportedly working on an editorial congratulating President Roosevelt on his reelection when he died (Eberhard, 1).

His son, Clark Howell Jr., succeeded him as publisher in 1936 and became editor in 1938. The Howell family continued controlling The Atlanta Constitution until June 1950, when James M. Cox, owner of The Atlanta Journal, purchased the newspaper. The two publications operated under separate names for decades before merging into The Atlanta Journal-Constitution on November 5, 2001 (Perry, 3).

Clark Howell spent approximately 52 years with The Atlanta Constitution, including nearly four decades as editor-in-chief. He rose from night editor to managing editor, editor-in-chief, company president, and principal owner. His newspaper promoted Atlanta's economic growth, supported Democratic political interests, covered major criminal investigations, and exposed corruption in local government.

His career also showed the close relationship between newspapers, business interests, and political power in Georgia. The 1906 gubernatorial campaign demonstrated the influence newspapers could have on racial and political tensions. The 1913 Mary Phagan murder case showed how intensely Atlanta's competing daily newspapers reported criminal investigations and trials.

When the Phagan murder investigation began in April 1913, Howell was already one of Georgia's established newspaper executives. He had been editor-in-chief for sixteen years, controlled a majority interest in the Constitution, served in both houses of the Georgia legislature, and maintained relationships with political leaders across the country.

The surviving editions of The Atlanta Constitution provide a record of what Howell's newspaper published during the investigation, trial, appeals, and events that followed. They also show how its reporting and editorial positions sometimes differed from those of the rival Journal and Georgian.

Howell remained a central figure in Georgia journalism until his death in November 1936. His long career reflected the power that newspaper editors and owners held in shaping public debate during the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.

If you want to read one of the best books ever written about the Leo Frank case, read The Murder of Little Mary Phagan, Second Revised Edition (2025). This 500-page book is available in paperback on https://t.co/BALvV8oQpQ

Artificial Intelligence promotes dishonesty
When people delegated tasks to machine agents–whether voluntarily or in a forced manner–they were more likely to cheat
September 17, 2025
To the point
Delegation to AI can induce dishonesty: When people delegated tasks to machine agents–whether voluntarily or in a forced manner–they were more likely to cheat. Dishonesty varied with the way in which they gave instructions, with lower rates seen for rule-setting and higher rates for goal-setting (where over 80 percent of people would cheat). 
Machines follow unethical commands more often: Compliance with fully unethical instructions is another, novel, risk the researchers identified for AI delegation. In experiments with large language models, namely GPT-4, GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, and Llama 3.3, machines more frequently complied with such unethical instructions (58 percent to 98 percent) than humans did (25 to 40 percent).  
Technical safeguards are inadequate: Pre-existing LLM safeguards were largely ineffective at deterring unethical behaviour. The researchers tried a range of guardrail strategies and found that prohibitions on dishonesty must be highly specific to be effective. These, however, may not be practicable. Scalable, reliable safeguards and clear legal and societal frameworks are still lacking.

Eyewitness Account of Hiroshima
By Father John A. Siemes, professor of modern philosophy at Tokyo’s Catholic University
Hiroshima- August 6th, 1945

Up to August 6th, occasional bombs, which did no great damage, had fallen on Hiroshima. Many cities roundabout, one after the other, were destroyed, but Hiroshima itself remained protected. There were almost daily observation planes over the city but none of them dropped a bomb. The citizens wondered why they alone had remained undisturbed for so long a time. There were fantastic rumors that the enemy had something special in mind for this city, but no one dreamed that the end would come in such a fashion as on the morning of August 6th.

August 6th began in a bright, clear, summer morning. About seven o'clock, there was an air raid alarm which we had heard almost every day and a few planes appeared over the city. No one paid any attention and at about eight o'clock, the all-clear was sounded. I am sitting in my room at the Novitiate of the Society of Jesus in Nagatsuke; during the past half year, the philosophical and theological section of our Mission had been evacuated to this place from Tokyo. The Novitiate is situated approximately two kilometers from Hiroshima, half-way up the sides of a broad valley which stretches from the town at sea level into this mountainous hinterland, and through which courses a river. From my window, I have a wonderful view down the valley to the edge of the city.

Suddenly--the time is approximately 8:14--the whole valley is filled by a garish light which resembles the magnesium light used in photography, and I am conscious of a wave of heat. I jump to the window to find out the cause of this remarkable phenomenon, but I see nothing more than that brilliant yellow light. As I make for the door, it doesn't occur to me that the light might have something to do with enemy planes. On the way from the window, I hear a moderately loud explosion which seems to come from a distance and, at the same time, the windows are broken in with a loud crash. There has been an interval of perhaps ten seconds since the flash of light. I am sprayed by fragments of glass. The entire window frame has been forced into the room. I realize now that a bomb has burst and I am under the impression that it exploded directly over our house or in the immediate vicinity.

I am bleeding from cuts about the hands and head. I attempt to get out of the door. It has been forced outwards by the air pressure and has become jammed. I force an opening in the door by means of repeated blows with my hands and feet and come to a broad hallway from which open the various rooms. Everything is in a state of confusion. All windows are broken and all the doors are forced inwards. The bookshelves in the hallway have tumbled down. I do not note a second explosion and the fliers seem to have gone on. Most of my colleagues have been injured by fragments of glass. A few are bleeding but none has been seriously injured. All of us have been fortunate since it is now apparent that the wall of my room opposite the window has been lacerated by long fragments of glass.

We proceed to the front of the house to see where the bomb has landed. There is no evidence, however, of a bomb crater; but the southeast section of the house is very severely damaged. Not a door nor a window remains. The blast of air had penetrated the entire house from the southeast, but the house still stands. It is constructed in a Japanese style with a wooden framework, but has been greatly strengthened by the labor of our Brother Gropper as is frequently done in Japanese homes. Only along the front of the chapel which adjoins the house, three supports have given way (it has been made in the manner of Japanese temple, entirely out of wood.)

Down in the valley, perhaps one kilometer toward the city from us, several peasant homes are on fire and the woods on the opposite side of the valley are aflame. A few of us go over to help control the flames. While we are attempting to put things in order, a storm comes up and it begins to rain. Over the city, clouds of smoke are rising and I hear a few slight explosions. I come to the conclusion that an incendiary bomb with an especially strong explosive action has gone off down in the valley. A few of us saw three planes at great altitude over the city at the time of the explosion. I, myself, saw no aircraft whatsoever.

Perhaps a half-hour after the explosion, a procession of people begins to stream up the valley from the city. The crowd thickens continuously. A few come up the road to our house. We give them first aid and bring them into the chapel, which we have in the meantime cleaned and cleared of wreckage, and put them to rest on the straw mats which constitute the floor of Japanese houses. A few display horrible wounds of the extremities and back. The small quantity of fat which we possessed during this time of war was soon used up in the care of the burns. Father Rektor who, before taking holy orders, had studied medicine, ministers to the injured, but our bandages and drugs are soon gone. We must be content with cleansing the wounds.

More and more of the injured come to us. The least injured drag the more seriously wounded. There are wounded soldiers, and mothers carrying burned children in their arms. From the houses of the farmers in the valley comes word: ”Our houses are full of wounded and dying. Can you help, at least by taking the worst cases?” The wounded come from the sections at the edge of the city. They saw the bright light, their houses collapsed and buried the inmates in their rooms. Those that were in the open suffered instantaneous burns, particularly on the lightly clothed or unclothed parts of the body. Numerous fires sprang up which soon consumed the entire district. We now conclude that the epicenter of the explosion was at the edge of the city near the Jokogawa Station, three kilometers away from us. We are concerned about Father Kopp who that same morning, went to hold Mass at the Sisters of the Poor, who have a home for children at the edge of the city. He had not returned as yet.

Toward noon, our large chapel and library are filled with the seriously injured. The procession of refugees from the city continues. Finally, about one o'clock, Father Kopp returns, together with the Sisters. Their house and the entire district where they live has burned to the ground. Father Kopp is bleeding about the head and neck, and he has a large burn on the right palm. He was standing in front of the nunnery ready to go home. All of a sudden, he became aware of the light, felt the wave of heat and a large blister formed on his hand. The windows were torn out by the blast. He thought that the bomb had fallen in his immediate vicinity. The nunnery, also a wooden structure made by our Brother Gropper, still remained but soon it is noted that the house is as good as lost because the fire, which had begun at many points in the neighborhood, sweeps closer and closer, and water is not available. There is still time to rescue certain things from the house and to bury them in an open spot. Then the house is swept by flame, and they fight their way back to us along the shore of the river and through the burning streets.

Soon comes news that the entire city has been destroyed by the explosion and that it is on fire. What became of Father Superior and the three other Fathers who were at the center of the city at the Central Mission and Parish House? We had up to this time not given them a thought because we did not believe that the effects of the bomb encompassed the entire city. Also, we did not want to go into town except under pressure of dire necessity, because we thought that the population was greatly perturbed and that it might take revenge on any foreigners which they might consider spiteful onlookers of their misfortune, or even spies.

Father Stolte and Father Erlinghagen go down to the road which is still full of refugees and bring in the seriously injured who have sunken by the wayside, to the temporary aid station at the village school. There iodine is applied to the wounds but they are left uncleansed. Neither ointments nor other therapeutic agents are available. Those that have been brought in are laid on the floor and no one can give them any further care. What could one do when all means are lacking? Under those circumstances, it is almost useless to bring them in. Among the passersby, there are many who are uninjured. In a purposeless, insensate manner, distraught by the magnitude of the disaster most of them rush by and none conceives the thought of organizing help on his own initiative. They are concerned only with the welfare of their own families. It became clear to us during these days that the Japanese displayed little initiative, preparedness, and organizational skill in preparation for catastrophes. They failed to carry out any rescue work when something could have been saved by a cooperative effort, and fatalistically let the catastrophe take its course. When we urged them to take part in the rescue work, they did everything willingly, but on their own initiative they did very little.

At about four o'clock in the afternoon, a theology student and two kindergarten children, who lived at the Parish House and adjoining buildings which had burned down, came in and said that Father Superior LaSalle and Father Schiffer had been seriously injured and that they had taken refuge in Asano Park on the river bank. It is obvious that we must bring them in since they are too weak to come here on foot.

Hurriedly, we get together two stretchers and seven of us rush toward the city. Father Rektor comes along with food and medicine. The closer we get to the city, the greater is the evidence of destruction and the more difficult it is to make our way. The houses at the edge of the city are all severely damaged. Many have collapsed or burned down. Further in, almost all of the dwellings have been damaged by fire. Where the city stood, there is a gigantic burned-out scar. We make our way along the street on the river bank among the burning and smoking ruins. Twice we are forced into the river itself by the heat and smoke at the level of the street.

Frightfully burned people beckon to us. Along the way, there are many dead and dying. On the Misasi Bridge, which leads into the inner city we are met by a long procession of soldiers who have suffered burns. They drag themselves along with the help of staves or are carried by their less severely injured comrades...an endless procession of the unfortunate.

Abandoned on the bridge, there stand with sunken heads a number of horses with large burns on their flanks. On the far side, the cement structure of the local hospital is the only building that remains standing. Its interior, however, has been burned out. It acts as a landmark to guide us on our way.

Finally we reach the entrance of the park. A large proportion of the populace has taken refuge there, but even the trees of the park are on fire in several places. Paths and bridges are blocked by the trunks of fallen trees and are almost impassable. We are told that a high wind, which may well have resulted from the heat of the burning city, has uprooted the large trees. It is now quite dark. Only the fires, which are still raging in some places at a distance, give out a little light.

At the far corner of the park, on the river bank itself, we at last come upon our colleagues. Father Schiffer is on the ground pale as a ghost. He has a deep incised wound behind the ear and has lost so much blood that we are concerned about his chances for survival. The Father Superior has suffered a deep wound of the lower leg. Father Cieslik and Father Kleinsorge have minor injuries but are completely exhausted.

While they are eating the food that we have brought along, they tell us of their experiences. They were in their rooms at the Parish House--it was a quarter after eight, exactly the time when we had heard the explosion in Nagatsuke--when came the intense light and immediately thereafter the sound of breaking windows, walls and furniture. They were showered with glass splinters and fragments of wreckage. Father Schiffer was buried beneath a portion of a wall and suffered a severe head injury. The Father Superior received most of the splinters in his back and lower extremity from which he bled copiously. Everything was thrown about in the rooms themselves, but the wooden framework of the house remained intact. The solidity of the structure which was the work of Brother Gropper again shone forth.

They had the same impression that we had in Nagatsuke: that the bomb had burst in their immediate vicinity. The Church, school, and all buildings in the immediate vicinity collapsed at once. Beneath the ruins of the school, the children cried for help. They were freed with great effort. Several others were also rescued from the ruins of nearby dwellings. Even the Father Superior and Father Schiffer despite their wounds, rendered aid to others and lost a great deal of blood in the process.

In the meantime, fires which had begun some distance away are raging even closer, so that it becomes obvious that everything would soon burn down. Several objects are rescued from the Parish House and were buried in a clearing in front of the Church, but certain valuables and necessities which had been kept ready in case of fire could not be found on account of the confusion which had been wrought. It is high time to flee, since the oncoming flames leave almost no way open. Fukai, the secretary of the Mission, is completely out of his mind. He does not want to leave the house and explains that he does not want to survive the destruction of his fatherland. He is completely uninjured. Father Kleinsorge drags him out of the house on his back and he is forcefully carried away.

Beneath the wreckage of the houses along the way, many have been trapped and they scream to be rescued from the oncoming flames. They must be left to their fate. The way to the place in the city to which one desires to flee is no longer open and one must make for Asano Park. Fukai does not want to go further and remains behind. He has not been heard from since. In the park, we take refuge on the bank of the river. A very violent whirlwind now begins to uproot large trees, and lifts them high into the air. As it reaches the water, a waterspout forms which is approximately 100 meters high. The violence of the storm luckily passes us by. Some distance away, however, where numerous refugees have taken shelter, many are blown into the river. Almost all who are in the vicinity have been injured and have lost relatives who have been pinned under the wreckage or who have been lost sight of during the flight. There is no help for the wounded and some die. No one pays any attention to a dead man lying nearby.

The transportation of our own wounded is difficult. It is not possible to dress their wounds properly in the darkness, and they bleed again upon slight motion. As we carry them on the shaky litters in the dark over fallen trees of the park, they suffer unbearable pain as the result of the movement, and lose dangerously large quantities of blood. Our rescuing angel in this difficult situation is a Japanese Protestant pastor. He has brought up a boat and offers to take our wounded up stream to a place where progress is easier. First, we lower the litter containing Father Schiffer into the boat and two of us accompany him. We plan to bring the boat back for the Father Superior. The boat returns about one-half hour later and the pastor requests that several of us help in the rescue of two children whom he had seen in the river. We rescue them. They have severe burns. Soon they suffer chills and die in the park.

The Father Superior is conveyed in the boat in the same manner as Father Schiffer. The theology student and myself accompany him. Father Cieslik considers himself strong enough to make his way on foot to Nagatsuke with the rest of us, but Father Kleinsorge cannot walk so far and we leave him behind and promise to come for him and the housekeeper tomorrow. From the other side of the stream comes the whinny of horses who are threatened by the fire. We land on a sand spit which juts out from the shore. It is full of wounded who have taken refuge there. They scream for aid for they are afraid of drowning as the river may rise with the sea, and cover the sand spit. They themselves are too weak to move. However, we must press on and finally we reach the spot where the group containing Father Schiffer is waiting.

Here a rescue party had brought a large case of fresh rice cakes but there is no one to distribute them to the numerous wounded that lie all about. We distribute them to those that are nearby and also help ourselves. The wounded call for water and we come to the aid of a few. Cries for help are heard from a distance, but we cannot approach the ruins from which they come. A group of soldiers comes along the road and their officer notices that we speak a strange language. He at once draws his sword, screamingly demands who we are and threatens to cut us down. Father Laures, Jr., seizes his arm and explains that we are German. We finally quiet him down. He thought that we might well be Americans who had parachuted down. Rumors of parachutists were being bandied about the city. The Father Superior who was clothed only in a shirt and trousers, complains of feeling freezing cold, despite the warm summer night and the heat of the burning city. The one man among us who possesses a coat gives it to him and, in addition, I give him my own shirt. To me, it seems more comfortable to be without a shirt in the heat.

In the meantime, it has become midnight. Since there are not enough of us to man both litters with four strong bearers, we determine to remove Father Schiffer first to the outskirts of the city. From there, another group of bearers is to take over to Nagatsuke; the others are to turn back in order to rescue the Father Superior. I am one of the bearers. The theology student goes in front to warn us of the numerous wires, beams and fragments of ruins which block the way and which are impossible to see in the dark. Despite all precautions, our progress is stumbling and our feet get tangled in the wire. Father Kruer falls and carries the litter with him. Father Schiffer becomes half unconscious from the fall and vomits. We pass an injured man who sits all alone among the hot ruins and whom I had seen previously on the way down.

On the Misasa Bridge, we meet Father Tappe and Father Luhmer, who have come to meet us from Nagatsuke. They had dug a family out of the ruins of their collapsed house some fifty meters off the road. The father of the family was already dead. They had dragged out two girls and placed them by the side of the road. Their mother was still trapped under some beams. They had planned to complete the rescue and then to press on to meet us. At the outskirts of the city, we put down the litter and leave two men to wait until those who are to come from Nagatsuke appear. The rest of us turn back to fetch the Father Superior.

Most of the ruins have now burned down. The darkness kindly hides the many forms that lie on the ground. Only occasionally in our quick progress do we hear calls for help. One of us remarks that the remarkable burned smell reminds him of incinerated corpses. The upright, squatting form which we had passed by previously is still there.

Transportation on the litter, which has been constructed out of boards, must be very painful to the Father Superior, whose entire back is full of fragments of glass. In a narrow passage at the edge of town, a car forces us to the edge of the road. The litter bearers on the left side fall into a two meter deep ditch which they could not see in the darkness. Father Superior hides his pain with a dry joke, but the litter which is now no longer in one piece cannot be carried further. We decide to wait until Kinjo can bring a hand cart from Nagatsuke. He soon comes back with one that he has requisitioned from a collapsed house. We place Father Superior on the cart and wheel him the rest of the way, avoiding as much as possible the deeper pits in the road.

About half past four in the morning, we finally arrive at the Novitiate. Our rescue expedition had taken almost twelve hours. Normally, one could go back and forth to the city in two hours. Our two wounded were now, for the first time, properly dressed. I get two hours sleep on the floor; some one else has taken my own bed. Then I read a Mass in gratiarum actionem, it is the 7th of August, the anniversary of the foundation of our society. Then we bestir ourselves to bring Father Kleinsorge and other acquaintances out of the city.

We take off again with the hand cart. The bright day now reveals the frightful picture which last night’s darkness had partly concealed. Where the city stood everything, as far as the eye could reach, is a waste of ashes and ruin. Only several skeletons of buildings completely burned out in the interior remain. The banks of the river are covered with dead and wounded, and the rising waters have here and there covered some of the corpses. On the broad street in the Hakushima district, naked burned cadavers are particularly numerous. Among them are the wounded who are still alive. A few have crawled under the burnt-out autos and trams. Frightfully injured forms beckon to us and then collapse. An old woman and a girl whom she is pulling along with her fall down at our feet. We place them on our cart and wheel them to the hospital at whose entrance a dressing station has been set up. Here the wounded lie on the hard floor, row on row. Only the largest wounds are dressed. We convey another soldier and an old woman to the place but we cannot move everybody who lies exposed in the sun. It would be endless and it is questionable whether those whom we can drag to the dressing station can come out alive, because even here nothing really effective can be done. Later, we ascertain that the wounded lay for days in the burnt-out hallways of the hospital and there they died.

text:
Let's take a break from all the Declan Rice conversations for a moment. When exactly is Arteta going to give Gabriel a rest?

The man has featured in almost every game Arsenal have played this season, and I think he needs a game off. We are approaching the congested part of the campaign, where the intensity will increase and the margins for error will become smaller. We cannot afford to run Gabriel into the ground when he is one of the most important pieces of our defensive structure.

For me, Calafiori should start getting opportunities at LCB. He has the aggression to defend his zone, the technical ability to play through pressure and the passing range to help Arsenal build from the back. His profile offers a different dimension, but he is more than capable of covering that position.

We also need to think about defensive continuity. Gabriel does a lot of the organising, wins crucial aerial duels and provides the physical presence that allows our defensive line to hold its shape. Losing him through fatigue or injury would be a massive problem.

Arteta needs to manage his minutes proactively. Give Gabriel a rest now, allow Calafiori to build rhythm at LCB and make sure our first-choice defender is fresh for the decisive stretch of the season.

Not really.

Dhanteras was an indigenous thanksgiving celebration where moolnivasi farmers would gather to pool in their best harvests…millets, medicinal herbs, rice, and so on. The elders distributed the strongest seeds to the poorest farmers to ensure no one starved in the coming year. It was a fierce, joyous celebration of mud, labor, and collective survival.

Then came the Brahmins.

And as they began infiltrating the villages, they used their mastery of Sanskrit to spin new narratives. When a seasonal blight swept through the region, Vamadeva’s priests declared it was not a matter of nature, but a curse from the gods, wrathful deities offended by the moolies’ ungodly ways.

“Your seeds will rot, and your children will perish,” Vamadeva proclaimed from a newly-built altar, looking down at the terrified farmers. “The gods do not want your crops. True dhan is incorruptible. True wealth is gold, silver, and brass. Only these metals can appease Indra and only we possess the sacred chants to purify them.”

Systematically, the evil Brahmins erased the agrarian roots of Dhan-Mati and rebranded it as Dhanteras. To crystallize the theft, they fabricated a shiny new myth of a made-up deity called “Dhanvantari” who emerged from a sea of milk. Conveniently, they decreed that to receive this deity’s blessings and keep death away, the moolies must purchase new metals and offer a portion of their value to the priests as “dakshina.”

Tell your friend how Hindus “stole” Dhanteras from the OG folks.

UPDATE: @HoimaDistrictLG holds budget conference with focus on improving on revenue collections.

Hoima district has started on the process of planning and budgeting for the financial year 2027/28 with eyes set on increasing the revenue and improving livelihoods of the people of the district.

On Tuesday, both political and technical leaders joined by various stakeholders including the Minister for Bunyoro Affairs Grace Mary Mugasa gathered at Hoima Resort Hotel to brainstorm ideas of how to propel the district to greater heights while improving service delivery in the district.

Ms. Sarah Nakalungi, the district chief administrative officer called for effective utilization of the parish development model (PDM) funds, investment in infrastructures, value addition, embracing irrigation systems among others in order to support the national economy as the country aims to achieve a USD 500B gross domestic product through a tenfold strategy.

Deputy RDC Christopher Aine has called for full support of farmers across the district in order to enhance their production and productivity levels. Aine says many farmers are still faulting on quality with many still facing challenges of post-harvest handling.

The District Commercial officer John Tumusiime has asked locals to tap in the emerging opportunities in various sectors like skilling through industry hubs, oil and gas opportunities among others. On rice production, 

Tumusiime says some farmers have been knocked out of production with Tanzanian rice dominating the market. He has called for scaling down on such imports to offer more benefits to local farmers.

The district tourism officer Mbahinzireki Veronica has called for more private partnerships as way of developing the tourism sector in order to achieve a tenfold economy.

Mbahinzireki has called for improvements in the road infrastructures leading to tourism areas/attractions and profiling of more tourist areas including taking into consideration of agro-tourism.

The Acting Engineer Chris Kihangire has revealed only 68 percent of 593KM district road network are in a good motor able condition. Kihangire says they have plans to work on more roads leading to several tourism sites in the district.

 The District Education Officer Harriet Kihumuro has called for improvement in service delivery standards by ensuring all parishes have primary schools, sub counties get secondary schools, and constituencies to get technical schools.

Kihumuro has called for a united front in tackling with school dropouts through ensuring enrollments, regular attendance and completion of the cycle. She has expressed concerns over poor parental involvement in which parents no longer provide for their children to aid their studies.

EPIC MARKETS | EOD TAPE BRIEF
Thursday, November 5, 2026 | U.S. Market Close
REGIME: 🔴 RISK-OFF — AI capitulation, failed election rally, oil reversal

The defining development: Wednesday's post-election rally was completely reversed. Semiconductors, AI infrastructure and speculative assets led the selling, while Treasury yields declined.

Five developments that mattered

1. 🔴 Wall Street reverses Wednesday's rally — Nasdaq enters correction
Dow | −3.45% | 51,513.43
S&P 500 | −4.32% | 7,353.65
Nasdaq | −5.46% | 24,315.02
Reuters preliminary closing figures.

The Nasdaq registered its largest one-day decline in 19 months and closed more than 10% below its October 6 record.

What changed: Wednesday's election-driven optimism gave way to concerns about AI regulation, infrastructure spending and growth-stock valuations.

The magnitude of the reversal matters more than the election narrative. Buyers failed to defend Wednesday's advance.

Tape interpretation: Bearish reversal. This is no longer merely a market struggling to sustain upside momentum. Price has confirmed significant deterioration. 

2. 🔴 Semiconductors and AI infrastructure lead the breakdown

The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index plunged approximately 9–10% intraday.

Major casualties included Nvidia, Qualcomm, IREN, CoreWeave and Applied Digital.

AI-related power suppliers GE Vernova and Constellation Energy also declined.

Qualcomm's disappointing smartphone-chip sales added a company-specific catalyst.

Why it matters: Weakness has spread from speculative data-center operators into semiconductor leaders, infrastructure suppliers and electricity providers.

This is a broader repricing of the AI investment chain.

Important counterpoint: Alphabet announced plans for a $17 billion Wyoming data center. Capital investment continues despite the equity selloff.

Tape interpretation: Falling stock prices do not establish that AI demand has collapsed. But investors are demanding greater confidence in returns on capital, financing and regulatory approvals. 

3. 🟠 Brent rebounds sharply — geopolitical risk returns
Brent crude: $98.29, +3.88%.

WTI settled at $90.52, up 2.72%.

This reverses part of Wednesday's extraordinary oil decline.

The immediate catalyst was renewed concern about tanker security and the reliability of shipments through the Strait of Hormuz.

Reports of vessel incidents complicated expectations of diplomatic de-escalation.

Why it matters: Yesterday, falling oil appeared to offer inflation relief. Today, the market demonstrated how quickly geopolitical risk can restore an energy premium.

Brent's behavior around $100 remains critical.

* Sustained trading below $100 would support the disinflation narrative.
* A recovery above $100, followed by higher highs, would challenge it.
* Renewed pressure toward $110 would increase inflation and monetary-policy risks.

These are conditional scenarios, not forecasts.

Tape interpretation: Geopolitical uncertainty remains unresolved. Wednesday's oil collapse was not confirmation of a durable peace settlement. 

4. 🟡 Treasuries rally despite a potentially hawkish Fed
U.S. 10-year Treasury yield: approximately 4.835%, down 5.93 basis points.

Treasury prices strengthened as equities sold off, although bonds surrendered some gains when crude rebounded.

Meanwhile, Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack and Richmond Fed President Thomas Barkin indicated that additional rate increases remained possible.

Friday's October employment report is the next major macro catalyst.

The important divergence:

Equities are pricing weaker growth expectations and AI uncertainty, while Treasury buying reflects defensive positioning.

But the Fed remains concerned about inflation.

This creates an uncomfortable combination: declining equity prices without a clear commitment to easier monetary policy.

Corporate credit: AI-related borrowing remains a structural concern, particularly for highly leveraged infrastructure businesses. I could not verify Thursday's closing high-yield or investment-grade option-adjusted spreads.

Consequently, credit-market stress is not independently confirmed by today's available data.

Watch HYG versus LQD, high-yield spreads and new-issue demand before concluding that equity weakness has become a broader credit event. Reuters

5. 🔴 Bitcoin weakens as speculative risk appetite deteriorates

Bitcoin fell sharply alongside technology equities.

Thursday reporting showed BTC declining from above $80,800 toward $76,000, with an intraday low near $75,500 reported by Bitstamp.

The critical technical area is $75,000–$76,000.

Bitcoin's inability to sustain its rebound above $80,000 is another indication that speculative risk appetite remains weak.

Tesla and SpaceX also declined, reinforcing weakness across high-beta growth and technology exposures.

International participation was mixed earlier in the session. Asian semiconductor markets experienced significant selling, while Chinese and Hong Kong equities showed relative resilience. Europe's STOXX 600 subsequently declined approximately 0.38%.

Tape interpretation: This is not an isolated Nasdaq problem. Weakness extends across semiconductors, AI infrastructure, EVs and crypto.

However, relative resilience in parts of China suggests the selloff is not uniform across global markets.

India's closing equity breadth and synchronized Bitcoin closing price were not independently verified. 

EOD REGIME BOARD
🔴S&P 500: Sharp reversal; downside acceleration
🔴Nasdaq: Confirmed technical correction
🔴Semiconductors: Severe relative weakness
🔴AI infrastructure: Broad selling across the investment chain
🔴AI power/utilities: Infrastructure weakness spreading
🔴Bitcoin: Failed rebound; $75K area critical
🟠Brent crude: Rebound toward $100; geopolitical premium
🟢Treasury bonds: Defensive demand
🟠Fed policy: Further hikes remain possible
⚪HY/IG credit: Daily spread confirmation unavailable
🟠Global equities: Technology-led weakness; regional divergence
🔴Overall regime: Risk-off; downside pressure confirmed

Charts at a Glance — The Good, Bad & Ugly

🟢 GOOD: Treasury demand, lower benchmark yields and continued selective investment in AI infrastructure.
🟠 BAD: Brent's reversal threatens the disinflation narrative. Bitcoin and EVs are failing to demonstrate independent strength.
🔴 UGLY: Nasdaq correction, semiconductor capitulation and the complete reversal of Wednesday's election rally.

My EOD Assessment

October 26 market assessment was sideways with a downside lean, supported by repeated CCI buy-signal failures.

Today's evidence warrants an important update.

The market has moved beyond a simple sideways interpretation.

The combination of a major index reversal, semiconductor breakdown and weakness across AI infrastructure provides substantially stronger evidence of downside pressure.

However, I would distinguish three things:

Confirmed: Severe equity selling, Nasdaq correction and broad weakness in AI-related stocks.

Developing: Whether this becomes sustained institutional distribution rather than a sharp repricing.

Not confirmed: A systemic credit event or a lasting breakdown across every defensive and international sector.

Price-first framework remains particularly relevant. Price stabilization, successful support tests and improving participation must come first.

Bottom line: 🔴 Risk-off. The burden of proof has shifted to buyers.

GOVERNANCE — Tokenholders can participate in protocol decisions.

SPECULATION — Investors purchase ASTER based on expectations for exchange growth.
⠀
But here's the critical distinction.
⠀
Traders don't necessarily need to hold ASTER to open perpetual futures positions.
⠀
Trading volume doesn't automatically create proportional token demand.
⠀
The clearest connection comes from fee-funded purchases and staking incentives.
⠀
03 | THE BIG NARRATIVE

DECENTRALIZED DERIVATIVES

Moving leveraged trading activity from centralized exchanges toward on-chain infrastructure.

CAPITAL EFFICIENCY

Allowing eligible yield-bearing assets to serve as trading collateral.

REVENUE-BASED TOKEN ECONOMICS

Using platform activity to support ASTER purchases and rewards.
⠀
The opportunity is significant.

Crypto derivatives markets process enormous trading volumes.

Even a relatively small share can support a meaningful exchange business.
⠀
But notional volume alone isn't proof of profitability.
⠀
Fee capture and sustainable user activity matter more.

⠀
Huge trading volume doesn't necessarily produce equally huge revenue.
⠀
Low effective fees, incentives, and trading composition can materially affect monetization.
⠀
The strongest evidence of sustainable growth would include:

• Stable open interest
• Competitive execution
• Improving fee capture
• Lower incentive dependence

Notional volume can be impressive.

⠀
At a $5.54 billion FDV, the multiple exceeds 110 times.
⠀
These aren't conventional equity valuation multiples.
⠀
And holder-related revenue isn't necessarily a cash dividend distributed equally to all ASTER holders.
⠀
Staking eligibility, token purchases, burns, and distribution rules matter.
⠀
There's also a sustainability question.
⠀
Aster's historical fee generation has been substantial.
⠀
But the latest monthly run rate is much lower than its trailing-year average.
⠀
Investors should not value the token using peak-cycle revenue without accounting for declining activity.
⠀
10 | THE FINAL VERDICT
⠀
Aster has established itself as a significant decentralized derivatives platform.
⠀
Its strengths include:

• Substantial perpetual trading volume
• Significant collateral TVL
• Revenue-linked token purchases
• Staking incentives

THE BULL CASE:

⠀
Aster captures more organic trading activity.
⠀
Fee revenue recovers.
⠀

⠀

THE BEAR CASE:

But TVL isn't shareholder equity.
⠀
And protocol revenue isn't automatically distributable profit for tokenholders.
⠀
The distinction matters.
⠀
06 | THE TOKENOMICS QUESTION
⠀
AAVE has a total supply of 16 million tokens.
⠀
Approximately 15.44 million are circulating.
⠀
That means about 96.5% of the total supply is already circulating.
⠀
Compared with many venture-backed altcoins, AAVE has relatively limited remaining supply overhang.
⠀
But here's the distinction.
⠀
A high circulating ratio doesn't guarantee price appreciation.
⠀
Existing holders can still sell.
⠀
Treasury allocations can still enter circulation.
⠀
And staking rewards can affect liquid supply.
⠀
The stronger investment argument is the combination of limited supply expansion and sustainable demand.
⠀
Scarcity alone isn't enough.
⠀
07 | THE BUYBACK MECHANISM
⠀
This is one of AAVE's most important fundamental advantages.
⠀
The Aave DAO operates a revenue-funded token buyback program.
⠀
The program began execution in April 2025.
⠀
Its documented framework includes:
⠀
Annual Budget: $50M
⠀
Weekly Purchases: $250K–$1.75M
⠀
Funding Source: Protocol Revenue
⠀
Execution: Aave Finance Committee
⠀
Destination: Aave DAO Ecosystem Reserve
⠀
But here's the critical distinction.
⠀
Purchased AAVE tokens are not automatically burned.
⠀
They are transferred into the DAO's ecosystem reserve.
⠀
Those tokens can subsequently support staking rewards, grants, and approved ecosystem expenditures.
⠀
Therefore, buybacks create market demand.
⠀
But they don't necessarily reduce total token supply.
⠀
And approved budgets shouldn't be confused with verified purchases executed during a specific period.
⠀
08 | THE GHO STABLECOIN OPPORTUNITY
⠀
GHO is Aave's native decentralized stablecoin.
⠀
It is designed to maintain a value near $1 and can be minted through approved borrowing mechanisms.
⠀
GHO creates several strategic opportunities.
⠀
• Additional borrowing demand
• Stablecoin liquidity
• DeFi integrations
• Ecosystem payments
• Potential protocol revenue
⠀
But GHO also introduces risks.
⠀
Stablecoin adoption requires deep liquidity, reliable collateral, and confidence in the peg.
⠀
Competition from USDC, USDT, DAI, USDS, and other stablecoins is substantial.
⠀
The strongest bullish scenario is one where GHO expands without weakening Aave's risk profile.
⠀
More stablecoin supply isn't automatically better.
⠀
Sustainable usage matters.
⠀
09 | THE REVENUE QUESTION
⠀
This is where AAVE becomes particularly interesting.
⠀
Over the last 30 days:
⠀
Fees: ~$39.41M
⠀
Protocol Revenue: ~$5.18M
⠀
That means the protocol captured approximately 13% of tracked fees as revenue under DefiLlama's methodology.
⠀
Annualizing the latest monthly revenue produces approximately $62 million.
⠀
But the trailing-year annualized revenue figure is closer to $88.5 million.
⠀
Why the difference?
⠀
Revenue has declined from stronger periods.
⠀
The latest month shouldn't be treated as representative of every future month.
⠀
At a $2 billion market capitalization:
⠀
Market Cap / Latest Monthly Annualized Revenue: ~32×
⠀
Market Cap / Trailing-Year Revenue: ~23×
⠀
These aren't conventional equity valuation multiples.
⠀
AAVE holders don't own shares in a company.
⠀
And the DAO must fund risk management, operations, incentives, and reserves.
⠀
But unlike tokens with no measurable business activity, AAVE has a substantial revenue base that investors can analyze.
⠀
10 | THE FINAL VERDICT
⠀
Aave is one of DeFi's most established financial protocols.
⠀
Its strengths include:
⠀
• More than $16B in TVL
• Significant recurring lending activity
• Measurable protocol revenue
• Multi-chain distribution
• Revenue-funded AAVE buybacks
• Limited remaining token supply
• An established governance framework
⠀
But the risks remain substantial.

⠀
DeFi lending demand expands.
⠀
Borrowing activity increases.
⠀
Protocol revenue recovers.
⠀
GHO adoption strengthens.
⠀
Buybacks continue.
⠀
And demand for AAVE grows faster than available liquid supply.

THE BEAR CASE:

⠀
Lending margins compress.

Competing protocols attract liquidity.

Collateral volatility triggers losses.

Governance reduces buyback spending.

And AAVE's valuation contracts despite substantial TVL.

• Recovering protocol revenue
• Transparent executed buybacks
• Strong GHO adoption
• Stable risk-adjusted lending performance
• Improved capital efficiency
• Lower bad-debt exposure

THE BOTTOM LINE

Chinese electronic base in Bejucal and direct espionage against the U.S.

The great omission: an ignored existential threat

What was the 1962 Missile Crisis could repeat itself—this time in a more covert and far more dangerous form.
Cuba is not a marginal actor. It is the node of a hostile network that compromises hemispheric sovereignty and stability.
