text:
What this tells me is that Poseidon is more Phrygian facing than Thracian.  This might be a dynastic merging along said corridor of the Rhine/Danube within another royal house.

In Geography 12.8.18, Strabo describes the earthquake-prone Phrygian interior and explicitly discusses Poseidon's worship there.

He also preserves a tradition that Celaenae (Kelainai) was named for Celaenus, a son of Poseidon and Celaeno.

Strabo offers an alternative explanation for the city's name, so the genealogy is a tradition, not an established historical etymology. Nevertheless, Poseidon is associated with a named inland Phrygian city, rather than merely a coastal Greek settlement.

Strabo 12.8.15 describes Apameia, the successor to Celaenae, as one of Asia Minor's great commercial centers. It sits at the sources of the Marsyas and Maeander river system, linking inland Phrygia toward the western Anatolian coast.

https://t.co/0nOhI4uXz1

Phrygian association isn't restricted to the sea. It includes an inland river-headwater region, earthquakes, and a city with a Poseidon-derived foundation tradition.

Herodotus, Histories 7.73, reports that the Phrygians had previously been known as Bryges, living in Europe beside the Macedonians, before moving into Anatolia.

In 7.75, he describes the Bithynians as Thracians who formerly inhabited the Strymon valley.

https://t.co/TdhfWn6eUW

Strabo goes even further in Geography 7.3.2. He connects the Mysians, Phrygians, Mygdonians, Bebrycians, and Bithynians with the Thracian world, including a tradition connecting European Mysians near the Danube with their Anatolian counterparts.

https://t.co/QEir0xqjQK

These are ancient accounts of population origins and migrations, not proof that every claimed movement happened exactly as described. Modern scholars still debate the archaeological interpretation, particularly at Gordion.

But, do you see how easy it is to separate them now?

"Iran has exempted ships from India, China, Iraq and Qatar from its Strait of Hormuz restrictions, a senior Iranian lawmaker said on Tuesday.

“Ships from these countries pass freely, and the Americans do not intercept them either,” Amir Hayat Moqaddam, deputy chairman of the Iranian parliament’s National Security and Foreign Policy Committee, told the Iranian Students’ News Agency (ISNA).

Iran effectively shut the strait early in the US-Israel war on Iran, which began on February 28, and the United States reimposed a naval blockade on Iran’s southern ports in July.
So why have these four countries been granted passage through the critical strait, and can their ships really sail freely while the blockade remains in place?

What does Iran get in return for letting ships pass?

Why does it matter to these four countries?
All four are highly dependent on the Strait of Hormuz for exports.
Of the 10.23 million barrels a day of Gulf crude that passed through the strait in October, about 42 percent went to China and 13 percent to India, Muyu Xu, a senior crude oil analyst at the analytics firm Kpler, told Al Jazeera.
Asia is particularly reliant on Gulf oil and gas usually shipped out via Hormuz. Countries there have much to offer in return for allowing ships to pass.

Is this announcement new?
Not entirely.
Iran began letting some vessels from countries it considers friendly pass within weeks of the war starting. And in April, its military command said “brotherly” Iraq was exempt.

Will ships be able to get past the US blockade?
That depends on Washington.
US Central Command (CENTCOM) has said the blockade applies to “all vessels of all nations entering or leaving coastal areas or ports in Iran”, while vessels avoiding Iranian ports are not affected.
It has also said humanitarian shipments, including “food and medical supplies essential for the survival of the civilian populations”, can pass after inspection.
Ending the blockade is one of Tehran’s demands before it will commit to broader peace talks with the US, which will include discussions about Iran’s nuclear programme. Qatar-mediated talks currently centre on an Iranian proposal to reopen the strait if the US meets seven conditions, including this and lifting sanctions.

Will this make a difference to oil markets?
Not much, for now.
An exemption has not guaranteed safety. 
More than 120 commercial ships have been hit in the region since the war began, with October being the worst month, according to data from the International Maritime Organization and United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations."

text:
🤔DEBRIEFING: THE VOICE ON THE LINE

My read: the newest tool in fraud isn't a hacker breaking into a system. It's a voice. Your CEO's voice, on the phone, telling you to wire money for a deal you can't discuss with anyone. This week federal prosecutors charged three men with doing exactly that. And they used a name for the technology we've been tracking for months.

Here is what's on the record.

November 5, 2026. The U.S. Attorney in Manhattan unseals an indictment against three foreign nationals.

Jacob Soall, 41, of the U.K. and Marbella, Spain. Arrested in Spain on June 17. Sharon Hazan, 54, of Israel. Arrested in Spain on August 5. Convicted of bank fraud in the same court in 2008. Guy Sheetrit, 42, of Israel and the UAE. Arrested in the U.K. on September 7.

All three are waiting on extradition.

How it worked, according to prosecutors: They used what the government calls "super intelligence" to copy people's voices and faces. They called employees pretending to be the company's CEO, with news of a confidential deal. Then they called again pretending to be lawyers at major law firms, to make the deal sound real. Then the employees wired the money.

Soall allegedly worked from a handwritten script titled "Lawyer Call." It included lines meant to keep employees from talking to their coworkers.

Who got hit: A hospital system in Missouri. A hospital system in California. A bank in Rhode Island. A fintech company in the U.K. A mutual fund company in Massachusetts. A pet food company in Florida.
Total losses: about $129 million.

Where the money went: accounts in the United States, Spain, Portugal, Greece, the UAE, Singapore, Austria, Slovakia and China. Then it was converted into crypto and split up.

And the launderer. Prosecutors say Hazan bragged he had been laundering money since 1994, and that he moved more than $400 million in the last three years alone.
Now widen the lens.

Look at the words.

This year the government built an entire vocabulary around "super intelligence." A presidential order. A Super Intelligence Force under the Director of National Intelligence. A White House Accord on Super Intelligence.

Now a federal prosecutor uses the same term in a criminal case. Not "AI." Not "deepfake." "SI technology."
The U.S. Attorney: "SI technology offers tremendous potential." And some people will use it to steal.
Nothing in the case connects to those programs. But the language has moved from policy into the courtroom.
And look at the dates. The arrests happened in June, August and September. The public heard about it in November. Up to five months between the arrest and the announcement.

That's the pattern this project keeps tracking. The work gets done first. The public sees it later.
And look at who's in the middle again. Not the people on the phone. The man who moved the money. Same as the last two weeks: the cartel's launderer, the man who built shell companies, the billion-dollar crypto bridge, the port chief. The service in the middle.

And it broke the way they always break. A cloned voice can fool a person. It can't fool a wire transfer. Every payment touched a bank in one of nine countries. Every crypto conversion left a record on a chain.

It's not the flag. It's not the party. It's the network.

Coordinated 

Timelines. Patterns. The general's words, not mine. All I did was read the receipts. 

I am the guy on the couch, and you have been debriefed.

THE DEBRIEFING: THE FLAG IS THE PASSPORT

My thesis, so you can judge it for yourself: the financial war on Iran has moved past the money and onto the paperwork. Whoever controls identity controls movement, whether it's a bank account, a phone number or an oil tanker. The papers are now the target.

Every ship at sea needs a flag. The flag is the ship's passport. It's how the ship gets registered, certified as safe, insured and allowed into ports. A tanker without a valid flag is a ship nobody vouches for.

On Wednesday the Treasury Department sanctioned a network it says was selling fake passports for ships. According to Treasury, a business run out of India set up websites posing as the official ship registries of countries that had never authorized them, with names spanning nearly every continent. Tankers carrying Iranian oil sailed under those invented flags. When the press exposed one fake registry, Treasury says, the operators shut it down and opened another. One country publicly disowned the registry using its name, and that registry was still flagging ships.

Treasury says one of those tankers, sailing under a fake flag, was seized by the U.S. military back in April while carrying Iranian oil. The network behind it was named this week. The ship was seized first, and the people behind it were named months later.

The same action hit a ground-handling company at a Turkish airport. Treasury says it started servicing Iranian airlines in the weeks after the U.S. sanctioned all of them in September. That's the first company to step into the gap, and the first to get punished for it.

The Treasury Secretary's words: "under Operation Economic Outcast, you are either with us or against us," and "We know where you are." Banks were warned again that anyone who knowingly helps can be cut off from the U.S. dollar.

Put this next to the rest of the week. Prosecutors went after bank and phone-company insiders in Texas, a payment-company chairman in Vietnam, and a counterfeit flag registry. Each one is the person who issues the credential, not the person who uses it.

Timelines. Patterns. Their words, not mine. All I did was read the receipts. 

I am the guy on the couch, and you have been debriefed.

🤔THE DEBRIEFING: VENEZUELAN SENTENCED TO 12 YEARS FOR LAUNDERING OVER A BILLION DOLLARS

My read: crypto didn't make dirty money disappear. It gave it a bridge. Cash goes in on one side, comes out as dollars on the other, and the bridge is supposed to be where nobody looks. This week a man who ran one of those bridges, a billion dollars' worth, got 12 years. The bridge kept the receipts.

Here is what's on the record.

November 3, 2026. Federal court, Eastern District of Virginia. Jorge Figueira, 60, a Venezuelan national living in Miami, is sentenced to 12 years in prison for conspiracy to launder money. He agreed to a $1 billion money judgment.

How the bridge worked: Money came in. It was converted into a stablecoin, Tether, on the Tron blockchain. It hopped through a chain of wallets. It went to liquidity brokers, some registered in the U.K. and the U.S. It came back out as dollars, into shell-company bank accounts. Then it was paid out.
Who used it: "numerous and varied illicit actors," prosecutors said. Including drug trafficking organizations.

Where it went: the United States, Colombia, China, Panama and Mexico.

How much: more than $1 billion through the wallets and accounts the FBI identified.
Now the part that matters.
He was charged in January. The day after the complaint, Tether froze $182 million in his network's coins.
Ten months from charge to 12 years.

That's how fast it goes when the money sits on a blockchain. Every hop between wallets is written down forever. The FBI didn't have to find the money. It had to read it.

Now widen the lens.

Same courthouse. Five days apart.

October 29. Eastern District of Virginia. A Chinese national living in Honduras gets 12 years for laundering cartel money for the Jalisco cartel, under the terrorism statute. November 3. Eastern District of Virginia. A Venezuelan national in Miami gets 12 years for running a billion-dollar crypto bridge for drug organizations.

And the rest of the week: The chairman of a fiduciary firm with offices in five financial centers, arrested in California for laundering. Serbia shuts a bank overnight and sends prosecutors after the money that left. Paraguay seizes a bank and investigates loans to its owners' own companies.

Different countries. Same layer. The service in the middle. The people who move other people's money.

And look at Venezuela this week.

On November 5, bondholders get the green light to move on Venezuela's state oil debt. Foreign oil companies are signing 25-year contracts. Talks between the government and the opposition resume on the 11th.

The door opens for Venezuelan oil. A Venezuelan launderer goes to prison. Both sides of the same rope.

That's the pattern this project keeps tracking. The crime has to touch a system. The system keeps the record. And the cases climb through the people who keep the money moving.
It's not the flag. It's not the party. It's the network.

Coordinated

text:
Clean Mystery Review: What Readers Can Expect
#fiction #cozymystery #dogs 
A good **clean mystery review** should tell readers more than whether a book has a satisfying culprit. It should help them know how the story will feel when they settle in with a cup of coffee, a curious cat at their elbow, or a loyal dog warming their feet. For many mystery lovers, the best part is the puzzle itself: following clues, second-guessing suspects, and enjoying the company of characters worth visiting again.

Clean mysteries offer that pleasure without asking readers to wade through graphic violence, heavy profanity, or explicit scenes. They can still have real stakes, surprising turns, and villains with motives as tangled as a leash drawer after a rainy walk. Clean does not mean dull. It means the author lets suspense, relationships, setting, and smart detection carry the story.

## What Makes a Mystery Clean?

There is no single rulebook that every publisher or reader follows. One reader may want a story with no swearing at all, while another is comfortable with a mild word here and there. Some readers welcome a sweet romance; others prefer romance to remain in the background. That is why thoughtful descriptions matter.

Generally, a clean mystery avoids lingering descriptions of violence and keeps disturbing material off the page or handled with restraint. A crime may happen, because there would be little mystery without a question to solve, but the emphasis stays on investigation rather than gore. Language is mild, intimacy is closed-door or understated, and the overall reading experience remains comfortable for a broad range of adults and teens.

A clean mystery can also make room for grief, jealousy, family conflict, and fear. Those emotions give a whodunit weight. The difference lies in how the story treats them. Rather than using shock for its own sake, the book uses difficult moments to reveal character and deepen the puzzle.

## The Clues Matter More Than the Carnage

The most rewarding clean mysteries play fair with the reader. The answer may be surprising, but it should make sense once the detective gathers the right pieces. A misplaced key, a contradictory alibi, an old photograph, or a muddy paw print can become far more exciting than a gruesome discovery when each detail has a purpose.

This is where cozy and clean mysteries shine. The reader gets to investigate alongside the sleuth, noticing who hesitates, who knows too much, and who is being just a little too helpful. A strong mystery invites that delicious moment of suspicion: surely it cannot be the charming shop owner. Or can it?

The detective also matters. Readers often return to a series not only to learn who committed the crime, but to spend time with someone they trust. An amateur sleuth with local knowledge, a sheriff with patience, a veterinarian who notices an unusual injury, or a clever dog with a talent for observation can bring a fresh angle to familiar mysteries.

In the Doc and Daisy Mysteries, canine forensics gives the investigation a playful but credible twist. A dog may notice scents, behaviors, and small changes people overlook. Daisy's warm snout and sharp observations remind us that a mystery can be clever without becoming cold.

## Setting Is Part of the Investigation

A clean mystery is often at its best when the setting has a personality of its own. Small towns, historic districts, seaside communities, and close-knit neighborhoods create natural tension because everyone seems to know everyone else's business. They also offer plenty of suspects.

An inviting setting does not mean every resident is innocent. In fact, the prettiest porch can hide a long-held grudge, and the friendliest festival committee may have more secrets than a locked cookie tin. The contrast is part of the fun. Readers get charming local landmarks, memorable traditions, and a sense of community, then watch the sleuth gently tug at the loose thread.

Florida towns make especially lively mystery settings. Sunshine, salt air, eccentric neighbors, historic details, and unexpected wildlife can all add color to a case. A storm rolling in can change plans. A crowded community event can conceal a crucial conversation. Even a quiet walk near the water can leave behind a clue.

The setting should never merely decorate the page. In a satisfying mystery, it affects motives, opportunities, and evidence. If an old building has a hidden passage, the reader should understand why it matters. If a town has a treasured annual event, it should bring together the very people who would rather avoid one another.

## Kind Characters Do Not Mean Easy Conflicts

Some people hear “clean” and assume every character will be endlessly sweet. That is not necessary, and it would not be much fun. Strong clean mysteries need prickly neighbors, unreliable witnesses, rivals, and folks with questionable judgment. They simply do not need cruelty to be treated as entertainment.

The key is compassion. Even when a character makes a mess of things, readers can understand the pressure, fear, or mistake behind the behavior. A good sleuth is curious without being careless, determined without becoming harsh. That balance makes the final reveal more satisfying because justice feels earned rather than merely delivered.

Animal companions can deepen that warmth without turning the story into a cartoon. Pets notice routines. They respond to tension. They offer comfort after a difficult clue or a dangerous encounter. And, if we are honest, they can be excellent judges of suspicious strangers. A dog may not solve every case alone, but a well-timed bark or a determined tug toward an overlooked spot can be very persuasive.

## A Clean Mystery Review Should Mention the Trade-Offs

Readers deserve clear expectations. Clean mysteries are not all alike, and they are not the perfect fit for every mood. Those who want gritty police procedure, intensely dark psychological suspense, or graphic action may find a cozy clean mystery gentler than they prefer. Its pace may include conversations at the diner, neighborhood relationships, and the everyday work of putting clues together.

For many readers, that is exactly the appeal. The danger is real, but the book does not leave them feeling as though they have spent an evening in a crime scene. There is room for humor, friendship, family, and a hopeful sense that truth can be found.

It also depends on the individual title. Some clean mysteries involve serious subjects such as fraud, missing persons, or family secrets. A careful review should mention content that may trouble particular readers, even when the writing stays non-graphic. Honest guidance helps readers choose a book that suits their comfort level, not someone else's.

## Why These Stories Keep Calling Readers Back

The finest clean mysteries understand that solving a crime is only part of the pleasure. Readers come back for familiar streets, trusted friends, eccentric townspeople, and the feeling that a difficult problem can yield to patience and attention. They come back for clues hidden in plain sight and for the small triumph of spotting one before the sleuth does.

Most of all, they come back for hope. A clean mystery can acknowledge that people sometimes lie, hurt one another, and make terrible choices. Yet it can also offer kindness, courage, and a community willing to set things right. That is a comforting promise, especially when delivered with a little wit, a well-earned twist, and perhaps a wagging tail near the final clue.

The next time you choose a mystery, look for more than the word “clean” on the cover. Look for a puzzle that respects your intelligence, characters you would happily meet again, and a setting that feels alive. The right story will leave you satisfied, curious for the next case, and glad you followed the trail.

text:
Thinking of applying for Anthropic shares? Thursday’s tech sell-off may have bought you some time. The listing was expected this month but could now be delayed.

Use the time well. As my latest article for @MoneyWeek explains, when you’re weighing up a big flotation, the price matters far more than the date.

Jay Ritter at the University of Florida has tracked US flotations since 1980. For the biggest companies, shares rose 9.8 per cent on average on their first day. That gain went to whoever got shares at the offer price.

Buy once trading starts and you’ve paid for it. Over the next three years, those shares roughly matched the market, slightly behind it, while you carried one company’s risk.

There’s a catch. The better the deal, the fewer shares you’re likely to get. Better-informed investors pile into the attractive flotations, so ordinary applicants tend to be scaled back in the good ones and filled in full in the bad ones. Economists call it the winner’s curse.

Personally, I'm an indexer and not remotely tempted by IPOs. But even if I were, I’d want to know two things first: what price I’d be paying, and how few shares I’d get if the deal turned out to be a good one.

Am I missing something? Read my article, linked in the comments, and let me know.

4/8 — Other research provides important context.

The Florida findings did not appear in a scientific vacuum.

A 2022 Veterans Affairs investigation compared approximately 902,000 matched recipients in each vaccine group.

Moderna recipients experienced significantly lower rates of documented SARS-CoV-2 infection and COVID-19 hospitalization.

COVID-related deaths were numerically lower with Moderna, although the principal mortality comparison was not statistically significant.

Other investigations, including a CDC/Veterans Affairs analysis and a 2026 Indiana mortality study, have also identified circumstances in which Moderna appeared to provide stronger protection against certain COVID-19 outcomes.

These observations are relevant.

Differences in vaccine dose, dosing interval, immune responses, and durability of protection offer plausible explanations.

It is therefore reasonable to investigate whether Moderna offered better protection against COVID-19 during portions of the original vaccination campaign.

But there is a crucial distinction.

Evidence of superior protection against COVID-19 does not establish that Pfizer caused excess non-COVID deaths.

Those are separate scientific questions.

Evidence supporting one cannot simply be used to prove the other.

HYPERGROWTH LEN5 #3 SANDISK $SNDK FELL 22% IN ONE DAY:

Sandisk (SNDK) at $806.43, -$230.97 / -22.26% on Thursday, and $873.50 premarket, +$67.07 / +8.32% from that close.

Sandisk is #3 on the Hypergrowth Len5, and it lost more than a fifth of its price on Thursday on no news of its own. A week earlier the flash-memory maker reported revenue almost five times what it took in a year before. Data centers were its fastest-growing buyers, and the selling follows an election that raised the chance of new rules on data-center building. Thursday's close left the shares at about a third of their June record. Sandisk still forecasts higher sales, and the year-ago figures it has to beat get much larger from here.

Hypergrowth wants sales multiplying, and Sandisk's rose 378% from a year earlier in the quarter to October 2. What would knock it off the Hypergrowth Len5: revenue that stalls near this quarter's $11.03B. This quarter had to beat $2.31B from a year earlier. Next summer's quarter has to beat $8.97B.

The October 29 report showed data centers buying far more of Sandisk's chips:
- Revenue, money from customers: $11.03B, +378% from a year earlier.
- Data-center revenue: $4.80B, against $269M, and 44% of the total.
- Gross margin, the share of sales left after making the chips: 85.0%, against 29.8%.
- Profit: $8.1B, against $112M.
- Forecast for the December quarter, due tentatively January 28: revenue of $12.2B to $12.6B, about four times the $3.03B of a year earlier.
Our read: a margin that nearly tripled says higher memory prices, more than extra volume, made the quarter.

Thursday's selling ran at three times Sandisk's usual volume:
- 30.7M shares, against a 30-day average of 9.9M.
- Since the report: -39%.
- From the June 25 record close of $2,335.00: -65%.

At Thursday's close the shares cost about 7 times the past year's adjusted profit, which leaves out one-time items. Our read: sellers are pricing in a drop in that profit.

An 8-for-1 stock split on November 19 multiplies the share count and changes nothing about the business.

Sandisk's sales qualify it for Hypergrowth several times over, and sellers still took a fifth off its price in one day. The next number from inside the company is December-quarter revenue, and Sandisk's own floor for it is $12.2B.

text:
🔵#PAULKAGAME: THE PAN-AFRICAN LEADER WHO CHOOSES ACTIONS OVER EMPTY SPEECHES

Rwanda’s industrial ambitions faced American trade pressure. President Kagame refused to surrender the country’s vision of building its own industries.

Pan-Africanism is often celebrated in political speeches, conference halls and diplomatic gatherings. But when it comes to putting the principle into practice, the real test is whether African leaders are prepared to make difficult decisions to protect their countries’ economic interests.

President Paul Kagame’s position on Rwanda’s textile and footwear industries offers a compelling example of this distinction.

His message was straightforward: Africa cannot achieve genuine economic independence while remaining dependent on importing products it has the capacity to manufacture itself.

The controversy surrounding Rwanda and the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA) illustrates this position.

For years, Rwanda and other East African countries pursued measures to reduce imports of second-hand clothes and shoes, with the objective of creating opportunities for local manufacturers, attracting investment and developing domestic textile industries.

However, this ambition encountered resistance from the United States second-hand clothing industry, which argued that the proposed restrictions would harm American businesses and employment.

Washington subsequently put pressure on Rwanda to reverse its policy.

But President Kagame refused to abandon the country’s industrial ambitions simply to preserve preferential access to the American market.

His position was clear: Rwanda would develop its industries, whether external interests welcomed that decision or not.

In June 2017, Kagame articulated the choice facing Rwanda: continue importing second-hand clothing under the threat of losing trade benefits, or build the textile industries that Rwandans deserved.

He made it clear that Rwanda was prepared to accept the consequences of choosing industrialisation.

And the consequences came.

In July 2018, the Trump administration suspended duty-free AGOA treatment for Rwandan apparel products, citing Rwanda’s continued restrictions on imports of used clothing and footwear. Rwanda retained its AGOA eligibility for other products, but its apparel benefits remained suspended.

This episode raises an important question about the nature of international trade partnerships: how can African countries build competitive domestic industries if their attempts to protect emerging manufacturers repeatedly encounter pressure from established foreign commercial interests?

The contradiction is particularly striking when African countries are encouraged to industrialise while facing resistance when they introduce policies intended to create room for local production.

They do not want Africans to remain dependent on their own capacity to produce clothes and shoes? Then why should an African country be discouraged from building that capacity?

President Kagame’s position challenges precisely this contradiction.

His understanding of Pan-Africanism goes beyond calls for African unity and continental solidarity. It places economic sovereignty, industrialisation and the ability to make independent national decisions at the centre of the discussion.

The principle is simple: Africa cannot continue exporting raw materials, importing finished products and expecting to achieve meaningful economic independence.

Rwanda’s AGOA experience demonstrates the political and economic costs that can accompany a decision to pursue a different development path.

President Kagame’s message remains relevant: African countries must have the confidence to build their own industries, defend their economic interests and determine their development priorities.

Pan-Africanism is not merely about speaking proudly about Africa. It is also about making the difficult decisions necessary to build an Africa that can produce, manufacture and compete.

text:
$NVDA
Three House committee chairs have asked Jensen Huang to brief them behind closed doors on November 18, the day after Nvidia reports earnings. He has until November 11 to accept or offer another date.

The letter, dated November 4, comes from Brian Mast (Foreign Affairs), John Moolenaar (Select Committee on the CCP) and Rick Crawford (Intelligence). It asks about two things: Nvidia's security protocols against foreign adversary espionage, and Huang's interactions with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, whom the letter calls "a publicly reported People's Republic of China (PRC) intelligence asset."

"Publicly reported" points back to the New York Times story of October 29. Citing U.S. officials, the Times said intelligence agencies concluded Alice Huang passed information to Beijing while developing a close relationship with Jensen Huang. Nvidia said his interactions with her are "not unusual or unexpected" and that "meetings with customers are part of a CEO's job." China's foreign ministry called the reports baseless.

The letter is a request. It doesn't come with a subpoena, and it doesn't accuse Jensen Huang of anything.

Megaspeed isn't a new name. In October 2025 the Times reported that U.S. officials were looking at whether the Singapore company helped Chinese firms get restricted Nvidia chips, and Singapore said it was investigating too. Megaspeed had reportedly become Nvidia's largest buyer in Southeast Asia. Nvidia said its visits to Megaspeed's facilities found no evidence of diversion.

So what matters for the stock? I'd watch whether this pushes Washington to tighten checks on chips sold through third countries. Nvidia's next quarter doesn't hinge on one meeting.

Three dates to watch: Huang's reply by November 11, whether analysts bring it up on the November 17 call, and the November 18 briefing.

Gilbert Arenas was in the second year of a $111 million contract when a $1,000 pot on the Washington Wizards’ team plane changed everything. A teammate was already down about $6,000 in a card game when Arenas bought into the hand just to get under his skin. Days later, both men pulled guns on each other in the locker room.

In the video below, Arenas walks through the hand, card by card. “Losing in cards has nothing to do with money,” he says. “It’s the sh*t talking and the ego.” The teammate’s answer, as Arenas tells it: “People like you, I rob on the street.”

The NBA suspended him for the final 50 games without pay, about $147,200 a game, more than $7 million in all. He pleaded guilty to a felony gun charge.

The teammate was Javaris Crittenton. A year and a half later, he opened fire on an Atlanta street looking for a man he believed had robbed him. Jullian Jones, a 22-year-old mother of four, was walking with friends when the shots hit her. He got 23 years.

Arenas did not stay away from the table. In July 2025, federal agents came to his door at 6:30 in the morning with guns aimed at the house. Prosecutors say he ran high-stakes poker games at his Encino mansion. Players paid a cut of every hand. Women were hired to serve drinks, give massages and offer “companionship,” then taxed on their tips. One of the men charged with him is described as a suspected organized crime figure from Israel. Arenas pleaded not guilty.

Did he learn nothing from the card game that nearly cost him $7 million, or did he just learn which side of the table makes the money?

text:
A change in Israel's leadership could create new opportunities to rebuild relationships with Democrats, restore trust with congressional leaders and improve the atmosphere between Jerusalem and Washington.

But – and this is a big but – we should not fool ourselves into believing that changing the people at the top will automatically change how large parts of the Democratic Party view Israel. It won’t.

There are deep, substantive policy differences between Israel and significant parts of the Democratic Party.

These disagreements concern settler violence in the West Bank, the expansion of settlements and outposts, the lack of meaningful progress in Gaza, the absence of serious engagement with the Palestinian Authority, the government’s judicial overhaul, and a long list of additional issues.

These disagreements will not disappear simply because Netanyahu is replaced by Eisenkot or Bennett.

Even if Eisenkot were to become prime minister tomorrow, without substantive changes in Israeli policy, the grace period he might receive from Democrats would be short.

The atmosphere might improve. Meetings in Washington might become warmer. Statements from senior congressional Democrats might become less hostile. There would likely be some goodwill toward an Israeli leader not associated with Netanyahu’s policies.

But the goodwill will not last.

If Israel continues expanding settlements and outposts, fails to confront settler violence, and offers no credible diplomatic horizon, a new government will quickly discover that the underlying disagreements remain exactly where they were.

Changing the government without changing its policies will not solve the problem. And this is something the Israeli public needs to understand and make decisions accordingly.

AI may not need another data center campus

Local opposition blocked or delayed at least 75 U.S. data center projects worth about $130 billion in the first quarter of 2026. But AI capacity may not always need a brand-new campus.

At GTC Berlin, @nvidia announced that telecom operators are putting its AI servers into buildings they already run: data centers, metro sites and cell sites. Nokia’s radio software will run on those same servers, so operators can use one platform for network functions and AI workloads.

NVIDIA moves fast, and it tends to grow through partners. This time, those partners are the telecom operators whose sites are already spread across their markets. Several are putting the technology to work:

- T-Mobile made an AI radio access network call in Bellevue, Washington, connected to its existing 5G Standalone core.
- Orange is demonstrating real-time translation for emergency and field crews.
- Elisa runs an enterprise voice assistant at one of its network sites.
- BT, Deutsche Telekom and Elisa point to 2027 for field trials or commercial services.

Nearly 20 operators now have AI radio access network collaborations built on Nokia and NVIDIA technology.

The appeal is straightforward: the buildings, fiber and power connections are already there. That could help operators put computing closer to customers without starting with a new campus. It does not make power, cooling or local review irrelevant, but it gives communities a different proposal to evaluate.

For operators, decades of network investment could become a new source of revenue. For a CIO, it could mean AI capacity in a building near a plant or hospital, offered through a carrier already serving the business.

The full piece maps which AI work stays central, which moves to nearby sites and which runs on site: New AI Computing Moves Into Existing Telecom Sites https://t.co/XzCrfrvATP

If your carrier offered AI capacity in a nearby building in 2027, which workload would you move first? And could your contract let you take it to another operator later?

Telecom operators built sites in nearly every community over decades. NVIDIA is giving those sites a new job.

text:
The Rhetorical Pivot: How a Conflict Intended to Preempt a Threat Became a Domestic Fault Line

The ongoing military conflict against Iran, initiated by President Donald J. Trump with the stated goal of preventing Tehran from securing a functional nuclear weapon, has rapidly evolved from a matter of global security into a primary domestic political battleground. For supporters of the administration’s foreign policy, the intervention was a justified and necessary measure to protect the West and its regional allies from a nuclear-armed state sponsor of terrorism. However, after the recent midterm elections, conservative commentators and administration allies have offered a distinct critique, arguing that the Democratic Party has successfully reframed the conflict to leverage political control at home and abroad.
According to this view, the political opposition has turned a strategic defence initiative into a narrative of an "illegal, never-ending war" to manipulate public sentiment. Critics argue that rather than focusing on the global security implications of a nuclearised Iran, the opposition has capitalised on the immediate economic fallout—most notably rising domestic gas prices and inflation—to erode support for the administration’s "America First" agenda. By centring the national conversation on economic strain rather than national security, the newly empowered Democratic majorities in Congress are seen by detractors as positioning themselves to dictate terms to both domestic leaders and international partners.
Furthermore, some staunch critics go as far as to accuse the opposition of hypocrisy regarding military intervention. They argue that while progressive and Democratic platforms frequently condemn unilateral military action as a "forever war," their own globalist and ideological leanings historically involve heavy-handed interventions under the guise of international law or humanitarianism. From this perspective, the condemnation of the current conflict is less about an inherent opposition to warfare and more about a calculated effort to brand any Republican-led action as inherently illegitimate. By doing so, critics contend, the opposition seeks to reassure the American public of their own moral and diplomatic superiority while using the threat of funding cuts and legislative stalemates to hold the administration's foreign policy hostage.
Conversely, mainstream Democratic leaders and a growing number of independent voters view the situation through an entirely different lens. Figures such as Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer have maintained that opposition to the war stems from a constitutional duty to prevent unchecked executive overreach and avoid prolonged, costly foreign entanglements. They point out that the electorate's clear shift during the midterms reflects a genuine public weariness of the conflict's mounting domestic costs rather than a manufactured narrative. As the debate intensifies with a divided government in Washington, the conflict remains a stark example of how identical foreign policy actions can be interpreted as either a vital shield for global safety or an unnecessary domestic burden.

text:
Washington is spending billions to win a war it still can't define.

By mid-October, the Iran conflict had reportedly cost the US more than $47 billion, including roughly $30 billion in munitions.

Now Pete Hegseth is seeking another $350 billion in mandatory defense funding, while the administration faces growing political resistance.

The pressure is no longer coming just from Tehran.

Democrats have taken control of both congressional chambers, JD Vance has questioned the war's political cost, and lawmakers are preparing investigations into Pentagon decisions and Hegseth's leadership.

Yet Hegseth's November 5 message offered defiance, not answers. He called the campaign historic and dismissed criticism as political interference.

Three questions deserve concrete answers:

- $47 billion: How much more will this war cost?

- $30 billion: How quickly can depleted ammunition stockpiles be replenished?

- $350 billion: What measurable military capabilities will this additional funding actually deliver?

Destroying nuclear facilities is not the same as permanently eliminating nuclear ambitions.

That requires intelligence, verification and a credible strategy for the period after the strikes end.

A military campaign cannot be judged by targets destroyed alone.

It must be judged by whether its objectives are achieved, its costs remain sustainable and the threat is genuinely reduced.

Hegseth can demand another $350 billion and call every critic a political enemy. But taxpayers aren't funding a fucking speech.

They're funding an outcome. 🤔

text:
A country can be bombed into darkness. That's not the same as winning a war.

On November 5, Trump warned that he might have to destroy what remains of Iran and suggested reconstruction could take 25 years.

That's an extraordinary statement from a president who still hasn't publicly defined the military and political conditions that would make further destruction unnecessary.

Look at the strategic consequences.

Iran has roughly 90 million people. Its electricity network, water infrastructure, transport corridors, energy facilities and industrial capacity support an entire civilian economy.

Attacking these systems doesn't just weaken military logistics. It can disrupt hospitals, water treatment, food distribution, communications and economic activity on a national scale.

The legal threshold is not optional.

Under international humanitarian law, an object must qualify as a military objective before it can be lawfully attacked. Even then, the expected civilian harm cannot be excessive relative to the concrete and direct military advantage anticipated.

Military necessity is not a blank cheque to destroy civilian life.

There's also a strategic problem Washington cannot bomb away:

- Destroying facilities does not eliminate scientific knowledge or technical expertise.

- Disrupting energy production can create years of economic damage without guaranteeing political surrender.

- Civilian hardship can deepen resentment and make a postwar settlement harder to achieve.

- Infrastructure destruction can create reconstruction costs that extend far beyond the military campaign itself.

So what does victory actually mean?

If the objective is to prevent Iran from restoring nuclear or military capabilities, Washington needs measurable conditions:

Verified dismantlement, restrictions on enrichment, monitoring mechanisms and enforceable security arrangements.

Without those benchmarks, the military campaign risks becoming an open-ended destruction strategy.

Trump's statement does not confirm that another attack has been ordered.

But threatening the destruction of an entire country's remaining infrastructure without clearly defining limits is a dangerous escalation in rhetoric.

You can destroy power plants, bridges and factories. You cannot bomb 90 million people into a sustainable political settlement.

A war without a defined endpoint isn't strength;

it's a fucking strategy with no exit plan.

text:
40 years.

FOUR DECADES of being a @WWE  fan. From the larger-than-life heroes of my childhood to the legends, rivalries, WrestleManias and unforgettable moments that have been part of my life for as long as I can remember.

And today, I'm done.

I've said for years that the @TKOGrp  takeover and the Netflix deal would eventually destroy the WWE I grew up loving. I hoped I was wrong. But this? This is where I draw the fucking line.

We're talking about sending human beings into a region facing serious security threats, where an airport has already been struck by a missile, and where governments are warning their citizens against unnecessary travel.

And what does WWE reportedly do?

Offer production workers an extra $3,000 in hazard pay.

THREE THOUSAND DOLLARS.

Meanwhile, significant parts of the production are being handled safely from headquarters in Connecticut.

So apparently it's possible to protect some of your workforce, but others still need to be physically present to keep the show running?

And then we have TKO President Mark Shapiro discussing the financial consequences of cancelling events, the concerns of Wall Street investors and the importance of meeting year-end targets.

He says employee safety comes first.

Well, here's a fucking radical idea.

PROVE IT.

Because if you have to offer people hazard pay to convince them to travel somewhere, perhaps the conversation shouldn't be about how much extra money they'll receive. Perhaps it should be about whether they should be going there in the first place.

These aren't expendable assets on a corporate spreadsheet.

They're human beings. They're somebody's husband, wife, father, mother, son or daughter.

And that includes the wrestlers. The men and women who put their bodies on the line week after week, who entertain millions, who inspire children, who become heroes to people like me.

No championship, no television contract, no sponsorship agreement and no fucking shareholder dividend is worth somebody's life.

I don't blame the talent. I don't blame the crew. I have nothing but respect for the people who make this business what it is.

My anger is directed squarely at the people making these decisions.

WWE used to tell us that the fans were the heart and soul of the company.

Well, this fan has had enough.

I didn't spend 40 years supporting a balance sheet. I supported the people, the passion, the storytelling and the magic of professional wrestling.

And I refuse to continue financially supporting or watching a company whose current priorities I can no longer reconcile with my conscience.

So that's it. No more WWE. No more premium live events. No more subscriptions or merchandise.

To the wrestlers and crews who gave me four decades of memories, thank you. Genuinely. You deserved my loyalty, and you still have my respect.

To @TKOGrp  and its executives?

You can keep your Crown Jewel.

You can keep your Saudi millions.

You can keep your investors happy.

But you've just lost a fan of 40 years.

And I suspect I'm not the only one.

People before profits. Every single fucking time.

text:
$QGEN Q3 2026 earnings: Qiagen beats quarterly targets and agrees to EQT buyout

Qiagen, a maker of genetic and diagnostic lab tests, beat its third-quarter targets as it agreed to a private-equity buyout. Total revenue grew 3% to $548 million, but by our math sales from businesses owned a year ago grew less than 1% once the acquired Parse Biosciences unit is stripped out. Profit per share excluding one-offs rose 7% to $0.65 on higher-margin chemical kits, U. S. tariff refunds and share buybacks. Because EQT Private Equity agreed to buy the company, management suspended its full-year outlook and cancelled its conference call.

• Sales from businesses owned a year ago: ~𝟏% (at constant currency, by our math (+3% including Parse))
• Profit per share, excluding one-offs: $𝟎.𝟔𝟓 (+7% from a year ago (plan was at least $0.62))
• Operating margin, excluding one-offs: 𝟑𝟎.𝟒% (+0.8 percentage points from a year ago)
• Full-year 2026 outlook: 𝐖𝐢𝐭𝐡𝐝𝐫𝐚𝐰𝐧 (suspended during the €46.50 per share EQT takeover offer)

⚖️ 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭: 🟢 Bullish

The story got better because the €10.8 billion cash takeover offer resolves a year-long chief executive vacancy and removes the risk of a painful medium-term target reset. New automated sample machines and early U. S. approvals for bloodstream infection panels also lifted core lab demand. One caution: tuberculosis testing stayed flat on weak U. S. immigration screening, and a federal jury found that Parse willfully infringed three rival patents.

The question now is whether the buyout closes smoothly in mid-2027 or hits regulatory and shareholder hurdles that force Qiagen back onto its standalone plan. If the deal closes, operational debates end; if it fails, the company faces a €150 million break fee and sub-1% underlying growth. Shareholder tender results and regulatory filings over the next two quarters will decide.

Full article with charts - link in bio

🐂 𝐁𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🟢🟢 𝐄𝐐𝐓 𝐀𝐠𝐫𝐞𝐞𝐬 𝐭𝐨 𝐁𝐮𝐲 𝐐𝐢𝐚𝐠𝐞𝐧 𝐟𝐨𝐫 €𝟏𝟎.𝟖 𝐁𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧
For a year, Qiagen operated without a permanent successor for departing chief executive Thierry Bernard while rumours of a sale grew. On October 21, the Dutch molecular testing group ended that uncertainty. A holding company controlled by EQT Private Equity agreed to "make an all-cash voluntary public takeover offer to acquire all outstanding QIAGEN shares at €46.50 per share".

The deal values the business at €10.8 billion, or about $12.1 billion including $1.1 billion of net debt. Both governing boards unanimously backed the agreement as "in the best interest of QIAGEN and its business". Because a private buyer is stepping in, the leadership vacuum and the risk of a painful strategy reset under a new chief executive no longer hang over operations.

What to watch: shareholder tender results and regulatory clearances ahead of the expected mid-2027 closing. The buyer needs at least 50% of issued shares plus one share and Extraordinary General Meeting approval to complete the takeover.

🟢 𝐍𝐞𝐰 𝐈𝐧𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐮𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐅𝐃𝐀 𝐀𝐩𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐯𝐚𝐥𝐬 𝐋𝐢𝐟𝐭 𝐂𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝐋𝐚𝐛 𝐒𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬
Qiagen relies on new lab machines and test panels to drive second-half growth. That product rollout delivered in the third quarter. The company launched QIAmini, a compact automated sample-preparation machine for smaller labs, completing its rollout of three new systems this year. It also won U. S. clearance ahead of schedule for two bloodstream infection panels on QIAstat-Dx, its rapid diagnostic machine.

• Sample technologies sales: $187.4 million, up 10% at constant currency
• Sample technologies sales from businesses owned a year ago: up 3% at constant currency
• Sample technologies instrument sales: up about 10% at constant currency
• QIAstat-Dx diagnostic sales: $35 million, up 11% at constant currency
• Genomics and sequencing sales: $66.0 million, up 9% at constant currency

Sample technologies grew mainly because Qiagen bought Parse Biosciences, a single-cell research specialist, in December 2025. Qiagen said "Parse remains on track to exceed its 2026 sales target of approximately $40 million", which adds roughly 7 percentage points to the division's growth by our math.

What to watch: full-year instrument placement numbers for QIAsprint Connect and QIAsymphony Connect in the fourth-quarter report. Rising machine installations would confirm that labs will buy more chemical kits in 2027.

🟢 𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐬𝐮𝐦𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞𝐬 𝐌𝐢𝐱 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐓𝐚𝐫𝐢𝐟𝐟 𝐑𝐞𝐟𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐬 𝐋𝐢𝐟𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐎𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐢𝐧
Earlier this year, Qiagen expected its operating margin excluding one-offs to stay flat at 29.5% as it absorbed U. S. tariffs and research costs at Parse Biosciences. Instead, the operating margin excluding one-offs rose 0.8 percentage points from a year ago to 30.4%. Reported gross margin jumped 2.4 percentage points to 64.6% because the cost of making products fell from 37.8% of sales to 35.4%.

Two things drove the improvement. Chemical kits and software — which carry higher margins than lab machines — reached 91% of total revenue. Gross profit also benefited from "the impact of U. S. tariff refunds" and efficiency savings. Those gains easily covered a 0.7 percentage point rise in research and development spending, which reached 9.8% of sales as Qiagen funded Parse.

What to watch: gross margin excluding one-offs in the fourth quarter. A reading near 67% without further tariff refunds would show that efficiency gains and Parse kit sales are lifting profitability on their own.

🐻 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🔴🔴 𝐓𝐚𝐤𝐞𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫 𝐂𝐥𝐨𝐬𝐞𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐁𝐨𝐨𝐤 𝐨𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟖 𝐓𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐞𝐭𝐬
Qiagen highlighted that third-quarter sales grew 3% at constant currency, beating its 1% to 2% outlook. Yet "QIAGEN has suspended its 2026 outlook and will not provide financial guidance while the transaction is pending", and it cancelled its quarterly conference call. That leaves investors with no forward plan and no update on the 2028 targets.

The headline beat also relies on an acquisition. Excluding Parse Biosciences, which adds about $12 million of quarterly sales by our math, sales from businesses owned a year ago grew less than 1% at constant currency. Prior full-year plans required fourth-quarter sales growth to jump to between 5% and 8% at constant currency. If the takeover fails, Qiagen also warned it "may be required to pay the Bidder a termination payment of €150 million".

What to watch: fourth-quarter constant-currency sales growth in February 2027. A rate below 5% would show that the old full-year target would have missed without the takeover.

🔴 𝐓𝐮𝐛𝐞𝐫𝐜𝐮𝐥𝐨𝐬𝐢𝐬 𝐓𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐒𝐭𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐏𝐂𝐑 𝐒𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬 𝐊𝐞𝐞𝐩 𝐅𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐠
Outside of sample preparation and sequencing, demand in Qiagen's other product lines remains sluggish. QuantiFERON, its flagship blood test for latent tuberculosis that brings in a quarter of company revenue, stood still at $136 million. Qiagen said "continued softness in U. S. immigration testing was offset by demand in other latent tuberculosis (TB) testing groups".

Meanwhile, cautiously funded research labs continue to hold back on routine equipment and older kits. Total instrument revenue across the group rose just 1% at constant currency to $51.6 million. In the PCR division, which sells tools to copy and measure DNA, sales fell 5% at constant currency to $71.2 million. Strong demand for the newer QIAcuity digital PCR system could not make up for falling sales of older quantitative PCR kits, machines and third-party products.

What to watch: fourth-quarter QuantiFERON sales. After $380 million in the first nine months, the test needs $120 million in the fourth quarter to reach its $500 million full-year goal.

🔴 𝐑𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐮𝐜𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐂𝐨𝐬𝐭𝐬 𝐃𝐨𝐮𝐛𝐥𝐞 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐏𝐚𝐫𝐬𝐞 𝐋𝐨𝐬𝐞𝐬 𝐚 𝐏𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭
While profit excluding one-offs rose, reported net income fell 19% from a year ago to $105.7 million. Part of the drop came from taxes returning to 20.1% after a one-time U. S. tax deduction last year. The rest came from restructuring and integration charges, which more than doubled from $8.1 million to $19.2 million, or 3.5% of sales, as Qiagen relocated jobs under its $75 million cost programme.

Integration also brought a legal setback. In August 2026, a U. S. federal jury found that Parse Biosciences willfully infringed three single-cell patents held by Scale Biosciences and Roche, awarding $4.9 million in damages. Because infringement was willful, the judge can triple the penalty, adding up to $9.8 million. Qiagen recorded a $4.9 million reimbursement asset from the $28.8 million acquisition escrow account, so the verdict did not hit net income, but the ruling challenges Parse's intellectual property.

What to watch: the post-trial judgment in Delaware federal court. An injunction or a penalty enhancement beyond the escrow protection would hurt the return on the $231 million Parse purchase.

👓 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐓𝐡𝐞𝐦𝐞𝐬

𝐂𝐡𝐢𝐧𝐚 𝐃𝐞𝐦𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐃𝐫𝐚𝐠𝐬 𝐨𝐧 𝐀𝐬𝐢𝐚-𝐏𝐚𝐜𝐢𝐟𝐢𝐜 𝐒𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬
Regional sales moved in opposite directions during the third quarter. Revenue rose 4% in the Americas to $298.3 million and 3% in Europe, the Middle East and Africa to $176.9 million. In contrast, sales in the Asia-Pacific, Japan and Rest of World region slipped 1% to $72.6 million because "challenging macro-demand trends in China" outweighed growth in Australia, Malaysia and Indonesia.

— • — • —

💲 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐊𝐏𝐈𝐬

𝐅𝐫𝐞𝐞 𝐜𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐟𝐥𝐨𝐰 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐢𝐧𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐢𝐞𝐬 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟏𝟎𝟕 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
Free cash flow fell 10% from a year ago in the third quarter and 5% over the first nine months to $319 million. Cash flow slowed because Qiagen spent $35.3 million building inventory during the first nine months "in response to geopolitical conditions and to support new product launches", lifting balance-sheet inventory 6% since December to $320.0 million.

𝐍𝐞𝐭 𝐝𝐞𝐛𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐥𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐠𝐞 𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): 𝟏.𝟎𝐱 𝐚𝐝𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐄𝐁𝐈𝐓𝐃𝐀  ⇗ accelerating
Net debt stood at $812.7 million by our math at the end of September, with $830.1 million in cash and short-term investments against $1.64 billion of total debt. Net debt to Ebitda excluding one-offs edged down from 1.1x in June to 1.0x, but remains above 0.7x at year-end 2025 after January's $496.7 million share repayment and July's $72.3 million dividend.

𝐃𝐢𝐥𝐮𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐜𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐭 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): 𝟐𝟎𝟖.𝟏 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
Diluted shares fell 4.8% from 218.5 million a year ago because the Dutch group completed a synthetic share buyback in January 2026 that combined a direct capital repayment with a 20-for-19 reverse stock split. The lower share count lifted third-quarter profit per share growth by about 5 percentage points above net profit growth.

— • — • —

🔮 𝐆𝐮𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔 𝐍𝐞𝐭 𝐬𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬 𝐠𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐭𝐡 (𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐧𝐭 𝐜𝐮𝐫𝐫𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐲): 𝐒𝐮𝐬𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐝  ⇒ stable
✕ withdrawn, was ~1–2% CER
Withdrawn. Qiagen suspended its full-year sales outlook while the EQT Private Equity takeover offer is pending. Through the first nine months of 2026, net sales rose 2% as reported to $1.58 billion and were unchanged at constant exchange rates.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐟𝐢𝐭 𝐩𝐞𝐫 𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞, 𝐞𝐱𝐜𝐥𝐮𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐨𝐧𝐞-𝐨𝐟𝐟𝐬 (𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐧𝐭 𝐜𝐮𝐫𝐫𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐲): 𝐒𝐮𝐬𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐝  ⇗ accelerating
✕ withdrawn, was at least $2.43 CER
Withdrawn. The molecular diagnostics group also retracted its full-year earnings floor because of the takeover agreement. Over the first nine months, profit per share excluding one-offs rose 2% at constant currency to $1.80, after clearing the quarterly floor for at least six straight quarters.

— • — • —

❓ 𝐊𝐞𝐲 𝐐𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬

𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐦𝐮𝐜𝐡 𝐝𝐢𝐝 𝐔.𝐒. 𝐭𝐚𝐫𝐢𝐟𝐟 𝐫𝐞𝐟𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐬 𝐚𝐝𝐝 𝐭𝐨 𝐦𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐢𝐧?
The quarterly report credits U. S. tariff refunds for part of the 2.4 percentage point jump in gross margin, without giving the dollar figure. Knowing the refund size would show how much of the 30.4% operating margin excluding one-offs is repeatable.

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐢𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐨𝐬𝐮𝐫𝐞 𝐭𝐨 𝐭𝐫𝐢𝐩𝐥𝐞 𝐝𝐚𝐦𝐚𝐠𝐞𝐬 𝐚𝐭 𝐏𝐚𝐫𝐬𝐞?
A federal jury found Parse Biosciences willfully infringed three patents, which allows the judge to triple the $4.9 million damages award to $14.7 million. Investors need to know if the acquisition escrow covers enhanced damages and whether an injunction is possible.

𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐦𝐚𝐧𝐲 𝐧𝐞𝐰 𝐚𝐮𝐭𝐨𝐦𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐬𝐲𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐦𝐬 𝐰𝐞𝐫𝐞 𝐩𝐥𝐚𝐜𝐞𝐝 𝐢𝐧 𝐐𝟑?
Sample technologies instrument sales rose 10% at constant currency following the launches of QIAsprint Connect, QIAsymphony Connect and QIAmini. Qiagen previously promised placement counts at year-end, and cancelling the conference call left third-quarter installation numbers undisclosed.

𝐖𝐡𝐢𝐜𝐡 𝐫𝐞𝐠𝐮𝐥𝐚𝐭𝐨𝐫 𝐩𝐨𝐬𝐞𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐥𝐨𝐧𝐠𝐞𝐬𝐭 𝐫𝐞𝐯𝐢𝐞𝐰 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐄𝐐𝐓'𝐬 𝐨𝐟𝐟𝐞𝐫?

text:
Meet Martha Garside. She is seventy-four years of age, lives in a damp-coursed stone terrace just outside Holmfirth, and has never trusted a weather forecast in her born days. Martha’s uniform is as fixed as the Pennine mist: thick, ribbed beige stockings that somehow manage to sag no matter how hard she pulls them, a stout navy skirt that has seen off three prime ministers, a pinny that smells faintly of boiled cabbage and carbolic soap, and a head full of curlers that she treats like crown jewels.

If you make the mistake of stepping on her meticulously scrubbed front flagstones with muddy boots, you won't get a polite cough. You will get the full force of her rolled-up Yorkshire Post, delivered with the sniper-like precision of a woman who spent forty years shouting at local lads for scrumping apples.

She rules her patch of the valley with an iron ladle, viewing the local men—especially those daft enough to roll old tin baths down hills or build flying machines out of garden fencing—as permanent candidates for the local asylum.

Her conversation consists entirely of heavy sighs, sharp tucks of the chin, and observations on how nobody knows the value of a proper shilling anymore. She doesn't suffer fools, she doesn't do pleasantries, and if you offer her a cup of tea, she’ll check to see if you've wiped the spout first.

🇮🇷| November 5–6: A Letter Delivered to the Kremlin, Two Drones Brought Down Over Qeshm, and the Rules of the Strait of Hormuz Reaffirmed

November 5–6, 2026. Tehran. Five developments, five markers of a single, coherent strategy.

💥 Front One: The Messenger at the Kremlin

On the evening of November 5, at the Kremlin in Moscow, Major General Mohsen Rezaei, Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, delivered a letter from the Leader of the Islamic Revolution, Seyyed Mojtaba Hosseini Khamenei, to Russian President Vladimir Putin.

A Kremlin spokesperson confirmed that the meeting was attended by Igor Kostyukov, head of Russia’s military intelligence agency (GRU), and Yuri Ushakov, the presidential aide for foreign policy.

This was no mere "diplomatic formality." It was a "strategic alignment." By having the head of the GRU at the table, Putin signaled that the discussion went beyond "bilateral relations" to encompass intelligence, security, and military coordination.

During a phone call with Putin on November 2, Rezaei had already expressed gratitude for the Russian president’s "clear praise" of martyred leaders and other Iranian heroes, as well as his "support" for the resistance of the Iranian people while emphasizing the importance of continuing strategic cooperation between Iran and Russia.

Thanks offered over the phone four days prior; a personal letter from the Leader delivered at the Kremlin four days later. This is not just a "warming of relations" it is the re-welding of two nations bound together by the chains of sanctions.

🎯 Front Two: Electronic Warfare Over Qeshm

On the evening of November 5, the Public Relations Department of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) announced that a fifth and a sixth U.S. MQM-170 reconnaissance drone had been "brought down" over Qeshm Island by advanced electronic warfare systems operated by the IRGC Aerospace Force.

"Brought down" not "shot down." The distinction is precise. To "shoot down" implies destruction; to "bring down" implies taking control.  Electronic warfare systems infiltrate a drone’s control architecture, severing the link between the operator and the aircraft, before guiding it down to a landing site of their own choosing.

This is not "shooting down a drone." This is "seizing the enemy’s eyes and forcing them to see exactly what we want them to see."

The MQM-170 is an American reconnaissance drone, typically employed for tactical-level intelligence gathering, battlefield surveillance, and target designation. Its seizure over Qeshm Island implies that the images it captured, the signals it intercepted, and the data it transmitted may have fallen under the control of Revolutionary Guard engineers potentially even before the drone touched down.

The sixth one. Not the first, not the second but the sixth MQM-170. Add to this the 56 MQ-9s, and you have a cumulative track record. In the realm of electronic warfare, such a record signifies genuine capability. It is not a matter of luck or a fluke; it represents a systematic, repeatable, and fully matured operational capacity.

📜 The Third Front: The Rules of Hormuz, Reaffirmed

The Public Relations Department of the Revolutionary Guard Navy announced that two oil tankers one east of the Strait of Hormuz and the other within it were intercepted while attempting to transit through unauthorized shipping lanes.

Having deactivated all navigation and identification systems, the vessels sought to exit the Strait of Hormuz with the assistance of "aggressive, terrorist American forces." They struck mines, caught fire, and came to a halt.

One sentence in the statement bears repeating verbatim: "By the grace of Allah and through the efforts of the brave warriors of the Revolutionary Guard Navy, the Strait of Hormuz remains closed. This status will not change until seven specific conditions are met."

"Until seven conditions are met."

This is not a "threat." It is a formal declaration of a policy framework. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz is neither a "temporary measure" nor a "bargaining chip" or a "concession" to be traded away. It is a fixed state one that will remain in place until the seven conditions Iran’s demands of the United States are satisfied.  The opening of the Strait of Hormuz is contingent upon these conditions.

This is not a "blockade." It is the "physical manifestation of conditions."

Two oil tankers are ablaze and the statement warns: more will follow, until seven specific conditions are met.

⚔️ The Fourth Channel: A Telephone Line to the UAE

On the evening of November 5, Foreign Minister Araghchi spoke by phone with his Emirati counterpart, Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan. They discussed "recent regional developments" and exchanged views within the framework of "diplomatic efforts aimed at maintaining regional stability."

What is the UAE’s position? It hosts U.S. military assets at the Al Dhafra Air Base. Its F-16s have previously shot down Iranian drones over the beaches of Dubai. It has deployed Israeli-made EL/M-2084 radar systems. It supplies 40% of Israel’s oil. Its port of Fujairah has been struck at least 19 times.

Yet, Araghchi is on the line with them not to issue "protests" or "threats," but to "discuss regional developments" and engage in "diplomatic efforts to maintain regional stability."

What the UAE hears is not "we are going to attack you," but rather "we are open to talks." However, the prerequisite for such talks as outlined in the statement regarding the Strait of Hormuz is the fulfillment of those seven conditions.

The communication channel remains open, but the rules have not changed.  

📜 The Fifth Front: Fadavi, Forty Thousand Names and the Recognition of a Superpower

Brigadier General Ali Fadavi, head of the advisory group to the Commander-in-Chief of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), addressed a crowd in the city of Ardestan, Isfahan Province:

"Internal divisions lead to failure. A unified voice must be our goal; for by maintaining such unity, we cannot be defeated neither in military warfare nor in economic warfare."

"The uniform of the Revolutionary Guard is the most sacred of uniforms. To date, more than 40,000 members of the Revolutionary Guard have been martyred."

"The criminal United States launched a war against us in February 1979, inciting separatist groups from Kurdistan to Gonbad-e Kavus to fight us, and subsequently pushed Saddam to wage an eight-year war against us."

"Our malevolent enemies have continuously waged war against us in the Persian Gulf, instigating a second and third 'imposed war,' and even bringing the criminal Zionist entity into the conflict against us."

"God is the pillar of this system, which is why Iran has become a global superpower. Yet, the world only realized this once the United States entered the fray and was defeated. Only then did the world come to understand that Iran is a superpower."

"Forty thousand members of the Revolutionary Guard." This is not merely a "statistic"; it is the weight of the system itself. An institution that even as early as the eighth month of a war could state that "40,000 members have been martyred" is not merely "managing a crisis." It is upholding a legacy of memory. These 40,000 names serve as the tangible foundation for the very concept of "unity."

"The world only realized Iran is a superpower once the United States entered the war and was defeated." This statement is not an act of "boasting"; it is a redefinition of the war’s outcome. The United States entered the conflict and it did not win. On the battlefield, the U.S. saw 56 MQ-9 drones and 6 MQM-170 drones brought down. Dozens of American vessels were set ablaze in the Strait of Hormuz. U.S. bases across eight different nations were struck by Iranian missiles. And within its own borders, the United States saw its policies rejected by its own people at the ballot box. This is what it means to be "defeated."  The term "superpower" was not something Iran proclaimed for itself; it was a status declared by the outcome of the conflict.

🔻 Five threads, one single logic

The Kremlin: A letter from the Leader was delivered personally to Putin, in the presence of the head of the GRU and a foreign policy aide. This was no mere formality, it was an alignment of positions.

Qeshm: A sixth MQM-170 drone was seized via electronic warfare. It wasn’t shot down; it was "landed" effectively commandeering the enemy’s own eyes.

Strait of Hormuz: Two oil tankers are ablaze. The statement is clear: the Strait will not reopen until seven specific conditions are met. The rules have been established.

Abu Dhabi: The communication lines remain open, yet the rules remain unchanged. The prerequisites for any dialogue are those laid out in the statement regarding the Strait of Hormuz.

Ardestan: Forty thousand names united. A superpower. The world will only truly understand this once the United States has been defeated.

Five threads, one consistent approach: every action taken by the enemy whether military strikes, economic blockades, diplomatic pressure, or public accusations serves only to confirm Iran’s strategic resolve.

The statement concerning the Strait of Hormuz serves as the most precise footnote to the day’s events: the Strait will not reopen until seven conditions are satisfied. This is not a matter of "we might consider it" or "we are open to talks," it is a firm "until seven conditions are met."

The phone lines are open. The tankers are burning. Control of the drones has been seized. And in the Kremlin, a letter has been received.

Long live Iran. Long live the Resistance. Long live the Axis of Resistance.

text:
WHAT THE MIDTERM ELECTIONS MEAN FOR CRYPTO

Bitcoin quickly recovered after the U.S. midterm elections.

After Democrats won control of Congress, Bitcoin fell below $76,000. Investors feared that new crypto laws might face delays.

However, Bitcoin bounced above $80,500 by Wednesday, gaining over 6%. It later fell back but remained around $76,000.

Bitcoin is also near an important support level and a possible 80-day cycle low predicted by analyst Juan Villaverde.

Meanwhile, Bitcoin and Ethereum ETFs attracted $128 million in new money on Wednesday. This is encouraging after several days of investors withdrawing funds.

But one good day does not mean a new bull market has started.

Elections May Create Short-Term Fear

Markets often react strongly to political news.

Bitcoin’s quick recovery shows that elections can cause sharp price movements without changing the long-term value of good crypto projects.

Historically, Bitcoin gained an average of about 54% in the 12 months following the last three midterm elections.

However, these gains were also linked to Bitcoin’s market cycles. We cannot say elections caused them or guarantee that history will repeat itself.

Interest rates, ETF investments, and demand from large investors may matter more than political events.

Crypto Laws Could Face Delays

Crypto supporters reportedly spent $200 million helping elect candidates who support digital assets.

However, some important candidates lost. In Ohio, Sherrod Brown, known for supporting stricter crypto regulations, won his Senate race.

Still, crypto support is not limited to one political party. Some Democrats support clear rules that allow the industry to grow, while others want stronger protections against fraud.

The same differences exist among Republicans.

The new Congress could bring more debate, delays, and changes to crypto laws. But fresh lawmakers may also bring better ideas.

Two Important Crypto Laws to Watch

1. The CLARITY Act

This bill aims to clarify which government agencies regulate crypto.

Today, the SEC and CFTC both have roles in the market, but their responsibilities are not always clear.

The bill could give crypto businesses clearer rules.

It failed to advance in the Senate in September, mainly because lawmakers disagreed about ethics and conflicts of interest.

A new agreement is still possible if both parties work together.

2. The GENIUS Act

This law has already passed. It establishes rules for payment stablecoins, which are digital currencies designed to maintain a stable value, often $1.

Government agencies must now put the rules into practice.

The new Congress may debate who can issue stablecoins, how they should be backed, and what banks can offer.

What Does This Mean for Your Crypto?

Bitcoin’s basic supply and network rules are unlikely to change because of Congress.

Ethereum and other blockchain projects could face greater changes.

Clear regulations may encourage businesses to build new applications and services.

However, stricter rules could increase costs or limit certain products.

Crypto exchanges, stablecoin companies, and DeFi projects may also face new challenges.

This could create a bigger difference between strong projects and weak ones.

For investors, this is an important opportunity to identify quality projects.

YOUR NEXT MOVE

The next two years may bring plenty of uncertainty and debate about crypto.

Instead of worrying about every political headline:

- Review your crypto holdings and their long-term value.
- Keep some cash ready for attractive buying opportunities.
- Watch the CLARITY Act and stablecoin regulations.
- Focus on projects with real purpose, strong fundamentals, and sustainable growth.

Crypto has survived many political changes.

The election may change the road ahead, but it has not ended crypto’s journey.

Stay patient, stay prepared, and keep your eyes on the bigger picture.
