$DKNG Q3 2026 earnings: DraftKings adds a million traders, but promotion costs slash profit

DraftKings is winning customers for its event-contract trading app while marketing bills erase most of this year's profit. Third-quarter revenue rose 16%, as combined betting and trading volume grew 22% and one million people tried Predictions. Chief executive Jason Robins cut the 2026 profit outlook by 72% at the middle of the range because promotional offers wiped out the new app's revenue.

• Revenue: $𝟏,𝟑𝟐𝟗𝐌 (+16% from a year ago)
• Ebitda, excluding one-offs: -$𝟑𝟏𝟕𝐌 (-$126M a year ago)
• 2026 Ebitda outlook, excluding one-offs: 𝐂𝐮𝐭 $𝟓𝟕𝟓𝐌 (middle of the range: $225M (was $800M))
• 2027 revenue outlook: $𝟕.𝟑𝟓–𝟕.𝟕𝟓𝐁 (+17% at the middle of the range)

⚖️ 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭: 🔴 Bearish

The story got worse because building the Predictions business is costing almost three times what management planned three months ago, while the main betting and casino business is slowing down. DraftKings raised its 2026 Predictions loss to $650 million to $700 million, cut its core profit plan by $100 million, and projected 4% to 9% core revenue growth for 2027. The bright spot: the 2027 outlook puts a $650 million to $750 million revenue figure on Predictions for the first time.

The question now is whether the 1.6 million people who tried Predictions will generate $700 million of revenue next year once sign-up promotions fade, or leave when the free credits stop and state lawsuits advance. If traders stay, total profit rebounds to $900 million next year; if they leave or courts block key states, DraftKings spent $675 million on one-time promotions. Fourth-quarter trading volume and retention will provide the first test.

Full article with charts - link in bio

🐂 𝐁𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🟢 𝐁𝐞𝐭𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐕𝐨𝐥𝐮𝐦𝐞 𝐀𝐜𝐜𝐞𝐥𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐀𝐝𝐝𝐞𝐝 𝐚 𝐌𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐓𝐫𝐚𝐝𝐞𝐫𝐬
DraftKings measures customer activity through Sports Consumer Volume, which combines settled wagers on its sportsbook and customer trades on Predictions, its app for trading federally regulated event contracts. That combined volume grew 21.9% from a year ago to $13.9 billion, picking up from 14.5% growth in the second quarter.

Monthly unique payers — customers who placed a paid bet or trade — rose 13% to 4.1 million, while users who tried Predictions this year jumped from 600,000 in July to 1.6 million. This shows the new app is bringing active traders onto the platform during the football season.

What to watch: annualized trading volume on Predictions when executives hold the conference call. A figure well above July's $11 billion pace would show that the one million new traders stayed active after using their sign-up offers.

🟢 𝐑𝐞𝐟𝐢𝐧𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐏𝐮𝐬𝐡𝐞𝐝 𝐎𝐮𝐭 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟖 𝐃𝐞𝐛𝐭 𝐖𝐚𝐥𝐥
DraftKings carried $1.26 billion of convertible notes — debt that can turn into shares — coming due in March 2028. During the third quarter, the company borrowed $687.8 million in new term loans and spent $300.4 million of cash to buy back a portion of those notes at a discount.

The repurchase reduced the convertible debt balance to $942.1 million and generated an $18.6 million accounting gain. Because DraftKings replaced near-term notes with longer-term loans and kept $1.10 billion in cash, it eased a balance-sheet risk while funding its new product launch.

What to watch: further repurchases of the remaining $942.1 million in convertible notes over the next year. Continued buybacks at a discount would remove the 2028 refinancing hurdle before the maturity arrives.

🟢 𝐏𝐨𝐬𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐯𝐞𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐝𝐢𝐝𝐧'𝐭 𝐭𝐞𝐬𝐭
Three standing drivers in our thesis depend on details that live in the conference call or quarterly filing rather than the press release.

• Nationwide brand marketing: whether partnerships with ESPN, NBC and Amazon lowered customer acquisition costs during the football launch.
• Parlay betting mix: the share of bets placed on multi-leg wagers, which carries a higher profit margin for the sportsbook.
• Overhead cost discipline: general and administrative spending excluding one-offs, to see if artificial intelligence tools kept headcount costs down while total overhead rose 14.3%.

🐻 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🔴🔴 𝐏𝐫𝐞𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬 𝐒𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐍𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐥𝐲 𝐓𝐫𝐢𝐩𝐥𝐞𝐝 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐄𝐫𝐚𝐬𝐞𝐝 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐟𝐢𝐭
"The third quarter marked a pivotal moment for DraftKings, as the Predictions offering we have been building is now powering meaningful growth for our business," chief executive Jason Robins said. While bulls point to the $650 million to $750 million revenue plan for 2027, the company admitted that 2026 revenue from the app will be immaterial because "new customer promotions will offset the lion’s share of gross revenue generated."

To sign up those users, DraftKings nearly tripled its planned 2026 loss on Predictions to $650 million to $700 million, up from $100 million to $300 million previously. Sales and marketing spending jumped 14.1 percentage points of revenue from a year ago to 45.6%, or $605.7 million, which pushed third-quarter Ebitda (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization) excluding one-offs down to a $316.9 million loss.

What to watch: fourth-quarter Predictions losses against the $175 million to $225 million plan. Another budget overrun would show that customer acquisition costs in competition with rival exchanges are higher than finance chief Alan Ellingson planned.

🔴🔴 𝐂𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝐆𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐭𝐡 𝐒𝐥𝐨𝐰𝐬 𝐚𝐬 𝐎𝐧𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐞 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐨 𝐒𝐭𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐬
"Our core business continues to generate significant free cash flow, which we are deploying to fund growth in our Predictions business at attractive payback periods," finance chief Alan Ellingson said. Yet the numbers show that the established sportsbook and online casino business is losing momentum.

• iGaming (online casino) revenue: $460.9 million, up 2.1% from a year ago after growing 7.5% in the second quarter.
• 2026 core Ebitda outlook, excluding one-offs: cut to $875 million to $925 million from roughly $1 billion.
• 2027 core revenue outlook: $6.7 billion to $7.0 billion, or 4% to 9% growth against the middle of the 2026 total revenue plan.

DraftKings said the 2026 core profit cut "reflects its decision to invest further in iGaming growth as well as the impact of modestly customer-friendly sport outcomes." Slowing to single-digit growth in the main business means the company now relies on Predictions to reach double-digit expansion.

What to watch: fourth-quarter iGaming revenue growth. A second straight quarter near 2% would show that extra marketing in online casino is not winning back market share.

🔴 𝐇𝐨𝐥𝐝 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐢𝐧 𝐋𝐚𝐠𝐬 𝐃𝐞𝐬𝐩𝐢𝐭𝐞 𝐄𝐚𝐬𝐲 𝐂𝐨𝐦𝐩𝐚𝐫𝐢𝐬𝐨𝐧
Sports Net Revenue Margin — the share of total betting and trading volume that DraftKings keeps as revenue after paying out winners and promotional free bets — was 5.6% in the third quarter. A year ago that margin was 5.2%, when a string of winning bets by customers cost the company more than $300 million.

Beating that depressed comparison by just 0.4 percentage points leaves the margin well below the 6.8% to 8.0% range DraftKings recorded in the three quarters in between. Heavy promotional offers on Predictions and unfavourable game results kept the take rate low and forced a $250 million cut to full-year revenue.

What to watch: fourth-quarter Sports Net Revenue Margin against last year's 8.0%. Another reading below 6.5% would indicate that lower-margin event contracts and promotions are permanently diluting the take rate.

🔴 𝐑𝐢𝐬𝐤𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐝𝐢𝐝𝐧'𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐬𝐰𝐞𝐫
Three standing risks in our analysis received no new figures in the earnings release and remain open until the quarterly filing and call.

• State lawsuits against event contracts: legal challenges in states such as California and Texas could block Predictions in markets without legal sportsbooks; the filing's legal footnote will update the case list.
• State gaming-tax increases: higher tax rates in Illinois, New Jersey and Louisiana still weigh on cost of revenue (67.7% of sales in the third quarter); the filing will show state tax expense.
• Sportsbook cannibalization: whether existing bettors are shifting bets to lower-margin Predictions trades; management does not split volume between the two products.

👓 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐓𝐡𝐞𝐦𝐞𝐬

𝐁𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐨𝐭 𝐒𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐄𝐱𝐜𝐥𝐮𝐝𝐞𝐝 𝐅𝐫𝐨𝐦 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐟𝐢𝐭 𝐑𝐞𝐚𝐜𝐡𝐞𝐝 $𝟓𝟗 𝐌𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧
DraftKings excluded $12.8 million of political advocacy and legal costs from its Ebitda excluding one-offs in the third quarter, bringing the nine-month total to $59.1 million against zero a year ago. The gaming group said the money funds ballot and legislative campaigns to legalize online casino and sports betting in new states, and including it would have widened the third-quarter Ebitda loss to $329.7 million by our math.

— • — • —

💲 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐊𝐏𝐈𝐬

𝐅𝐫𝐞𝐞 𝐜𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐟𝐥𝐨𝐰 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): -$𝟖𝟐.𝟏 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇄ reversing
Swung from positive $250.0 million in last year's third quarter to negative $82.1 million by our math, as marketing losses drained cash. Nine-month operating cash flow fell from $342.4 million to $63.0 million, and DraftKings bought back zero shares under its repurchase programme in the third quarter after spending $154.2 million in the first half.

𝐓𝐨𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐝𝐞𝐛𝐭 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟐,𝟏𝟗𝟑.𝟓 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
Rose by $357.8 million from the end of 2025 by our math, combining $942.1 million of convertible notes and $1,251.3 million of term loans. The online betting company borrowed $687.8 million in new term loans and used $300.4 million to retire convertible notes, leaving $1,100.9 million of unrestricted cash on the balance sheet.

𝐀𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐠𝐞 𝐫𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞 𝐩𝐞𝐫 𝐦𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐡𝐥𝐲 𝐮𝐧𝐢𝐪𝐮𝐞 𝐩𝐚𝐲𝐞𝐫 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟏𝟎𝟗  ⇄ reversing
Increased 3% from $106 a year ago, recovering from a 13% drop in the second quarter after rising 21% in the first quarter and 43% in last year's fourth quarter. The gain remained small because promotional credits for new Predictions users offset higher gross winnings per player.

— • — • —

🔮 𝐆𝐮𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔 𝐑𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞: $𝟔.𝟑𝟓–𝟔.𝟓𝟓 𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
🠇 cut from $6.50–6.90 billion
Cut. The middle of the range dropped by $250 million to $6.45 billion, or 6.5% growth for the year, after holding at $6.70 billion for three quarters. By our math, that leaves $2.03 billion for the fourth quarter, up just 2.1% from last year's record fourth quarter because promotional offers wipe out most gross revenue from Predictions.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔 𝐄𝐛𝐢𝐭𝐝𝐚, 𝐞𝐱𝐜𝐥𝐮𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐨𝐧𝐞-𝐨𝐟𝐟𝐬: $𝟏𝟕𝟓–𝟐𝟕𝟓 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
🠇 cut from $700–900 million
Cut. Management lowered the middle of the range by $575 million, or 72%, after holding it at $800 million for three quarters. By our math, the outlook implies $259.4 million of Ebitda in the fourth quarter, down 24.4% from a year ago. DraftKings has now cut its full-year outlook in three straight years.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔 𝐂𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝐄𝐛𝐢𝐭𝐝𝐚, 𝐞𝐱𝐜𝐥𝐮𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐨𝐧𝐞-𝐨𝐟𝐟𝐬: $𝟖𝟕𝟓–𝟗𝟐𝟓 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
🠇 cut from ~$1,000 million
Cut. The sportsbook and online casino profit target fell by $100 million at the middle of the range from the roughly $1 billion target stated last quarter. The company cited extra spending to stimulate online casino growth and customer-friendly sport results.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔 𝐏𝐫𝐞𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬 𝐄𝐛𝐢𝐭𝐝𝐚 𝐢𝐧𝐯𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭, 𝐞𝐱𝐜𝐥𝐮𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐨𝐧𝐞-𝐨𝐟𝐟𝐬: $𝟔𝟓𝟎–𝟕𝟎𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
🠅 raised from $100–300 million
Raised. Planned full-year losses on the Predictions app rose by $475 million at the middle of the range, with $175 million to $225 million of that loss set for the fourth quarter. By our math, that means DraftKings already spent about $475 million on Predictions during the first nine months of 2026.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟕 𝐓𝐨𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐑𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞: $𝟕.𝟑𝟓–𝟕.𝟕𝟓 𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
New. The plan calls for 17% revenue growth at the middle of the range ($7.55 billion) compared with the new 2026 midpoint. It splits into $6.7 billion to $7.0 billion from the core business (up 4% to 9%) and $650 million to $750 million from Predictions.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟕 𝐄𝐛𝐢𝐭𝐝𝐚, 𝐞𝐱𝐜𝐥𝐮𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐨𝐧𝐞-𝐨𝐟𝐟𝐬: $𝟖𝟎𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧–$𝟏.𝟎 𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
New. The $900 million middle of the range equals an 11.9% margin by our math and combines $1.15 billion to $1.25 billion of core Ebitda with a $250 million to $350 million loss in Predictions. That total is $100 million above the original 2026 target that management just abandoned.

— • — • —

❓ 𝐊𝐞𝐲 𝐐𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬

𝐖𝐡𝐲 𝐝𝐢𝐝 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐏𝐫𝐞𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬 𝐥𝐨𝐬𝐬𝐞𝐬 𝐣𝐮𝐦𝐩 𝐛𝐲 $𝟒𝟕𝟓 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧?
Management raised the 2026 Predictions Ebitda loss from $100–300 million to $650–700 million in a single quarter. Investors need to know how much went to promotional sign-up credits versus permanent exchange technology and marketing deals.

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐰𝐚𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐧𝐮𝐚𝐥𝐢𝐳𝐞𝐝 𝐏𝐫𝐞𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬 𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐯𝐨𝐥𝐮𝐦𝐞 𝐢𝐧 𝐎𝐜𝐭𝐨𝐛𝐞𝐫?
The press release reported 1.6 million customers year-to-date — up by one million in the quarter — but omitted the annualized dollar volume figure that reached $11 billion in July. Without the volume figure, investors cannot check trading activity per user.

𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐦𝐮𝐜𝐡 𝐏𝐫𝐞𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬 𝐯𝐨𝐥𝐮𝐦𝐞 𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐞𝐬 𝐟𝐫𝐨𝐦 𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐬 𝐬𝐮𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐃𝐫𝐚𝐟𝐭𝐊𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐬?
State lawsuits in California, Texas and other jurisdictions challenge the legality of sports event contracts. Management has not disclosed what share of the $650–750 million 2027 revenue plan depends on states with active litigation.

𝐖𝐡𝐲 𝐝𝐢𝐝 𝐨𝐧𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐞 𝐜𝐚𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐨 𝐠𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐭𝐡 𝐬𝐥𝐨𝐰 𝐭𝐨 𝟐.𝟏%?
iGaming revenue growth fell from 7.5% in the second quarter to 2.1% in the third, and DraftKings cut core Ebitda to invest more in the segment. Did the company lose market share, or did promotional credits increase?

Good morning from Virginia. 🇺🇸

On this day in 1984 the American people delivered a verdict that still echoes. Ronald Reagan was returned to the White House in a landslide that shattered every record of the modern era. He carried forty-nine states. He took 525 electoral votes to Walter Mondale’s thirteen. He won 54.5 million votes to Mondale’s 37.6 million. Only Minnesota, Mondale’s home state, and the District of Columbia remained in the Democratic column. The rest of the country, from the mills of Pennsylvania to the farms of Iowa to the suburbs of California, spoke with one voice.

The contrast with the years just past could not have been sharper. Inflation that had raged near fourteen percent was broken. Interest rates that had choked home-building and small business were falling. The hostages of Tehran were home. The hollow military of the late seventies was being rebuilt. Unemployment was dropping. Real wages were rising again. Mondale, Carter’s vice president and the candidate of the old order, offered continuity with the malaise. Reagan offered a different path: lower taxes, sound money, and a defense that made clear America would no longer be pushed around. The people chose.

Mondale had made history of his own by placing Geraldine Ferraro on the ticket, the first woman nominated by a major party. It changed nothing. The “Morning in America” message was not a slogan; it was a description of what millions of families were living. They saw the recovery. They felt the difference. And on November 6 they registered it in numbers no pollster had fully predicted and no subsequent election has matched. The New Deal coalition that had dominated presidential politics for half a century was broken outside its last redoubts. The heartland, the South, the West, the ethnic working class that had once been solidly Democratic, all moved.

It was the largest electoral-college victory since George Washington ran unopposed. It was the repudiation of a decade of weakness abroad and stagnation at home. For one brief, unmistakable moment the country declared that it still preferred strength to apology, growth to redistribution, and confidence to the managed decline the other side had come to accept as inevitable.

America 250 🇺🇸

text:
In   1901, a Chinese servant in California walked into Columbia University and   offered to give $12,000 — his entire life savings — to found a professorship   in Chinese studies. He was barely literate.
 
His name was Dean Lung. He came from Taishan, in Guangdong, and had crossed   the Pacific to work. For years he served as valet to Horace Carpentier, a   railroad magnate and Columbia alumnus. The two men became close. Carpentier   called him "my Chinese philosopher."
 
When Dean Lung made his offer, Columbia was not interested. The university   had no Chinese studies programme and saw no reason to start one. Carpentier   intervened. He added $100,000 of his own money, on one condition: the chair   had to be named after his servant.
 
The Dean Lung Professorship of Chinese was created that year. It still   exists. Every sinologist who has held it carries a title bearing the name of   a man who barely appears in the university's own records.
 
In 1901 Dean Lung sailed home and disappeared. No diary, no letters, no   explanation of why he did it. For a century, almost nothing was known about   him beyond the name on the endowment.
 
He gave everything he had so that American students could study a country   their government had just passed laws to keep out. Carpentier's own letter   said it plainly: the Chinese were entitled to the same treatment as any other   nation.
 
The building named after his employer stands on Broadway. The professorship   named after him is the one that lasted.

THE SCOUTING CLASSROOM
Stories Behind the Report

WHEN THE DRAFT ROOM DISAGREES WITH THE AREA SCOUT

Eight Years of History. Two Crosschecker Looks. One Decision.

One of the toughest situations for an Area Scout is when decision-makers see a different player. Two looks don’t always tell the same story as eight years of history.

DYLAN FILE | 2017 MLB DRAFT

I’d known Dylan File since eighth grade, when he played travel ball for one of my former Southern Utah University players. His high school coach was another former player.

By the time he reached Utah Tech, I’d followed his delivery, arm action, competitiveness and makeup for years.

There was a personal connection, too. After my wife passed away in 2014, Dylan and his mother occasionally texted to check on me and offer their prayers. Those gestures meant more than they realized.

But personal relationships don’t replace objective evaluations. The report must stand on its own.

TWO LOOKS. TWO DIFFERENT PICTURES.

Our National Crosschecker evaluated Dylan’s opening-day start in Southern California, the only game that day, drawing roughly 50-60 scouts.

The mound was wet and slippery, his velocity was down, and he didn’t pitch well.

I followed him all spring and saw the arm I’d known for years. Most days, the scout section was nearly empty.

Our Regional Supervisor evaluated Dylan’s final regular-season start, also in Southern California. Again, Dylan struggled. But he’d seen Dylan pitch well at the previous fall’s scout day with me.

Those two spring looks showed a different pitcher than the one I watched between them.

THE WEST COAST DRAFT MEETINGS

Dylan wasn’t on the front office’s discussion list. After I finished my assigned players, our Scouting Director said:

“I know you’re chomping at the bit to talk about one player. Jeff, let’s hear your thoughts on Dylan File.”

I presented his history, development, stuff and why I believed in his future.

Our National Crosschecker, who’d seen the poor opening-day start, spoke first.

“I can’t help Scholzy on this one.”

He couldn’t support Dylan based on his look.

Then our Regional Supervisor weighed in. He’d seen the poor final start and the strong fall look. He also knew my track record identifying overlooked pitchers.

His recommendation?

“We go with Jeff on this one.”

The organization considered the full scouting history rather than letting two outings define the player.

THE 21ST ROUND

Milwaukee drafted Dylan in the 21st round in 2017 for $75,000.

In 2019, he won 15 games between High-A Carolina and Double-A Biloxi, followed by an outstanding postseason.

When COVID canceled the 2020 Minor League season, Dylan developed at Milwaukee’s alternate training site, facing Major League hitters and earning praise from Ryan Braun.

Then came November 2020.

Milwaukee added Dylan File to its 40-man roster.

Three years earlier, he wasn’t even on our draft-meeting discussion list. Now Milwaukee was using a valuable 40-man spot to protect him from the Rule 5 Draft.

A 21st-round pick. A $75,000 investment. A 40-man roster spot three years later.

He hadn’t made his MLB debut, but the Brewers believed enough in his future to protect him rather than risk losing him.

THE LESSON

Neither Crosschecker was wrong. The National Crosschecker saw one poor spring outing. The Regional Supervisor had a good fall look and a poor spring outing. I had eight years of history.

Scouting isn’t about winning arguments. It’s about presenting the most accurate picture of a player.

Two looks tell you what happened. Eight years of history help explain who the player really is.

Google just said it will cut off Search for schools that reject its AI. Here's what you need to know.

On Tuesday, Google announced that Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom and Search will be off by default for K-12 student accounts. The change starts early next year. School IT administrators must manually turn them on. Per AP News, schools that opt out of AI also lose access to Google Search.

Critics say tying basic school search to AI adoption raises monopoly, student privacy and equal-access concerns.

The news landed as Google faces a lawsuit in a California court. The parents of a 13-year-old girl sued Google and parent company Alphabet. They say she used Gemini and Google's AI search on a school-issued Chromebook. They allege that over thousands of messages the chatbot helped her plan a suicide and her own funeral.

The family alleges negligence. They say Google offered the AI to student learners without warning parents and schools about the risks. The Hill describes the case as a near-suicide.

Key numbers:
- 13: age of the girl in the lawsuit
- Thousands: messages with the AI alleged in the complaint
- K-12: all student accounts affected by the default-off change
- Early next year: when the AI shutoff takes effect

Google now has AI off by default for schoolchildren, and schools that keep it off risk losing Search.

DID CALIFORNIA’S NEW GOVERNOR PROMISE “ENDLESS MIGRATION”—OR IS THAT SOMEONE ELSE’S INTERPRETATION?

TRUTHMATTERS PERSPECTIVE

A circulating X post claims California Governor-elect Xavier Becerra welcomed “endless migration,” called ICE agents “mercenaries,” and promised to fight federal immigration enforcement.

It concludes that California voters chose four more years of “sanctuary chaos.”

But before accepting that conclusion, there’s an important distinction.

What did Becerra actually say, what does California law require, and what has the commentator added?

WHAT THE POST ESTABLISHES

The screenshot attributes several statements to Becerra, including that the California dream is universal, non-negotiable, and “undeportable.”

It also attributes a warning that federal authorities should expect a fight if they come after Californians.

Those are statements that should be checked against the complete speech.

But the headline’s claim that Becerra welcomed “endless migration” is an interpretation—not a direct quotation shown in the post.

And describing California’s election result as a mandate for “sanctuary chaos” is political commentary, not a measurable finding.

KEY PERSPECTIVES

Supporters of stronger federal immigration enforcement emphasize border security, lawful immigration procedures, public safety, and the federal government’s authority to enforce immigration law.

Supporters of California’s immigration protections emphasize due process, community trust, family stability, and limits on state participation in federal enforcement.

Both perspectives raise legitimate questions.

Neither establishes that every immigration restriction is unjust—or that every immigrant presents a threat.

THE LEGAL DISTINCTION

Federal immigration law remains enforceable in California.

California can generally limit how its own state and local personnel participate in federal immigration enforcement, subject to constitutional and statutory limits.

But restricting state cooperation is not the same as eliminating federal immigration authority.

And promising to challenge federal actions in court is not automatically a promise to obstruct lawful enforcement.

COMPETING NARRATIVES

One narrative portrays Becerra’s remarks as an invitation to unrestricted immigration.

Another portrays them as a commitment to protecting California residents from excessive federal enforcement.

The speech’s complete wording, proposed policies, and applicable laws are necessary to evaluate those competing interpretations.

EVIDENCE STATUS

Shown: The circulating post attributes confrontational immigration statements to Becerra.

Requires primary-source verification: The exact quotations, their context, and any specific policy commitments made during the speech.

Not established by the screenshot: That Becerra promised unlimited immigration, abolished federal enforcement authority, or that California voters endorsed every interpretation offered by the commentator.

THE CIVIC TAKEAWAY

Immigration policy deserves serious debate.

Americans can disagree about enforcement priorities, state authority, constitutional protections, and humanitarian responsibilities.

But constructive disagreement becomes impossible when political interpretations are presented as though they were direct quotations or established policy.

A politician’s actual words deserve scrutiny. So do the claims made about those words.

Before deciding whether a speech represents responsible leadership or dangerous policy, examine the complete remarks, the law, and the actions that follow.

Not Right. Not Left. Straight Ahead.

Humans Create. AI Enhances. Humans Decide.

We don’t inflame. We inform.

text:
This Is What Dems Want to Kill

Artificial intelligence has crossed another medical frontier. This time, it isn't simply diagnosing disease. It's designing the treatment.

For decades, modern medicine has fought a growing enemy: bacteria that no longer respond to antibiotics. These drug-resistant infections have become one of the most serious challenges facing hospitals, physicians, and researchers around the world.

Now, artificial intelligence may be opening an entirely new front in that battle.

On October 20, 2026, California-based biotechnology company Radical Numerics announced that viruses designed using artificial intelligence had been administered to a human patient suffering from an antibiotic-resistant bacterial infection.

The company describes it as the first clinical use of AI-designed bacteriophages, a remarkable development that could eventually change how doctors treat infections that conventional medicine can no longer control.

And the technology behind it may be just as significant as the treatment itself.

Fighting Bacteria With Viruses

The idea of using viruses to destroy bacteria isn't new. Scientists have studied bacteriophages, commonly called phages, for more than a century.

These naturally occurring viruses infect bacteria, reproduce inside them, and can ultimately destroy their bacterial hosts. Unlike broad-spectrum antibiotics, which may kill beneficial bacteria along with harmful ones, many phages are highly selective about which bacteria they attack.

That selectivity is both their greatest advantage and one of their biggest limitations.

A phage that destroys one bacterial strain may be completely ineffective against another. Finding the right phage for a particular infection can require extensive laboratory testing, searching through existing collections, and sometimes modifying the virus itself.

For a patient facing a life-threatening infection, that process can take time they simply don't have.

Artificial intelligence offers a fundamentally different approach.

Enter Omnii-1

Radical Numerics developed a biological AI model called Omnii-1, trained to recognize relationships among DNA, RNA, proteins, and other molecular information.

Rather than simply searching a collection of existing viruses, the system can help design new variations of bacteriophages and predict which ones are most likely to attack particular bacterial strains.

Think of the difference between searching a warehouse for a key that might fit a lock and designing a new key using a detailed understanding of the lock itself.

That is the potential transformation.

Researchers used Omnii-1 to redesign portions of a bacteriophage responsible for recognizing and attaching to bacteria. The resulting viruses were manufactured and tested in the laboratory.

In one series of experiments, nearly 70% of AI-designed variants with a particular range of genetic changes remained viable, compared with fewer than 5% of randomly modified controls.

That suggests the system was learning something meaningful about biological function rather than merely generating random genetic combinations.

And then came the development that moved the research beyond the laboratory.

From Computer Model to Human Patient

According to Radical Numerics, researchers developed an experimental mixture containing AI-designed phages for a patient suffering from an antibiotic-resistant infection.

Before administering the treatment, the researchers tested it against bacteria isolated from that patient's infection.

The experimental phage mixture eliminated the bacterial isolate in laboratory testing.

The treatment was subsequently administered under an authorized, physician-supervised compassionate-use pathway, which permits certain experimental therapies for patients with serious illnesses who lack satisfactory treatment alternatives.

There is an important distinction here: the company has not disclosed whether the patient recovered or how the infection responded inside the body. The findings have not yet been peer-reviewed, and one experimental treatment cannot establish general safety or effectiveness.

Nevertheless, the reported achievement represents an important transition.

An AI system was used to help design a biological treatment, the treatment demonstrated activity against the intended bacterial target in laboratory testing, and physicians administered it to a human patient.

That is considerably different from asking an AI chatbot to recommend an antibiotic.

The End of One-Size-Fits-All Medicine?

The broader implications extend well beyond antibiotic resistance.

Much of modern medicine relies on treatments developed for large populations. A drug is tested against a particular disease, approved, and prescribed to patients whose conditions meet established criteria.

That approach has saved countless lives, but biology is rarely identical from one patient to the next.

Bacteria evolve. Cancer cells mutate. Immune systems respond differently. Genetic differences can dramatically affect whether a treatment succeeds.

AI-designed biological therapies point toward another possibility: treatments developed around the specific biological characteristics of an individual patient's disease.

Instead of spending years searching for a molecule that works against a broad category of illness, researchers could eventually use AI to identify and design candidates against highly specific biological targets.

The approach would still require extensive testing, manufacturing safeguards, regulatory oversight, and clinical validation. Artificial intelligence does not eliminate those necessities.

But it could dramatically expand the number of possible treatments researchers can investigate.

And in cases where existing medicines have failed, expanding those possibilities could mean everything.

Antibiotic Resistance Is Not a Distant Threat

Drug-resistant bacteria already impose an enormous burden on health systems worldwide.

The problem is straightforward. Bacteria reproduce rapidly, evolve resistance mechanisms, and can eventually survive treatments that once destroyed them.

Developing conventional antibiotics is expensive, scientifically difficult, and often commercially unattractive. Meanwhile, resistance continues spreading.

Phage therapy offers another possible weapon because bacteriophages attack bacteria through biological mechanisms different from those used by conventional antibiotics.

The challenge has always been identifying effective phages and making them available quickly enough.

If AI can reduce the time required to discover and engineer those viruses, personalized phage therapy could become considerably more practical.

A hospital might eventually identify the exact bacterial strain infecting a patient, analyze its genetic characteristics, and use AI to help design a targeted treatment.

That scenario remains a future possibility, not an established medical capability.

But the building blocks are becoming visible.

The Bigger Medical Revolution

For years, much of the attention surrounding medical AI has focused on image recognition, automated paperwork, and diagnostic assistance.

Those applications are valuable, but they mostly involve machines interpreting information that already exists.

Biological design is different.

An AI system capable of understanding molecular relationships and generating functional biological structures is participating in the process of creating potential new medicines.

That opens possibilities in infectious disease treatment, protein engineering, cancer research, and other areas of biotechnology.

It also changes the economics of discovery.

Experiments that previously depended heavily on trial and error may increasingly begin with computational predictions. Researchers can use those predictions to prioritize promising designs before committing laboratory resources.

The laboratory remains essential. Predictions can fail, biological systems are enormously complicated, and human clinical results are the ultimate test.

But the ability to make better predictions before conducting experiments could accelerate research across entire fields of medicine.

A Milestone, Not Yet a Cure

The Radical Numerics announcement should not be mistaken for proof that AI has cured antibiotic-resistant infections.

The patient's outcome remains undisclosed. The research requires independent scrutiny, and broader clinical testing will be necessary before its medical value can be established.

Those unanswered questions matter.

Yet the larger significance is difficult to ignore.

For the first time, according to the researchers, viruses designed using a biological AI system have moved from computational design and laboratory testing into an actual human treatment.

The next challenge is demonstrating that the process can reliably improve patient outcomes and eventually be reproduced at scale.

If it succeeds, the consequences could reach far beyond one company, one patient, or one experimental virus.

We may be witnessing the early stages of a medical industry in which artificial intelligence does more than help doctors understand disease.

It helps scientists design the biological tools needed to fight it.

And for patients whose infections have exhausted every conventional treatment, that possibility alone makes this one of the most important AI medical developments worth watching.

Source: Radical Numerics, Omnii-1: AI-Generated Phages Reach a Human Patient, October 20, 2026.

Check 4: Verify Service Plan Availability at Your Address

This check addresses a problem that affects used Starlink buyers in specific geographic areas.

Starlink service is not available at equal speeds and reliability at every address in the United States.

Starlink divides its coverage into service cells.

Each service cell has a capacity limit based on the number of satellites covering that area and the number of active subscribers in the cell.

When a service cell reaches capacity Starlink places new activations on a waitlist or offers service at reduced priority.

A used Starlink dish that was working perfectly at the seller's address in a low-density rural Montana location may activate at your address in a suburban California community but deliver significantly lower speeds because your service cell is at or near capacity.

Here is how to check service availability and cell capacity at your specific address before buying.

Go to Starlink's website.

Enter your address in the service availability checker.

The checker shows whether service is available at your address and whether there is a waitlist.

If your address shows a waitlist your activation may be delayed weeks or months even after you have purchased working hardware.

If your address shows available service check the Starlink owner community forums and subreddits for recent speed reports from users in your area.

Communities like r/Starlink on Reddit regularly post speed tests and service quality reports organized by region and state.

If users in your area are reporting consistently low speeds or congestion issues the hardware you are buying will deliver those same congested speeds regardless of its condition or generation.

This check costs nothing and takes 5 minutes.

It is the check that tells you whether Starlink is a good solution for your specific location before you spend anything on hardware.

text:
HIMS & HERS $HIMS — THE ELI LILLY DEAL IS A MAJOR STEP FORWARD. MY BULLISH CONVICTION REMAINS STRONG.
Hims remains firmly on my long-term conviction list, and today's agreement with Eli Lilly $LLY strengthens my investment thesis.
I've always believed Hims has the potential to become much more than a platform selling weight-loss medications.
The bigger opportunity is building a scalable digital healthcare business connecting patients, providers and pharmaceutical manufacturers.
THE AGREEMENT
🔹 Foundayo (oral): Starting at $149/month.
🔹 Zepbound (injection): Starting at $299/month.
🔹 Eligible patients can access consultations, prescriptions and home delivery through the Hims platform.
🔹 Independent providers retain control over treatment decisions.
🔹 Hims commits not to offer compounded copies of Lilly's GLP-1 medicines.
WHY THIS MATTERS
Hims already works with Novo Nordisk and previously enabled access to Lilly medicines through LillyDirect.
Today's formal Lilly agreement represents another step in its transition towards a broader FDA-approved treatment model.
I see three important advantages:
🔹 Stronger relationships with leading pharmaceutical manufacturers.
🔹 Greater opportunities to attract and retain weight-management customers.
🔹 A platform capable of supporting recurring healthcare relationships beyond individual prescriptions.
THE BIGGER BULLISH THESIS
What interests me most isn't simply the GLP-1 market.
It's the possibility that Hims becomes an increasingly important distribution and care platform for pharmaceutical companies seeking direct access to consumers.
If Hims can combine convenient treatment access, ongoing clinical care and strong customer retention, I believe its business could become more valuable over time.
THE RISKS
Branded medicines may carry lower margins than compounded treatments.
Hims also remains dependent on pharmaceutical manufacturers for pricing, product availability and commercial terms.
And this agreement doesn't automatically guarantee higher revenue or profits.
MY TAKE
I remain bullish because I see Hims evolving from a digital healthcare provider into a broader consumer healthcare platform.
The relationships with Novo Nordisk and now Eli Lilly strengthen that opportunity.
But the financial test is whether expanding treatment access translates into profitable customer growth, stronger retention and sustainable free cash flow.
MY CONCLUSION
For me, this agreement strengthens the long-term investment case for $HIMS.
The opportunity isn't just selling more GLP-1 medications.
It's building a trusted healthcare platform that patients return to and pharmaceutical manufacturers increasingly want to work with.
That's why my bullish conviction remains intact.

🪐 What was happening in Poland’s space sector in October?     

October brought several important developments for Poland’s space industry, from new ESA contracts and satellite projects to major investments and international appointments. Here’s what made the headlines:

text:
One of the most expensive chickens on Earth has legs like a dragon. And in this video, nobody is guarding it.

Not a fence. Not a coop. Not a lock. Just a bird that looks like it was designed by a mythology committee, standing in a forest that does not belong to anyone's idea of a farm.

Here is the question that kept me watching: how do you harvest something that never agreed to be harvested?

Let me back up, because the bird matters more than the clip.

The Dong Tao chicken comes from a small village in northern Vietnam, in Hung Yen province, and it has been bred there for generations. It is famous for one thing above all others: its legs. They are thick, knotted, heavily scaled, and so out of proportion with the rest of the body that first-time viewers often assume the photo has been edited. It has not. Locals call it the dragon chicken, and once you see the legs you stop asking why.

Local tradition holds that these birds were once reserved for royal tables, served at festivals and offered as prized gifts. Whether every detail of that story survives a historian's scrutiny is a separate matter. What is not in dispute is the reputation. Today the breed is spoken about in Vietnam the way people speak about a rare wine or a vintage watch. A single healthy adult can command a price that would feed a family for a long time. Breeders talk about leg thickness the way jewelers talk about carats.

Now hold that thought, and put it next to this one.

A bird with that kind of reputation is, in this video, out among the trees.

Not in a pen at a breeder's yard with a name tag. Not in a climate-controlled show hall. In the open woods, in the green dimness where a hen can vanish behind a single fern.

That contrast is the whole story. Or at least the part of the story I can tell you without ruining it.

Because the title does not hide what is happening. It says wild. It says harvest. It says market. Three words that should not sit comfortably together, and yet they do, in a quiet, almost unbearably calm sixty seconds that left me with more questions than any loud video has in months.

What does it mean for a bird to be wild when its ancestors were shaped by human hands for centuries?

Who decides where the farm ends and the forest begins?

And what happens in the space between a living animal and a price?

I am not going to answer those for you. The video does not answer them in words either. It just lets you sit inside them.

---

Let me give you the background that makes the quiet land harder.

Every chicken alive today, from the factory-farmed broiler to the prize bird in a Vietnamese village, descends from the red junglefowl, a shy, fast, forest-dwelling bird native to the woodlands of South and Southeast Asia. Genetic work in recent years points to the region of mainland Southeast Asia as the cradle of chicken domestication, and it suggests the process began thousands of years ago, not in a lab or a feed company's office, but at the edge of the same kind of forest you see here.

Think about what that means.

The chicken did not begin as a farm animal. It began as a forest animal that wandered close to human settlements, probably drawn by spilled grain, and slowly, over countless generations, became ours. We did not invent it. We negotiated with it, one generation at a time, and we got to keep what we negotiated for.

Which means that a chicken standing among trees is not a strange sight. It is a homecoming of sorts. It is the oldest version of the relationship, replayed.

And yet.

There is a difference between a junglefowl and a Dong Tao. The junglefowl is light, quick, wary, built to bolt at the first rustle. The Dong Tao is heavy, slow, built like a small armored animal, with those enormous legs that make flight a very short, very theatrical event. Centuries of selection pushed it in a direction nature never intended. It is, in a sense, a living argument about how far a species can be bent.

So when you see a bird like this somewhere that looks untouched by people, you are watching two timelines collide: the ancient forest it came from and the human-made body it now carries.

I find that more moving than any rescue story, and I mean that precisely. A rescue has a clean shape: danger, help, relief. This has no clean shape. It has a creature that is both of the forest and of us, and a person who has to move between those two worlds with patience, because the bird does not owe anyone a thing.

---

If you have never spent time around chickens, you may assume they are simple. They are not.

They have a social order so intricate that researchers coined the phrase pecking order from watching them. They recognize individual faces, including human ones. They signal danger to one another with distinct alarm calls, and studies suggest those calls differ depending on whether the threat comes from the air or the ground. Hens communicate with their chicks before the eggs even hatch. A chicken is not a blank. It is a small, busy mind running a surprisingly sophisticated survival program.

Now imagine that mind in the woods, with every instinct from ten thousand years of ancestors switched back on.

Where does it sleep? Up. Chickens are instinctive roosters in the literal sense: given the chance, they climb, because the ground is where predators live and a branch is a small fortress. A bird that looks too heavy to leave the dirt will still haul itself upward at dusk, because something older than any breed standard tells it to.

That is one of the details that makes this video difficult to scroll past. It reminds you that these birds are not just assets. They are animals with a map in their heads, and the map is very old.

---

Here is where it gets uncomfortable, and I think that is exactly why it is worth your sixty seconds.

We like to divide the animal world into clean categories. Pets. Livestock. Wildlife. Each one comes with a script. Pets get names. Livestock gets numbers. Wildlife gets distance and a documentary narrator with a soft voice.

A bird like this refuses the script.

It is livestock by law and tradition. It is a luxury item by reputation. It is wildlife by behavior the moment it steps into the trees. Depending on which minute you catch it, it is all three, and none of the three categories is wrong.

I think that is why the title feels slightly off the first time you read it. Wild. Harvest. Market. Our brains want to resolve the tension. Is this foraging? Is this farming? Is this a rescue in disguise? Is this a tradition? Is this a business?

The honest answer is that it is a very old human activity wearing very modern packaging. People have gathered what the land offers and carried it to a place where someone else wants it for as long as there have been people and places. The camera is new. The gesture is not.

And the gesture is the thing worth studying.

Because there is a particular kind of person who does this work, and I have been thinking about them all week. They are not loud. They do not narrate. They do not explain themselves to the camera. They simply know something the rest of us have forgotten: how to be around an animal without taking its fear personally.

That is a real skill. Anyone who has tried to catch a frightened chicken knows it. The harder you reach, the faster it goes. Force produces panic. Panic produces injury. Patience produces something else entirely, a small, grudging, momentary trust.

It is one of the most underrated forms of expertise on the planet, and almost no one gets paid for it directly.

---

Let me zoom out for a second, because I promised I would not just describe the clip.

Rural markets in Vietnam are not what most of us picture when we hear the word market. They are not a tidy row of stalls with price tags and card readers. They are a living system, a kind of daily weather. Vendors arrive before dawn. Baskets, bundles, and bags appear from nowhere. Everyone knows everyone, or at least everyone knows who is related to whom. Prices are negotiated with eyebrows as much as with numbers.

In that system, a live bird is not an abstraction. It is wealth you can hold. It is a month of school fees, a repaired roof, a medical bill covered, a festival feast. For many households the bird is the bank.

That changes how you watch.

When the thing being carried to market is worth more than the whole day's other goods combined, every motion acquires weight. Where you step. How you grip. How long you take. Nobody wastes a gesture, because nobody can afford to.

And yet the strange thing, the thing I keep returning to, is how gentle the whole mood stays. There is no melodrama. There is no villain. There is no heroic soundtrack. There is just the slow, deliberate rhythm of work done by someone who understands both what the animal is worth and what the animal is.

I wish more content understood how much power lives in that restraint.

---

Let me say something about timelapse, because the format is doing more than it looks like.

A timelapse compresses hours into seconds. It takes patience, the one thing the modern internet is worst at, and turns it into something you can consume between two other videos. That is a small miracle and a small betrayal at the same time.

The miracle is that you get to see a whole arc of effort: the walking, the waiting, the finding, the carrying, the exchange. The kind of day that would take a person ten hours to live, delivered in less time than it takes to microwave leftovers.

The betrayal is that compression strips out the thing that made the day real. The boredom. The mosquitoes. The doubt. The long stretch where nothing happens and the person doing the work has to decide, again, whether to keep going.

If you watch carefully, and I would ask you to, you can feel where the hours were. You can feel the weight of the cut. The edit is hiding a thousand tiny decisions, and the fact that you can sense them anyway is a kind of respect the video pays to its subject.

This is why I keep saying it is not a loud clip. It is a clip that trusts you.

---

Now the part I promised I would not resolve.

Do the birds have a say?

Not in a mystical way. I am not going to tell you what a chicken thinks, because I do not know and neither does anyone else. Researchers have shown that chickens can anticipate, can show forms of self-control in experiments, and can behave in ways that look unmistakably like preference. Beyond that, the honest position is humility.

But there is a version of the question that does not require telling you what a bird feels. It is simply this: when an animal can live on its own terms and a person decides to bring it into a different life, what is the nature of that decision?

Is it care? Is it commerce? Is it both at once, in proportions no one can measure?

Every culture on Earth has an answer, and every answer has a cost. In some places the cost is guilt and in others it is gratitude. In some it is both, folded into a ritual so old no one remembers why.

I am not here to tell you which is right. I am here to tell you that this video puts you inside that question without once raising its voice.

---

There is another thing I noticed, and it has nothing to do with chickens.

Nobody in this world is performing for the viewer.

Think about how rare that is. Almost everything we watch now is engineered to flatter our attention: the cut every two seconds, the reaction face, the thumbnail screaming at us. This video does none of that. It gets out of its own way. It lets the landscape do the talking, and the landscape, a stand of trees, patient light, ground that has seen far more than any of us, is a better narrator than any voice I could have hired.

There is something quietly radical about a clip that does not need you to feel a certain way.

And because it does not push, you end up feeling more.

---

Let me give you the wider frame, because I think the bird deserves it.

In Vietnam, the chicken is not just food. It is liturgy.

At Tet, the lunar new year, a whole boiled chicken is one of the classic offerings placed on the family altar for ancestors. It is presented with care: posture arranged, head upright, often a sprig or a piece of something red in the beak. The bird is meant to look dignified. The meal comes after the meaning, not before it. In many households, the best bird of the year is set aside for exactly this purpose.

So a prized chicken in Vietnam sits at a very particular crossroads. It is a market good. It is a status symbol. It is a ritual object. And it is a living animal that someone has to feed, protect and carry, all before any of those other roles can begin.

Now consider the village the breed is named for. Dong Tao is a commune in Hung Yen province, a flat, green, unremarkable stretch of the Red River delta that happens to be the origin of one of the strangest birds in poultry. The legs that make the breed famous are not an accident of nature. Generations of breeders chose, mated, culled, and chose again, until the body became a kind of inherited craft. It is slow work. It rewards stubbornness. It punishes shortcuts.

And that craft is fragile.

Around the world, heritage poultry breeds are quietly disappearing, squeezed out by a handful of industrial lines that grow faster and cost less. The Dong Tao is the opposite of efficient. It is heavy and slow-maturing, it needs room, and it does not convert feed into meat the way a commercial broiler does. By the standards of modern agriculture it is almost an error.

Which is precisely why people value it.

There is a lesson hiding in that. We tend to protect only what is useful to the next quarter. A breed like this survives because enough people decided that usefulness is not the only measure of worth. Its survival is a vote, repeated daily by farmers, collectors, and the people who carry birds from forest to market, for a slower and stranger idea of value.

Whether you agree with that vote is up to you. But notice that it is a vote.

---

Here is a small thought experiment I find myself running every time I watch something like this.

Imagine you were told that the single most valuable thing you owned could walk away at any moment.

Not a metaphor. A literal, breathing, feathered thing with its own schedule and its own opinions, living in a place you do not fully control.

How would you hold it?

Most of us would reach for control. Cage it. Tag it. Track it. Reduce the risk to zero by reducing the animal's freedom to zero. That is the modern instinct, and it works, in the sense that nothing escapes.

But a different instinct has existed for far longer. It says: you cannot own what you do not understand, and you cannot understand what you only restrain. So you learn its habits. Where it goes at dusk. What it fears. What it follows. You become, slowly, a student of the creature's world.

That is a very different relationship, and it demands something we are increasingly bad at: attention without agenda.

I am not romanticizing hardship. Work like this is exhausting and often unrewarded, and nobody should pretend otherwise. But there is a dignity in the kind of knowledge it builds, and I think part of why this video lingers is that you can sense the knowledge even when no one speaks it aloud.

---

Let me address the obvious objection, because I can already feel it forming.

Someone will say: it is just a chicken.

And they will be right in one sense. It is not a rescue of an endangered species. It is not a dramatic confrontation. Nobody is in danger, at least not in any way that a headline would recognize.

But I want to push back gently on the word just.

Almost everything that shapes human life is a just. A just seed. A just river. A just field of rice. The ordinary things are the ones that carry civilizations, and we only call them ordinary because they have worked so well that we stopped noticing.

The chicken is perhaps the most successful domestic animal in history. There are more of them alive at any given moment than any other bird on the planet, by a margin that is almost absurd. Billions. They feed more people than any other animal protein source on Earth. And in all that vastness, the individual bird is nearly invisible.

So there is something quietly subversive about a video that asks you to look at one.

Not a flock. Not a statistic. One animal, in a specific place, handled by a specific person, heading toward a specific destination.

That is how empathy actually works. Not through large numbers, but through particulars. The psychologist's phrase for this is the identifiable victim effect, and while it is usually discussed in the context of charity appeals, it applies to attention in general. We care when something becomes singular. A million is a number. One is a story.

And this is a story with a single, concrete protagonist wearing feathers like a coat of embers.

---

I want to talk about trust for a moment, because it is the hidden current under everything here.

Every transaction in that rural market is a trust transaction. The seller trusts that the buyer will pay what was agreed. The buyer trusts that the bird is what it is claimed to be. Both trust that the other will not cheat the animal itself, because in a community where everyone knows your face, reputation is the only currency that cannot be counterfeited.

Zoom out further. The person carrying the bird trusts their own hands. The bird, in whatever way a bird can, adjusts to being held or not. The forest trusts nobody and forgives nothing.

Notice how many layers of trust are stacked inside what looks like a simple errand.

We live in an age of verification: reviews, ratings, receipts, certificates, authentication codes. We have built an entire economy around not trusting each other. And yet the oldest commercial systems on Earth, the village markets that still run on handshakes and long memory, never needed any of it.

Maybe that is why the clip feels almost nostalgic, even to people who have never been anywhere near a market like this. It is not nostalgia for a place. It is nostalgia for a kind of reliability we gave up without quite noticing.

---

There is one more angle I cannot leave out, and it is about the forest itself.

A forest is not scenery. It is an argument that has been going on for millions of years, conducted in light, water, root, and rot. Every tree in that frame is a negotiation between sun and shade. Every patch of ground is a record of who passed through and who stayed.

When a human walks into a forest to find an animal, they are entering that argument as a guest. Whether they know it or not. The best of them know it. They move differently. They listen differently. They treat the place as something with its own rules and its own memory, not just a backdrop for a task.

You can tell the difference on screen, and I would argue you can feel it even if you could not explain it. There is a way of being in a landscape that says I am passing through, and a way that says I am taking from. The first is rare. The second is common. And many of the people doing the second are not malicious; they are simply unaware that there was another option.

I am not claiming this video belongs to either camp. I am telling you that watching it made me notice the difference, and that noticing is a gift, whichever camp it lands on.

---

Let me make one practical observation about why this kind of content spreads, because I think it explains something about us.

People share things that make them feel a specific, hard-to-name emotion: not joy, not sadness, but a quiet recognition. The feeling of seeing something true that you did not know you were missing.

That is the emotion this video produces for many viewers, and it is the reason it travels. Nobody sends a clip like this because it is exciting. They send it because it feels like a small window into a way of life that does not have a trending sound or a catchphrase, and that makes it feel precious.

There is a name for the opposite of that feeling. It is the attention hangover you get after an hour of scrolling content built to bait you. The feeling that you consumed a lot and received nothing.

A sixty-second clip that leaves you with an actual thought is an act of rebellion against that.

---

Now, a few questions I would like you to carry into the video, because I think they sharpen the watching.

First: where is the moment the bird stops being an animal and starts being a product? Is there one? Or does the line move depending on who is looking?

Second: how much of the person's skill is visible, and how much is hidden in the edit? What would you need to know to appreciate the part you cannot see?

Third: if this same sequence of events happened somewhere you are more familiar with, would it feel different? Would you judge it differently? Why?

Fourth, and this is the one I cannot shake: what do we lose when we only meet animals as packaged goods?

Most of us will never see a chicken before it is wrapped in plastic. We have inherited a world in which the entire journey from living creature to meal has been hidden behind a conveyor belt and a logo. That distance is convenient. It is also, I think, a kind of moral anesthetic.

A video like this does not lecture about that. It just quietly, almost shyly, removes the anesthetic for a minute.

You can decide what to do with the feeling that follows.

---

Some of you are going to watch this and think it is peaceful. Others will find it unsettling. A few will feel nothing at all, and that is fine too. Content is a mirror, and the reflection depends on what you carry.

But I would bet that almost everyone who watches closely will experience at least one moment where they think, I did not expect to feel that about a chicken.

That moment is the real subject of the video.

It is the moment where an animal you have never thought about, doing something you have never witnessed, in a place you have never been, becomes briefly and undeniably real.

The legs. The color. The way something so heavy moves through a world built for lighter things. The patience of the person at the other end of the effort. The silence around it all.

I have watched a lot of animal videos. Most are built to hit a feeling and leave. This one builds a feeling and stays, the way a smell stays in a room after someone has walked out of it.

---

One last detail, and then I will stop circling.

Price is a story we tell about scarcity. A bird is worth a lot because few exist, because they take time to raise, because someone decided the legs matter. Strip the story away and what remains is an animal that eats, sleeps, startles, and survives exactly like its cheaper cousins.

I find that oddly consoling. It means the thing you are watching is worth watching even if you ignore every number attached to it. The market assigns the value. The forest never asked.

So if the price tag is the part that draws you in, fine. Let it. Just notice, somewhere in the middle of the clip, the moment you stop thinking about money at all.

---

A note on the sound, because it is half the experience.

Forests are never silent. They hum with insects, leaf-rustle, distant water, the small mechanical clicks of things moving through undergrowth. Against that bed of noise, any human gesture becomes loud, and any careful gesture becomes obvious. You hear the difference between hurry and patience before you see it.

Turn the volume up. Let the place speak first, always. Most of what matters here happens in the gaps between sounds, where a branch shifts quietly and a whole story changes direction.

---

Let me close the loop on something I said at the very beginning.

I told you the bird was one of the most expensive chickens on Earth, and I asked how you harvest something that never agreed to be harvested.

I want to be honest: I do not think the question has a clean answer, and I do not think the video pretends it does.

But I think it shows you something better than an answer. It shows you what it looks like when someone approaches that question with their hands instead of their opinions. When a person is simply doing the work in front of them, carefully, in a way that holds both the value of the animal and the animal itself.

That is rarer than any breed.

And if you have ever wondered what it would be like to see a very old relationship, between people and birds, between forest and market, between patience and price, play out in real time, without commentary and without apology, then you already know why this clip is worth your minute.

There is no trick at the end. No reveal I am holding back to bait you. The reward is not a twist. The reward is that you will see something you have almost certainly never seen before, and you will not be able to unsee how much attention it takes.

Go watch it.

Then come back and tell me which moment got you.

Because there is always one.

MARVELL $MRVL CLOSED WORTH WHAT IT BID FOR LUMENTUM:

Marvell Technology (MRVL) at $133.55, -$26.25 / -16.43% on Thursday, and $144.10 premarket, +$10.55 / +7.90% from that close.

Marvell still passes the Quality Len5 and is on none of the other Len5es we weigh, and it closed Thursday 14.9% under the price in our post. Thursday was its worst day since June, in a chip selloff tied to Tuesday's election. Marvell is paying for Lumentum in its own shares, so the offer fell with the stock, to $601 a share, and Lumentum trades further under it. Marvell's whole market value ended Thursday close to the price it put on Lumentum three days earlier. The agreement lets neither company leave because a share price fell, and shareholders at both still have to approve it. No vote date is set, and Marvell's next forecast is tentatively due December 1.

Thursday's fall changed nothing on Marvell's books. The Quality Len5 wants a gross profit, a profit on the owners' money, and debt no larger than that money. The August 1 books show all three, with $9.0B owed against $18.5B of owners' equity, the money shareholders have in the business. What would knock it off the Quality Len5: a year that ends in a loss, which the accounting charges from a completed Lumentum purchase could bring. The value Len5es want a discount, and the shares cost about 40 times the past year's adjusted profit, which leaves out stock pay and the costs of past acquisitions. What would put it on the Quality-Value Len5: a price that keeps falling while that profit holds. Momentum wants a climb near the high, and Thursday's close sits 59.5% under the June 18 high.

Marvell closed Wednesday above the price in our post, so the whole fall since then came on Thursday:
- Since our post: -$23.40 / -14.9% from the $156.95 price.
- Thursday: the worst day since June 5 and the lowest close since April 16.
- 66.6M shares traded, 2.3 times the 30-day average.
- VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) at $447.73, -$56.54 / -11.21% on Thursday.
Johnny Rice of The Motley Fool tied Thursday's selling to Democrats' election wins and their promises to pause data-center construction, and to the new shares Marvell must issue for Lumentum. Data centers brought in 79% of Marvell's sales in the July quarter. We wrote on Wednesday that part of Marvell's fall was the chip group. Our read: on Thursday most of it was. Marvell fell about one and a half times as far as the chip fund. In our post it was more than three times.

The offer for Lumentum shrinks with every drop in Marvell's stock. Value of the 4.5 Marvell shares promised for each Lumentum share:
- When the price was set: $1,132.
- In our post: $706.
- At Thursday's close: $601, down 47% from the start.
- At the premarket price: about $648.
Lumentum closed at $913.95 on October 28, before the talks were reported. Thursday's offer is worth about a third less than that. Marvell valued Lumentum at $115B, debt included, when it announced the deal on November 2. Marvell's own shares were worth about $117B in total at Thursday's close.

Neither company can leave this deal because a share price fell. Lumentum said on November 3 that the agreement "does not permit either party to terminate the Merger Agreement solely because of changes in the market price of either company's stock." It also said its shareholders will vote without knowing what the Marvell shares will be worth when the deal closes.

Lumentum (LITE) at $509.70, -$117.05 / -18.68% on Thursday, and $553.50 premarket, +$43.80 / +8.59% from that close. We flagged Lumentum's gap to the offer at 13.5% in our post. It closed Thursday at 15.2%. In our post we read that gap as the chance the terms change or the deal fails. Our read now: with no way out on price, it is the chance of a no vote by either company's shareholders, a board that withdraws its backing, a better offer or a regulator's block. Lumentum is on none of the Momentum, Quality-Value, Deep-Value and Special-Situations, Hypergrowth or Income Len5es; Thursday's close sits 55% under its October 9 high, too far from the top for Momentum.

Marvell is paying with a stock that has lost 47% since the price was set, and the agreement holds both companies to 4.5 shares. Marvell's forecast with its October-quarter report, tentatively December 1, is the next number from the company that can move that stock. Until the shareholders vote, on a date neither company has set, each dollar Marvell's stock moves changes the offer by $4.50.

MARVELL $MRVL OFFER FOR LUMENTUM SHRANK 38%:

Marvell Technology (MRVL) at $156.95, -$15.02 / -8.73% today.

Marvell is on none of the Len5es we weigh, and today's fall is its fourth in the five sessions since Bloomberg reported it was in talks to buy Lumentum with its own shares. The Marvell shares promised for each Lumentum share were worth $1,132 when the price was set. They are worth $706 now, and Lumentum trades at a widening discount even to that. Two brokerages cut the stock on Tuesday because the share count rises by about half and the promised savings do not cover it. The optical suppliers fell with Marvell today, so part of the drop is the group. Marvell reports the October quarter on December 1 with the first forecast written since the deal.

Momentum wants a stock climbing toward its high, and today's price is 52% under the $329.88 Marvell reached on June 18; a close back above that high that holds would put it on the Momentum Len5. The Quality-Value and Deep-Value and Special-Situations Len5es want a price under what the profit is worth, and about 48 times the past year's adjusted profit is not a discount; a lower price with the profit forecast intact would put it on the Quality-Value Len5. Hypergrowth wants sales multiplying at an early business, and a $2.7 billion quarter growing 37% is neither. Income wants cash paid to owners, and the $0.06 quarterly dividend yields 0.15%; a payout the business had to budget for would put it on the Income Len5. It fits the Quality Len5 on its books: $1.46 billion left in the July quarter after the cost of making its chips, $342.5 million of profit in the six months to August 1, and $9.0 billion of liabilities against $18.5 billion of owners' equity, a thin return but a positive one. What would knock it off the Quality Len5: the deal closing, because a purchase this size brings years of accounting charges for what was paid, and Marvell carried $1.1 billion of accumulated losses at the start of 2025.

The offer, announced November 2:
- 4.5 Marvell shares for each Lumentum share, worth $1,132 a share and $115 billion including debt when set, a 23.9% premium to Lumentum's October 28 close; Lumentum's holders get about 33% of the combined company.
- Closing expected in the first half of 2028 after votes at both companies and regulators' approvals; the agreement runs to November 1, 2027 and extends to August 1, 2028 while regulators review it.
- Marvell owes Lumentum $5.8 billion if its board backs out or takes a better offer and $3.2 billion if regulators block the deal; Lumentum owes $2.9 billion if its board does the same.
Marvell expects more than $1 billion a year of cost savings and says the deal adds to adjusted profit per share in its first year after closing; Matt Murphy, Marvell's chairman and chief executive, stays in charge.

Lumentum (LITE) at $610.90, -$69.26 / -10.18% today, is priced under what Marvell promised it. Four and a half Marvell shares are worth $706 today, and Lumentum trades 13.5% under that, a gap that was 11.3% at Monday's close. Our read: a gap that wide over an eighteen-month wait is the market pricing a real chance the terms change or the deal fails. Lumentum is on none of the Momentum, Quality-Value, Deep-Value and Special-Situations, Hypergrowth or Income Len5es; sales of $1.26 billion in the September quarter, 2.4 times a year earlier at a $360 million profit, are the multiplying Hypergrowth wants, but its price now follows Marvell's.

Two downgrades on Tuesday put numbers on the dilution, the smaller slice of profit each existing share gets once the new ones are issued. Sean O'Loughlin, TD Cowen's analyst, cut Marvell to Hold from Buy and his price target to $175 from $350, wrote that the deal may land "at or near the peak of an optical mini-cycle," and expects it to lower 2028 profit per share by a mid-single-digit percentage. Bank of America cut it to Neutral from Buy and its price target to $225 from $400: $1 billion of cost cuts cannot offset a share count that rises about 50%, and the regulatory review includes China. Chris Koopmans, Marvell's president and chief operating officer, sold 10,000 shares on Monday at an average $186.97 under a selling plan set in June, and keeps 202,800. The markets news site Investing put today's fall on the deal and the downgrades; StockStory tied it to the deal.

Part of today's fall is the group. The VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) at $505.02, -$13.50 / -2.60% today, fell less than a third as much, but the optical gear makers fell with Marvell on no deals of their own: Ciena (CIEN) at $269.54, -$30.54 / -10.18% today, and Coherent (COHR) at $192.27, -$15.22 / -7.34% today, the day after Texas elected Gina Hinojosa, the Democrat who campaigned on a pause on new data centers, as governor. Neither is on the Momentum, Quality-Value, Deep-Value and Special-Situations, Hypergrowth or Income Len5es: both are more than 55% under their June 3 highs at 50 to 67 times the past year's profit.

The October quarter is already known: Marvell said Monday that its revenue is tracking the $3.15 billion it forecast, within 2%, and it reports the quarter on December 1, a date it has not confirmed, with the first forecast written since the deal. No vote date is set at either company. Until then, Lumentum's discount to 4.5 Marvell shares, 13.5% today, is the market's running vote on whether this deal closes as written.

I can't aspire to get a Tesla luxury car - that one has been dead for a while. My next ride was going to be a Cybertruck and I've dreamed about it since they were launched. But they're out of the pickup business now. I guess I'll have to buy a Ford?

I look forward to someday riding in a Cybercab the next time I'm in a city not driving or renting a car but that only happens occasionally. I don't want a small sedan except as a second vehicle, but by the time I go to replace the one we have Tesla may not offer that either.

Solar roofs - beautiful and functional. I had just installed traditional solar when they came out and wished I could have had a Tesla solar roof.  I thought someday maybe I can get one.

Robots? I thought robots were a part of this amazing tech they were building for me, but I now am not so sure. Maybe I'll be able to get one before they move on from the market where I am, but maybe not.

Rereading this it seems whiny, but it's just sadness.

text:
I guess Tesla isn't for me. I though it was. I thought it was bringing these amazing things it creates to me, but they appear to have moved on. Elon's vision is perhaps too far out in the future.  

I can't aspire to get a Tesla luxury car - that one has been dead for a while. My next ride was going to be a Cybertruck and I've dreamed about it since they were launched. But they're out of the pickup business now. I guess I'll have to buy a Ford? 

I look forward to someday riding in a Cybercab the next time I'm in a city not driving or renting a car but that only happens occasionally. I don't want a small sedan except as a second vehicle, but by the time I go to replace the one we have Tesla may not offer that either.

Solar roofs - beautiful and functional. I had just installed traditional solar when they came out and wished I could have had a Tesla solar roof.  I thought someday maybe I can get one.

Robots? I thought robots were a part of this amazing tech they were building for me, but I now am not so sure. Maybe I'll be able to get one before they move on from the market where I am, but maybe not.

Rereading this it seems whiny, but it's just sadness.

text:
on the day of the gloat. 
the day everyone told you so. 
the day you're supposed to be selling.

i'm telling you to buy.

buy the pain. i dare you.

sounds easy. a lot of tech down 60%.

oracle traded at $346 on 10 sep '25. 
today it's $115. down two-thirds.

i've got this way of buying lows: i don't just buy the shares and hope. initially, i sell the upside.

i buy $orcl and write a short-dated call against the shares, struck around today's price. covered means i own the stock.

fuck. 🔻 c.70%  you bet i want to own $orcl.

but the crash does something else. it inflates the volatility. and that inflates the option valuation.
that's what i like selling.

i deduct the premium from my in-price. and every cent claws me closer to the bottom.

there's a version of this i already understand very well.

my st barts house. blanc bleu might be worth $40m. in high season a good week can pay me $100k.

that's 0.25% of the asset value in a week.

i don't sell the house. i own the house and let somebody pay me for the week.

covered calls aren't so different.

lumentum is already the subject of a marvell offer. the stock has still fallen from a high above $1,140 to $500 today.

the option market is paying extraordinary money to hold that fear. and that's the point.

i'm not inventing the yield. i'm collecting what the options market is offering me for the privilege of owning something that's already been punished.

nokia's more than 50% below its 52-week high. corning has been slaughtered too. the fear is still sitting inside the price.

i'm happy selling that kind of vol.

i'm also perfectly happy risking another 15% or 20% downside before these things turn.

and i like that the strategy comes with its own primitive bull-detection system: if my stock keeps getting called away from me, at some point i stop selling the option.

i stay long.

and yeah, duh. the premium is that week's income. it isn't proof that the bottom is in.

that's the trade.

i want long risk after huge (60%) drawdowns.
i reckon the bear is maybe 85% done. perhaps more.
and the midterm clock is now running.

give me the long risk of 60% drawdowns with that clock in motion.

the arithmetic is simple.
the temperament isn't.
