text:
Mark Carney's Clean & Green, Liberal Super Welfare Budget for Canada
* It's a welfare budget with corporate welfare and more welfare for the lower-income, Indigenous, and Greens.
- Deficit this year: $62.3 billion; $50 billion deficit in each following year.
- $142 billion in new tax cuts along with corporate tax relief & incentives dubbed Christmastime for the rich.
- A mega tax deduction allows Canadian development expenses to be deducted at 100%.
- Clean tech tax credits for industry and $93 billion in overall clean economy incentives through 2034 and a $50 billion national clean electricity strategy.
- $22 billion in new affordability and social infrastructure spending, which includes roughly $16 billion dedicated to housing and welfare supports.
- Indigenous reconciliation allocates roughly $26.6 billion to Indigenous water infrastructure, housing, education, and family welfare supports.
- The Canada groceries and essentials welfare benefit supplement gets a one-time 50% increase for the 2026–27 benefit year. -The Canada Caregiver Credit is now a fully refundable tax credit, targeted at lifting approximately 15,000 caregivers and vulnerable individuals out of poverty.
- Low-wage worker tax credits give single workers without children from $1,709 to $1,859. The maximum family benefit increases from $2,943 to $3,143.
- The budget offers $44.7 billion over 11 years, aimed at putting Canada on a path to end homelessness. 
+++

Drone war in Africa went from rare to normal in about three years, and almost nobody is defending against it

31 African countries now have military drones. Turkey has signed 32 drone supply deals, 28 of those since 2021. China sells CH4 and Wing Loong drones But who gets these weapons is not always obvious from official deals

UAE bought Chinese drones and gave them to Haftar militia in Libya. In Sudan, rebel RSF forces fly Chinese drones while government forces fly Turkish ones. Countries selling drones gain political influence without sending soldiers. Over 900 drone strikes have hit 15 African countries so far, causing more than 3,000 deaths

Russia Ukraine war did not stay in Europe. It spilled into Africa through private armies. 

Wagner group, now called Africa Corps, works in Mali and Central African Republic, mining gold that gets sold through Dubai. Turkey sells drones and gets security partnerships in return. UAE sends Chinese weapons to armed groups it supports in Libya and Sudan.

Small explosive drones and modified quadcopters are making air attacks possible for groups that could never afford fighter jets. When armed groups get drone power, governments lose their air superiority edge. 

Counter drone defenses become next big military purchase. Africa drone wars are testing new combat technology at real scale. Those lessons will spread to every future conflict

Cheap drones now matter more than expensive ones. Worldwide, the trend is away from a few costly drones and toward many cheap ones you can afford to lose

Africa governments spent big on imported, expensive drones, while rebels, often helped by foreign states, moved fast with cheap ones. Governments must now do what rebels did - go cheap, go local, defend against small drones, and cut off rebels’ access to parts and pilots

text:
Played a bit of the Ocarina of Time Remake with my son yesterday. We also played through the 3DS version together a few years ago.

My son was immediately blown away by the art direction. All I kept hearing was: "Dad, it looks so real!"

When he got the Kokiri Sword, he actually reached out and touched the screen to see if he could grab it... lol.

Personally, I've always been somewhat disappointed by Ocarina of Time, and that hasn't changed today. After the brilliant A Link to the Past, Ocarina of Time just felt emptier and more confused to me. 

And frankly, none of that has really been addressed.

Hyrule Field's design was still somewhat excusable back in 1998, given how incredibly limited the Nintendo 64 was from a technical standpoint. But today, especially when the game is using the technology from BotW and TotK? Yikes.

Something that already bothered me back then, but that I couldn't quite articulate properly at the time, was that a huge part of Zelda's magic came from the fact that there was always something interesting to do. The Moment-to-Moment was exquisite in those earlier games.

Every screen in Zelda 1 or ALTTP held some kind of secret or some opportunities of interactivity. There were always enemies to fight or something to interact with. Fight your way through a few bushes over here in the overworld and suddenly you stumble into a little grove where the Flute Boy is playing his flute. Whoa! Interesting!

Then along came Ocarina of Time, where you'd spend two minutes doing absolutely nothing but holding the analog stick forward to walk across a boring, empty Hyrule Field.

Try to do this design exercise: Graph out Hyrule Field from top-down and then try to come up with what interesting gameplay mechanics hide behind every cell. You'll quickly find that there's really not that much at all going on... 

And sure, Hyrule Field looks prettier now, but it's still just as empty and uninteresting as it was back then.

That means the entire overworld, which was so magical in Zelda 1 and ALTTP because every new dungeon item unlocked entirely new ways to interact with the environment, discover new areas and so on, is unfortunately no longer there in the same way.

Instead, you get this typical open-world terrain that you just walk through. On your very first trip from Kokiri Forest to Hyrule Castle, you fight exactly ONE tiny enemy and spend roughly two minutes doing nothing but holding your analog stick forward without anything remotely interesting happening.

From a level design perspective, that's something I would NEVER approve at Moon.

I would've turned Hyrule Field into a proper overworld where every single segment offers interesting opportunities for interaction. And after every dungeon, every new item you got should make you giddy about going back to the overworld to find out what amazing new discoveries are available now!

Over here, you can jump into the river and discover an NPC hiding beneath the bridge who gives you an interesting quest. Over there, you can use your Boomerang to interact with something. Around that corner, there's something you can do with the Hookshot. Further back, you can blow open a new path using Bombs. Down that little alley, you can lift a heavy rock that reveals a cave leading into an elaborate underground network, which eventually opens up a secret entrance into Hyrule Castle Town, where you can find a Heart Container.

And so on, and so forth. But none of that stuff happens here.

Back in 1998, Hyrule Field was a nice little tech demo that allowed Nintendo to show off how the N64 could render some really big triangles, just to make the poor old PlayStation look bad.

But from a design perspective, it was already pretty lousy back then. And to simply copy that design 1:1 today? Nah. Every designer at Nintendo should be crying foul and know that this could be done so much better nowadays.

Now, I'm sure some people will come along and start rambling about staying faithful to the original...

Oh, give me a break.

I just took Zelda 1 apart myself and turned it into a 16-bit game. Zelda 1 didn't actually need that many improvements because Miyamoto was still putting his hands on every single screen like a ruthless design dictator back then. But even there, you could improve certain empty areas (like the empty desert where absolutely nothing happens) simply by introducing interesting new designs and opportunities for interaction.

What we're getting here, once again, is essentially just a graphical update. And I mean, graphically the game is really nice! But as always in games, graphics != fun.

We already had a pure graphical update with Ocarina of Time 3D, so... did we really need yet another one? What happened to Nintendo only making a new game when they figure out featuring new ways to play?

From a pure game design perspective, there was SO much more potential here, and I find it quite disappointing that Nintendo's designers apparently decided against really flexing their creative muscles.

Any reasonably competent designer could've squeezed a lot more fun out of this simply by understanding what makes the Zelda formula work and then consistently questioning whether the moment-to-moment experience is actually enjoyable.

If we're being honest with ourselves, Ocarina of Time these days is a solid 7.5–8/10 game whose design unfortunately doesn't quite measure up to its predecessors due to the technical limitations back then. Those limitations don't exist anymore, so why are we still getting those same old restricted designs?

Back in 1998, you could overlook some of those shortcomings because the game was still an absolute bombshell thanks to innovations like Z-targeting and so on. It showed the entire industry where video games could go next in the same way Super Mario 64 did.

But nowadays, all of that stuff has become the de-facto standard.

So the main focus should've really been on the level design and the interplay between the overworld and the dungeons - and that's precisely where OoT is decidedly hit-and-miss.

I genuinely wish the international gaming press had a better understanding of game design instead of largely behaving like a bunch of graphics whores.

Giving Ocarina of Time a 10/10 for its design just goes to show that, unfortunately, a lot of games journalists don't really understand game design in the deep manner that they ought to in the first place.

We've seen plenty of games after OoT that did terrains like that that kinda looked nice, but really didn't offer much fun. And sadly, nobody at Nintendo sought to address this issue when it's clear that they all understand how to do it better these days.

This is a good thought experiment, and theoretically true. However, it won’t happen like this because of… well, people. Their fundamental distrust of AI, and the moral headwinds already colliding with it.

Many people, in the West in particular, have fallen into an ‘AI doom’ mindset. They will reject and resist the adoption of AI, even if it could offer them a ‘frictionless’ conduit to navigating life.

I expect the resistance will be made worse if the distrusted classes—the government, the manager or, worst of all, the ‘tech bro’—are seen to preach the benefits of adoption.

‘RESIST.’

Given how politicised this has already become, ‘anti-AI-ism’ will increasingly be preached as a moral virtue.

If using AI becomes a moral transgression, refusing its benefits becomes a point of pride.

‘I don’t use AI, therefore I am a better person.’

A new secular religion for our times: rage, rage, rage against the machines.

See, for example, even the earliest debates about AI in art: anyone who uses AI to create is a thief, deserving of scorn.

In education, new Texas Govenor Gina Hinojosa has seized on the zeitgeist.l - warning that children taught by AI will become ‘a generation of sociopaths instead of productive citizens’.

That will resonate deeply with parents.

Of course, this thinking is fundamentally flawed because it sets up the choice as binary and zero-sum.

Choose: the side of AI or the human? Darkness or light? The ultimate human storytelling device: a battle between good and evil.

Those who understand that this is neither binary nor zero-sum will be the ones who choose adoption.

This will give them tremendous and compounding advantages. Ironically, they may then be persecuted for having achieved those advantages through the ‘dark arts’.  Will they be sacrificed on the altar of anti-AI-ism?

Make no mistake: there will be active resistance to AI adoption, fuelled by the intoxicating brew of moral superiority and wrapped in the language of a battle for the soul of humanity itself.

So no, I don’t foresee ‘friction collapse’ driven by AI adoption anytime soon.

text:
agents are going to cause a breakdown of human behavior assumptions underlying today's systems. i've started thinking about it as friction collapse. without friction, a number of norms will collapse.

consider selling tickets to a concert/event. today, you can post them at a certain time and it's first come first serve. soon everyone's agent will persistently monitor, and as soon as they are posted for sale, thousands of people will instantaneously be trying to buy the same ticket. how do you even resolve this? sell the ticket to the person whose agent gets there fractions of a second before?

we're seeing the same thing with job applications, restaurant reservations, but basically anything that relies on participation requiring effort is going to break down. sales emails/calls, participation in government benefits, apartment rentals, doctors appointments, RFP responses. customer support won't be able to handle the user who will not drop their point of dissatisfaction. with no friction, these systems just don't work anymore.

business models will break down:
- flights/hotels will be consistently cancelled and rebooked at the lowest price (great use case for your agent if you don't have this already set up)
- subscriptions will be cancelled
- retailers won't be able to arbitrage price differences as the agent will find the cheapest place to buy anything
- insurance denials (health/auto/home/etc.) will be fought tooth and nail
- bank interest rates will be optimized and avoidable charges will be avoided

a lot of what we perceive as stable social coordination is actually an equilibrium sustained by human inefficiency. rationing is a product of human slowness. signaling effort/interest/intent is a key part of our social infrastructure. inertia is a key to many business models. information asymmetry is everywhere. and attention is monetized thoroughly.

with agents, none of these things are true. humans will simply demand what they want and have their agents get it for them. there is going to be a fundamental renegotiation of how markets allocate resources, how people signal intent, and how businesses capture value.

text:
10 habits of people who always seem to have great energy
⠀
1. They get outside soon after waking
Morning light tells their body clock the day has started and helps time their natural energy rise. They don't wait for coffee to do it.
⠀
2. They wake up at the same time every day
A steady wake time keeps their body clock on schedule, so their energy shows up at the same time each morning.
⠀
3. They skip sunglasses in the morning
They let morning light reach their eyes, since that's the signal their clock needs most.
⠀
4. They wait a bit before their first coffee
Letting their body wake itself up first helps them avoid the sharp afternoon crash.
⠀
5. They step outside around midday
Midday is the brightest light of the day. A short walk after lunch gives their focus and mood a boost right when most people start to fade.
⠀
6. They don't let gray days stop them
Even a cloudy sky is far brighter than any office, so they go out anyway and stay a little longer.
⠀
7. They move outdoors when they can
Walking outside gives them daylight and the calming effect of the world moving past them, two things a treadmill can't offer.
⠀
8. They catch the sunset
A few minutes of evening light helps them wind down and makes indoor lights at night bother them less.
⠀
9. They keep their evenings dim
Lamps instead of overhead lights and screens turned down protect their melatonin and their sleep.
⠀
10. They protect their sleep
Great energy during the day starts with good sleep at night. Bright days and dark nights are how they get it.
⠀
Great energy isn't luck. It's mostly light, timed right ☀️

text:
Most men think that love is built by spoiling their women, but that is actually how you lose them. You see, you will buy gifts, do a lot of favours, and always try everything to make sure she is happy. You have to understand that, yes, those things are good, but that is not how love is built.

Let me show you today how you build love with your woman. If you want your woman to be able to love you, and love you for real, then make sure that she invests in you. In what way? Give her a few assignments here and there. Tell her, "Please, pick this for me. Do this for me. Do that for me."

Anytime a lady is doing something for a man, she asks herself, "Am I doing this because I just want to do it, or am I doing it because this person is valuable?" The more she does things for you, the more she knows that you are valuable to her.

But most men don't get this. They think, "The more I relieve her of duties and responsibilities, the more she is going to love me." It doesn't work like that.

Remember, marriage is a kingdom; it's not a democracy. It is a place where whatever the king says, his word is final, and whatever he brings out has to have meaning to whoever is around him. Think of a king who is constantly serving instead of being served. Will the people love him? No, it doesn't work like that.

I'm not saying that anyone should take advantage of anyone else, but what I mean is that there has to be mutual investment. What do you invest as a man? You invest in protection, you invest in a future, and you invest in provision. But what does she invest in return?

No, you relieve her of all her duties. There is nothing she literally does. You want her to wake up late. She cannot even make tea for you. She can never do this or that for you, and you think she is going to fall in love with you. No.

Women fall in love where they invest, where they invest their time, attention, emotions, and hard work. That is where they fall in love, and that is why you see bad boys winning. How do they win? They give her something to ponder, something to chase.

Look at how she treats bad boys and how she treats good boys. Good boys always offer everything. They always say, "Babe, do you need this?" "Yes." "Babe, you should not struggle. You should not do this. I have it catered for."

But bad boys will do the opposite. They will tell her, "I'll be there at this time. Find your way there." The woman will find her own fare. She will come, and the bad boy will give her the experience. It's always a good experience, but out of sight, out of mind. text:
If you’re an InboxKit user, ask your account manager one question this week:

“Will you still offer Microsoft in 3 months?”

Whatever the answer is, hear me out.

Word in the industry is that some of the big inbox providers are about to stop offering Outlook.

Not a pause. Not “temporary issues.” Gone.

You could wake up to 0 inboxes and a campaign still scheduled for 9am.

Here’s how to not be that guy, gents.

🟥 WHY OUTLOOK KEEPS DISAPPEARING
→ Microsoft is the most volatile provider in cold email
→ Cheap Outlook usually means tenants from cold email reseller pools
→ Hundreds of cold emailers share one pool, and one pool shares one fate
→ When Microsoft tightens up, the whole pool dies together
→ A provider built on that pool can’t fix it. All they can do is turn it off

🟪 THE TICKING BOMB NOBODY ASKS ABOUT
Most inbox providers have exactly one source for their tenants.
One supplier. One pool. One point of failure.
→ That source gets flagged, so every customer gets flagged
→ That source raises prices, so your price goes up overnight
→ That source quits, so your provider “sunsets Outlook”
→ You never see it coming because you never knew it existed
Your provider’s dashboard looks diversified. Their supply chain is one guy.
Ask them: “How many sources do your Microsoft tenants come from?”
If the answer is 1, or they dodge, you’re standing on the bomb.

🟧 WHAT TO DO THIS WEEK
→ Export your domain list, DNS records and sequencer connections now, not after the “we’re sunsetting Outlook” email
→ Keep your domains. Domain reputation belongs to you, not your provider
→ Migrate in batches. Never move 100% of your volume on one day
→ Warm new inboxes before the old ones die: 3–5 days minimum, 10–14 if you’re patient

🟨 WHAT A REAL OUTLOOK TENANT LOOKS LIKE
→ High-spend real businesses
→ Not cold email reseller pools
→ Premium license
→ More than one source behind it, so one supplier dying doesn’t take you down

🟩 HOW TO RUN IT SO IT LASTS
→ 2–3 cold emails per inbox per day. Always
→ 100 inboxes per domain × 3 = 300 sends per domain per day
→ No links. No open tracking. Track inbox placement
→ Spintax, so 100 inboxes aren’t sending the same fingerprint
→ Microsoft SNDS for reputation and complaints. It’s free
→ Judge reply and bounce rate per domain. One domain dips, pause it

⬛ HOW COLD EMAILERS ACTUALLY DIE
It’s never one bad day. It’s the same 6 mistakes:
→ Ran 100% of volume through one provider with one source behind it
→ Bought the cheapest tenants on the market and shared a pool with 500 strangers
→ Pushed 10 a day per inbox because “last week it was fine”
→ Kept links and open tracking on, then blamed Microsoft for the spam folder
→ Watched blended reply rate while 3 domains quietly died underneath it
→ Had zero backup inboxes warming, so one outage meant 2 weeks with no sends

None of these show up on day one.

They show up the week you hit quota, the week the client renews, the week you finally scale.

Then the guy posts “cold email is dead.”

It’s not dead, bro. It just stopped forgiving you.

I don’t trust one source with my sends or my clients’ 65M+ a day.

If you want to know where I source my infrastructure, comment “INFRA” and I’ll DM you.

text:
🚨Joe O’Cearuill JJ Gabriel’s father on his conversation with Michael Carrick and Jason Wilcox over Manchester United’s contract offer:

🗣️ Joe O’Cearuill: “I had a very honest conversation with Michael Carrick and Jason Wilcox about JJ’s future, and I think some people at Manchester United will be angry when they hear why we said no.

But I’m his father before I’m anybody’s friend at a football club.

JJ is 16 years old.

We are not going to make a decision about his future because of the Manchester United badge alone.

I asked them one simple question.

‘Where exactly do you see JJ playing?’

There was a pause.

And that pause told me a lot.

I said, ‘You want him to stay, but you can’t give me a clear pathway. You can’t tell me when he becomes part of the first team.’

JJ doesn’t want to spend years being told he is one of the best young players at Manchester United while waiting for someone to decide when he is ready.

He wants responsibility.

He wants competition.

Most importantly, he wants a pathway.

The contract discussion became serious.

Our proposal was a £5 million signing package, with performance bonuses taking it beyond £8 million, alongside a clear development pathway.

We also wanted regular first-team training and a defined number of senior appearances once he reached the appropriate age.

Manchester United weren’t prepared to agree to those terms.

Real Madrid were.

And that changed everything for me.

I told Carrick, ‘This isn’t about who pays the most money. It’s about who is prepared to make a commitment to my son’s development.’

‘If you want him to stay, show us where he fits.’

‘Don’t tell me he has potential. Tell me what you’re going to do with it.’

Michael was respectful, but I understood there were limitations.

He has a squad to manage.

Jason has a club to manage.

But I have a 16-year-old whose next decision could shape the next ten years of his career.

Then Real Madrid came into the picture.

Their message was different.

They didn’t say, ‘Come here and wait.’

They said, ‘Come here and compete.’

They were prepared to meet the financial package, accept the bonuses and give us a much clearer pathway toward senior football.

That mattered enormously.

I told United, ‘If you cannot give him what another club is willing to give him, you cannot be surprised when he chooses the other club.’

This isn’t disrespect toward Manchester United.

But Manchester United cannot expect every talented young player to stay forever because of the history of the shirt.

History matters.

Ambition matters too.

JJ wants to play for the biggest clubs in the world.

And when Real Madrid tell my 16-year-old son they believe he can become one of their players, I have to take that seriously.

Some people will say he should have stayed.

Some will say he is too young.

Some United fans will be furious.

I understand that.

But I would rather people be angry with our decision today than JJ wake up at 20 and ask why I didn’t fight harder for his career.

We didn’t reject Manchester United because we don’t respect the club.

We rejected the proposal because we didn’t believe it was the best one for JJ.

Real Madrid showed more ambition.

They showed more clarity.

And they were willing to put their money behind their words.

JJ is only 16.

He has a lot to learn.

But he also has huge ambition.

I’m not going to apologize for protecting that.

Manchester United had the opportunity to convince us.

They didn’t.

Real Madrid did.

So now JJ is going to Madrid to compete.

Not to be Cristiano Ronaldo.

Not to be Jude Bellingham.

Not to be anybody else.

To become JJ Gabriel.

And if Manchester United fans are angry, I understand.

But my responsibility isn’t to make Manchester United fans happy.

My responsibility is to make sure my son gets the best opportunity to become the footballer he believes he can be.”

text:
$SLVM Q3 2026 earnings: Sylvamo exits its loss-making European mills, and Americas profits rebound

Sylvamo, the maker of office and printing paper, agreed to sell its money-losing European mills while higher prices lifted profit across the Americas. Continuing Ebitda, excluding one-offs, nearly doubled from last quarter to $128 million as paper price hikes added $25 million and Latin American margins rebounded. Even so, profit per share excluding one-offs fell 26% from a year ago because North American sales shrank and $6 million to $7 million of quarterly European corporate overhead stayed behind.

• Sales from continuing operations: $𝟔𝟒𝟓𝐌 (-2.6% from a year ago (+5% from last quarter))
• Profit per share, excluding one-offs: $𝟏.𝟑𝟑 (-26% from a year ago ($0.35 last quarter))
• Ebitda, excluding one-offs: $𝟏𝟐𝟖𝐌 (20% margin, up from 11% last quarter)
• Eastover sheeter outlook: 𝐏𝐮𝐬𝐡𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐨 𝐐𝟑 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟕 (expanded by 200,000 tons of cutting capacity)

⚖️ 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭: 🟢 Bullish

The story got better because chief executive John Sims found a buyer for Europe, ending a cash drain that management had previously put off fixing until 2027. One caution: the paper maker pushed the startup of its new Eastover paper-cutting machine to the third quarter of 2027 while keeping its three older machines running, and nine-month free cash flow remains negative.

The question now is whether exiting Europe and raising prices will turn into debt reduction once the fourth-quarter Eastover mill outage passes. Bulls see a high-margin Americas business poised to cash in on mill upgrades, while skeptics point to rising paper imports, stranded corporate overhead and delayed equipment startups. The European sale price and fourth-quarter inventory drawdown will settle it.

Full article with charts - link in bio

🐂 𝐁𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🟢🟢 𝐁𝐢𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐎𝐟𝐟𝐞𝐫 𝐄𝐱𝐢𝐭𝐬 𝐋𝐨𝐬𝐬-𝐌𝐚𝐤𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐄𝐮𝐫𝐨𝐩𝐞𝐚𝐧 𝐌𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐬
Sylvamo makes uncoated freesheet, the standard office and printing paper. Its European mills lost $64 million on an operating basis in the first half of 2026, and three months ago chief executive John Sims had pushed any decision on their future into 2027. That overhang is now ending.

Sims announced a put option agreement with Midas Atlantic Partners and The Najafi Companies for "a binding offer to acquire our Europe business, including our uncoated freesheet paper mills in Saillat, France, and Nymolla, Sweden". The paper maker moved Europe into discontinued operations and recorded a $342 million noncash impairment charge to write down the business.

Exiting Europe removes a business that burned $49 million of operating cash over the first nine months of 2026. It leaves the US company "concentrated in Latin America and North America, where we see the greatest opportunities to create value", Sims wrote, with an 18% to 20% Ebitda margin across both remaining regions this quarter.

What to watch: the purchase price and net cash proceeds in the quarterly filing or deal closing announcement. A clean exit without Sylvamo funding large closure liabilities would confirm that the European cash drain is gone for good.

🟢🟢 𝐏𝐚𝐩𝐞𝐫 𝐏𝐫𝐢𝐜𝐞 𝐈𝐧𝐜𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐬𝐞𝐬 𝐋𝐢𝐟𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐟𝐢𝐭 𝐀𝐜𝐫𝐨𝐬𝐬 𝐀𝐦𝐞𝐫𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐬
Management had promised a second-half earnings rebound after maintenance shutdowns and weak Latin American margins dragged down the spring quarter. In the third quarter, higher prices and fewer mill outages nearly doubled Ebitda, excluding one-offs, from $66 million to $128 million.

• Prices and product mix: up $25 million from last quarter on "previously communicated paper price increases"
• Planned maintenance outage costs: down $38 million from last quarter, as scheduled
• Mill operations and other costs: $6 million lower from better factory performance
• Latin America Ebitda margin, excluding one-offs: 18%, up from 3% last quarter on $258 million of sales

The Latin American rebound shows that the second quarter's margin drop to 3% was mostly outage timing and delayed shipments rather than a broken business. In September, Colombia also canceled import duties on Brazilian paper, which "restores access to a market we previously served", the Memphis-based group said.

What to watch: fourth-quarter price and mix changes in Latin America and North America. A second straight quarter of price gains would show that customer price hikes are holding despite rising paper imports.

🐻 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🔴🔴 𝐄𝐚𝐬𝐭𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫 𝐒𝐡𝐞𝐞𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐃𝐞𝐥𝐚𝐲𝐞𝐝 𝐀𝐧𝐝 𝐔𝐧𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐨𝐜𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐂𝐨𝐬𝐭𝐬 𝐒𝐭𝐚𝐲
Sims says the European exit will make Sylvamo a stronger company while its Eastover, South Carolina mill upgrades drive future profit. However, the release reveals a nine-month delay on a key Eastover machine and leftover corporate overhead that cuts against that clean story.

At Eastover, management chose to "keep our three existing cutsize sheeters operational and add a new state-of-the-art sheeter rather than replacing one". A cutsize sheeter cuts large paper rolls into standard office sheets. While keeping all four machines adds 200,000 short tons of cutting capacity, startup moved to "early in the third quarter of 2027" instead of ramping up in late 2026.

Meanwhile, continuing operations must absorb $6 million to $7 million per quarter of "corporate costs previously allocated to our European operations", the company said. Selling and administrative overhead rose 3.5 percentage points of sales from a year ago to 12.7%, which helped pull operating profit, excluding one-offs, down 26% to $53 million.

What to watch: whether management cuts that $24 million to $28 million of yearly stranded overhead or delays the $30 million to $40 million Eastover profit target set for 2027. Full-year 2026 results in February will give the first read on 2027 cost savings.

🔴 𝐑𝐢𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐈𝐦𝐩𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐬 𝐀𝐧𝐝 𝐅𝐫𝐞𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐭 𝐂𝐨𝐬𝐭𝐬 𝐒𝐪𝐮𝐞𝐞𝐳𝐞 𝐍𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐡 𝐀𝐦𝐞𝐫𝐢𝐜𝐚
North America provides nearly two-thirds of Sylvamo's continuing revenue, and the company needs strong domestic demand to replace paper supply it lost when International Paper closed its Riverdale line in May. Instead, North American sales fell 8% from a year ago to $414 million, and segment operating profit fell 19% to $65 million.

Even against the weak second quarter, North American sales volume fell while foreign paper imports into both North and Latin America grew from a year ago. At the same time, supply chain pressures cost the company $6 million more than last quarter because "elevated diesel prices and reduced driver availability increased trucking costs in the U. S.", the paper maker said, alongside "persistedly high oil prices".

What to watch: North American sales volume and input costs in the fourth quarter, when the Eastover mill takes its major upgrade outage. Falling volume alongside rising imports would mean competitors are taking market share while Sylvamo raises prices.

🔴 𝐃𝐢𝐯𝐢𝐝𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐬 𝐄𝐱𝐜𝐞𝐞𝐝 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐅𝐥𝐨𝐰 𝐖𝐡𝐢𝐥𝐞 𝐃𝐞𝐛𝐭 𝐑𝐢𝐬𝐞𝐬
Even without the European cash burn, Sylvamo's continuing businesses have not generated enough cash this year to cover its capital spending and shareholder payouts. Third-quarter free cash flow turned positive at $16 million, down from $64 million a year ago, leaving nine-month free cash flow at negative $15 million.

Despite the negative nine-month cash flow, the board paid $54 million in dividends over the first three quarters and kept buybacks at zero. To fund the $69 million gap by our math and build paper inventory ahead of fourth-quarter mill outages, continuing net debt rose by $147 million since December to $907 million.

What to watch: fourth-quarter free cash flow and the promised year-end inventory drawdown. Management previously said working capital would release cash in the fourth quarter, and missing that drawdown would leave debt elevated heading into 2027.

🔴 𝐑𝐢𝐬𝐤𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐝𝐢𝐝𝐧'𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐬𝐰𝐞𝐫
The earnings release did not provide numbers for four standing issues that depend on the conference call or the quarterly filing.

• European deal price and cash terms: the release announces the binding offer and a $342 million write-down, but does not disclose the sale price or closing timeline.
• Suzano pulp tax dispute in Brazil: no update on whether supplier Suzano has started billing $15 million to $20 million a year in tax at the Três Lagoas mill after winning an August court appeal.
• Shareholder rights plan and Atlas Holdings: no word on whether the board decided in September to extend the takeover defense expiring at the end of November.
• 2030 factory efficiency targets: management noted Lean operational gains, but gave no baseline numbers for its 2030 machine efficiency or cash-cost goals.

— • — • —

💲 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐊𝐏𝐈𝐬

𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐮𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐨𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬 𝐢𝐧𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐢𝐞𝐬 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟑𝟔𝟗 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
Inventories for continuing operations rose 41.4% from $261 million at the end of December, consuming $92 million of operating cash over the first nine months. The paper maker built up stock in North America to supply customers while the Riverdale contract ended and the Eastover mill shuts down for fourth-quarter upgrades.

𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐮𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐨𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬 𝐧𝐞𝐭 𝐝𝐞𝐛𝐭 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟗𝟎𝟕 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
Total debt minus cash on the continuing balance sheet rose 19.3% from $760 million at the end of 2025, by our math ($1,000 million of short- and long-term debt less $93 million of cash). Net debt borrowings climbed as the group funded $156 million in nine-month capital projects and $54 million in dividends.

𝐂𝐚𝐩𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐣𝐞𝐜𝐭 𝐬𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟓𝟒 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇒ stable
Cash invested in capital projects ran at 8.4% of sales in the third quarter, compared with $58 million in the second quarter and $50 million a year ago. Nine-month capital spending for continuing operations reached $156 million, up from $142 million in the same period last year as Eastover upgrades continued.

— • — • —

🔮 𝐆𝐮𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞

𝐄𝐚𝐬𝐭𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫 𝐧𝐞𝐰 𝐜𝐮𝐭𝐬𝐢𝐳𝐞 𝐬𝐡𝐞𝐞𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐮𝐩: 𝐄𝐚𝐫𝐥𝐲 𝐐𝟑 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟕 (~𝟐𝟎𝟎,𝟎𝟎𝟎 𝐬𝐡𝐨𝐫𝐭 𝐭𝐨𝐧𝐬 𝐜𝐚𝐩𝐚𝐜𝐢𝐭𝐲)  ⇘ decelerating
🠇 cut from Install Q3 2026, ramp Q4 2026
Cut. Management pushed the startup of its new paper-cutting machine at the Eastover mill from late 2026 to early in the third quarter of 2027. The US company changed the scope so it will add the machine alongside its three existing sheeters rather than replacing one, adding about 200,000 short tons of sheet-cutting capacity once running.

text:
The yak that gets pushed backward in this fight is often the one that wins.

It sounds wrong.

But the animal that gives ground is protecting something worth far more than a patch of grass.

Biology has a name for it.

I did not believe it either, until the morning an old herder named Dorje put a cup of salted butter tea in my hands, pointed at two bulls on the slope below his tent, and said, "Watch the one who loses. Never the one who wins."

PART ONE: THE TUESDAY I WON AND LOST

I was thirty-one years old, I owned a color-coded spreadsheet for every corner of my life, and on a Tuesday in July I won the biggest argument of my career and lost everything it was supposed to protect.

The argument was about a contract. Fourteen months of work sat on one table in a glass meeting room: a regional freight deal worth about four hundred thousand dollars a year, my name on every slide, my promotion quietly stapled to the signature. The client's procurement chief wanted exactly one concession. A small one. Payment terms moved from thirty days to forty-five. Nothing that would have hurt us.

I said no.

I said no politely, then firmly, then with a slide titled "Why Our Terms Are Non-Negotiable." I had data. I had a flawless chart. I was right about every number in that room, and I kept pushing until the procurement chief closed her laptop, thanked everyone for their time, and walked out.

My director found me in the corridor afterward. He wasn't angry, and that was the worst part. He said, very gently, "You won the argument. Congratulations. We lost the client."

Then he said something I typed into my phone, because I thought it was the cruelest sentence anyone had ever said to me.

"You fight every fight like it's the last patch of grass on earth."

I took two weeks of leave I hadn't touched in three years. I had no plan. My phone, with its usual sense of humor, offered me a message from a neighbor of my grandfather's: Dorje's knees were bad, the family herd had gone up to the summer pasture, and nobody from our side had visited in two years.

So I went looking for the only person I knew who had never once used a slide to win an argument.

PART TWO: THE AIR UP THERE

The road to the summer pasture ends long before the pasture does. After that you walk, or you ride behind someone who knows the way, and you learn quickly that the sky above 4,000 meters is a different substance.

At 4,500 meters, air pressure is only about 58 percent of what it is at sea level. The air still contains the same 21 percent oxygen, but each breath delivers roughly 40 percent less of it to your lungs. I know that now as a statistic. That first afternoon I knew it as a pounding headache and the feeling of climbing stairs with a wet blanket on my shoulders.

Dorje's herd did not seem to notice. About sixty yaks were spread across the green slope like spilled ink, grazing as calmly as lowland cattle graze at a thousand meters.

That is not an accident. The domestic yak, Bos grunniens, lives comfortably between roughly 3,000 and 5,500 meters, and its wild cousin, Bos mutus, ranges across the Tibetan Plateau and is listed as Vulnerable by the IUCN. Compared with lowland cattle, yaks carry larger lungs and hearts for their body size, plus blood that handles scarce oxygen more efficiently. A 2012 genome study published in Nature Genetics found that yak genes linked to oxygen use and energy metabolism show the fingerprints of natural selection for life in thin air.

Even the Latin name records their voice. Grunniens means "the grunting one." Yaks do not moo. They grunt, low and rough, and I heard it everywhere that week, like a conversation between very large, very tired accordions.

Dorje met me at the tent door. He was shorter than I remembered, with a face the weather had been editing for seventy years. He did not ask why I had come. He handed me tea, real butter tea, thick with yak butter and salt, the drink the plateau runs on: calories and warmth in one cup.

Then he turned his chin toward the slope.

"Two of them are going to settle something," he said. "Sit down. Drink. Breathe slowly. You are going to want to understand this."

PART THREE: TWO BULLS

Dorje had names for them. The big one was Smoke, a black bull in his prime, heavy through the shoulders, with a hump of muscle that rolled when he walked. The challenger was Ash, younger, narrower, with a pale patch across his back like a scar of old frost.

They did not charge at each other the way cartoons promise. First came the posturing: heads low, a slow sideways walk, grunts that vibrated in my sternum from fifty meters away. Then, without any signal I could see, the distance closed and their horns met with a crack like a dropped plank.

And then they pushed.

If you have only seen bulls fight in movies, you picture goring and chaos. Real yak contests are mostly a shoving match, forehead to forehead, horns hooked and braced, two animals worth hundreds of kilograms each leaning with everything they have. Wild bulls can approach a tonne. Domestic bulls are usually lighter, but nobody would want to stand between them.

Ash was the one who started to win. I could see it. Step by step, Smoke's hind legs gave ground, his hooves tearing long dark furrows in the turf. Five meters. Ten. Fifteen. The younger bull's neck was a cable. The older bull was sliding down the slope, and I heard myself whisper, "He's losing."

"Don't watch the winner," Dorje said, so calmly that I almost didn't hear it. "Watch the one who loses."

So I watched.

At around fifteen meters, Smoke did something I had not expected. He did not panic. He did not turn and bolt. He simply stopped resisting, twisted his head sideways, broke the lock, and walked away. Not a run. A walk. His tail was relaxed. A minute later he was grazing, as if the last six minutes had been a mild disagreement about where to stand.

Ash stood where the contact had ended, sides heaving, mouth open, flecks of foam on his chin. He raised his head and grunted at the empty air, a victory speech with no audience. Then his legs folded and he lay down in the grass, breathing like a bellows.

"Ash won the ground," Dorje said. "Now count what it cost him."

I looked at the two bulls. One lying down, panting at 4,500 meters. One eating.

"The yak that gets pushed backward," Dorje said, "is often the one that wins. Not today. Not on the grass. But in the long season. That is what my father told me. I never knew why. I only know it is true."

I wanted to argue. That is my default setting. But I had just lost a fourteen-month contract by refusing to move an inch, so I closed my mouth, finished my tea, and decided to find out why.

PART FOUR: THE SCIENTIST BY THE STREAM

The why arrived the next morning in the form of a field ecologist named Lin, who was camping beside a stream half a kilometer below Dorje's tent. She was studying how domestic herds and wild grazers share the high pastures, and she carried binoculars, a notebook with a cracked waterproof cover, and the permanent squint of someone who counts animals for a living.

I told her what Dorje had said. She laughed, not unkindly.

"Dorje is half right," she said. "And the half he's right about has been studied for fifty years."

She pulled out the notebook and drew two stick figures. One she labeled Hawk. One she labeled Dove.

"In 1973, John Maynard Smith and George Price published a paper in Nature called 'The Logic of Animal Conflict.' It started with a question that had bothered biologists for a long time. Why do so many animals fight with ritual instead of with everything they have? If winning is everything, shouldn't evolution produce killers?"

"And?"

"Imagine a population where every animal is a Hawk. Always escalate, always fight to injury. Whenever two Hawks meet, one wins the resource and the other pays the cost of injury. Now put a number on it. Say the resource is worth ten points. Say serious injury costs thirty."

She wrote the numbers on the page. "Two Hawks meeting would each average five points of benefit and fifteen points of damage. Negative. A Hawk among Hawks loses on average. Now add a Dove, who displays, then retreats if the other escalates. A Dove among Hawks gets nothing, but it never gets hurt. That beats a negative number. The model says that when the cost of fighting is larger than the prize, the stable outcome is a mixture, and in this example only one animal in three should be fighting all out."

I stared at the page. "That is the contract."

"I'm sorry?"

"Nothing. Keep going."

She did. And as she talked, two rules assembled themselves in my head, the first two of the six I would eventually write on the inside cover of that cracked notebook she lent me.

RULE ONE: KNOW WHAT THE GRASS IS WORTH.

Every fight has a prize and a price, and the mistake that wrecks careers, marriages and friendships is paying a price that is bigger than the prize. The Hawk-Dove model is not about being gentle. It is arithmetic. If the thing you are defending is worth ten and the fight costs thirty, winning is a loss with better public relations. Before you push, write down two numbers: what you gain if you win, and what you lose in the process. I never wrote down either number on that Tuesday in July. The payment terms change was worth maybe two points to the client and nothing to me, and my stubbornness cost four hundred thousand dollars a year.

RULE TWO: ASSESS BEFORE YOU COLLIDE.

"Animals are not stupid about this," Lin said. "Look at red deer on the Isle of Rum in Scotland. Tim Clutton-Brock and Steve Albon studied them for years. Stags don't just crash antlers. First they roar, and the roaring is an honest signal, because roaring is exhausting. Then, if the roaring is a draw, they walk side by side in parallel, sizing each other up. Only if both are still unconvinced do they lock antlers. Most contests end long before the antlers touch, because the information has already been exchanged."

She tapped the page. "Fighting is the last step of assessment, not the first. And it's dangerous. Antler and horn contests cause real injuries, and in many species a serious wound in the rut can mean a death sentence by winter."

I thought about the glass room and the slide titled Non-Negotiable. I had skipped every step of assessment. I had never asked the procurement chief what the forty-five days were really about. I walked in with my chart and the confidence of an animal that has never been wounded.

"Rule two," I wrote. "Roar first. Walk parallel. Find out what the other side is really fighting for. Only then push."

Lin watched me write and raised an eyebrow. "You know that's not Dorje's point yet."

"What is Dorje's point?"

"Wait for the weather," she said.

PART FIVE: THE NIGHT THE SKY CHANGED ITS MIND

The storm arrived on my fifth night, in July, because the plateau does not care about the calendar.

It began as a smear of dark cloud over the western ridge and ended as hail the size of peas hammering the tent canvas so hard I could not hear my own voice. The temperature fell from a pleasant afternoon to below freezing in under two hours. Up here, summer is a rumor and winter is a permanent resident.

Dorje shook me awake before the worst of it. "Come. Look. Bring the lamp."

We stood at the tent flap and watched the herd do something that I think about almost every day now. The yaks had gathered into a tight bunch, rumps to the wind, calves in the middle, hail bouncing off their long dark skirts of hair. Yaks wear a double coat: coarse outer hair that hangs almost to the ground and a fine, soft undercoat that people on the plateau have spun and woven for centuries. In weather like this, the coat is a house.

Smoke was in the middle of the bunch. Warm, protected, dry. He was eating hay Dorje had thrown out at dusk, chewing slowly, eyes half closed.

Ash was at the edge.

He stood outside the circle, facing the wind alone, head low, ribs visible under the wet coat. In the lamplight I could see a long gouge across his shoulder where a horn had raked him during the fight, now dark with crusted blood and rain. He was shivering. And he was not eating. He had spent the day trying to defend the ground he had won from three other young bulls, and the grass he had spent his day defending had gone unchewed.

"Count it," Dorje said.

I counted. A bull that spends the day fighting does not spend the day eating. At this altitude every breath of air is expensive, and every shove burns oxygen the body cannot spare.

Lin explained it to me the next morning, over a stove that refused to light until the third try. "In many large hoofed animals, males lose a startling amount of body weight during the rut. They fight, they patrol, they guard females, and they barely eat. Bison, elk, red deer, they all do it. Biologists call it the cost of reproduction, and it is one of the best-documented trade-offs in life history. Energy you spend on today's contest is energy you cannot spend on tomorrow's winter. And on this plateau, winter is not a metaphor. Temperatures can drop far below minus twenty."

RULE THREE: ENERGY IS THE ONLY CURRENCY IN THIN AIR.

Every plateau has a thin-air version. For yaks it is literal. For me, it was the attention I burned on a fight I should have settled in one sentence. For you, it might be the group chat you reply to at midnight, the colleague you correct in every meeting, the argument you are winning right now at the expense of a night's sleep. Your day contains a fixed number of good breaths. Spend them on the grass that feeds you through the winter, not on proving you can push a stranger fifteen meters.

Lin's second point came as she poured me a cup of something that tasted of smoke and tea. "Now the part Dorje won't say because he doesn't have the vocabulary. In biology, animals that lose a contest and take damage are often more likely to lose the next one. Researchers call this the loser effect. A review by Hsu, Earley and Wolf in 2006 pulled together evidence across species from crickets to mice. The effects are real, though how strong they are varies a lot, and the cause is usually injury and stress."

"So losing is bad."

"Losing badly is bad. Being pushed fifteen meters isn't injury. Smoke went home without a scratch. Ash went home with a hole in his shoulder."

RULE FOUR: A RETREAT YOU CHOOSE IS NOT A DEFEAT.

Smoke did not lose that fight. He ended it. The difference is everything. A chosen retreat leaves your body, your reputation, and your options intact. A forced collapse leaves you wounded and talked about. I had not retreated in that glass room. I had been carried out, on a stretcher of my own pride, and I walked home with a wound the size of a contract. Next time, I will end the contest at the point where the cost starts to outrun the prize, and I will do it with my tail relaxed.

I thought about Smoke's walk. His relaxed tail. The way he started grazing before the dust had settled. He had not looked beaten. He had looked finished.

PART SIX: THE SECOND FIGHT

On the eighth day, the herd gave me the rest of the lesson.

By then Ash had recovered some strength, but not enough. His coat was dull, his shoulder wound had scabbed over, and the weight he had lost showed along his ribs. A third bull, a stocky brown animal Dorje called Stone, who had been grazing quietly all week and had not fought anyone, strolled toward him in the late afternoon.

I knew what was coming. So did Ash. But he had a reputation to defend, so he lowered his head and met the challenge.

It lasted less than two minutes. Stone, fresh and fed, pushed Ash back thirty meters and left him bleeding at the edge of the slope. This time there was no dignity in the ending. Ash limped away with his head down, and the herd closed over the gap he left like water.

Smoke watched the whole thing from fifty meters off, chewing.

That evening, I put my theory to Lin, who had come up to share a pot of Dorje's tea. "So Dorje is right. The bull who yields wins."

"Careful," she said, and I could hear the scientist rebuilding her fences. "That is a pattern, not a law. In plenty of species, dominant males sire more offspring. Rank matters. A male who never fights never mates. Smoke is not winning because he avoids fighting. He is winning because he chooses which fights are worth their price. He fights when the cost is low and the prize is real. He yields when the cost is high and the prize is grass."

"Is there a name for that?"

"Several. Game theorists call it a conditional strategy, behavior that depends on the situation. Behavioral ecologists talk about life-history trade-offs, the balance between spending now and surviving later. Dorje calls it Tuesday." She smiled at her own joke, which I had never told her I'd understand.

"So what is the thing worth more than the grass?"

"Your body," Lin said. "Your next season. The version of you that is still standing in the spring."

RULE FIVE: KEEP YOUR FEET EVEN WHEN YOU GIVE GROUND.

I had been so focused on the retreat that I had missed something Dorje had pointed out on the second day. Smoke had been pushed fifteen meters back, but he never went down. Yaks stand on broad, tough hooves with sharp rims, built for loose turf and rocky ground. A yak's center of gravity is low, its head sits below its shoulders, and its legs are planted like the pillars of a bridge. You can push a yak backward, but it is very hard to topple one.

Position is negotiable. Footing is not. Smoke gave up fifteen meters of slope and kept every bit of his balance, and that is why the retreat cost him nothing. When I think about my career now, I ask two questions. What am I willing to yield, and what do I refuse to lose? Payment terms are slope. My integrity, my health, and my relationships are footing. I had defended the slope with my life and almost lost my footing in the process.

RULE SIX: THE HERD KEEPS SCORE, AND IT REMEMBERS HOW YOU FOUGHT.

On my last night, Dorje told me something that seemed small at the time and turned out to be the biggest thing I carried down the mountain.

"Smoke has not fought for three seasons," he said. "Not because he is afraid. The herd knows him. When he walks, they move. When he grunts, they listen. He fought a hundred fights when he was young. Now he doesn't need to."

This is not just a herder's observation. In the 1920s, the Norwegian zoologist Thorleif Schjelderup-Ebbe described the pecking order in chickens, the first detailed account of a dominance hierarchy. Since then, researchers have found stable social rankings in cattle, horses, primates, wolves, and countless other social species. The function is the same everywhere: settle conflicts once so that you do not have to settle them again every day. A reputation is a fight you only have to win once.

Think about what a herd learns from a single contest. It learns who fights fair. It learns who overpays for small prizes. It learns who stays calm when the ground shifts. Ash's loss to Stone mattered less than the way Ash fought it: tired, wounded, defending a rank he could no longer afford. Every animal on that slope updated its map of him.

Your reputation works the same way. People rarely remember the small concession you made in a negotiation. They remember whether you fought like someone who was afraid or like someone who was in control.

PART SEVEN: GOING BACK DOWN

I left on the tenth day. Dorje walked me to the edge of the pasture with a stick in one hand and his bad knee announcing every step. At the last rise, he stopped, looked at the herd below us, and said the only piece of advice he would ever give me directly.

"A yak does not push to win. He pushes to learn what he needs to know. When he knows, he stops."

I carried the notebook down the mountain with six rules in it and a lot of headache medicine in my bloodstream.

Three weeks later, my director called me into the same glass room. The same procurement chief had agreed to one more meeting, not because I had asked, but because I had sent her a short, honest email saying that I had pushed too hard and wanted to understand what the forty-five days were really about.

It turned out the forty-five days were about her own company's quarterly cash cycle. They had nothing to do with our price and everything to do with her calendar. Once I understood that, the answer was almost embarrassingly simple. We gave her the forty-five days. In exchange, we asked for a three-year term instead of a one-year term, and a small volume commitment. She signed in twenty minutes.

I gave ground on the slope and kept my footing. The contract was worth a little more than the one I had lost. I did not tell my director about the yaks. He would have laughed. Or worse, he would have asked for the slides.

But on the drive home that evening I realized something that has stayed with me ever since. I had been wrong about what winning looks like. I thought it looked like Ash, panting in the grass with his victory speech to nobody. It looks like Smoke, walking away with his tail relaxed and his shoulders intact, already chewing, already on to the next thing.

THE SIX RULES, IN ONE PLACE

1. Know what the grass is worth. Before any fight, write down the prize and the price. The Hawk-Dove model shows that when the cost of fighting exceeds the prize, all-out aggression is a losing strategy on average.

2. Assess before you collide. Red deer roar and walk in parallel before they lock antlers, and most contests end before contact. Gather information first, and fight last.

3. Energy is the only currency in thin air. In many large mammals, males lose a large share of body mass during the rut. At 4,500 meters, with air pressure near 58 percent of sea level, every wasted effort costs more.

4. A retreat you choose is not a defeat. Animals that suffer injury and defeat can be more likely to lose later contests, so exit on your terms before the damage, not after.

5. Keep your feet even when you give ground. Yield position, never footing. Smoke lost fifteen meters and kept his balance, and that is why the retreat cost him nothing.

6. The herd keeps score. Dominance hierarchies, from chickens to cattle, exist so that conflicts get settled once. Your reputation is the sum of how you fought, not how many fights you won.

Biology has a name for what Smoke did on that slope. Several names, actually: a conditional strategy, a life-history trade-off, an evolutionarily stable choice between the hawk and the dove. Dorje has a shorter one.

He calls it knowing which grass is yours.

The yak that gets pushed backward in this fight is often the one that wins. Not because it is weak. Because it knows exactly what it is protecting, and it is not the patch of grass.

Save this for the next time you feel the urge to win an argument you cannot afford.

AFTERWORD: WHAT THE SCIENCE DOES AND DOES NOT SAY

The characters in this story are invented, but the biology is real, and it deserves honest edges. Dominance matters: in many species, high-ranking males do father more offspring, so yielding is never automatically smart. The Hawk-Dove numbers above are a teaching example, not measurements taken from yaks. Winner and loser effects vary widely between species and situations. And nobody can promise that a yak who walks away from a push will outlive the one who wins it.

What the research does support is narrower and more useful: contests are costly, animals gather information before they escalate, and the choice to fight or yield depends on what is at stake. Domestic yaks number roughly fourteen million, most of them in China, and the people who live beside them on the high plateau have spent thousands of years reading exactly these signals. That patience is worth borrowing.

If you take only one thing from the slope, take the question Dorje asked every morning before breakfast: what am I actually protecting today? Most days, the honest answer is smaller than the fight you were about to pick.

November 5 Saints Zachary (Zechariah,Zacharias, Zaccaria, Zakariya) and Elizabeth, parents of Saint John the Baptist.
Patronage: Saint Elizabeth:
expectant mothers
Fulda, Germany, diocese of
pregnant women
Patronage: Saint Zachary: expectant mothers.
.
Little is known about either saint, with the exception that they were of advanced age upon conceiving and bearing the cousin of Jesus, the Forerunner of the Son of Justice, Saint John the Baptist. Though all we know of them is recorded in the Gospel of Luke (chapter 1), detailing Our Blessed Mother’s visitation to her kinswoman, Elizabeth, given the honor bestowed upon them by the Lord we can be certain of their piety, strength of character, and love.
.
[5] There was in the days of Herod, the king of Judea, a certain priest named Zachary, of the course of Abia; and his wife was of the daughters of Aaron, and her name Elizabeth.
[6] And they were both just before God, walking in all the commandments and justifications of the Lord without blame. [7] And they had no son, for that Elizabeth was barren, and they both were well advanced in years. [8] And it came to pass, when he executed the priestly function in the order of his course before God, [9] According to the custom of the priestly office, it was his lot to offer incense, going into the temple of the Lord. [10] And all the multitude of the people was praying without, at the hour of incense.
[11] And there appeared to him an angel of the Lord, standing on the right side of the alter of incense. [12] And Zachary seeing him, was troubled, and fear fell upon him. [13] But the angel said to him: Fear not, Zachary, for thy prayer is heard; and thy wife Elizabeth shall bear thee a son, and thou shalt call his name John: [14] And thou shalt have joy and gladness, and many shall rejoice in his nativity. [15] For he shall be great before the Lord; and shall drink no wine nor strong drink: and he shall be filled with the Holy Ghost, even from his mother' s womb.
[16] And he shall convert many of the children of Israel to the Lord their God. [17] And he shall go before him in the spirit and power of Elias; that he may turn the hearts of the fathers unto the children, and the incredulous to the wisdom of the just, to prepare unto the Lord a perfect people. [18] And Zachary said to the angel: Whereby shall I know this? for I am an old man, and my wife is advanced in years. [19] And the angel answering, said to him: I am Gabriel, who stand before God: and am sent to speak to thee, and to bring thee these good tidings. [20] And behold, thou shalt be dumb, and shalt not be able to speak until the day wherein these things shall come to pass, because thou hast not believed my words, which shall be fulfilled in their time.
[21] And the people were waiting for Zachary; and they wondered that he tarried so long in the temple. [22] And when he came out, he could not speak to them: and they understood that he had seen a vision in the temple. And he made signs to them, and remained dumb. [23] And it came to pass, after the days of his office were accomplished, he departed to his own house. [24] And after those days, Elizabeth his wife conceived, and hid herself five months, saying: [25] Thus hath the Lord dealt with me in the days wherein he hath had regard to take away my reproach among men.(Luke 1: 5-25)
.
Following Our Blessed Mother’s visit from the Archangel Gabriel, and her acceptance of the will of the Lord, she left her home and traveled alone, at great peril, to visit Elizabeth.
.
[39] And Mary rising up in those days, went into the hill country with haste into a city of Juda. [40] And she entered into the house of Zachary, and saluted Elizabeth.
[41] And it came to pass, that when Elizabeth heard the salutation of Mary, the infant leaped in her womb. And Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Ghost: [42] And she cried out with a loud voice, and said: Blessed art thou among women, and blessed is the fruit of thy womb. [43] And whence is this to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me? [44] For behold as soon as the voice of thy salutation sounded in my ears, the infant in my womb leaped for joy. [45] And blessed art thou that hast believed, because those things shall be accomplished that were spoken to thee by the Lord.
[56] And Mary abode with her about three months; and she returned to her own house.
(Luke 1: 39-45, 56)
.
Following Mary’s departure, Elizabeth gave birth to Saint John the Baptist, and Zachary was so filled with the Holy Spirit, he sang of song of prophesy and praise!
.
[57] Now Elizabeth' s full time of being delivered was come, and she brought forth a son. [58] And her neighbours and kinsfolks heard that the Lord had shewed his great mercy towards her, and they congratulated with her. [59] And it came to pass, that on the eighth day they came to circumcise the child, and they called him by his father' s name Zachary. [60] And his mother answering, said: Not so; but he shall be called John.
[61] And they said to her: There is none of thy kindred that is called by this name. [62] And they made signs to his father, how he would have him called. [63] And demanding a writing table, he wrote, saying: John is his name. And they all wondered. [64] And immediately his mouth was opened, and his tongue loosed, and he spoke, blessing God. [65] And fear came upon all their neighbours; and all these things were noised abroad over all the hill country of Judea.
[66] And all they that had heard them laid them up in their heart, saying: What an one, think ye, shall this child be? For the hand of the Lord was with him. [67] And Zachary his father was filled with the Holy Ghost; and he prophesied, saying: [68] Blessed be the Lord God of Israel; because he hath visited and wrought the redemption of his people: [69] And hath raised up an horn of salvation to us, in the house of David his servant: [70] As he spoke by the mouth of his holy prophets, who are from the beginning:
[69] Horn of salvation: That is, A powerful salvation, as Dr. Witham translates it. For in the Scripture, by horn is generally understood strength and power.
[71] Salvation from our enemies, and from the hand of all that hate us: [72] To perform mercy to our fathers, and to remember his holy testament, [73] The oath, which he swore to Abraham our father, that he would grant to us, [74] That being delivered from the hand of our enemies, we may serve him without fear, [75] In holiness and justice before him, all our days.
[76] And thou, child, shalt be called the prophet of the Highest: for thou shalt go before the face of the Lord to prepare his ways: [77] To give knowledge of salvation to his people, unto the remission of their sins: [78] Through the bowels of the mercy of our God, in which the Orient from on high hath visited us: [79] To enlighten them that sit in darkness, and in the shadow of death: to direct our feet into the way of peace. [80] And the child grew, and was strengthened in spirit; and was in the deserts until the day of his manifestation to Israel.
(Luke 1: 57-80)
.
The name Elizabeth, which has been borne by several saints, means in Hebrew "worshiper of God." We can be certain of this truth as she has the distinction of being one of the first to know about Mary's great blessing as the Mother of God. A descendant of the priestly line of Aaron, she was a kinswoman—how close we are not told—of the Virgin Mary. According to the Gospel, Elizabeth had lived a blameless life with her husband in one of the hill-towns of Judea: “righteous in the eyes of God, observing all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord blamelessly.” However, having reached an advanced age with her prayers for a son unanswered, she thought that her barrenness was a reproach. Following the miraculous conception, and Zachary’s visit from Saint Gabriel, Elizabeth is visited by Our Blessed Mother, and realizes the great honor and task that the Lord has set before her. The Gospel story tells us further that at Elizabeth's delivery her friends and neighbors rejoiced with her, and when the child was brought to be circumcised, they were going to call him after his father Zachary, but his mother said, "His name shall be John."
.
Saint Zachary, whose name in Hebrew means “Jehovah hath remembered,” served as the High Priest in the Temple of Jerusalem, and had also lived an honorable and pious life. However, he was mocked and questioned by some, due to the fact that he had never produced a son. Following his visit from Saint Gabriel, Zachary was struck dumb, and his speech was not restored until he concurred with his wife’s assertion that their child be named John, despite no one of that name coming from their lineage.
.
Tradition, supported by Saint Basil and Cyril of Alexandria, asserts that when Herod set out to kill the Christ, he heard of the special circumstances surrounding Saint John's birth and tried to hunt him down. Saint Elizabeth took John, who was 18 months old, into the wilderness. They came to a mountain, and she spoke to it and a cave opened in it with a fresh stream and a fruitful date palm sprang up at its mouth. She escaped Herod's men by hiding in the cave. Saint Zachary died a martyr, killed in the Temple "between the porch and the altar" by command of Herod, because he refused to disclose the whereabouts of his son. Holy legend continues to tell us that the blood spilled in his martyrdom turned to stone as testimony against the reign of Herod. As the Roman Martyrology does not report this incident, it is unclear as the circumstances of this holy couple’s lives and deaths.
.
The lives of Saints Elizabeth and Zachary were lives of dedication to the Lord, faith in His ways, and hope in His love. Despite their advanced age, their disappointment in not conceiving a child, and the mockery they endured from their neighbors, both Zachary and Elizabeth continued to place their faith and trust in the Lord… and were rewarded by bringing forth the Precursor to Jesus, Saint John the Baptist. What might we accomplish if we look to the Lord with faith, hope, and confidence, rather than clinging to our doubts?
.
Eternal Father, I wish to honor Saints Zachary and Elizabeth, and I give Thee thanks for all the graces Thou hast bestowed upon them. I ask Thee to please increase grace in my soul through the merits of this saint, and I commit the end of my life to them by this special prayer, so that by virtue of Thy goodness and promise, Saints Zachary and Elizabeth might be my advocate and provide whatever is needed at that hour. Amen.

text:
leave your gift there before the altar, and go your way. First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift
Matthew 5:24

The altar stood in the Temple as the appointed place for presenting sacrifices to God. Jesus directs the worshiper to interrupt even a sacred offering when he remembers that another person has a legitimate grievance against him. God is not honored by outward devotion joined to a refusal to pursue peace and righteousness.

Reconciliation receives immediate priority. The worshiper must take the initiative, even when the offense may not have begun with him. Love for God is inseparable from love for one’s neighbor, and the disciple’s pursuit of peace reflects the character of the God he worships. The command fulfills the righteousness God required throughout Scripture, including the call to love one’s neighbor and seek justice rather than offer empty ritual.

The worshiper is to return and complete the offering after seeking peace. Jesus does not dismiss worship or sacrifice; He orders worship according to God’s priorities. A reconciled heart does not earn acceptance before God, but genuine devotion to God produces humility, repentance, forgiveness, and earnest efforts to restore broken relationships.

text:
De Invocatione, Veneratione, et Reliquiis Sanctorum, et Sacris Imaginibus.: On the Invocation, Veneration, and Relics of Saints, and on Sacred Images:  Council of Trent, Session XXV.
.
The holy Synod enjoins on all bishops, and others who sustain the office and charge of teaching, that, agreeably to the usage of the Catholic and Apostolic Church, received from the primitive times of the Christian religion, and agreeably to the consent of the holy Fathers, and to the decrees of sacred Councils, they especially instruct the faithful diligently concerning the intercession and invocation of saints; the honor [paid] to relics; and the legitimate use of images: teaching them, that the saints, who reign together with Christ, offer up their own prayers to God for men; that it is good and useful suppliantly to invoke them, and to have recourse to their prayers, aid, [and] help for obtaining benefits from God, through his Son, Jesus Christ our Lord, who is our alone Redeemer and Saviour; but that they think impiously who deny that the saints, who enjoy eternal happiness in heaven, are to be invocated; or who assert either that they do not pray for men; or that the invocation of them to pray for each of us even in particular is idolatry; or that it is repugnant to the Word of God, and is opposed to the honor of the one mediator of God and men, Christ Jesus;263 or that it is foolish to supplicate, vocally or mentally, those who reign in heaven.
.
Also, that the holy bodies of holy martyrs, and of others now living with Christ,—which bodies were the living members of Christ, and the temple of the Holy Ghost,264 and which are by him to be raised unto eternal life, and to be glorified,—are to be venerated by the faithful; through which [bodies] many benefits are bestowed by God on men; so that they who affirm that veneration and honor are not due to the relics of saints; or that these, and other sacred monuments, are uselessly honored by the faithful; and that the places dedicated to the memories of the saints are in vain visited with the view of obtaining their aid, are wholly to be condemned, as the Church has already long since condemned, and now also condemns them.
.
Moreover, that the images of Christ, of the Virgin Mother of God, and of the other saints, are to be had and retained particularly in temples, and that due honor and veneration are to be given them; not that any divinity, or virtue, is believed to be in them, on account of which they are to be worshipped; or that any thing is to be asked of them; or that trust is to be reposed in images, as was of old done by the Gentiles, who placed their hope in idols; but because the honor which is shown them is referred to the prototypes which those images represent; in such wise that by the images which we kiss, and before which we uncover the head, and prostrate ourselves, we adore Christ, and we venerate the saints, whose similitude they bear: as, by the decrees of Councils, and especially of the second Synod of Nicæa, has been defined against the opponents of images.
.
And the bishops shall carefully teach this,—that, by means of the histories of the mysteries of our Redemption, portrayed by paintings or other representations, the people is instructed, and confirmed in [the habit of] remembering, and continually revolving in mind the articles of faith; as also that great profit is derived from all sacred images, not only because the people are thereby admonished of the benefits and gifts bestowed upon them by Christ, but also because the miracles which God has performed by means of the saints, and their salutary examples, are set before the eyes of the faithful; that so they may give God thanks for those things; may order their own lives and manners in imitation of the saints; and may be excited to adore and love God, and to cultivate piety. But if any one shall teach or entertain sentiments contrary to these decrees: let him be anathema.
.
And if any abuses have crept in amongst these holy and salutary observances, the holy Synod ardently desires that they be utterly abolished; in such wise that no images [suggestive] of false doctrine, and furnishing occasion of dangerous error to the uneducated, be set up. And if at times, when expedient for the unlettered people, it happen that the facts and narratives of sacred Scripture are portrayed and represented, the people shall be taught, that not thereby is the Divinity represented, as though it could be seen by the eyes of the body, or be portrayed by colors or figures.
.
Moreover, in the invocation of saints, the veneration of relics, and the sacred use of images, every superstition shall be removed, all filthy lucre be abolished; finally, all lasciviousness be avoided; in such wise that figures shall not be painted or adorned with a beauty exciting to lust; nor the celebration of the saints and the visitation of relics be by any perverted into revelings and drunkenness; as if festivals were celebrated to the honor of the saints by luxury and wantonness.
.
In fine, let so great care and diligence be used herein by bishops, as that there be nothing seen that is disorderly, or that is unbecomingly or confusedly arranged, nothing that is profane, nothing indecorous, seeing that holiness becometh the house of God.
.
And that these things may be the more faithfully observed, the holy Synod ordains, that no one be allowed to place, or cause to be placed, any unusual image, in any place or church, howsoever exempted, except that image has been approved of by the bishop; also, that no new miracles are to be acknowledged, or new relics recognized, unless the said bishop has taken cognizance and approved thereof; who, as soon as he has obtained some certain information in regard of these matters, shall, after having taken the advice of theologians, and of other pious men, act therein as he shall judge to be consonant with truth and piety. But if any doubtful or difficult abuse has to be extirpated; or, in fine, if any more grave question shall arise touching these matters, the bishop, before deciding the controversy, shall await the sentence of the metropolitan and of the bishops of the province, in a provincial Council; yet so that nothing new, or that previously has not been usual in the Church, shall be resolved on without having first consulted the most holy Roman Pontiff.
