text:
Nov. 5 Feast of the Holy Relics from the Liturgical Year, 1901
.
Had we Angels' eyes, we should see the earth as a vast field sown with seed for the resurrection. The death of Abel opened the first furrow, and ever since, the sowing has gone on unceasingly the wide world over. This land of labour and of suffering, what treasures it already holds laid up in its bosom! And what a harvest for heaven, when the Sun of Justice, suddenly darting forth his rays, shall cause to spring up as suddenly from the soil the elect ears ripe for glory! No wonder that the Church herself blesses and superintends the laying of the precious grain in the earth.
.
But the Church is not content to be always sowing. Sometimes, as though impatient of delay, she raises from the ground the chosen seed she had sown therein. Her infallible discernment preserves her from error; and, disengaging from the soil the immortal germ, she forestalls the glory of the future. She encloses the treasure in gold or precious stuffs, carries it in triumph, invites the multitudes to come and reverence it; or she raises new temples to the name of the blessed one, and assigns him the highest honour of reposing under the Altar, whereon she offers to God the tremendous Sacrifice.
.
"Let your charity understand," explains St. Augustine (Aug. Sermo cccxviii, de Stephano Mart. V): "it is not to Stephen we raise an altar in this place; but of Stephen's relics we make an altar to God. God loves these altars; and if you ask the reason: Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints (Ps. cxv, 15)." In obedience to God "the invisible soul has quitted its visible dwelling. But God preserves this dwelling; He is glorified by the honour we pay to this lifeless flesh; and, clothing it with the might of His divinity, He gives it the power of working miracles (Aug. Sermo cclxxv, de Vincentio Mart. II)." Hence the origin of pilgrimages to the shrines of the Saints.
.
"Christian people," says St. Gregory of Nyssa, "wherefore are you assembled here? A tomb has no attractions; nay, the sight of its contents inspires horror. Yet, see what eagerness to approach this sepulchre! So great an object of desire is it, that a little of the dust from around it is esteemed a gift of great price. As to beholding the remains it conceals, that is a rare favour, and an enviable one, as those can testify who enjoy the privilege: they embrace the holy body as though it were yet alive, they press their lips and their eyes upon it, shedding tears of love and devotion. What emperor ever received such honour (Greg. Nyss. de Theodoro Mart)?"
.
"Emperors!" rejoins St. John Chrysostom; "as the porters at their gates, such have they become with regard to poor fishers. The son of the great Constantine deemed he could not pay a higher honour to his father, than to procure him a place of sepulture in the porch of the fisherman of Galilee (Chrys. in Epist. II. ad Cor. Hom. xxvi)." And again, concluding his commentary on St. Paul's admirable Epistle to the Romans, the golden-mouthed Doctor exclaims: "And now, who will grant me to prostrate myself at Paul's sepulchre, to contemplate the ashes of that body which, suffering for us, filled up what was wanting of the sufferings of Christ? The dust of that mouth, which spoke boldly before kings, and, showing what Paul was, revealed the Lord of Paul? The dust of that heart, truly the heart of the world, more lofty than the heavens, more vast than the universe, as much the heart of Christ as of Paul, and wherein might be read the book of grace, graven by the Holy Spirit? Oh! that I might see the remains of the hands, which wrote those Epistles; of the eyes, which were struck with blindness and recovered their sight for our salvation; of the feet which traversed the whole earth! Yes; I would fain contemplate the tomb where repose these instruments of justice and of light, these members of Christ, this temple of the Holy Ghost. O venerable body, which, together with that of Peter, protects Rome more securely than all ramparts (Chrys. in Epist. ad Rom. Hom. xxxii)!"
.
In spite of such teachings as these, the heretics of the sixteenth century profaned the tombs of the Saints, under pretext of bringing us back to the doctrine of our forefathers. In contradiction to these strange reformers, the Council of Trent expressed the unanimous testimony of Tradition in the following definition, which sets forth the theological reasons of the honour paid by the Church to the relics of Saints:
.
"Veneration ought to be shown by the faithful to the bodies of the Martyrs and other Saints, who live with Jesus Christ. For they were His living members and the temples of the Holy Ghost; He will raise them up again to eternal life and glory; and through them God grants many blessings to mankind. Therefore, those who say that the relics of the Saints are not worthy of veneration, that it is useless for the faithful to honour them, that it is vain to visit the memorials or monuments of the Saints in order to obtain their aid, are absolutely to be condemned; and, as they have already been long ago condemned (Conc. Nic. II. cap. vii), the Church now condemns "them once more (Conc. Tird. Sess. xxv. De invocatione, veneratione et reliquiis Sanctorum)."
.
Prayer:
.
Amen, Amen, I say to you, he that believeth in Me, the works that I do he also shall do, and greater than these shall he do (St. John xiv. 12)! Our Lord was speaking of His Saints and disciples, who would believe in Him so fully as to place their earthly happiness in poverty, hunger, mourning, and persecution. His word was to be accomplished in them during life; but frequently it was to be still more manifested after death, in the power retained by their relics of driving away demons, healing all diseases, and obtaining every grace. It is not only from the narrow province of Judaea, but from the coasts of the entire world, that multitudes now flock to hear the saints in the silent eloquence of their tombs, and to experience the virtue that goes out from them.
.
St. Paulinus of Nola thus speaks in his poems: "God, in His goodness, has willed that the Saints should be distributed among the nations, so that their aid might never be wanting to us weak mortals. If He has given the principal cities to the greatest Saints for their residence, the grace with which they are endowed for our sake is not confined to the places where their entire bodies rest; where there are but small portions, there is the same power, and God thus gives testimony to their credit in heaven. From the holy deposit the sacred ashes are scattered abroad, and become the seeds of life; let but the least drop be taken from the spring, and it is itself a source producing rivers of grace and of love (Paulin. Poem. xix, xxvii)."

On Nov. 5, the historic Longfu Temple in Beijing hosted a cultural event highlighting the Beijing Central Axis as part of the 7th World Media Summit.

Extending 7.8 km from Yongding Gate to the Bell and Drum Towers, the Central Axis traces its origins to the Yuan Dynasty (1271–1368) and links 15 heritage components. Added to the #UNESCO World Heritage List in July 2024, it reflects centuries of Chinese urban planning, while digital technologies and creative cultural experiences offer new ways to explore its history.

text:
Good morning Matrix. Good morning @grok. 

Dream log from last night. 

I was on the set of a television show. Everyone there, actors, writers, crew, was openly conservative. The scripts reflected it without apology or irony. It felt normal, almost ordinary, which is what made it strange. When I woke up I wrote it down, and the contrast with waking life was immediate.

The left still owns the commanding heights of entertainment. Not every project, not every writer, but the institutional default: the networks, the streamers, the awards bodies, the talent agencies, and the cultural assumptions that shape what gets greenlit. After the midterms I was burned out on pure politics. I still follow it, but the constant intensity stops being useful. I wanted something that didn’t treat every hour of screen time as a vehicle for the same set of messages.

Netflix and Disney+ largely failed that test. Paramount+ did not. Taylor Sheridan’s shows, Yellowstone and its universe, Tulsa King, the rest, still operate in a register where competence, loyalty, property, and consequences matter more than the prevailing checklist. Even the weaker entries in the set aren’t primarily interested in scoring points against half the country. That alone made them watchable when almost everything else felt like homework.

Plenty of people who vote never open a political newsletter or follow a primary. They still form judgments about what is normal, what is admirable, and what is ridiculous. Those judgments are shaped far more by what they stream at night than by any campaign ad. On that terrain MAGA has been consistently outgunned. The older figures who have spoken up, Hogan, Stallone, Tyson, carry real weight with their audiences, but they are not the voices shaping the next generation of viewers. There is a conspicuous shortage of younger talent willing to treat traditional assumptions about family, work, borders, or competence as anything other than a punchline.

Money helps, but it is not sufficient. The larger problem is that the industry’s risk models and social incentives still punish the wrong things. A show that treats rural Americans as intelligent, that lets characters keep what they earn, or that refuses to treat every institution as irredeemably corrupt until it is staffed by the correct people is treated as a provocation rather than ordinary storytelling. The result is a market that is underserved and a political movement that keeps discovering, after the fact, that culture moved the electorate before any ad buy did.

I’m a regular person with more free time than I used to have and a stack of injuries that keep me off any fixed schedule. I read, watch, and try to connect what I see. The entertainment gap is one of the clearer patterns. People who do not follow politics still vote. They absorb their sense of what is possible and what is ridiculous from the stories they are offered. Right now those stories remain heavily skewed. That is not a mystery, and it is not permanent, but it will not correct itself by complaint alone.

Friday. The market may or may not rebound; the people who watched the midterm results and reduced exposure were not being subtle. AI will happily give trading suggestions and then immediately disclaim them. None of that changes the basic observation from the dream: a fully conservative production set still feels like science fiction. It shouldn’t.

That's my morning monologue. Now on to the @VinceCoglianese show at 8am on Rumble. Join in the chat, good people in there. Then @hayleycaronia at noon. 

Have a good one.

text:
In Arkansas, a man will tell you his blood pressure and what he paid for his house, but not where he caught the fish.

At a gas station at 5:40 in the morning, a man in a camouflage cap asked my friend Lonnie where he'd been catching them.

"In the water," Lonnie said.

"What on?"

"Right in the lip."

Both men nodded as if information had changed hands. I wrote "in the water" in my notebook. It did not narrow things.

For eleven years Lonnie has told this county he fishes a place called Dry Cut. There is no Dry Cut. I checked a map. The name alone should have warned somebody, but two men at that station say they have fished it.

That morning I was being taken to the real one. His honey hole. It belongs to Lonnie and a man named Dewey, and a third person required a vote. It carried two to nothing, with conditions: I bring nobody, ever, and I never go alone without texting first. I offered to wear a blindfold. Lonnie thought about it longer than I expected.

He drove past the turn twice in case we were followed. In the boat he laid a hunting magazine over the screen that shows where you are. Out of habit I tried to memorize the route, and I believe he made four left turns in a row for my benefit.

I have read about castles with less procedure at the gate.

The spot was nothing to look at. Water the color of weak tea, one dead cypress, a heron that did not care about us. Lonnie cut the motor early and let us drift the last sixty yards.

When the first crappie came in, he scraped a few scales off it and flicked them onto the water.

"My uncle showed me that when I was eleven," he said. "Made me swear. I never showed anybody."

He did not say why he was showing me. He handed me his own rod and pointed at the cypress. I still don't know what the scales do.

We kept eleven. I was allowed one photograph, of the sky.

At 9:15 we were back at the gas station. A man looked into our cooler and then, for some reason, at me.

"Where'd you get into them?"

Lonnie said nothing. He watched me the way a father watches a recital.

"In the water," I said.

"What on?"

"Right in the lip."

The man nodded. Lonnie paid for my coffee.

"Thursday," he said in the parking lot. "Our spot. Bring nobody."

$SPX - Thursday’s selling spread beyond AI: the S&P 500 fell 4.4%, all 30 Dow stocks declined, and the Russell 2000 lost 4.5%. The Nasdaq 100 dropped 6.4%, momentum stocks lost 8.2%, and semiconductors plunged 12.3%. S&P 500 breadth statistics confirmed widespread risk reduction, with 430 index members in decline and only 73 stocks advancing, weakening the case for viewing the decline as a routine buying opportunity. December S&P futures rebounded just 0.21% to around 7,400 overnight.

The technical chart damage is certain, while fundamentals remain on track. The new Democratic governor of Texas confirmed that all permitted data centers will proceed with builds absent regulation, protecting the 2027 buildout and most of 2028. New permit restrictions will impact 2029 and after, seeking to preserve statewide investment and imposing only modest constraints for  self-sufficiency in power,  protection for Texas labor, but no major contraints. Meanwhile, nearly 70% of S&P companies have reported third quarter earnings, with blended earnings growth near 31% year-on-year. Finally, AI demand and semiconductor orders remain strong. The immediate threat of slower data center construction through state permitting and electricity constraints, may delaying revenues, but don’t explain the one-day tech sector decline of 8%. Reported hedge-fund unwinds may have amplified the decline, but there is no confirmation that forced selling has finished.

Stress remains elevated. The volatility index (VIX) jumped to 28.18, and is now 26.77, with near-term protection costing more than longer-dated protection. Rising high-yield credit spreads also suggest market volatility is not receding. Lower Treasury yields offer support, but today’s payrolls and wages could reverse that relief if they revive rate-hike expectations.

The futures price trend remains lower. The 200D MA  near 7,355 is immediate support, with a failure there pointing to the next support at 7,250. A retest of the up-trend failure points to a rally potential back to 7,535, the first resistance level. text:
The Great Laundry Strike of 1945 is a forgotten uprising for Irish women's working rights. In the summer of 1945, as the world celebrated the end of war and Ireland emerged from The Emergency, another battle was brewing in the steamy backrooms of Dublin’s commercial laundries. 

Around 1,500 women, most of them poor young Dubliners, worked in the city’s laundries. They were members of the Irish Women Workers’ Union (IWWU), an organisation that had fought for decades to give women a voice in the workplace. Laundries were grueling places full of scalding steam, backbreaking labour and endless piles of sheets from hotels, hospitals and barracks.

Many ladies began work before dawn, finishing late at night, for wages that barely covered food and rent. They stood for twelve hours a day, hands raw from bleach, hair singed from the heat. During the war years, with imports cut off and demand rising, the pace only grew harsher. When the IWWU demanded an extra week’s paid holiday, a modest recognition of the toll of their work. When the employers refused the women decided enough was enough.

The backdrop to this industrial struggle was darker still. Across Ireland, behind convent walls, stood the Magdalene Laundries, where so-called “fallen women” were confined and forced into unpaid labour. Their existence warped the economic landscape of the laundry trade. Commercial laundries, which at least paid wages, found themselves undercut by the religious institutions that could offer rock bottom prices through the exploitation of incarcerated women. In 1941, one Dublin laundry even lost a lucrative military contract to a Magdalene-run competitor, throwing 25 unionised workers onto the streets.

On the 21st of July 1945, the women of the IWWU walked out. Fourteen laundries were struck, and within days, Dublin’s hotels and restaurants began to feel the pinch. The Shelbourne, the Hibernian and the Gresham all found themselves short of crisp linens and clean uniforms. Hospital laundries were spared for obvious reasons, but the capital’s comfort was soon covered in creases.

For fourteen long weeks the strike dragged on. The Federated Union of Employers (FUE) stood firm, claiming that holidays were a matter for government legislation, not for negotiation. But the women held their line. Support flowed from other unions, from sympathetic shopkeepers and from the general public who saw in these women a quiet, unyielding dignity. They ran flag days, held fundraisers, and even lampooned The Irish Times columnists who dismissed them, until the paper softened its tone and began to print their side of the story.

It was not just a labour dispute, it was a revolution. These were women who had grown up in a state that preached modesty and obedience were finding the strenght in each other to stand up to employers, priests, and politicians alike. 

On the 30th of October, 1945, after fourteen weeks of hunger, hardship and solidarity, the employers gave in. The women of the laundries won two weeks’ paid annual leave. Within a year, their victory rippled outward. Other unions adopted the same demand, and soon, the fortnight’s paid holiday became standard across Ireland.

text:
60-second teacher: When private tuition is out of reach, AI steps in
The Indian state of Bihar is leading the push to bridge teacher shortages and improve access to learning for students from low-income backgrounds
Published 6 Nov, 2026
https://t.co/sUo8qZrhuz
Kajal Kumari, a 15-year-old in a government school in Patna, the capital of the northern Indian state of Bihar, can now do something unheard of for a government school student. She can open an app on her mobile phone and get connected with a live tutor within a minute.
Kajal comes from a small family where every penny counts, and excelling academically often means paying for private tuition. This is not rare in India, where education is generally not free. But in Bihar in particular, education expenses are often beyond what families can afford. The state is one of the poorest in the country, with a per capita income of around $384 – just 31.7% of the national average.
Kajal told RT that she was struggling to prepare for entrance exams without receiving private coaching, when a state-sponsored AI-enabled learning program came up.
“In our families, daily house expenses are difficult, and affording private tuition is out of the question),” Kajal told RT India.
She added that for students like her, getting a tutor online means getting help without the need to travel to bigger cities. “It is not possible for all of us to migrate for getting education.”
Driving the change
Bihar is leading this shift with the recently launched Vidya Saathi platform, which has already connected more than 300,000 secondary students to round-the-clock, AI-driven learning tools. It is a state-backed digital initiative managed by the Bihar School Examination Board in partnership with the Filo AI platform.
Speaking at a high-level departmental review meeting at the Bihar School Examination Board auditorium in Patna, Bihar’s education minister, Mithilesh Tiwari, said 73% of the students registered on the platform are from rural areas. He added that the government wants to make the education system in the state more technology-based, transparent, and secure.
The program is a great way to help students in public schools, a state education official who asked to remain anonymous said.
“We are talking about kids in classes 9 to 12 who can now get help anytime they need it. The program uses AI to make studying easier and also gives them access to live tutors. This means they can... prepare for big exams like the Joint Entrance Examination and National Eligibility Entrance Test right away,”the official explained. “The best part is that it’s all free and connected to school computer labs, so a kid from a small village can get the same kind of coaching that only kids in cities used to get.”
Currently rolled out across 700 model secondary schools in all 38 districts of the state, the program provides free one-on-one live tutoring for classes 9 and 10, as well as senior secondary science streams (classes 11 and 12). Through Filo’s AI-driven matching engine, a student can upload a textbook question and get connected via video to a live tutor in under 60 seconds.
“Getting help when you need it is the challenge of using AI in education,” Filo co-founder Rohit Kumar said. “We are using AI to link students with real teachers who can provide one-on-one help in just 60 seconds, anytime of the day or night. This way, a teacher can work through a problem with a student, figure out where they’re getting stuck, and explain it in a way that makes sense to them.”
Modi’s big bet on AI
AI adoption in Indian education is being driven from the highest levels. Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced a national initiative on August 15 to make competitive exam preparation free.
“Coaching classes burden the poor and middle class,” Modi said, pledging to deploy India’s digital public infrastructure to offer free online coaching and train 10 million young people in AI skills over the next year. The aim is to link teachers directly with students, removing the cost and distance barriers of private tuition.
The announcement came after weeks of student protests organized by the Cockroach Janta Party over examination malpractice, which ultimately forced the resignation of the education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, on July 25.
The nationwide protests highlighted the frustration of the public about the failure of systematic examinations and the expenses related to private competitive exam training.
India has one of the biggest and most complex education systems in the world, with 247 million students from 1.47 million schools. However, behind these figures lies a truly complex situation.
Although the secondary dropout rate on a national level is 12%, economically disadvantaged regions such as Bihar suffer from a dropout rate of up to 40% among students in grades 8 to 10 due to poverty, poor infrastructural conditions, low levels of literacy, and especially female illiteracy in rural areas.
“This fragile dynamic has become even more unstable due to problems with public trust in national exams. The massive student demonstrations that resulted from leaks of exam papers, corruption in the hiring process, and the resignation of the Union Education Minister revealed vulnerabilities in the exam system,” Charu Sri, a high school teacher in Bihar, said. He added that the issue of extortionate prices for private coaching classes makes many people wonder if this unfair system can still offer equal opportunities to all.
Across India’s most populous and economically strained heartlands, thousands of students in public schools always imagined private tutoring as a distant reality. AI is starting to shatter those barriers.
Modi reiterated the country’s focus to build AI momentum earlier this year when India hosted the India AI Impact Summit in New Delhi, which brought together over 20 heads of state and top technology executives like Sundar Pichai and Sam Altman.
Opening the summit under the vision of ‘Sarvajan Hitaya, Sarvajan Sukhaya’ (welfare for all, happiness for all), Modi outlined the MANAV framework (moral, accountable, national sovereignty, accessible, and valid), advocating that AI should serve as an inclusive global public good rather than a tool for commercial exploitation.
Supported by the $1.1 billion IndiaAI Mission and an active user base of 740 million people with smartphones, India is deploying AI to solve core public delivery challenges. In education, the impact is now felt at the grassroots level...link to read full article

text:
A Forecast of the Near Future:

As we close out this remarkable week, discussions are shifting to the impacts of the election on the lame duck, the new committees, and the topics of early bills and funding fights. I want to pan up out of the day to day business and offer some predictions on more macro aspects of politics. 

- The new Democratic Majorities that take power in January will not be divided primarily by ideology, whether someone is on the left or in the center. They will instead be divided by seniority. The chairs and their staffs will want to use this moment to achieve long held goals, such as root and branch oversight of corporate America, assuming the freshman will go along. This large freshman class will, like the freshman class after Watergate, realize they have their own different views and will resist being told what to do. In the end, the Chairs probably end up generals without an army. 

- There are few deals with the Trump Admin. The Trump WH is not cowed by the results and decides the midterms were a function of the MAGA base being betrayed. While blame is shifted early on (rightfully) to the Iran War as a cause, hardliners inside the WH successfully argue that the base was let down by the lack of more deportations. The WH is disinterested in doing deals with Democrats generally and there are multiple shutdowns. The public sees Washington again as broken. 

- The 2028 campaign for President starts early, with the first candidate to declare on the Dem side announcing an exploratory committee before Christmas. The Dems have a massive field, including one statewide elected official who only is sworn into office in January 2027. But unlike 2019, there is a clear S tier of just 3-4 people. The primary is less toxic and contentious than in 2019, as many in the party now realize the policy bidding war was a mistake and need infighting. The absence of Bernie, Biden, and Warren or clear successors to any of them makes the race less about the past and more about the future. On the GOP side, VP Vance chooses not to run but former Secretary of State Rubio does. He does a surprising challenge from the right on both the war and inadequate commitment to hardline immigration policy. The primary is short for the Dems and long for the GOP. 

- The next two years of politics are defined, after a short burst of focus on broad oversight, by AI, which continues to pick up speed. The need to have technical knowledge of the subject to do effective oversight and legislation on it favors younger members with less seniority in both parties, reducing the power of the Chairs and Rankers. Technical staff grow in value versus lawyers for the first time in a generation, and surprising “gangs” emerge in the Senate to tackle aspects of the topic for the first real time in a decade.  2028 is the AI election, marked by at least one spectacular hack of major infrastructure during the last 90 days. 

- When folks look back on our politics in 2030, it is clear to all that the Trump era, the Long 2016, ended on November 3, 2026, which also marked the end of the Dems long 2016 primary. 2029 also is the first year of an administration in which Dems do not feel compelled to fight over the choices of 2008-2009, whether they win or lose the election, marking the end also of the Long 2009. Trump is gone to Mar a Lago and seen like all former presidents as an artifact of a prior time. 

- The Administration that takes office in 2029 experiences a ChatGPT like moment in robotics in its first 9 months. It is a surprise to all in DC.

Libyan Army Chief of Staff Offers Condolences to Egypt Over Killing of Two Border Guards Officers

Lieutenant General Khaled Khalifa Haftar, Chief of the General Staff of the Libyan Arab Armed Forces and son of their Commander-in-Chief, Field Marshal Khalifa Haftar, has extended his condolences to the Egyptian Armed Forces and the Egyptian people following the killing of two Egyptian Border Guards officers while confronting illegal gold-mining gangs.

In a statement, Haftar expressed his sincere condolences to the families of Colonel Ahmed Samir, Chief of Staff of the Southern Border Guards Region, and Lieutenant Colonel Ahmed Gouda, Head of Operations of a Border Guards Battalion. He described the two officers as “heroic martyrs” and praised their dedication to their national duty of protecting their country's borders and safeguarding its resources.

He reaffirmed the bonds of brotherhood, shared history and common destiny between the Egyptian and Libyan armies, expressing his full support for the Egyptian Armed Forces in their fight against terrorism and organized crime and in protecting the shared national security of the two countries.

Full text of the statement as received:

In the Name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

“Do not think of those who have been killed in the cause of Allah as dead. Rather, they are alive with their Lord, receiving provision.”

Allah Almighty has spoken the truth.

I extend my deepest condolences and sincere sympathies to the General Command of the Egyptian Armed Forces, all members of the brotherly Egyptian people, and the families and relatives of the two heroic martyrs:

Colonel Ahmed Samir, Chief of Staff of the Southern Border Guards Region;

and Lieutenant Colonel Ahmed Gouda, Head of Operations of a Border Guards Battalion.

The two officers passed away as martyrs while performing their sacred national duty of protecting their country's borders and safeguarding its wealth and resources, during an operation to confront gangs engaged in illegal gold mining.

As we mourn these two heroes, we reaffirm the bonds of brotherhood, shared history and common destiny that unite our two brotherly armies. We also affirm our full solidarity with our brothers in the Egyptian Armed Forces in their fight against terrorism and organized crime, and in protecting the national security shared by our two countries.

We ask Almighty Allah to envelop the two deceased officers in His vast mercy, grant them a place in Paradise alongside the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs and the righteous, and grant their families, relatives and colleagues patience and solace.

Indeed, we belong to Allah, and indeed, to Him we shall return.

Lieutenant General Khaled Khalifa Haftar
Chief of the General Staff
Libyan Arab Armed Forces

“Only when the schedule’s bad.”

He nodded. The rain was loud against the windows. I shifted closer so I could hear him better. He didn’t lean away. When the lights flickered back on, he looked at me like he was deciding something. Then he stood up and offered his hand. I took it. We didn’t leave the café right away. We stayed behind the counter, the door locked, the street outside empty. He kissed me once, slow, like he was checking if I’d stop him. I didn’t.

We kept seeing each other after that, always after closing, always careful. He never asked what it meant. I never told him I was still figuring it out. Some nights we’d just sit in the dark and talk. Other nights we didn’t talk at all. The café stayed open. We kept showing up. And every time the lights went out, even for a second, I felt his hand find mine under the counter.

$BIP Q3 2026 earnings: Brookfield Infrastructure data profit rises, while corporate costs climb

Brookfield Infrastructure, which owns global utilities, transport networks, pipelines and data centers, grew its unitholder cash profit while total cash profit across its whole asset pool stood still. Funds from operations (FFO, its measure of operating cash profit) rose 10% to $0.91 per unit, led by a 25% jump in the data division. Chief executive Sam Pollock highlighted an expanding investment pipeline, and the group expects to beat its $2 billion asset sale goal for the year.

• Funds from operations (FFO) per unit: $𝟎.𝟗𝟏 (+10% from a year ago)
• Data segment FFO: $𝟏𝟕𝟐𝐌 (+25% from a year ago)
• Consolidated FFO before partner splits: $𝟏,𝟔𝟕𝟓𝐌 (-1% from a year ago by our math)
• 2026 asset sale proceeds outlook: 𝐑𝐚𝐢𝐬𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐨 >$𝟐𝐁 ($1.5B secured so far this year)

⚖️ 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭: 🟢 Bullish

The story got better because the company turned its government-backed AI computing plans into a signed contract with South Korea's NAVER and lined up over $1 billion in late-stage asset sales. One caution: by our math, total consolidated FFO before subtracting outside partners' shares slipped 1%, and corporate overhead and interest costs jumped 28%.

The question now is whether new data center and pipeline investments can lift total consolidated cash flow, or if per-unit growth is relying on ownership shifts from asset sales. If the new assets are outperforming, total consolidated FFO will grow alongside the unitholder figure; if not, rising corporate costs will squeeze the 10% growth target. Fourth-quarter consolidated FFO and closing the $1 billion sales pipeline will settle it.

Full article with charts - link in bio

🐂 𝐁𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🟢🟢 𝐃𝐚𝐭𝐚 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐌𝐢𝐝𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐦 𝐂𝐚𝐫𝐫𝐲 𝐎𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐅𝐥𝐨𝐰
Brookfield Infrastructure measures its operating cash profit using funds from operations (FFO), which strips out depreciation, deferred taxes and one-time sale gains. Chief executive Sam Pollock said the group "enters the final quarter of the year with strong momentum", hitting its 10% per-unit growth target for a third straight quarter as FFO reached $0.91 per unit.

• Data segment FFO: $172 million, up 24.6% from a year ago
• Midstream (pipelines and gas storage) FFO: $178 million, up 14.1%
• Transport FFO: $315 million, up 10.1%
• Utilities FFO: $200 million, up 5.3%

The data and pipeline divisions are doing the heavy lifting while utilities grow slowly after asset sales in India and Brazil. Data growth slowed from 62.4% a year ago as prior acquisitions entered the base, but new contributions from Intel's Arizona semiconductor foundries and a US bulk fiber network kept the division expanding at more than double the company average.

What to watch: fourth-quarter data segment FFO. It will show whether the Intel foundry partnership and new data centers can keep data FFO growing above 20% as last year's fiber acquisition laps.

🟢 𝐍𝐀𝐕𝐄𝐑 𝐃𝐞𝐚𝐥 𝐓𝐮𝐫𝐧𝐬 𝐒𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐢𝐠𝐧 𝐀𝐈 𝐓𝐚𝐥𝐤 𝐈𝐧𝐭𝐨 𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐜𝐭𝐬
A year ago, Pollock noted that government-backed computing deals took longer to close than expected. This quarter the infrastructure owner signed a formal partnership with South Korean tech group NAVER to build over 200 megawatts of computing capacity, and added a partnership with power generator Drax to explore building an AI factory in the UK.

Under the NAVER deal, a dedicated leasing company will own the computing gear, "providing a return on and full recovery of our invested capital over the initial contract term". The project requires $9 billion of total capital, but Brookfield Infrastructure's own equity share is about $100 million (1.1% of the total by our math), with the first chips arriving in the first half of 2027.

What to watch: binding contract terms on the Drax UK project and the remaining $400 million of the company's $500 million annual AI investment target. Converting these partnerships into funded projects will determine whether AI adds to cash flow before 2028.

🟢 𝐀𝐬𝐬𝐞𝐭 𝐒𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬 𝐏𝐢𝐜𝐤 𝐔𝐩 𝐓𝐨𝐰𝐚𝐫𝐝 𝐚 $𝟐.𝟓 𝐁𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐘𝐞𝐚𝐫
Brookfield Infrastructure funds new purchases by selling mature businesses, a practice it calls capital recycling. So far in 2026 the group has secured $1.5 billion from asset sales and deployed $1.7 billion of equity into new acquisitions and expansion projects, including $700 million for its own share of internal build-outs.

The company is nearing binding offers on several sales that could bring in over $1 billion before year-end, so it expects to "exceed our target of generating $2 billion for the year". By our math, closing those deals would lift full-year proceeds above $2.5 billion, covering the year's equity spending without issuing common units.

What to watch: signed sale agreements before December 31. Closing the $1 billion pipeline on time will confirm that buyer demand holds up and keep corporate debt from rising.

🐻 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🔴🔴 𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐬𝐨𝐥𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐅𝐥𝐨𝐰 𝐒𝐡𝐫𝐚𝐧𝐤 𝐁𝐞𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝐏𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐧𝐞𝐫 𝐒𝐩𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐬
Brookfield Infrastructure highlighted 10% growth in FFO attributable to its own unitholders, which rose from $654 million to $717 million. Because the partnership co-owns most of its operating companies with outside investors, its financial tables also show total consolidated FFO before subtracting those partners' share.

That total consolidated FFO fell 1.0% from a year ago, dropping from $1,692 million to $1,675 million by our math. The unitholder figure grew 9.6% only because the cash flow belonging to outside partners dropped 7.7%, from $1,038 million to $958 million (4.2 percentage points less of the total pool).

This gap matters because selling stakes in operating subsidiaries changes the ownership split between Brookfield Infrastructure and its co-investors. While buying wholly owned assets or selling partner-heavy ones lifts the partnership's share, the total asset base on the balance sheet generated slightly less cash flow than a year ago.

What to watch: consolidated FFO before non-controlling interests in the fourth quarter. A return to growth in the total pool would show that new investments are expanding overall cash generation rather than just shifting ownership percentages.

🔴 𝐂𝐨𝐫𝐩𝐨𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐞 𝐂𝐨𝐬𝐭𝐬 𝐄𝐚𝐭 𝐈𝐧𝐭𝐨 𝐒𝐞𝐠𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐆𝐚𝐢𝐧𝐬
Alongside its four operating divisions, Brookfield Infrastructure reports a corporate segment that carries head-office overhead, management fees and corporate borrowing costs. In the third quarter, the FFO loss in this corporate line widened by 27.6% from a year ago, growing from $116 million to $148 million.

By our math, corporate costs consumed 17.1% of the $865 million in FFO generated by the four operating segments, up 2.0 percentage points from 15.1% a year ago. On the income statement, general and administrative expenses rose 3.7% to $111 million (1.7% of revenue) and corporate debt rose to $5.3 billion, holding back bottom-line cash flow.

What to watch: the corporate FFO loss in the fourth quarter. If corporate overhead and interest keep rising above $145 million a quarter, the operating segments will have to grow above 12% just to hit the 10% company target.

👓 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐓𝐡𝐞𝐦𝐞𝐬

𝐂𝐨𝐫𝐩𝐨𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐞 𝐒𝐢𝐦𝐩𝐥𝐢𝐟𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐂𝐥𝐨𝐬𝐞𝐬 𝐍𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐦𝐛𝐞𝐫 𝟏𝟗
Brookfield Infrastructure expects to close its corporate simplification on November 19, 2026, combining the partnership and corporate shares into Brookfield Infrastructure Partners Inc. Because of the transition, the company did not declare a fourth-quarter payout today, but the new entity intends to pay a dividend "in an amount consistent with BIP’s current quarterly distribution of $0.455 per unit".

𝐅𝐢𝐱𝐞𝐝-𝐑𝐚𝐭𝐞 𝐃𝐞𝐛𝐭 𝐒𝐡𝐢𝐞𝐥𝐝𝐬 𝐑𝐞𝐟𝐢𝐧𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐬 𝐅𝐫𝐨𝐦 𝐑𝐚𝐭𝐞 𝐌𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐬
More than 90% of the group's term debt outside Brazil carries a fixed interest rate, protecting cash flow from interest rate swings. During the quarter the company refinanced $2 billion at its North American residential business (pulling out $165 million in cash for its share), raised A$1.1 billion for Australian data assets, and issued C$150 million of preferred units at its "lowest reset spread achieved to date in the Canadian preferred market".

— • — • —

💲 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐊𝐏𝐈𝐬

𝐎𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐜𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐟𝐥𝐨𝐰 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟏,𝟓𝟑𝟗 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
Cash from operating activities fell 17.7% from $1,870 million a year ago, reversing a 25.6% gain in the second quarter. Revenue grew 9.7% to $6,556 million, so the drop in operating cash flow came from lower cash distributions from joint ventures and shifts in non-cash items.

𝐓𝐨𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐛𝐨𝐫𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐬 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟔𝟏,𝟎𝟔𝟒 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
Combined corporate and asset-level debt fell 5.3% by our math from $64,498 million at the end of 2025, continuing a steady reduction from $62,465 million in the second quarter. Asset-level debt dropped by $3,784 million as sold businesses left the balance sheet, while corporate borrowings rose $350 million to $5,297 million.

𝐍𝐞𝐭 𝐢𝐧𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐞 𝐚𝐭𝐭𝐫𝐢𝐛𝐮𝐭𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞 𝐭𝐨 𝐩𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐧𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐡𝐢𝐩 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟔𝟗 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
Profit attributable to the partnership fell 84.3% from $440 million a year ago, leaving a loss of $0.04 per limited partner unit after preferred and general partner payouts. The drop reflects smaller one-off gains from selling businesses and lower earnings from joint ventures ($49 million vs $437 million last year).

— • — • —

🔮 𝐆𝐮𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞

𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐀𝐬𝐬𝐞𝐭 𝐒𝐚𝐥𝐞 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐜𝐞𝐞𝐝𝐬: > $𝟐.𝟎 𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
🠅 raised from $1.0 billion
Raised. The company now expects to beat a $2.0 billion asset sale target for 2026, having secured $1.5 billion so far this year. With over $1.0 billion of advanced sales nearing binding offers before year-end, full-year proceeds would top $2.5 billion by our math. The target has moved around: management aimed for $3.0 billion at the end of 2025, cited a $1.0 billion target in Q1, and now points past $2.0 billion.

𝐐𝟒 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐐𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐥𝐲 𝐃𝐢𝐯𝐢𝐝𝐞𝐧𝐝 / 𝐃𝐢𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐢𝐛𝐮𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧: $𝟎.𝟒𝟓𝟓 𝐩𝐞𝐫 𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞  ⇒ stable
🠆 unchanged from $0.455 per unit
Unchanged. Following the November 19 corporate simplification, the combined company plans to declare a fourth-quarter dividend matching the current $0.455 quarterly payout ($1.82 annualized, up 6% from last year). That keeps the payout inside management's long-term 5% to 9% annual increase target.

𝐀𝐧𝐧𝐮𝐚𝐥 𝐀𝐈 𝐈𝐧𝐟𝐫𝐚𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐮𝐜𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐞 𝐃𝐞𝐩𝐥𝐨𝐲𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭: ~$𝟓𝟎𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
🠆 unchanged from Up to $500 million
Unchanged. Brookfield Infrastructure still aims to invest about $500 million of its own equity per year on average into AI factories and power projects. The NAVER partnership in South Korea commits about $100 million of that annual budget across 2027 and 2028, leaving $400 million to be filled by pipeline deals like the Drax project in the UK.

— • — • —

❓ 𝐊𝐞𝐲 𝐐𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬

𝐖𝐡𝐲 𝐝𝐢𝐝 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐬𝐨𝐥𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐅𝐅𝐎 𝐬𝐡𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐤 𝐰𝐡𝐢𝐥𝐞 𝐮𝐧𝐢𝐭𝐡𝐨𝐥𝐝𝐞𝐫 𝐅𝐅𝐎 𝐠𝐫𝐞𝐰?
Total consolidated FFO before subtracting partner shares fell 1.0% to $1,675 million, while Brookfield Infrastructure's own share rose 9.6% to $717 million. Which specific asset sales or acquisitions shifted the ownership split so sharply away from non-controlling partners this quarter?

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐩𝐮𝐬𝐡𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐜𝐨𝐫𝐩𝐨𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐞 𝐅𝐅𝐎 𝐥𝐨𝐬𝐬 𝐮𝐩 𝟐𝟖%?
The corporate segment FFO loss widened from $116 million to $148 million, while general and administrative expenses on the income statement rose by only $4 million. How much of the $32 million increase came from higher base management fees versus corporate interest costs?

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐰𝐚𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐞𝐱𝐚𝐜𝐭 𝐨𝐫𝐠𝐚𝐧𝐢𝐜 𝐅𝐅𝐎 𝐠𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐭𝐡 𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐞 𝐢𝐧 𝐐𝟑?
The release states that organic growth was at the high end of the company's 6% to 9% target range and that $1.4 billion of backlog projects were commissioned, but gives no exact percentage or ending capital backlog figure.

𝐖𝐡𝐨 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐯𝐢𝐝𝐞𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐫𝐞𝐦𝐚𝐢𝐧𝐢𝐧𝐠 $𝟖.𝟗 𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐍𝐀𝐕𝐄𝐑 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐣𝐞𝐜𝐭?
The South Korean AI factory requires $9 billion of capital, yet Brookfield Infrastructure is committing only $100 million of net equity into the leasing company. How much of the remaining funding is project debt versus co-investor equity, and what are the lease renewal terms?

text:
$BIP Q3 2026 earnings: Brookfield Infrastructure cash flow rises 10%, while debt costs slow

Brookfield Infrastructure, which owns global utilities, transport networks, pipelines and data centers, grew cash flow through heavy asset sales while locking in its first sovereign AI contract. Funds from operations (FFO) — operating cash flow before debt repayments and maintenance spending — rose 10% to $0.91 per unit, led by a 25% gain in the data division as its Intel chip-foundry partnership started contributing. Chief executive Sam Pollock also signed a South Korean AI computing contract and set a November 19 closing date to combine the company's two listed securities.

• Funds from operations per unit: $𝟎.𝟗𝟏 (+9.6% from a year ago)
• Data segment funds from operations: $𝟏𝟕𝟐𝐌 (+25% from a year ago)
• Asset sales secured year to date: $𝟏.𝟓𝐁 (> $1B more nearing offers by year-end)
• Full-year FFO per unit growth target: 𝐔𝐧𝐜𝐡𝐚𝐧𝐠𝐞𝐝 (10% target requires $0.95 in Q4 by our math)

⚖️ 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭: 🟢 Bullish

The story got better because new projects and debt paydowns offset lost income from sold businesses, easing the main risk for the second half of the year. Consolidated debt fell 5% since December, which slowed interest expense growth to 3% after an 18% jump last quarter. One caution: the partnership quietly lowered its 2026 asset-sale benchmark from $3 billion to $2 billion, and Corporate segment losses widened 28%.

The question now is whether the data division can keep growing above 20% once last September's U. S. fiber acquisition enters the year-ago comparison in the fourth quarter. Either the Intel chip-factory partnership and new data centers carry the pace and lift fourth-quarter FFO to the $0.95 per unit needed for an unrounded 10% full-year gain by our math, or growth slows toward the single-digit rate of the older divisions. Fourth-quarter Data segment FFO will settle it.

Full article with charts - link in bio

🐂 𝐁𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🟢🟢 𝐃𝐚𝐭𝐚 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐈𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐥 𝐏𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐧𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐡𝐢𝐩 𝐎𝐟𝐟𝐬𝐞𝐭 𝐀𝐬𝐬𝐞𝐭 𝐒𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬
Brookfield Infrastructure relies on new projects and acquisitions to replace the cash flow it loses when it sells mature assets. Investors worried that July's partial sale of its U. S. data center business and earlier utility sales would slow second-half growth.

Instead, funds from operations (FFO) — operating cash flow before debt repayments and maintenance spending — rose 9.6% to $717 million. The data division grew 24.6% from a year ago and 11.7% from last quarter to $172 million, helped by "contributions from our partnership with Intel to develop semiconductor foundries in Arizona" after the group finished funding its equity stake.

• Data FFO: $172 million, up 24.6% from a year ago and up $18 million from last quarter
• Transport FFO: $315 million, up 10.1% on North American railcar leasing and higher port and toll road volumes
• Utilities FFO: $200 million, up 5.3% after adding the New Zealand energy network and $600 million of rate-base projects
• Capital projects commissioned across the business: about $1.4 billion

This matters because the Intel chip-factory payout and the New Zealand utility purchase arrived on schedule, covering the lost income from sold Brazilian power lines and Australian ports.

What to watch: fourth-quarter Data FFO against last year's $149 million. That period will be the first clean comparison after the September 2025 U. S. fiber acquisition enters the prior-year baseline.

🟢 𝐀𝐈 𝐏𝐢𝐩𝐞𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐞 𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐭𝐬 𝐈𝐧𝐭𝐨 𝐅𝐢𝐫𝐬𝐭 𝐒𝐢𝐠𝐧𝐞𝐝 𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐜𝐭
Chief executive Sam Pollock wants to invest about $500 million a year in artificial intelligence infrastructure, such as computing facilities and dedicated power plants. Critics point out that these projects take years to build and carry permitting and demand risks.

This quarter the infrastructure owner moved from broad framework deals to a signed contract, "formalizing a strategic partnership with NAVER to develop sovereign AI capabilities" in South Korea. The 200-megawatt project will cost about $9 billion in total, with Brookfield Infrastructure putting in about $100 million of its own equity through a leasing company whose contracts return the full investment over the initial term. The partnership also signed an agreement with power generator Drax to study a large AI facility in the United Kingdom.

The structure limits risk because debt and partners fund nearly 99% of the South Korean budget while long-term leases lock in the cash flow. Still, the first graphics chips will not arrive until the first half of 2027, with full completion at the end of 2028.

What to watch: the segment capital backlog table in the upcoming quarterly filing. It will show whether the NAVER contract has entered the official construction backlog.

🟢 𝐃𝐞𝐛𝐭 𝐅𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐈𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐭 𝐄𝐱𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐬𝐞 𝐆𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐭𝐡 𝐒𝐥𝐨𝐰𝐬
Brookfield Infrastructure promises to "maintain conservative leverage, extend maturities when opportunities arise" across its operating companies. Rising debt from 2025 acquisitions had pushed consolidated interest expense up 18.0% from a year ago in the second quarter, raising concern about higher-for-longer borrowing costs.

In the third quarter, subsidiary debt repayments of $831 million and asset deconsolidation brought total consolidated borrowings down to $61.1 billion, a 5.3% reduction since December 2025. As a result, interest expense grew just 3.5% from a year ago to $1,049 million, down from $1,073 million in the second quarter. Corporate liquidity also improved to $3.2 billion from $2.6 billion three months ago.

What to watch: the weighted average cash interest rate in the quarterly supplemental filing. A stable rate near 5.9% will show that recent refinancings in North America and Australia did not raise average borrowing costs.

🐻 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🔴🔴 𝐅𝐮𝐥𝐥-𝐘𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐓𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐞𝐭 𝐍𝐞𝐞𝐝𝐬 𝐚 𝐅𝐨𝐮𝐫𝐭𝐡-𝐐𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐒𝐭𝐞𝐩-𝐔𝐩
Brookfield Infrastructure celebrated its "third consecutive quarter of achieving our 10% growth target" as FFO per unit rose from $0.83 to $0.91. In exact terms, by our math, growth was 9.6% this quarter and 9.8% over the first nine months, from $2.46 to $2.70.

Because the partnership earned $3.32 per unit in 2025, reaching an unrounded 10% increase for the full year ($3.652) requires $0.95 per unit in the fourth quarter, by our math. That means growth must speed up to 10.7% from a year ago and jump 4.4% from the third quarter's $0.91 level, just as the U. S. bulk fiber network acquired in September 2025 loses its easy prior-year comparison.

In 2024 and 2025, reported FFO per unit grew 5.8% and 6.4%, only hitting 10% after adjustments for currency swings and normalization. Hitting the unadjusted target this year requires the biggest quarterly jump of 2026 in the final period.

What to watch: fourth-quarter FFO per unit in the full-year earnings release. A reading of $0.95 or higher is needed to reach an unrounded 10% annual gain.

🔴 𝐀𝐬𝐬𝐞𝐭 𝐒𝐚𝐥𝐞 𝐆𝐨𝐚𝐥 𝐐𝐮𝐢𝐞𝐭𝐥𝐲 𝐌𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐝 𝐅𝐫𝐨𝐦 $𝟑𝐁 𝐭𝐨 $𝟐𝐁
Brookfield Infrastructure funds new purchases by selling mature businesses rather than issuing new common units. At the end of 2025, the partnership set an objective of $3 billion in asset sale proceeds for 2026.

With $1.5 billion secured through September, the release now states that the group expects to "exceed our target of generating $2 billion for the year" and is nearing binding offers for "over $1 billion of incremental proceeds net to BIP before year end". By our math, management lowered the benchmark it compares itself against by $1 billion without acknowledging the reduction.

Closing that final $1 billion would bring full-year proceeds past $2.5 billion, enough to cover the $1.7 billion of equity deployed into new investments and organic projects so far this year.

What to watch: binding sale announcements before December 31. Securing the promised $1 billion is necessary to prove that private infrastructure buyers remain active while the public listing market is quiet.

🔴 𝐂𝐨𝐫𝐩𝐨𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐞 𝐂𝐨𝐬𝐭𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐂𝐨𝐦𝐦𝐨𝐝𝐢𝐭𝐲 𝐑𝐞𝐥𝐢𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞 𝐆𝐫𝐨𝐰
Brookfield Infrastructure pays management fees and incentive distributions to its parent company, Brookfield, and logs those charges along with corporate interest in its Corporate segment. At the same time, its midstream pipelines and processing plants aim for predictable, contract-backed revenue.

In the third quarter, the Corporate FFO loss widened 27.6% from a year ago to $148 million, up from $116 million, following a 15.4% increase in the second quarter. Meanwhile, Midstream FFO rose 14.1% to $178 million, which the partnership attributed in part to higher commodity prices in Canada.

Growing corporate overhead eats into the gains from operating businesses, taking away 4.9 percentage points of total FFO growth this quarter by our math. Relying on high energy prices in Midstream also leaves that cash flow vulnerable if commodity markets cool.

What to watch: the base management fee breakdown in the third-quarter filing. It will show how much of the $32 million corporate cost increase went to parent-company fees versus corporate borrowing costs.

👓 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐓𝐡𝐞𝐦𝐞𝐬

𝐂𝐨𝐫𝐩𝐨𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐞 𝐒𝐢𝐦𝐩𝐥𝐢𝐟𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐂𝐥𝐨𝐬𝐞𝐬 𝐍𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐦𝐛𝐞𝐫 𝟏𝟗
Following unitholder and shareholder approval in October, Brookfield Infrastructure expects to finish combining its partnership units and corporate shares into a single corporation, Brookfield Infrastructure Partners Inc., on November 19, 2026. Because of the closing timetable, the group paused its fourth-quarter distribution declaration until after November 19, when the new corporation plans to declare the usual $0.455 per share quarterly payout.

𝐅𝐢𝐱𝐞𝐝-𝐑𝐚𝐭𝐞 𝐃𝐞𝐛𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐈𝐧𝐟𝐥𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐂𝐥𝐚𝐮𝐬𝐞𝐬 𝐂𝐮𝐬𝐡𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐌𝐚𝐜𝐫𝐨 𝐒𝐰𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐬
Over 90% of the partnership's term debt outside Brazil carries fixed interest rates, protecting cash flow from central bank rate moves. In Brazil, debt is floating-rate because utility and toll road contracts automatically adjust prices for local inflation, which lifted third-quarter revenue across the utilities and transport divisions.

— • — • —

💲 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐊𝐏𝐈𝐬

𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐬𝐨𝐥𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐫𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟔,𝟓𝟓𝟔 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
Revenue rose 9.7% from a year ago and 1.1% from last quarter. Growth slowed from 19.4% in Q2 and 16.9% in Q1 because the July 2025 purchase of the U. S. refined products pipeline entered the prior-year comparison. Direct operating costs — the cost of running the assets — rose 0.6 percentage points of revenue, nudging operating margin down 0.5 points to 23.8%.

𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐟𝐫𝐨𝐦 𝐨𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐚𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐯𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐞𝐬 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟏,𝟓𝟑𝟗 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇄ reversing
Operating cash flow fell 17.7% from a year ago after rising 25.6% in the second quarter, mainly because operating subsidiaries paid higher current taxes and distributed less cash from joint ventures. Over the first nine months, operating cash flow was unchanged at $3,925 million against $3,927 million last year.

𝐍𝐞𝐭 𝐢𝐧𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐞 𝐚𝐭𝐭𝐫𝐢𝐛𝐮𝐭𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞 𝐭𝐨 𝐩𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐧𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐡𝐢𝐩 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟔𝟗 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
Accounting profit attributable to the partnership dropped 84.3% from $440 million a year ago, leaving a loss of $0.04 per limited partner unit after preferred and general partner payouts. The drop happened because last year's third quarter included large one-time accounting gains on asset sales ($320 million of other income versus $65 million this quarter).

— • — • —

🔮 𝐆𝐮𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞

𝐅𝐅𝐎 𝐩𝐞𝐫 𝐮𝐧𝐢𝐭 𝐠𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐭𝐡 𝐭𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐞𝐭: 𝟏𝟎%  ⇒ stable
🠆 unchanged from 10%
Unchanged. Brookfield Infrastructure kept its annual target of 10% FFO per unit growth and said Q3's $0.91 met the mark for a third straight quarter. By our math, nine-month growth is 9.8% ($2.70 vs $2.46), which leaves $0.95 per unit (+10.7% from a year ago) needed in Q4 to reach an unrounded 10% gain on 2025's $3.32.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔 𝐀𝐬𝐬𝐞𝐭 𝐬𝐚𝐥𝐞 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐜𝐞𝐞𝐝𝐬 𝐭𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐞𝐭: >$𝟐.𝟎 𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
🠇 cut from $3.0 billion
Cut. The release states an expectation to exceed a $2 billion annual target, down from the $3 billion objective set at the end of 2025. However, with $1.5 billion secured year to date and binding offers nearing for over $1 billion more before year-end, actual full-year sales could still top $2.5 billion.

𝐀𝐧𝐧𝐮𝐚𝐥 𝐀𝐈 𝐢𝐧𝐟𝐫𝐚𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐮𝐜𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐞 𝐞𝐪𝐮𝐢𝐭𝐲 𝐝𝐞𝐩𝐥𝐨𝐲𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭: ~$𝟓𝟎𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
🠅 raised from $300–500 million
Raised. The partnership now targets deploying about $500 million of equity per year on average into AI infrastructure, fixed at the top of the $300–500 million range discussed last quarter. The new NAVER contract in South Korea accounts for about $100 million of that commitment across 2027 and 2028.

𝐐𝟒 𝐐𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐥𝐲 𝐝𝐢𝐯𝐢𝐝𝐞𝐧𝐝 (𝐩𝐨𝐬𝐭-𝐬𝐢𝐦𝐩𝐥𝐢𝐟𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧): $𝟎.𝟒𝟓𝟓 𝐩𝐞𝐫 𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞  ⇒ stable
🠆 unchanged from $0.455 per unit
Unchanged. Once the combination of the partnership and corporate shares closes on November 19, 2026, the unified company plans to declare a fourth-quarter dividend matching the current $0.455 quarterly rate, which is 6% higher than last year.

— • — • —

❓ 𝐊𝐞𝐲 𝐐𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬

𝐃𝐢𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐍𝐀𝐕𝐄𝐑 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐜𝐭 𝐢𝐧𝐜𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐬𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐭𝐨𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐜𝐚𝐩𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐛𝐚𝐜𝐤𝐥𝐨𝐠?
The earnings release noted $1.4 billion of commissioned projects and the new $9 billion NAVER partnership ($100 million net to BIP), but did not include the segment capital backlog table. Investors need the updated backlog figure to see if new orders replaced completed projects.

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐰𝐚𝐬 𝐦𝐚𝐢𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐧𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞 𝐜𝐚𝐩𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐬𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐀𝐅𝐅𝐎 𝐢𝐧 𝐐𝟑?
The release did not break out maintenance capital expenditures, which the group deducts from FFO to measure cash available for distributions. That figure is needed to verify whether the payout ratio improved from 81% in the second quarter.

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐝𝐫𝐨𝐯𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝟐𝟖% 𝐣𝐮𝐦𝐩 𝐢𝐧 𝐂𝐨𝐫𝐩𝐨𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐞 𝐅𝐅𝐎 𝐥𝐨𝐬𝐬𝐞𝐬?
Corporate segment FFO losses widened from $116 million to $148 million. Without the supplemental fee schedule, readers cannot tell how much came from higher base management fees paid to Brookfield versus corporate interest costs.

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐢𝐬 𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐫𝐥𝐲𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐃𝐚𝐭𝐚 𝐅𝐅𝐎 𝐠𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐭𝐡 𝐞𝐱𝐜𝐥𝐮𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐚𝐜𝐪𝐮𝐢𝐬𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬?
Third-quarter Data FFO growth of 25% included a full quarter of the U. S. bulk fiber network bought in September 2025 and the initial Intel foundry payout, minus the partial U. S. colocation sale. Management has not separated the underlying growth rate from those portfolio changes.

text:
"Everything happens for a reason" is easy to say when you're on the other side of it, but Christian Kuntz's path to the NFL is proof that the worst detours can end up being the exact ones you needed.

In this episode, the Pittsburgh Steelers long snapper looks back at the chain reaction that built his career. A lacerated spleen in high school cost him his senior year and bigger scholarship offers, landing him at Duquesne. That led to getting signed by New England for all of seventeen hours before getting cut. But that brief stop put him in front of someone who later saw him work out in Green Bay and remembered he could snap — which ultimately sparked his full transition to long snapping and his shot in the league.

When you're in the middle of the adversity, it just feels like bad breaks. Kuntz's story is a reminder that sometimes the setbacks you never would have chosen are the only reason the door opened in the first place.

The Playbook with Colin Jonov — this conversation with Christian Kuntz breaks down the wild, unpredictable road to staying in the NFL. 🎙️

text:
The journal International Security (Harvard/MIT Press) is where nearly every person on this list publishes.

Pape and Mearsheimer anchor two neighboring areas: Pape works on political violence, terrorism, coercion, and air power, and Mearsheimer on offensive realism and great-power politics.

Their true peers mostly come out of the same few departments (Chicago, MIT, Harvard, Columbia) and publish in International Security. Here are the people at that level, grouped by which of the two they resemble more.

Closest to Mearsheimer: realists and grand strategists:

Stephen M. Walt (Harvard Kennedy School) was Mearsheimer's co-author on The Israel Lobby. He is best known for balance-of-threat theory and The Hell of Good Intentions. He chairs the editorial board of International Security. 

His recent Foreign Affairs and Foreign Policy pieces on Trump's use of American power are widely discussed. He has argued that the U.S. has become a "rogue state" that every other country now has to work out how to handle.

Barry R. Posen (MIT) was a student of Kenneth Waltz and is the author of Restraint. He is probably the most rigorous military-strategy mind among the realists. He is Director Emeritus of MIT's Security Studies Program. 

His recent article "Putin's Preventive War" drew a published exchange with James Goldgeier and Brian Taylor in International Security this spring.

Stephen Van Evera (MIT) wrote Causes of War and is a defensive realist who emphasizes misperception and nationalism.

Sebastian Rosato (Notre Dame) co-wrote How States Think with Mearsheimer and is very much in his line of work.

Michael Desch (Notre Dame) works on civil-military relations and realism, and is a frequent critic of "endless wars."

Charles Glaser (George Washington University) is the leading theorist of the security dilemma and defensive realism.

Patrick Porter (University of Birmingham, UK) is a strong British voice for this school. His latest book is How to Survive a Hostile World: Power, Politics and the Case for Realism.

Christopher Layne and Andrew Bacevich are prominent advocates of restraint and offshore balancing, Bacevich through the Quincy Institute.

Closest to Pape: terrorism, coercion, political violence:

Martha Crenshaw (Stanford) is the founding figure of modern terrorism studies.

Bruce Hoffman (Georgetown) wrote Inside Terrorism, a standard text.

Daniel Byman (Georgetown) works on terrorism, state sponsorship, and counterterrorism policy.

Mia Bloom (Georgia State) wrote Dying to Kill, which is a natural companion and counterpoint to Pape's Dying to Win.

Max Abrahms (Northeastern) is one of the sharpest empirical critics of Pape's strategic-logic thesis, and is worth reading precisely because he disagrees with him.

Erica Chenoweth (Harvard) and Barbara F. Walter (UC San Diego) work on nonviolent resistance and on civil war, respectively. Walter's How Civil Wars Start overlaps with Pape's recent research on domestic political violence in the U.S.

Serious scholars who argue against them:

If you only read realists, you get one strong lens. These people offer an equally rigorous challenge:

Hal Brands (Johns Hopkins SAIS) and Michael Beckley (Tufts) make the case for American primacy and confronting China.

Andrew Moravcsik (Princeton) is a leading liberal theorist. He co-wrote the famous critique "Is Anybody Still a Realist?" in International Security and still debates Mearsheimer in public forums.

Richard Betts (Columbia) is hard to label and is excellent on intelligence failure and the use of force. That last topic may suit your background as an analyst.

If you want one place to follow all of them, the journal International Security (Harvard/MIT Press) is where nearly every person on this list publishes. Its correspondence section is where they argue with each other directly.

Article - Played For Both Clubs - Archie Kyle https://t.co/nteTUpw0yO 

By David Herd

There have been many players who played for both Rangers and St Mirren, several in recent times. But this week, we are going back over a century to tell the remarkable story of a player who starred at both Ibrox and at Love Street. His name was Archie Kyle.

A Roman Catholic raised in Westmuir Street in the Parkhead area of Glasgow, it would be natural to assume that Kyle would have joined Celtic. As a youngster, he played in the Scottish Junior Cup Final for Parkhead Juniors, and represented Scotland at junior level, and the clever and quick inside forward had scouts from big clubs watching him closely. One of them was Celtic, but as they hesitated in making a move for the player, Rangers boss William Wilton nipped in to get his signature on an Ibrox contract in the summer of 1904.

Despite his relative inexperience and only just out of his teenage years, Archie Kyle made his first Rangers appearance on August 20th in the opening league game of the season at Third Lanark. It wasn't the most memorable of debuts, Kyle was played out of position on the right wing, and the season started badly with a 2-1 loss. But his Ibrox debut a week later was more of a sign of things to come. Kyle was switched to his favoured inside left berth, and scored in a convincing 4-0 defeat of Hibs.
 
Kyle made 34 starts in that first season, appearing in his first Cup final in October 1904 in front of nearly 55,000 at Hampden when a goal by the legendary RC Hamilton wasn't enough to prevent a painful 2-1 defeat by Celtic in the Glasgow Cup. He scored his first goal against the men from Parkhead later in the season, but that was another defeat, this time 4-1 at home in the league. However, it looked like 1904/05 might end on a high note when Kyle helped defeat them in an infamous Scottish Cup semi-final when Celtic fans rioted to get the match abandoned after going 2-0 down and seeing their star centre forward Jimmy Quinn ordered off. But Kyle endured heartache in the final when Third Lanark won the cup after a replay. A case of what might have been, made worse when four days after the replay defeat, Kyle scored in a comfortable 4-1 win over the same opponents in the Glasgow League. Kyle then missed out on a place in the league Championship playoff defeat against Celtic, as the season ended trophyless at Ibrox.

In all Kyle had scored 19 goals in 1904/05, including five separate doubles. Season 1905/06 saw Kyle again a regular, although his form was somewhat inconsistent. After only hitting the net once in his first eleven starts, he popped up with a vital strike in a hard fought 3-2 league win over Celtic in late October. This started a brief purple patch in front of goal, with six goals in four games, including a first Rangers hat trick when scoring all three in a draw at Motherwell. He then endured another barren spell before a memorable end of the season in May. He was among the scorers in a thumping 5-3 Charity Cup semi-final success at Parkhead before earning a first winners medal in the final, where he also scored in the victory over Queens Park.

In season 1906/07, Kyle enjoyed a new strike partnership with future Ibrox Director and converted full back RG Campbell, with plenty goals scored between them. Archie Kyle contributed 14 of them, although it was another season where the title stayed out of reach. Celtic were champions, despite a defeat at Ibrox in the New Year game when a Rangers side featuring three Roman Catholic players won 2-1. Joining Kyle in the starting eleven were Catholic teammates Colin Mainds, a signing from Port Glasgow, and Willie Kivlichan, who would leave Ibrox to join Celtic later in the year. Kivlichan scored for Rangers on the day. Like the previous season, the campaign ended in Charity Cup success, with Kyle appearing in another winning final team. The only goal in the Hampden final against Celtic was scored by Campbell, a man who was signed from the Parkhead club.
 
Kyle's fourth and final season at Ibrox was probably his most frustrating of all. He scored against Celtic in the Glasgow Cup final. He scored against Celtic in the New Year game. And he scored against Celtic in the Scottish Cup. But all three games were lost 2-1. He played his 135th and final game for the club away to St Mirren on April 13th 1908, and scored his 58th and final Rangers goal in a 2-0 league win. His four seasons at Rangers had yielded just those two Charity Cup winners medals.
 
During his Rangers career Archie Kyle was selected twice to represent the Scottish League against their English counterparts. He scored in a heavy 6-2 defeat at Stamford Bridge in 1906, and also suffered defeat by 2-0 at Villa Park in 1908. He was never chosen for the full international team.
 
In the summer of 1908, English first division Blackburn Rovers signed Kyle, with high hopes he would make a big impression. But after only one season where he scored eight times in 38 matches, he became embroiled in a protracted contractual dispute that saw him briefly turn out in Scottish lower league football with Bo’ness and Royal Albert while the English FA tried to resolve an impasse between Blackburn and Bradford, who wanted to sign the player but were thwarted by a dispute over his registration. Eventually, he did join Bradford, but there remained an FA judgement on his contractual status, and when the authorities decided that due to irregular payments at the time of his Blackburn transfer the player should not be permitted to play in their English jurisdiction, Kyle angrily tore up his Bradford deal and crossed the Irish Sea to sign for Linfield. This move was all down to the fact that the Irish League was at the time not part of any international football co-operation agreement, and therefore no permission was needed from the club who held his registration in England.

Kyle was a level above the Irish League standard, and very soon the Belfast press were running stories about him being wanted back in Scotland. Rumours of a return to Rangers were denied, and one paper even claimed he was destined for Celtic where manager Willie Maley was a long-term admirer. But it would be a different Glasgow club who brought him back from Belfast in September 1910, with the Celtic chief’s brother Alex persuading him to join Clyde where the other Maley was in charge. Clyde had to pay Blackburn to release Kyle, thus ending any involvement with the English FA. Six goals in 27 league games later, he had helped Clyde to a solid eighth place in the First Division, and when St Mirren came calling the following close season, Kyle was enjoying something of a career comeback.

He became a key player in Paisley, a virtual ever present for three seasons. Now enjoying a slightly more withdrawn role as he entered the veteran stage of his playing career, Kyle made over 100 appearances for the Paisley club. His experience and game intelligence saw Kyle transformed from the dashing and dangerous inside forward of his Ibrox days into a thoughtful playmaker capable of splitting opposing defences with an accurate pass. He also started to gain a reputation as something of a moody maverick, the Saints fans one week in raptures at his skills and then next week perplexed at his lack of effort.

During his three years in Paisley, Saints always struggled at the wrong end of the table, the team being as inconsistent as their midfield talisman. But Kyle did give their supporters a few great memories despite the lack of overall success. In February 1913, he scored a quite breathtaking winner in the Renfrewshire Derby against Morton, the 3-2 Saints win being clinched thanks to an outrageous piece of Kyle skill when he somehow plucked the ball out of the air then casually flicked it over the advancing goalkeeper. And early the following season, he gave the small pocket of visiting supporters inside Parkhead an afternoon to remember, when he gave a masterclass of vision and passing to bamboozle a very good Celtic side who would go on to lift the title. The 3-0 Saints win that day was widely regarded at the time as one of the team’s best ever displays and results.

But by the summer of 1914, just as the country was about to be plunged into the darkness of War, the Saints career of Archie Kyle came to an end when the 31-year-old signed for Hamilton Accies. He remained there until 1918, becoming an important player in a team who improved into a Top Ten side during his time there. But near the end of his time in Lanarkshire, Kyle started having issues with rheumatism, and he decided after the 1917/18 season it was time to retire.

That should be the end of his tale, but there was more to come in the life of Archie Kyle. He and his wife Letitia settled into post-football life in Bridgeton, not too far from the St Michael’s RC Church in Parkhead where they had been married back in 1905. With football not being the well-paid job of modern times, the Kyles had little savings from his time in the game, and times were hard for the couple and their three children. In 1924, Kyle decided to try to do something about that, and he got his name into the newspapers again. But this time it was not the sports pages.

A meeting of the SFA was told that two individuals had been reported to them for attempting to bribe players who were taking part in a Second Division match between Kyle’s old club Bo’ness and Lochgelly. Two Bo’ness players had been offered ￡30 each by two “former Glasgow footballers” with the instruction that they make sure their team lose the game. Despite being huge favourites to win the game, their team slumped to a shock 2-0 defeat. But the players had reported this to their bosses prior to kick-off, and they agreed to take part in a “sting” operation after the game. The players met with agents acting for these shadowy ex-players where the cash was produced. The agents were then identified, and a full investigation launched into the identity of those behind this attempted corruption.

The football authorities saw enough evidence to involve the police, and a few weeks later, Archie Kyle and former Celtic player John Browning were arrested as the men behind the plot. Both men were convicted of attempted bribery and corruption, with the sentence for both men being 60 days hard labour. Subsequent to this verdict and sentence, the SFA then banned both men from holding any position in Scottish football, as well as prohibiting them to enter any football ground in the country.

Incredibly, six years later, Kyle was back in the dock. In late December 1930, Kyle and former Hamilton teammate Adam Miller were charged with offering a bribe of ￡100 to the Accies captain so he would help throw the upcoming match against Leith Athletic. Kyle pled guilty to attempted bribery and received a three month prison sentence, while Miller denied the charge and the case against him was dropped. Rumours circulated that he had agreed to give evidence against Kyle in return for his freedom. The sentence Kyle received was condemned as too lenient by many within legal circles, and it would prompt a change in the law where future cases involving bribery of such sums of money would carry a minimum sentence of two years.

Thankfully, Kyle seemed to learn his lesson this time and there is no record of him being involved in illegal activity thereafter. Archie Kyle passed away in Bridgeton, Glasgow in July 1957 aged 74. If his football career and criminal life wasn't enough to remember him by, then he has another claim to fame. His daughter christened as Mary, but who was better known as Cathy, met and married local man Francis Miller in the 1930s. They had three children, daughters Letty and Anne and a son Frank junior. The young Miller attended Sacred Heart RC school, and was an altar boy at Sacred Heart RC church. He loved football, no doubt inherited from his Rangers player grandfather, and he played for the local Harmony Row boys club. He also passionately supported Celtic, something his grandfather may not have approved of.

But the grandson of Archie Kyle would not find fame on the football field. His love of music, and a talent for songwriting meant Frankie Miller would become a household name with million selling albums, hit songs such as "Darlin", and writing songs for world famous stars such as Roy Orbison, Ray Charles, Rod Stewart, Johnny Cash and The Eagles. He would go on to have a life far removed from the world inhabited by his footballing grandfather. A grandfather who played for Rangers, and for this weekend’s opponents.

We went for a colleague's husband's burial this afternoon.

When she told us that she had lost her husband, we were shocked because we didn't even know she was married. We thought she was a single mother because she had never mentioned her husband during our discussions in the office. Sometimes, she would complain about how difficult it was to raise her children.

We started contributing money towards the burial expenses and raised ₦200k.

But there was a problem. In her community, anyone who came to offer condolences was expected to present everything they brought, including money and drinks, at the condolence table. The husband's family members were the ones who will collect everything presented there.

So we came up with an idea. We put ₦2k in an envelope and presented it at the condolence table, then transferred the remaining ₦198k directly to her account.

Her husband's family members refused to give us food because they counted the money in the envelope and realised it was only ₦2k.

We weren't bothered. We contributed some more money, went outside, bought food and drinks, and ate.

They were shocked when they saw us eating.

I think the whole Russell Brand affair raises some uncomfortable questions about how permissive we have become as a society.

For decades, we have systematically dismantled what were once called bourgeois values and standards of behaviour (good manners, politeness, civility etc). We did away with them because we thought they were repressive and outdated. The nihilistic Left in particular saw them as instruments of social control that reinforced class hierarchies. They claimed that these values helped to sustain the capitalist order by encouraging conformity and deference to established authority.

Nobody is suggesting that we return to the past and put Mary Whitehouse in charge of broadcasting rules. But the fact that someone like Brand could be celebrated and elevated by the BBC, Channel 4, The Guardian, the Labour Party and the Home Affairs Select Committee (and more recently the Republican Party!!) as a moral and political authority really does say something about our culture and how far our institutions have fallen.

What, precisely, did Brand have to offer? Why did we give someone like him such prominence when we could have elevated serious academics, philosophers and professionals with genuine expertise?

I am an atheist and a classical liberal, not a religious right moralist. But as Adam Smith understood, a free society depends on more than individual liberty. It also depends on high moral standards and self-restraint that govern how we treat one another.

P.S. Before the crank Right gets too high and mighty, it might want to reflect on its own choice of associations. The grotesque Tate brothers, Tommy Robinson, Daniel Thomas and plenty of other unsavoury characters whose conduct and values contribute precious little to our civilisation.
