text:
Most bidders left. The Navy still pushed its pick back.

The Navy wants a jet to replace the T-45 Goshawk, which has trained Navy and Marine Corps aviators for carrier flying since the early 1990s. The program is called the Undergraduate Jet Training System.

Proposals were due Oct. 30. Textron Aviation Defense says it bid the M-346N, offered with Leonardo. Stavatti Aerospace says it bid too.

The other big names left. Lockheed Martin passed in April. Boeing left in June. Northrop Grumman came off SNC's team in September, and SNC didn't bid at the deadline, saying it "could not responsibly bid" under "the current contract structure."

The September request for proposals set the Oct. 30 deadline and put the award at June 30, 2027. On Nov. 3, with the bids in, the program office said the Navy is "in source selection with the intent to award the UJTS procurement in 4QFY27." Fourth quarter of fiscal 2027 runs July through September.

Bids to award, September plan: 8 months.
Bids to award now: up to 11.

Any slip past Sept. 30, 2027 moves the award into fiscal 2028.

text:
THE CEO WHO SPENT ONE NIGHT AS A HOMELESS MAN

I watched a security guard throw a homeless man out of my company’s lobby.

Then I watched the same man return the following morning wearing a $3,000 suit.

His name was Michael Bennett.

And he owned the entire building.

I know because I was the security guard.

I had worked at Bennett Financial Group in Manhattan for almost six years. My job was simple: check visitors, monitor cameras, and make sure nobody entered without authorization.

One freezing Thursday evening, a man walked into the lobby wearing an old brown coat and worn-out shoes.

His beard was untrimmed, and he carried a plastic shopping bag.

“Sir, can I sit here for a few minutes?” he asked.

I looked at the security policy.

“I’m sorry. This building is for employees and registered visitors.”

“It’s freezing outside.”

“I understand, but I can’t allow you to stay.”

He didn’t argue.

He simply nodded and walked toward the revolving doors.

But before leaving, he turned around.

“Do you know who owns this building?”

“Mr. Bennett,” I replied.

The man smiled faintly.

“Interesting.”

Then he disappeared into the snow.

The following morning, I arrived for my shift at 7:00 a.m.

At 8:15, the elevators opened.

The same man stepped out.

Except this time, he wore a tailored navy suit, polished shoes, and an expensive watch.

Behind him were two executives and the company’s legal director.

I immediately stood up.

“Good morning, sir.”

He looked directly at me.

“Good morning. Do you remember me?”

I swallowed.

“Yes, sir.”

He smiled.

“I’m Michael Bennett. I believe we’ve met.”

My stomach dropped.

The CEO.

The owner of the company.

The man I had refused to let sit in the lobby the previous evening.

I expected to lose my job.

Instead, he asked me to accompany him to the conference room.

Inside, several senior executives were waiting.

Michael took his seat at the head of the table.

Then he explained what had happened.

He had spent the previous evening visiting several businesses he owned without announcing his identity.

He wanted to understand how ordinary people were treated when nobody important was watching.

He had visited three buildings.

At one, a receptionist gave him a cup of coffee.

At another, a manager threatened to call the police.

At our building, I had followed company policy but refused to offer him even a few minutes of shelter.

He looked at me.

“Why didn’t you let me stay?”

I hesitated.

“Because I was afraid of losing my job, sir.”

He nodded.

“That’s an honest answer.”

Then he turned to the executives.

“This is exactly the problem.”

He explained that the company had spent millions on employee welfare programmes while its own security staff were afraid to show basic compassion.

He wasn’t angry that I had followed the rules.

He was concerned that the rules offered no reasonable way to handle an emergency.

He ordered an immediate review of the building’s visitor and emergency assistance policies.

A week later, the company introduced a programme allowing security personnel to offer temporary shelter, water, and emergency assistance to vulnerable people without risking disciplinary action.

But Michael wasn’t finished.

He invited me into his office.

“I’ve been reviewing your employment record,” he said.

I sat down.

“You’ve worked here for six years without a single disciplinary issue. Your supervisors say you’re reliable, but you’ve never applied for a promotion.”

I shrugged.

“I never thought I qualified.”

He opened a folder.

“Before working here, you studied business administration, correct?”

“Yes, sir. I couldn’t finish because my father became ill.”

He nodded.

text:
Podcast Summary | The Joe Rogan Experience: #2577 - Gregory Forth

Overview
Anthropologist Gregory Forth brings a rare data point to the hominin survival debate: he heard consistent local accounts of small, hairy, upright creatures on Flores well before Homo floresiensis was discovered in 2003 and announced in 2004. The core tension is that fossils establish an ancient species, while Forth’s ethnography rests on local reports that these animals still inhabit high, unsettled forest in the Lio region. He does not claim the species definitely survives; he argues the coincidence between fossil reconstructions and local descriptions is remarkable enough to justify serious field research. The most striking detail may be the rethinking of how Flores was peopled and how its fauna behaved; recent analyses suggest pygmy stegodons near the discovery site were likely killed by Komodo dragons, with possible stone-tool marks indicating hominins only scraped meat from bones rather than hunted the animals.

Key Themes
- The local “hairy little people” are described by inhabitants as natural animals rather than forest spirits, a distinction that gives the reports more weight.
- The creatures are repeatedly placed at high altitude in mountainous, unsettled forest, which Forth suggests implies a food supply there and makes coastal sightings less credible.
- Flores is mammal-poor; the only indigenous native mammals are bats and rodents, and monkeys, pigs, deer, and porcupines were introduced by people, so a small hominin would face an unusual ecological stage.
- The type specimen’s dentition suggests a largely vegetarian diet, though Forth does not rule out opportunistic meat-eating.
- The Flores “ape men” are argued to be more credible than North American Bigfoot because fossil evidence and a matching evolutionary history exist, unlike in the Pacific Northwest.
- Dating revisions turned the most recent Flores specimens from roughly 12,000–13,000 years old to 50,000–60,000, but the unresolved question of how hominins reached an island without a known land bridge remains central.
- Classification disputes matter: most paleoanthropologists place floresiensis in Homo, while others argue it is more primitive and derives from an older, separate branch.
- Eyewitness accounts tend toward naturalistic descriptions, while secondhand retellings drift toward the fantastic, which Forth offers as a kind of evidence for the credibility of firsthand reports.
- Ethical questions shadow the question: if such a creature were captured, it would be neither clearly an animal nor a person, complicating decisions about zoos and study.

Detailed Summary
Forth’s fieldwork on Flores began in 1984, and he heard accounts of small humanlike creatures long before the Homo floresiensis find. Local reports placed them in the Lio region of eastern Flores, mostly at high altitude in mountainous, unsettled forest. The best-known specimens are roughly three to three-and-a-half feet tall, or up to four feet in some estimates. One secondhand report cited about 1.4 meters. The creatures are described as primarily vegetarian, and the type specimen shows no definite canines and teeth in good shape for its age. Chimpanzees are cited as largely vegetarian but known to eat monkeys, illustrating that a mostly vegetarian diet does not exclude meat.

The witness accounts are uneven by design. Forth recorded more than 30 encounter reports and spoke with over 120 to 130 people who knew something about the creatures. He considered about a dozen much more interesting than the rest. Some less credible reports could have been misidentifications of the long-tailed macaque, or occurred near the coast where encounters would be unexpected. The clearest sightings, in Forth’s view, are more consistent with the standard “ape man” image.

The first story he heard came in the Ngada region. A legend held that the creatures, called “ebo,” were wiped out by ancestors of the Ngada, with two escaping to another territory and incestuously maintaining the species — a narrative Forth considers embellished. In that legend, the creatures lived in a cave high on a mountain, came down to join village feasts and dances, were given food, and were portrayed as stupid, eating pumpkin-skin plates and being made drunk on palm wine or palm gin. Local genealogies and family histories suggest such supposed interactions occurred at least 200 to 300 years ago, and a separate account described creatures living in a cave on a nearby volcano extinct about 200 to 300 years earlier.

The storytellers insisted the creatures were real, natural animals rather than forest spirits. Forth heard encounter accounts months before the Flores bones were discovered and more than a year before the discovery was announced publicly. He argues the local notion predates the fossil discovery, citing the name “Lai” recorded in a Lai-language dictionary. A German missionary’s Lai–German dictionary research from the 1920s was published in 1933 and included mentions of “Lai” consistent with local accounts. A Dutch Catholic missionary in the Ngada region had never heard of the “Ebugo,” the Ngada “ape men,” despite stories being widely known nearby.

Forth treats the match between reconstructions of Flores hominins and local descriptions as remarkable. He remains skeptical of firm belief but says the coincidence would require a huge, well-hidden conspiracy to fool him and is worth further exploration. He began researching the “Li” hominoids in earnest in 2005 around age 60 and left off in 2018 in his 70s, describing himself as never particularly athletic and now physically limited. A colleague plans an expanded search on a particular mountain in the Leo region, with drones and other technology under consideration. The argument is that an island setting and a smaller team reduce noise and disturbance compared with typical Bigfoot searches. Forth is working with a man in the Netherlands who placed camera traps at a volcano and wants to return with a team.

Two British hikers independently reported seeing a creature on a Flores mountain in March 2019. Interviewed separately, one described a small bipedal human-like “ape man” and the other a very large monkey — interpretations that align with the range of local descriptions, some more monkey-like and others more human-like. The hikers had not read Forth’s writings before their encounter and found his name later through internet research on Flores apes and monkeys. One initially wrote that what they saw “sounds like” the creature known locally as “Obugo.” A secondhand report put the highest size estimate around four feet. Another account described a big upright monkey with no tail, about three feet or more tall. A late anthropologist friend working on Sumbawa, immediately east of Flores, had a similar sighting in the 1980s and gave detailed descriptions on more than one occasion, allowing Forth to mention it in more than one book.

The evidence for a species is extremely rare and incomplete. Fossil remains found in central Flores were about 700,000 years old and smaller than Homo floresiensis; they are presumed possible ancestors. Possible stone-tool evidence may go back about a million years or more, though Forth notes some tools are ambiguous and not all authorities accept them as artifacts. Stone tool industries alone cannot distinguish species in that part of the world; skeletal evidence in close association is needed. The oldest date for Homo sapiens on Flores was once about 11,000 years ago and has since been pushed back to roughly 50,000 years. Initial age estimates for the Homo floresiensis remains were only 12,000 to 13,000 years old, treated as a major problem; a senior investigator reportedly said discovering something like Homo floresiensis at that age would be more surprising than discovering a space alien. That dating was later revised to roughly 50,000 to 60,000 years, though Forth says nothing is certain.

The first bones were initially dismissed by some as abnormal modern humans, for example a brain condition such as microcephaly. That view is now largely unsupported. Floresiensis had a small body and a brain about the size of a chimpanzee’s; small body size does not correlate with microcephaly, which concerns the head. A key dispute concerns classification. Most paleoanthropologists classify floresiensis as Homo, but some, including Chris Stringer, argue it is more primitive and derives from an older, separate branch near australopithecines. Peter Brown proposed a separate genus name, Sundanthropus, which was rejected, and Forth considers some stated reasons weak. The discovery challenged linear views of human evolution, supporting a “bushy” family tree like a menorah, with side-by-side branches rather than a single improving line.

Similar small hominin remains were found in the Philippines at Luzon, discovered after floresiensis and described as a separate species, Homo luzonensis. Evidence of small hominins also exists in China at Red Deer Cave, in the same region as the larger Homo erectus. Homo naledi in Africa, discovered by Lee Berger’s team, is dated to about 200,000 years ago; it buried its dead, had unusually elaborate symbolic culture for its circumstances, and evidence of stone tool use. No comparable culture is noted for floresiensis.

How the region’s wildlife reached Flores remains a puzzle. Many animals arrived by natural means, swimming, flying, or rafting, while others, including monkeys and porcupines, were introduced by people. Komodo dragons are strong swimmers and regularly swim between islands. Rats are described as able to reach almost everywhere; Alberta is noted as an exception, with mice present and rats kept out. The region’s sizable mammals include various mice and rats, including a giant, aggressive tree rat that locals hunt with dogs and tools, and people are often injured by them. Forth argues it is unlikely Homo floresiensis could have hunted the giant tree rats, which are difficult and vicious; smaller rodents might have been catchable. The small creatures are reputed to occasionally steal chickens or very small piglets. Pigs, monkeys, and porcupines were introduced by people, and dogs may have been present several hundred to a thousand years, possibly longer.

Komodo dragons can grow to about 10 feet long and have venom glands, sharp teeth, and a deadly tail. Recent analyses suggest pygmy stegodon remains near the discovery site were likely killed by Komodo dragons, with possible stone-tool marks indicating hominins only scraped meat from bones rather than hunting the animals. Pygmy stegodons were roughly the size of a cow. Lower sea levels during ice ages existed, but there is no known land bridge to Flores; stegodons are said to have swum there. Accidental rafting on large clumps of earth or vegetation driven out to sea by tsunamis is presented as a possible dispersal mechanism, requiring more than one individual and both sexes. The arrival of humans brought pigs, dogs, deer, and other domesticates, potentially providing prey that helped sustain giant lizards; humans may also have contributed to the extinction of pygmy elephants.

The discussion turns to why the Flores case outranks Bigfoot. Forth treats the Flores “ape men” as stronger than local traditions of much larger two-to-three-meter bipedal creatures on Sumba. He notes that local knowledge of wild animals varies between communities, offering the example of a rare indigenous wild rabbit or hare in western Indonesia and Sumatra that many local people did not know or have a name for. The human family tree is described as bushy, and paleoanthropology can be conservative and resistant to change, sometimes harming researchers who challenge prevailing views; Forth defends caution as appropriate given uncertainty. Clovis-first resistance is cited as an example; evidence from White Sands, New Mexico footprints dates to roughly 22,000 years ago, and dates keep being pushed earlier.

The ethics of discovery are treated seriously. If such a creature were captured, it would be neither clearly an animal nor a person, complicating decisions about zoos and study. Forth would prefer that such creatures, if they exist, be left alone, while acknowledging the scientific value of discovery and personal vindication. Proving existence is harder now because AI video makes distinguishing real from fake footage nearly impossible. Studying such creatures would be best done through long-term field research and habituation, citing Jane Goodall and gorilla researchers as models. Sedating an unknown hominin for study carries risks because its allergies and drug reactions are unknown and it could be killed accidentally.

The North American context is treated more skeptically. Native American traditions contain many names for a tall, hairy “wild man” of the woods, which the speakers treat as notable because those traditions reportedly did not include many invented creatures. The 1884 “Jacko” report is presented as one of the more interesting historical cases: an allegedly captured small ape-like creature near Yale, British Columbia, during Canadian Pacific Railway construction, about 100 miles from the coast, published in the Daily British Colonist on July 4, 1884, and described as roughly 4 feet 2 inches or a bit larger. No photos were taken. Commentators have suggested the creature was an infant Bigfoot. Modern historians and cryptozoologists widely regard the story as a newspaper hoax or journalistic fiction, and a physical anthropologist’s book arguing Jacko was an escaped circus or zoo chimpanzee is treated as implausible given the remoteness of the area and absence of zoos or circuses in British Columbia at the time.

The speakers connect Bigfoot belief to that 1884 context: great apes were newly known to Western publics, Darwin’s ideas were recent, and people had only vague ideas of what apes looked like, making misidentification plausible. Forth says his arguments have been found credible by some paleoanthropologists and biologists, but they avoid saying so publicly because of academic conservatism and fear of losing funding or reputation. The host acknowledges Bigfoot is fun to believe, which complicates his own judgment; the expert states he does not find Bigfoot credible. A genuine scientific search, rather than a reality-show search, is described as worth doing.

Dijon’s Eucharistic story is not a claim that a miraculous Host can still be seen. The object described in the received account was destroyed during the French Revolution. The present Catholic destination is the Church of Saint-Michel, where the Host was kept during its final years and where an annual Mass of reparation preserves the memory of its destruction. That distinction is essential for an honest pilgrimage page. The event itself was reported far from Dijon. Annual Mass of reparation for the destroyed Holy Host offers a natural day to enter that story.

Saint-Michel Church and the Reparation Memory of Dijon stands in Dijon, France. Dijon’s Eucharistic story is not a claim that a miraculous Host can still be seen. The object described in the received account was destroyed during the French Revolution. The present Catholic destination is the Church of Saint-Michel, where the Host was kept during its final years and where an annual Mass of reparation preserves the memory of its destruction. That distinction is essential for an honest pilgrimage page. The event itself was reported far from Dijon. The Diocese of Dijon’s historical account begins in Monaco in 1430. A woman acquired an ostensory that was probably stolen and that still contained a large consecrated Host. When she tried to detach the Host with a knife, blood was reported to appear and an image of Christ with the instruments of the Passion was said to form on it. These are claims transmitted by Catholic historical and devotional sources; Catholic Tourist does not present them as the result of modern scientific testing. Pope Eugene IV later gave the Host to Philip the Good, Duke of Burgundy. Philip in turn entrusted it to Dijon, where it became one of the city’s most important objects of devotion. It was kept at the ducal Sainte-Chapelle, a building that once stood beside the Palace of the Dukes of Burgundy but was demolished in the nineteenth century. Dijon’s municipal medieval heritage dossier confirms that the Sainte-Chapelle conserved the Holy Host and that it inspired a large annual procession. The distinction between the historic Sainte-Chapelle and the current Church of Saint-Michel prevents a common misunderstanding. Saint-Michel was not the original 1430 event site and it was not the principal shrine throughout the Host’s centuries in Dijon. It entered the story at the Revolution. On January 18, 1791, according to the diocesan account, the Host was transferred from the Sainte-Chapelle to Saint-Michel and placed in the tabernacle of the Virgin’s altar. Revolutionary authorities requisitioned Saint-Michel on February 9, 1794, for use as a Temple of Reason. On February 10, five municipal agents burned the Host in front of the church. The exact point of the destruction is not documented. A star in the pavement outside Saint-Michel now carries the memory, but it should be described as a memorial marker rather than archaeological proof of the precise spot. The Host therefore no longer survives. There is no reliquary, monstrance, or consecrated species from the 1430 account available for pilgrims to view at Saint-Michel. Dijon’s Eucharistic story is not a claim that a miraculous Host can still be seen. Its connection with Annual Mass of reparation for the destroyed Holy Host gives pilgrims a specific reason to understand the people, prayer, history, and present-day community gathered here.

Each year, this place comes into sharper focus through Annual Mass of reparation for the destroyed Holy Host on 02-10. The observance gives pilgrims a reason to return to the story and to the community that still keeps it. Anyone planning a visit should confirm the current program with the shrine, parish, or diocese, because Masses, processions, access routes, and crowd arrangements can change even when the annual commemoration remains the same.

The saints connected with this destination are St. Elizabeth of the Trinity — prayed at Saint-Michel and is represented there by relics documented in diocesan coverage. Those relationships matter: a patron, founder, visitor, martyr, relic, and tomb do not tell the same story. Here the saint is not a name added to a building. A Christian life becomes visible through an altar, a road, a burial place, a community, or a landscape where faith was actually practiced.

The Diocese of Dijon transmits the received 1430 account and documents the Host’s revolutionary destruction and the annual reparation Mass. The Host no longer survives, and Catholic Tourist makes no independent scientific claim about the medieval event. The story must preserve that exact ecclesial category and must not turn permission for devotion, a diocesan judgment, or a received tradition into a broader claim than the responsible authority made. That distinction matters. Church recognition, ecclesiastical custody, public devotion, local tradition, archaeology, and tourism promotion do not all answer the same question. Saying plainly what is known—and what remains a received tradition—protects the truth without taking the wonder out of the story.

Visit Saint-Michel as the final place of custody and the living church of reparation, while remembering that the 1430 event began in Monaco and the Host’s long Dijon shrine was the now-lost Sainte-Chapelle. The destination guide identifies Saint-Michel’s final custody: Pray in the church where the Host was kept from 1791 until its destruction in 1794., The lost Sainte-Chapelle: Remember the demolished sanctuary where Dijon’s Holy Host had been venerated for centuries., The pavement star: Read the exterior marker as a memorial to the burning, not proof of its undocumented exact location., Annual reparation: Join the February 10 Mass when the current parish schedule permits., and St. Elizabeth of the Trinity: Connect Saint-Michel’s Eucharistic memory with the Dijon Carmelite saint who prayed here.. A good visit does not treat these as boxes to check. Begin with the devotional or historical center, notice the details around it, and then leave room for worship or quiet reflection. A photograph can preserve the look of a moment; pilgrimage needs enough time for the meaning of the place to settle in.

Beautiful sites are especially vulnerable to being consumed quickly. At Saint-Michel Church and the Reparation Memory of Dijon, the challenge is to let beauty perform its older work: not self-display, but direction. Stone, wood, paint, light, landscape, and ritual can direct attention toward mysteries they do not contain or control. Even when the artistic achievement is extraordinary, Christian art remains most intelligible in relation to worship. The pilgrim can admire the maker’s skill while asking what truth the work was meant to confess and what kind of life that confession invites.

A little preparation protects that deeper visit. No stable daily opening schedule was verified from the parish page. Confirm before making a dedicated visit. Ask the parish for current confession availability; do not assume it accompanies every visit or annual observance. The church is in central Dijon. Contact the parish for the current step-free entrance and interior accessibility. Saint-Michel stands east of Dijon’s historic center and is walkable from the Palace of the Dukes and central tram stops. No miraculous Host survives at Saint-Michel. The exterior star is a memorial; the exact burning point is not documented. Confirm the annual Mass time and respect parish worship and photography restrictions. The official source should outrank an old itinerary, especially during feast days, restoration work, seasonal closures, or major pilgrimages. Entry to the main church also may not include every chapel, relic, museum room, or devotional area connected with its history.

There is also a healthy difference between curiosity and credulity. Saint-Michel Church and the Reparation Memory of Dijon can be approached with real openness without exaggerating what the sources establish. Catholic faith does not depend on turning every tradition into a scientific finding or every testimony into a universal decree. Careful language protects the people who live with the devotion, the pilgrims who are trying to understand it, and the credibility of the Church’s witness. The truest version of a story is usually more interesting than the viral version because it contains real people, real limits, and a place that can still be visited.

The most useful question after learning this history is not “Did I know this already?” but “What does this place ask me to remember?” Saint-Michel Church and the Reparation Memory of Dijon may preserve courage, conversion, sorrow, gratitude, missionary patience, artistic labor, or confidence in intercession. Memory becomes Christian when it leads beyond admiration toward communion: prayer for the living, gratitude for those who came before, repentance for failures, and renewed attention to Christ. Pilgrimage begins before the journey when attention changes. A traveler can arrive at Saint-Michel Church and the Reparation Memory of Dijon merely asking what there is to photograph, or arrive asking what generations of Christians learned to pray here. The second question slows everything down. Architecture becomes more than backdrop; an image becomes more than an object; a tomb becomes more than a historical marker. A feast can tell us when to remember, but it cannot do the remembering for us. Let the history become prayer, gratitude, repentance, service, or one concrete act of charity. Before leaving the story, choose one detail worth carrying with you and remember the living community behind it. If you share it, tell it with the same care you would hope a visitor would bring to a place you love: without exaggeration, without contempt for honest questions, and without losing sight of the people who still pray there. India is tightening the screws on ethanol feedstock. Maize could be the biggest beneficiary.

After restricting sugar-based ethanol, the government has now imposed fresh curbs on FCI rice and damaged foodgrains for ESY 2026-27.

Key numbers:

• FCI surplus rice: Capped at 72 LMT, equivalent to 324 crore litres of ethanol.
• Quarterly rice allocation: Maximum 108 crore litres.
• Distillery-level restriction: FCI rice ethanol capped at 30% of each bidder's total offer.
• Damaged foodgrains: Maximum 160 crore litres annually.
• Combined rice + damaged grain allocation: Just 484 crore litres against an overall ethanol tender of 1,100 crore litres.

The implications for maize are significant.

With sugar-based feedstock restricted and FCI rice allocations constrained, ethanol producers may increasingly turn to maize to bridge the supply gap.

India's maize balance sheet could face another demand shock.

The battle for maize between ethanol, poultry feed and starch industries is getting fiercer.

text:
INDIA’S BROKEN RICE EXPORT BAN MAY BE BACK!

The battle for Indian rice is intensifying.

Three industries are competing for the same grain: ETHANOL, POULTRY FEED & EXPORTS.

And supplies are tightening.

Key developments:

• India is considering renewed restrictions on 100% broken white rice exports. The previous ban lasted from September 2022 to March 7, 2025.

• Broken rice FOB Kakinada has climbed to $336/tonne, up 5% MoM and 5.32% YoY. Some offers are already exceeding $360/tonne.

• Poultry feed grain prices have crossed ₹34,000/tonne in southern India, with Bihar at ₹30,000 and Punjab at ₹31,000–32,000.

• India needs approximately 11 billion litres of ethanol this season, but FCI plans to supply only 7.2 million tonnes of rice to ethanol producers.

• S&P Global Energy CERA projects India's 2026/27 rice production at just 146 million tonnes, down 8 million tonnes YoY.

The weather has made matters worse: southern India drought, El Niño-related disruptions, Cyclone Arnab and unseasonal rainfall in Chhattisgarh.

THE BIGGER PICTURE:

India's rice market is facing a three-way supply squeeze.

Ethanol producers need feedstock. Poultry manufacturers need cheaper grain. Exporters need access to global markets.

If domestic prices continue climbing, export restrictions could return — tightening global broken rice availability and reshuffling feed trade flows.

One critical question:

Will India prioritise its domestic ethanol and feed industries over broken rice exports?

This is no longer just a rice story. It's a competition for scarce feedstock.

Seven nights run downstream from Siem Reap to Ho Chi Minh City along the Mekong, beginning amid the ancient temples of Angkor and ending in the energy of Vietnam's largest city. In between lies an extraordinary run of river villages, rice paddies and living cultural heritage.

Seven Nights Along the Mekong: From the Temples of Angkor to Vibrant Ho Chi Minh City

Embark on a captivating seven-night journey downstream along the legendary Mekong River, sailing from Siem Reap to Ho Chi Minh City. Your adventure begins among the awe-inspiring temples of Angkor and concludes amid the dynamic energy of Vietnam's largest metropolis. Along the way, discover authentic riverside communities, emerald rice fields, and centuries of living cultural traditions.

Embark in Cambodia and Begin Your Mekong Voyage

Your journey starts in Siem Reap, where Cambodia's ancient heritage blends seamlessly with modern sophistication. Travel by motorcoach to Kampong Cham, where your elegant river ship awaits. Settle into your accommodations before joining fellow guests and the crew for a welcoming dinner, marking the beginning of your unforgettable Mekong experience.

Experience Authentic Village Life and Timeless Craftsmanship

Visit Angkor Ban, one of Cambodia's few villages that remained untouched during the Khmer Rouge era. Wander among traditional wooden stilt houses shaded by lush banana trees and gain insight into a way of life preserved for generations. Later, cruise to Silk Island, renowned for its enduring weaving traditions. Meet local artisans who create exquisite silk by hand, visit a village school, and enjoy an overnight stay as the Mekong gently carries you onward.

Explore Phnom Penh's Royal Heritage and Resilient Spirit

Arriving in Cambodia's capital, discover the unique character of Phnom Penh, where elegant riverside promenades, historic landmarks, and bustling markets reveal the city's rich heritage and enduring vitality. Throughout the day, opportunities for reflection and cultural enrichment abound, while the evening comes alive with a captivating performance celebrating the music and dance traditions of Khmer folklore.

Sacred Blessings, Panoramic Views, and Colonial Charm

Journey to Oudong, Cambodia's former royal capital, where a traditional Buddhist Blessing Ceremony offers a meaningful and serene cultural experience. Take in sweeping views across the surrounding countryside before returning to Phnom Penh. Later, explore the city's French colonial architecture and iconic landmarks by tuk tuk, including the revered Wat Phnom and its graceful tree-lined boulevards.

Cross the Border into Vietnam

Relax on board as your ship continues southward along the Mekong, crossing from Cambodia into Vietnam. Watch the scenery transform as riverside villages, floating communities, and lush agricultural landscapes showcase the ever-changing rhythm of life along Southeast Asia's most iconic waterway.

Discover Tan Chau and the Natural Beauty of the Delta

In the charming town of Tan Chau, experience a slower pace of life that remains deeply connected to local traditions. Explore by trishaw, visit family-run silk and rattan workshops, or join a guided walking tour for a closer look at everyday life. Alternatively, venture into the tranquil Tra Su Forest aboard a traditional sampan, gliding through waterways lined with lotus blooms, towering cajuput trees, and an abundance of birdlife.

Immerse Yourself in the Heritage of Sa Dec

Step ashore in Sa Dec, a town forever associated with French novelist Marguerite Duras. Browse the lively local market, visit the colorful Cao Dai Temple, and tour the historic Huynh Thuy Le House. During the afternoon, gain insight into regional craftsmanship at local candy and rice paper workshops or explore the beautifully preserved Kiet Old House. In the evening, celebrate your voyage with a festive farewell dinner aboard the ship.

Arrive in Ho Chi Minh City

After breakfast, disembark your ship and transfer to Ho Chi Minh City as your remarkable Mekong River journey comes to a close. Depart with lasting memories of extraordinary cultures, timeless traditions, and unforgettable experiences along one of the world's great rivers.

$VIAV KEY READ-THROUGHS FROM VIAVI SOLUTIONS’ FISCAL Q1 2027 EARNINGS CALL

VIAVI’s results support a selective infrastructure-investment thesis rather than an indiscriminate bullish view of technology capital spending. The strongest signals are the migration of optical testing into semiconductor manufacturing, continued coexistence of 800G and 1.6T production, increasing fiber and connector complexity, and strengthening demand for resilient navigation. December-quarter NSE revenue guidance implies 14.3% sequential growth, with management attributing approximately 40% of the increase to data centers, approximately 33% to aerospace and defense, and the remainder to service providers. That breadth matters, but wireless remains conspicuously weak. The principal cross-market implication is continued divergence between optical infrastructure, selected broadband upgrades, and autonomous-system electronics on the positive side, versus expectations of an imminent broad wireless investment recovery on the negative side.

The assessments below distinguish business impact from stock-price impact and demand corroboration from genuinely new orders. Several affected companies had already reported before VIAVI’s call, making this evidence more useful for assessing forward durability than predicting completed quarters. No undisclosed VIAVI customer relationship or supplier allocation is assumed. Information is bounded to November 4, 2026. Historical-memory retrieval was unavailable because of an embedding-provider error requiring configuration repair; the analysis instead relies on the supplied material and readable, dated corporate disclosures.

SEMICONDUCTOR TEST: CPO CREATES ADDITIONAL MANUFACTURING TEST STEPS, NOT JUST FASTER INSTRUMENT REPLACEMENT (READ-THROUGH 1)

Affected company: FormFactor (FORM: United States). Direction: positive. Magnitude: high strategic importance for optical probing and systems, moderate potential consolidated impact over several years, and limited incremental near-term earnings visibility from this call alone. Conviction: high on the demand mechanism, lower on the size of individual customer allocations.

The decisive evidence is VIAVI’s confirmation that semiconductor packaging and test shipments began in September, initially at approximately $1 million, predominantly supporting CPO. Management expects the business to accelerate in December and March and described up to 5 testing stages spanning wafer probing, known-good-die assessment, optical-engine testing, assembled substrates, and final testing. Khaykin characterized semiconductor testing as potentially “north of $100 million for Viavi just by itself,” explicitly excluding OCS.

The transmission mechanism to FormFactor is additional demand for optical access, alignment, probing, and automated measurement as photonics moves inside expensive semiconductor assemblies. Detecting an optical defect before integrating a photonic component with a high-value processor or switch can prevent the loss of a much more expensive assembly. That increases the economic value of earlier screening. The opportunity is therefore not limited to replacing an older tester with a faster tester; it includes adding optical testing to manufacturing stages that previously required predominantly electrical measurements.

FormFactor’s exposure is verified rather than merely thematic. Its Pharos optical-probe portfolio supports edge coupling, surface coupling, die-level testing, and CPO interfaces. Its October 28 results also reported more than 20% sequential Systems revenue growth on higher CPO demand. VIAVI’s disclosure independently corroborates the same transition from development activity toward production infrastructure. It does not establish a supply agreement between the companies or imply that FormFactor receives a fixed portion of VIAVI’s opportunity.

The near-term catalyst is continued Systems order conversion and production-related customer spending in subsequent quarterly disclosures. FormFactor had already reported its September quarter, so VIAVI is not an advance signal for that completed release. The longer-duration catalyst is expansion of optical testing across successive packaging stages during calendar 2027 and beyond. The principal constraint is that faster alignment, parallel testing, and improved throughput can reduce equipment requirements per device. The durable positive thesis is expanding production volume and test coverage, not a permanent preservation of inefficient early-stage manufacturing.

ELECTRONIC MEASUREMENT: OPTICAL NETWORK VALIDATION HAS A CLEAR NEAR-TERM CATALYST, BUT VIAVI’S MARGINS SHOULD NOT BE EXTRAPOLATED (READ-THROUGH 2)

Affected company: Keysight Technologies (KEYS: United States). Direction: positive for communications testing demand. Magnitude: moderate at the consolidated level, potentially stronger within high-speed Ethernet, optical interconnect, and AI-fabric validation. Conviction: high on shared-market demand, but insufficient evidence to quantify an earnings beat.

VIAVI reported strong demand across lab, production, and field instruments and guided NSE revenue from $376.1 million to approximately $430 million sequentially. Management’s approximate 40% data-center contribution to that increase implies roughly $21.6 million of additional quarterly revenue associated with that end market. The important signal is simultaneous growth across multiple testing stages rather than reliance on a single laboratory product cycle.

Keysight has directly relevant products. Its October 13 announcement introduced the SERT 1600GE and AresONE Plus 1600GE platforms for switch validation, routing, and AI-workload emulation. The announcement also identified collaboration with NVIDIA around Spectrum-6 validation. Increasing network speeds and more synchronized AI workloads raise the importance of testing congestion, interoperability, fault behavior, and effective fabric performance before deployment. These requirements create instrument and software demand even before the associated infrastructure generates revenue for its operator.

The most actionable timing distinction is that Keysight is scheduled to report on November 19. Its previously issued fiscal Q4 revenue guidance was $1.930 billion to $1.950 billion. VIAVI’s late-quarter demand commentary provides a favorable external indicator for Keysight’s communications order environment and subsequent outlook. However, Keysight already reported 56% growth in commercial communications in its July quarter, so a strong market was not previously undiscovered. VIAVI adds evidence of persistence, not proof that expectations are too low.

The negative qualification concerns margins and competitive share. VIAVI’s September operating margin included a tariff refund, benefited from expense timing, and reflected its own business mix and completed integration actions. Those factors cannot be transferred to Keysight. Similarly, VIAVI’s success does not demonstrate that Keysight gained share; the companies compete in important product categories. The supported trading implication is a positive demand backdrop into November 19, with order growth and forward guidance more informative than an assumption that Keysight should replicate VIAVI’s operating-margin expansion.

OPTICAL COMPONENTS AND SWITCHING: CPO AND OCS COMMERCIALIZATION STRENGTHENS LUMENTUM’S BUSINESS CASE, BUT THE STOCK EXPOSURE IS NOW MERGER-LINKED (READ-THROUGH 3)

Affected companies: Lumentum Holdings (LITE: United States) and Marvell Technology (MRVL: United States). Direction: positive for Lumentum’s operating opportunity and conditionally positive for Marvell’s proposed combination. Magnitude: potentially high for Lumentum over several years; no immediate consolidation benefit to Marvell. Conviction: high on optical commercialization, not on transaction returns or valuation.

VIAVI’s initial CPO-related manufacturing shipments are evidence that customer programs are progressing into tangible production infrastructure. Management separately described OCS as “one of the biggest sweet spots in the market” for test content per port and emphasized substantial testing time for large optical switches. These disclosures support both an expanding production base for packaged optical connectivity and increasing manufacturing activity in optical circuit switching.

Lumentum’s November 2 results provide the company-specific exposure. It reported a second major NPO/CPO win backed by purchase commitments exceeding $5 billion and described OCS as a potential multibillion-dollar annual revenue stream. VIAVI’s commentary is therefore independent corroboration of an already disclosed operating thesis, not a new $5 billion order announcement. The transmission mechanism is manufacturing capacity and qualification activity translating into demand for Lumentum’s lasers, optical subsystems, and OCS products as customer systems move toward deployment.

The economic distinction between CPO and OCS remains important. CPO can create high aggregate demand through large semiconductor unit volumes and multiple manufacturing stages. OCS can create high content per system despite lower system volumes. VIAVI’s hypothetical discussion of $50 million to $100 million of testing demand against a $2 billion customer revenue base is not a recurring industry royalty rate. Test capacity is purchased ahead of, and periodically during, production expansion. It should not be converted into a mechanical forecast for Lumentum shipments or margins.

The ownership and trading implications are unusually important. On November 2, Marvell and Lumentum announced an all-stock transaction under which Lumentum shareholders would receive 4.500 Marvell shares for each Lumentum share. Closing is expected in the first half of calendar 2028, subject to approvals and other conditions. Lumentum is therefore not simply a standalone optical-growth exposure: its equity value is also linked to Marvell’s share price, the exchange ratio, and completion risk. The announced transaction value is not a fixed cash floor.

Near-term catalysts are execution against Lumentum’s already issued December outlook, customer qualification milestones, and developments affecting the merger. Longer-term, VIAVI’s evidence strengthens the rationale for combining electrical design, optical components, and packaging capabilities. It does not validate the acquisition price, promised synergies, or post-transaction shareholder returns. Lumentum and Marvell positions should also not be treated as independent sources of portfolio diversification.

OPTICAL TRANSCEIVERS: THE 800G AND 1.6T OVERLAP SUPPORTS NEAR-TERM DEMAND, WHILE CPO CHALLENGES SIMPLE TERMINAL-VALUE ASSUMPTIONS (READ-THROUGH 4)

Affected company: Coherent (COHR: United States). Direction: positive for near-term transceiver demand; negative for the assumption that every future bandwidth increment preserves today’s standalone-module revenue structure. Magnitude: material within data-center products, with the consolidated outcome supported by Coherent’s broader component capabilities. Conviction: high on coexistence of speed generations and architectural change, but not on the timing of eventual module displacement.

VIAVI stated that 800G remains the highest-volume shipment category and that 1.6T is still early in its ramp. Management expects 1.6T to approach high production volumes in the second half of calendar 2027 and suggested that it might not surpass 800G until the end of that year at the earliest. This is a positive counterpoint to the proposition that growth in the newest generation immediately renders the preceding generation commercially obsolete.

The transmission mechanism is overlapping demand from installed infrastructure, incremental cluster builds, and new high-performance deployments. Continuing 800G volume supports utilization of existing manufacturing assets, while 1.6T adds higher-performance products and new qualification activity. Coherent has demonstrated multiple 1.6T transceiver architectures using silicon photonics, indium-phosphide lasers, and VCSEL technology. Its exposure is consequently broader than a single optical implementation.

Coherent reported its fiscal Q1 results on November 4, before the analytical cutoff, including $2.37 billion of revenue and an expectation of more than 60% fiscal-year pro forma revenue growth. VIAVI’s call is corroborative evidence for the durability of that outlook, not a prediction of Coherent’s already released results. The relevant subsequent catalysts are December-quarter execution, customer acceptance of 1.6T products, and evidence that production capacity converts into shipments without excessive inventory accumulation.

The negative longer-duration implication is more subtle than an immediate short thesis. VIAVI’s expansion into wafer-level and package-level optical testing indicates that part of the value chain is moving upstream from standalone modules. On links that adopt CPO, the economics of module assembly and discrete components can change, and conventional pluggable content cannot simply be extrapolated indefinitely.

That product-level threat does not establish a negative consolidated outlook for Coherent. The company also supplies optical materials, lasers, photonic devices, and other technologies that can remain relevant as architectures change. The correct distinction is a favorable near-term volume cycle alongside a need to reassess where content and margins reside over time. Higher optical bandwidth does not guarantee unchanged revenue per link for every incumbent product.

FIBER AND CONNECTORS: DENSITY AND MANUFACTURING COMPLEXITY SUPPORT CONTENT GROWTH BEYOND DATA-CENTER FLOOR SPACE (READ-THROUGH 5)

Affected companies: Corning (GLW: United States) and Amphenol (APH: United States). Direction: positive. Magnitude: high within relevant optical businesses, moderate to high for Corning’s consolidated growth trajectory, and moderate for Amphenol’s more diversified portfolio. Conviction: high on increasing complexity and demand for sophisticated optical connectivity, not on a universal fiber-content multiplier.

VIAVI identified fiber and connector manufacturing as a new customer opportunity beyond traditional pluggable testing. Management specifically discussed fiber densification, multicore fibers, and large parallel connectors, stating that its equipment is being pulled into the fiber-optic and connector manufacturing supply chain. This is evidence that the infrastructure transition is affecting the physical connectivity layer, not only chips and transceiver modules.

The transmission mechanism is additional optical pathways and more demanding connector performance within dense computing environments. Higher density increases the value of precision alignment, low insertion loss, reliable interfaces, inspection, and controlled manufacturing processes. For suppliers of differentiated fiber assemblies and connectors, revenue can benefit from greater content and complexity per deployment rather than depending exclusively on additional buildings or rack count.

Corning’s October 27 results independently support this mechanism. Optical Communications revenue increased 44% to $2.38 billion, Enterprise Networks grew 84%, and Gen AI product sales more than doubled. Management explicitly said its Gen AI sales growth exceeded GPU unit growth. VIAVI’s production-test commentary corroborates the proposition that optical infrastructure content can grow faster than compute-unit shipments. It does not establish an additional customer order beyond those Corning has already disclosed.

Amphenol’s ownership perimeter matters. It completed the acquisition of CommScope’s Connectivity and Cable Solutions business on January 12, 2026, adding substantial fiber-optic interconnect exposure. The associated operating benefit now belongs to Amphenol, not to the former owner of those assets. Amphenol’s October 28 results also reported exceptional IT datacom growth and a 1.19x book-to-bill ratio, although those figures cover a broader portfolio than fiber alone.

The near-term catalysts are order conversion, delivery capacity, and continued customer acceptance of higher-density interconnect products. The longer-duration opportunity is content expansion across optical architectures. A blanket negative view of Amphenol based on optical substitution for copper would be incomplete because it participates in both electrical and optical interconnects. Equally, not every architecture increases fiber count per transmitted bit: multiplexing and topology choices can change that relationship. The high-conviction positive is demand for differentiated connectivity, not an indiscriminate commodity-fiber volume forecast.

BROADBAND ACCESS: DOCSIS AND DISTRIBUTED ACCESS SPENDING IS REAL, BUT INSTALLATION ACTIVITY SHOULD NOT BE CONFUSED WITH ACCELERATING ORDERS (READ-THROUGH 6)

Affected company: Harmonic (HLIT: United States). Direction: positive for continued broadband deployment and equipment utilization, tempered by weaker recent order replenishment. Magnitude: material because Harmonic is now a pure-play broadband company. Conviction: high on an active upgrade cycle; insufficient evidence for an immediate incremental earnings upgrade.

VIAVI highlighted stronger demand for cable instruments supporting DOCSIS 4.0 and distributed access architectures, alongside early indications of a replacement cycle for equipment purchased during 2020 through 2022. These are more specific signals than a generic claim that telecommunications spending is recovering. They indicate field activity associated with measurable changes in access-network architecture.

The transmission mechanism to Harmonic is deployment of virtualized broadband platforms and distributed access equipment as operators modernize their networks. Instrument purchases can accompany installation, activation, troubleshooting, and acceptance testing. That makes VIAVI’s commentary useful evidence that upgrades are progressing beyond planning. However, the timing is not identical: testing demand can occur after Harmonic has already booked or shipped the associated equipment.

Harmonic’s November 2 results provide direct corroboration. Continuing-operations revenue increased 64% to $148.8 million, and its cOS solution had been commercially deployed with 167 customers serving 52.6 million customer-premises devices. Its June 16 sale of the video business means that the broadband signal now has substantially greater relevance to the listed company than it did when video represented a separate business.

The counterevidence is important. Harmonic’s quarterly bookings were $105.9 million, equivalent to approximately 0.71x revenue, and backlog plus deferred revenue declined approximately 9.1% sequentially to $534 million. Its December revenue guidance of $141 million to $151 million does not imply a strong sequential step-up from September. VIAVI’s strength therefore supports ongoing deployment and backlog conversion, but it does not override Harmonic’s own evidence on the timing of new orders.

The near-term catalyst is execution against December guidance and subsequent replenishment of the order book. The longer-duration positive is a multiyear migration in access-network architecture and a broader customer base. The critical investment distinction is that equipment-supplier deployment revenue can improve even while cable operators face competitive or subscriber pressures. This call is not evidence of better broadband pricing, subscriber growth, or operator returns on capital.

DEFENSE ELECTRONICS: RESILIENT NAVIGATION HAS MORE DIRECT EXPOSURE THAN GENERIC DEFENSE SPENDING, BUT EXAIL’S UPSIDE IS CONSTRAINED BY TRANSACTION STRUCTURE (READ-THROUGH 7)

Affected companies: Exail Technologies (EXA: France) and Thales (HO: France). Direction: positive for Exail’s navigation and autonomous-maritime businesses; conditionally positive for Thales following completion of its proposed acquisition. Magnitude: material for Exail’s operating exposure, substantially smaller at Thales’s consolidated level, and limited as a standalone near-term equity catalyst for Exail. Conviction: high on demand relevance, not on undisclosed program awards.

VIAVI reported strong demand for positioning, navigation, and timing products across aerial, ground, maritime, and underwater autonomous systems, including both retrofits and new platforms. Management also attributed approximately 33% of the projected NSE sequential revenue increase to aerospace and defense. The important read-through is a shift in defense equipment composition toward autonomous systems and resilient navigation, rather than a simple assumption that all defense suppliers benefit equally from higher budgets.

The transmission mechanism is increased demand for navigation systems that remain effective when satellite signals are unavailable, degraded, jammed, or spoofed. Exail’s proprietary fiber-optic gyroscope-based navigation systems and autonomous maritime platforms directly address these requirements. This is a shared end-market exposure, not evidence that Exail supplies VIAVI or participates in VIAVI’s U.S. Army test-range award.

Exail’s October 14 disclosure independently reported 24% growth in Navigation & Maritime Robotics revenue to €99 million, supported by maritime program production and inertial-navigation demand. It also described sustained navigation orders across civil and defense applications, particularly internationally. That provides a stronger company-specific foundation than merely applying a broad defense-sector multiple to VIAVI’s commentary.

VIAVI’s T/Rx selection by the U.S. Army should nevertheless remain attributed to VIAVI. It validates demand for realistic electromagnetic testing but cannot be reassigned to competing European suppliers. Export permissions, qualification requirements, procurement channels, and domestic sourcing preferences can prevent a global demand trend from translating into identical opportunities across countries.

The equity structure changes the actionability. Thales and Exail signed a tender-offer agreement incorporating a €134-per-share offer framework, with acquisition of the controlling family stake expected by Q3 2027 and the subsequent offer expected to complete by early 2028 at the latest, subject to approvals. Exail therefore should not be treated as an unconstrained public-market vehicle for navigation growth. Better operating performance can support transaction confidence and downside resilience, but does not automatically increase the agreed consideration.

Near-term catalysts are contract conversion and transaction developments. Longer-term, the operating benefit would accrue to Thales only if the acquisition completes. The useful portfolio exposure is resilient navigation and autonomy, but the appropriate listed instrument depends on ownership timing rather than simply selecting the company with the most direct product description.

WIRELESS NETWORKS: OPTICAL AND DEFENSE STRENGTH DOES NOT VALIDATE AN IMMINENT AI-RAN OR 6G EARNINGS CYCLE (READ-THROUGH 8)

Affected company: Ericsson (ERIC: Sweden). Direction: negative for near-term earnings upgrades premised on a broad AI-RAN or 6G spending acceleration. Magnitude: meaningful for the valuation narrative and RAN growth assumptions, but limited incremental evidence for an absolute near-term revenue downgrade. Conviction: high on the absence of a broad deployment signal; no basis for asserting that Ericsson’s existing customer programs are deteriorating.

VIAVI called wireless the remaining weak area and described an anemic spending environment. Management positioned AI RAN and 6G as future opportunities rather than current volume drivers. Khaykin’s distinction was explicit: “until things kick into high gear with the planned deployment, that’s when you’ll actually see volume picking up.” The discussion of a potential new terrestrial network associated with SpaceX did not include a disclosed purchase order, deployment commitment, or customer-specific revenue forecast.

The transmission mechanism is the difference between development spending and carrier deployment spending. Early research, interoperability work, and pilot systems can create laboratory activity without generating a large replacement cycle for radios, baseband equipment, and deployment services. A strong AI data-center capital-spending environment therefore does not automatically lift the addressable revenue pool for mobile-network equipment.

Ericsson’s own October 15 results reinforce the distinction rather than support a simplistic bearish conclusion. It reported 7% organic sales growth, driven primarily by Networks, while describing the overall RAN market as flat. NQ MORNING MARKET REPORT | NOVEMBER 6

NQ experienced a historic liquidation yesterday, with selling pressure accelerating into the ETH close and losses exceeding 7%. From the October high to the latest low, NQ has now declined more than 16%. This is no longer an ordinary correction or rotational pullback. We are witnessing a major repricing of risk and a significant deterioration in market structure.

The Globex session established a low at 26,366.25 and a high at 27,251, reflecting extraordinary volatility. After a liquidation of this magnitude, traders must recognize that traditional support and resistance levels can become less reliable as liquidity deteriorates and forced selling accelerates.

The most significant structural development is NQ breaking below the 50% mean retracement of the April 2026 low to the all-time high. This represents the midpoint of the entire advance that produced the ATH. Acceptance below this level would suggest that the market is no longer simply correcting the rally but potentially unwinding a substantial portion of the entire bullish impulse.

Over the last two weeks, sellers have systematically dismantled critical support. The repeated failures above 30,000, loss of the weekly 21 EMA, breakdown below the August low at 28,600, failure at the May low near 28,107, and subsequent liquidation through April’s poorly developed structure demonstrate the persistence of aggressive selling.

What makes this decline particularly concerning is the lack of meaningful buyer response. Each attempted recovery has failed to establish sustained acceptance at higher prices. The election rally offered temporary relief, but NQ’s persistent weakness relative to ES was an early warning that institutional selling pressure had not been exhausted.

Buyer Scenario: Buyers must first stabilize the auction and reclaim the Globex high at 27,251. More importantly, they must recover the 50% retracement of the April to ATH advance and demonstrate sustained acceptance above it. Until then, rallies remain vulnerable to renewed selling pressure.

Seller Scenario: Continued acceptance below the 50% retracement keeps the larger bearish auction intact. Failure to defend the Globex low at 26,366.25 increases the probability of continued liquidation toward the April low, which was established during ETH. The yearly open near 26,265 is another important reference, but in an environment of extreme volatility, levels should be treated as areas of interest rather than guaranteed support.

The magnitude of this decline demands respect. A market that has lost more than 16% from its high and over 7% in a single session is experiencing an extraordinary expansion in volatility. Countertrend rallies can be violent, stops can experience significant slippage, and liquidity can disappear precisely when traders need it most.

Today is about capital preservation. This is not the environment to manufacture trades, increase leverage, or gamble on catching a historic move. The temptation to participate in extraordinary volatility can be overwhelming, but opportunity means nothing if your account cannot survive the risk.

Remember, the objective is not to capture every move. It is to remain financially and psychologically capable of trading when conditions normalize.

Did your account survive yesterday? That is the question that matters.

Discipline. Courage. Excellence.

My job is not to make money. My job is to protect my ability to trade tomorrow.

Can you cool an AI processor without a fan?

Spanish startup YPlasma is developing an ultra-thin plasma film that generates airflow without moving parts. At just 0.2 mm thick, the technology could offer a quieter, more compact alternative to conventional cooling systems.

At electronica 2026, YPlasma will demonstrate its technology on an NVIDIA Jetson Edge AI module, operating across a 7 to 25 W power range, alongside a conventional fan-cooled system.

text:
Prayer for Friday, November 6, 2026.
Thirty-first Week in Ordinary Time.
We remember Saint Leonard of Noblac.

Good Father, thank you for the gift of this new day, for your faithful love, and for the hope you awaken in our hearts. Your grace goes before us, invites us to seek you, and sustains us along the way. Receive our gratitude for life and for every opportunity to love.

I entrust to you my family, my friends, and everyone I will encounter today. Guide our decisions and bless our work. Give us hearts attentive to your Word and willing to respond freely to your grace.

Lord, increase our faith. When doubts arise or weariness weighs upon us, help us remain united to you. May our trust rest in your faithfulness, and may the Holy Spirit teach us to persevere in hope.

Bless our plans and help us discern which ones draw us closer to you and serve the good of our brothers and sisters. Grant us honesty in our work, patience as we wait, and humility to change course when necessary. We entrust to you our efforts, their fruits, and the time they take to unfold.

Jesus, crucified and risen, accompany us through our difficulties. If our trials continue, sustain us with your love. Teach us to carry our cross in union with you and to offer our sufferings out of love, trusting in the power of your resurrection.

Give us courage to seek help and generosity to ease the suffering of others. May we never be indifferent to anyone who needs food, companionship, comfort, or justice. Make us instruments of your mercy.

Father, give us this day our daily bread and hearts willing to share it. Watch over our homes, those who are sick, and those who live in loneliness. Through the intercession of Saint Leonard of Noblac, we pray especially for those in prison, their families, and those who work to help them reintegrate into society.

Deliver us from evil and protect those in danger. Free us from hatred and the desire for revenge. Convert our hearts and the hearts of those who hurt us, and guide us along paths of truth and peace.

You know our needs before we express them. Hear our prayers and grant us whatever will help us draw closer to you. When your answer differs from what we expect, teach us to trust: Father, thy will be done.

We place this Friday in your hands. May your grace help us live it with joy, gratitude, and a spirit of service. When night comes, receive our thanksgiving, forgive our sins, and grant us rest in your peace.

We ask this through Jesus Christ, our Lord. Amen.

I begin this Friday with hope: God loves me, and his grace sustains me. I entrust my life and the lives of my loved ones to him, and I ask him for a faithful heart that recognizes his presence in both joy and trials.

Oración para el viernes 6 de noviembre de 2026.
XXXI semana del Tiempo Ordinario.
Recordamos a san Leonardo de Noblac.

Padre bueno, gracias por el regalo de este nuevo día, por tu amor fiel y por la esperanza que despiertas en nuestro corazón. Tu gracia nos precede, nos invita a buscarte y nos sostiene en el camino. Recibe nuestra gratitud por la vida y por cada oportunidad de amar.

Te encomiendo a mi familia, a mis amigos y a todas las personas que encontraré hoy. Ilumina nuestras decisiones y bendice nuestras tareas. Danos un corazón atento a tu Palabra y dispuesto a responder libremente a tu gracia.

Señor, aumenta nuestra fe. Cuando aparezcan las dudas o sintamos cansancio, ayúdanos a permanecer unidos a ti. Que nuestra confianza descanse en tu fidelidad y que el Espíritu Santo nos enseñe a perseverar en la esperanza.

Bendice nuestros proyectos y ayúdanos a discernir cuáles nos acercan a ti y al bien de nuestros hermanos. Danos honradez para trabajar, paciencia para esperar y humildad para rectificar cuando sea necesario. A ti confiamos nuestros esfuerzos, sus frutos y sus tiempos.

Jesús, crucificado y resucitado, acompáñanos en las dificultades. Si la prueba se prolonga, sostennos con tu amor. Enséñanos a llevar nuestra cruz unidos a ti y a ofrecer nuestros sufrimientos por amor, confiando en la fuerza de tu resurrección.

Danos también valor para buscar ayuda y generosidad para aliviar el dolor ajeno. Que nunca seamos indiferentes ante quien necesita alimento, compañía, consuelo o justicia. Haznos instrumentos de tu misericordia.

Padre, danos hoy nuestro pan de cada día y un corazón dispuesto a compartirlo. Cuida de nuestros hogares, de quienes están enfermos y de quienes viven en soledad. Por intercesión de san Leonardo de Noblac, te pedimos especialmente por las personas encarceladas, por sus familias y por quienes trabajan por su reinserción.

Líbranos del mal y protege a quienes están en peligro. Aparta de nosotros el odio y el deseo de venganza. Convierte nuestro corazón y el de quienes nos hacen daño, y guíanos por caminos de verdad y de paz.

Tú conoces nuestras necesidades antes de que las expresemos. Escucha nuestras súplicas y concédenos lo que nos ayude a caminar hacia ti. Cuando tu respuesta sea distinta de lo que esperamos, enséñanos a confiar: Padre, hágase tu voluntad.

En tus manos ponemos este viernes. Que tu gracia nos ayude a vivirlo con alegría, gratitud y espíritu de servicio. Al llegar la noche, recibe nuestro agradecimiento, perdona nuestras faltas y danos descanso en tu paz.

Te lo pedimos por Jesucristo, nuestro Señor. Amén.

Comienzo este viernes con esperanza: Dios me ama y su gracia me sostiene. Le encomiendo mi vida y la de mis seres queridos, y le pido un corazón fiel para reconocer su presencia tanto en la alegría como en la prueba.
