text:
Podcast Summary | Candace: What Caused The MAGA Midterm Meltdown? | Ep 410

Overview
The Republican midterm defeat is framed not as a single-event failure but as the cumulative bill for unmet promises, unpopular foreign policy, and a leadership class that told its own voters their concerns did not matter. The core argument runs through election data: Republicans lost the voters they needed most, and the issues they were told were irrelevant, above all the Iran war and unconditional support for Israel, turned out to be decisive. The implied lesson is that fear-based voting is eroding, the base will withhold its votes when promises go unkept, and anyone who promoted the wars and policies voters rejected has forfeited the right to lead the movement they now claim to speak for.

Key Themes
- The loss is attributed to Trump telling parts of his coalition he did not want their support, leaving those voters home or voting Democrat.
- The MAGA base is described as insufficient on its own: overwhelming approval among MAGA voters covers under a quarter of the country, while 72% of non-MAGA voters backed the other side.
- Turnout gaps mattered: 91% of Trump 2024 voters backed Republicans versus 97% of Harris voters backing Democrats.
- The Iran war and Israel policy are presented as the hidden center of the election, with exit data undercutting the claim that these issues were marginal.
- Figures elevated over the base, including Ben Shapiro, Mark Levin, and Laura Loomer, are cast as not America First and out of touch.
- The speaker argues a reckoning is owed to voters, including accountability demands such as releasing Brian Cole Jr. over the January 5, 2021 pipe bomb case.
- Blame directed at Tucker Carlson, Candace Owens, and conservative podcasters is rejected as deflection from policy failure.
- The result is framed as a possible return to an era of voter agency, where unkept promises are punished regardless of party.

Detailed Summary
The argument begins with a prediction claim: the host says the Republican routing was called roughly a day ahead and that a prior election-night broadcast held up well. The broader point is that the outcome was legible in advance because it followed a long pattern rather than a surprise event.

The central explanation is turnout and persuasion among the coalition itself. Trump is said to have told certain supporters he did not want their backing, and those supporters responded by staying home or voting for the other side. The host stresses that MAGA loyalty is a narrow base, not a national majority. The numbers cited: 99% approval among MAGA voters, but MAGA is under a quarter of the country, and 72% of non-MAGA voters cast ballots against Republicans.

The voter-file and exit data are used to show a motivation gap. Only 91% of Trump 2024 voters backed Republicans, compared with 97% of Harris voters backing Democrats. The host adds that many voters chose Democrats despite unfavorable views of the party, which signals dissatisfaction with Republicans rather than enthusiasm for the opposition. Nearly one in five voters with an unfavorable view of Democrats still voted Democratic.

A long list of grievances is offered as the substance behind that dissatisfaction: no Epstein arrests, the appointment of Howard Lutnick as commerce secretary, Operation Midnight Hammer and the Iran war, ongoing Gaza and Ukraine wars, continued support for Benjamin Netanyahu, security-state measures such as flock cameras, H-1B and student visa policy, no wall and allegedly no deportations, glyphosate immunity, unchanged vaccine schedules, Trump family cryptocurrency ventures including Trumpcoin, USD1, and World Liberty Financial, the board of peace over Gaza, unresolved questions about Charlie Kirk's killing, and criticism of Erica Kirk.

Institutional and legal accountability is another thread. The host says deficits run over a trillion dollars a year and that Republicans failed to pass the Save Act and voter ID despite controlling the House, Senate, and presidency. The host also says there have been no arrests tied to the deep state, the FBI operation into Trump's 2016 campaign, or the Epstein files, and that questions about Butler, Pennsylvania remain unanswered. The demand for releasing Brian Cole Jr., held in Washington, D.C. and accused of planting two pipe bombs on January 5, 2021, is raised with reference to Steve Baker's reporting.

A recurring tension is between the base and the commentators elevated above it. Ben Shapiro, Mark Levin, and Laura Loomer are described as not America First. The host asserts the tables have turned, meaning the base will accept votes from critics but not their voices inside the movement. The standard set: anyone who supported the Iran war, the Gaza war, or the Ukraine war should hold no leadership role in the conservative movement.

The foreign policy case is built on exit polling. Seventy-four percent called the Iran war a crucial or major factor in their vote, and almost two-thirds of that group voted against Republicans. On Israel, 51% say U.S. support is too strong, and 80% of that group voted Democratic. Sixty-eight percent of Jewish voters voted against Republicans, though Jewish people are described as about 3% of the country. On intensity, 12% say support is not strong enough, 37% say it is about right, and 26% of the about right group voted Democratic.

The host uses these figures to rebut the argument that Iran was a marginal issue. Levin is said to have cited a Fox survey calling Iran a 4% issue, while Shapiro argued Americans care more about domestic economic conditions and that winning, not foreign conflict itself, matters most. The host counters that the election data shows the woke right positions on Israel and the Iran war were actually mainstream. Trump's post praising Levin as a great American patriot and brilliant is cited as evidence of the influence the host is criticizing.

After the midterms, Levin reportedly blamed Tucker Carlson for sabotaging Trump, the GOP, and the midterms, calling him among the biggest traitors in history and a loathsome creature. The host contrasts this with Levin's earlier claim that the Iran war would be a non-factor. A similar pattern is applied to Benny Johnson and Will Chamberlain, who are said to have promoted the Iran war and now decry neoconservatism. Will Chamberlain is quoted saying the Iran war is catastrophically unpopular and must end, and that tariffs must go too. The host's point is that being correct only after the fact does not restore standing.

Other commentators are said to blame the podcasting world rather than policy. Melissa Strait of PragerU, Joel Pollock, Joel Barry, and Caleb Hull are described as pointing at Tucker Carlson, Candace Owens, and right-wing podcasters. Pollock traced a swing among young white men to the podcasting world and antisemitism going back to 2024. Caleb Hull blamed Candace Owens for hijacking the aftermath of Charlie Kirk's assassination instead of producing a red wave, a claim the host calls sick and twisted. The host dismisses podcast influence on scale, noting even large shows reach a few million views, a small share of the electorate.

The host concedes some of the critics' underlying claims are true: the GOP betrayed voters, Trump is controlled by the Epstein class, votes do not matter, and there is no election integrity. The rebuttal is that critics dislike conservative podcasters for telling the truth. Dana Loesch is cited as attributing the loss to factory workers in Erie, Pennsylvania, and regular guys named Steve in Columbus, Ohio, rather than Carlson. The host frames the midterms as no country for old neocons.

The scale of the defeat is described in stark terms: Democrats flipping seven Senate seats and possibly reaching 55 or 56, a large House majority with predictions of 80 to 90 seats and roughly 250 to 270 House seats. A Black Democrat reportedly won in Mississippi, a Democrat won in South Carolina for Lindsey Graham's seat, a Democrat won every statewide race in Texas, and Georgia and Texas are described as possibly lost. A Tennessee Republican governor reportedly won by only two points instead of an expected 20.

JD Vance's response is examined through his tweet, which cited data analysts obsessing over electorate composition and whether turnout matched 2024. Vance reportedly said polls showed a Democrat blowout but the data told a different story: turnout merely okay in some states, downright amazing in others, not catastrophic anywhere. The host says Vance is flailing to save his political career.

A four-item list attributed to a pollster is used to sharpen the critique: end the wars, focus on cost of living and inflation, put America first, and change the relationship to Israel. The host mocks America First being placed third. Matt Walsh is quoted describing a Greek tragedy in which two Republican presidents this century were derailed by unpopular foreign wars, warning the current president's party could be destroyed for a decade. Andrew Wilson is cited saying the biggest blind spot is how we deal with Zionism and Israeli relations, and that raising it on the right makes one a social pariah. Wilson is also criticized for predicting a small Democrat House majority and Republicans keeping the Senate about a week and a half before the election.

Trump's own statements are used to show the political cost. He is quoted saying the U.S. had a deal to stop paying Israel $4 billion a year by the end of the year, while also saying the U.S. would help Israel if needed, and separately claiming a 99% approval rating in Israel. The host frames that approval as purchased at the price of a devastating domestic result. Trump is also criticized for discussing a ballroom construction project after the loss, including a kitchen taking 30% of space, large staircases, marbles, bronzes, and comparing the ballroom size to China's Great Hall.

The reaction on the right is portrayed as erratic. Laura Loomer is said to have taken only a three-hour break from Twitter overnight and posted 17 tweets declaring America is over, warning of eight jihadi candidates entering Congress, plans for survival, stockpiling supplies, finalizing wills, and expecting political violence.

The host widens the critique beyond Republicans. Democrats are said to have learned nothing, with incoming leadership including Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries described as as pro-Israel as neocons and vulnerable to the same backlash. The warning is that Republicans will get shellacked again if they return with the same messaging. The host says Republicans could recover in two years, citing Ohio, Iowa, and Florida as states that flipped or withstood Democratic waves.

The final theme is voter agency. The host says voters are no longer motivated by fear of the other party, and politicians who do not keep promises are punished at the ballot box. Both parties' bases are described as willing to withhold votes. A family member reportedly did not vote for the first time in her life, in a household previously four out of four voters. Mississippi's Black Democrat win and a comparison to the mid-1990s, with Democrats across the South and Republicans across the North including Mitt Romney as Massachusetts governor, are used to suggest a return to unpredictable politics. Viewer comments about refusing to participate and pride in withholding support reinforce the point. The stated lesson: be careful what you promise on the campaign trail, because fear-based voting no longer works.

text:
Podcast Summary | This Past Weekend w/ Theo Von: #694 - Caleb Followill

Overview
Caleb Followill's story is less a conventional rock-star arc than a study in how a rootless, church-centered childhood shaped both a band and a person. Raised as the son of a traveling evangelist, living out of cars and moving town to town for revivals, he learned self-reliance and a survival instinct early, then carried that hunger into music. Kings of Leon's path ran through rejection in Nashville, a sudden and enormous UK following, and the isolating pressure of a career-defining album in Only by the Night. The throughline is ambivalence about fame: success created distance, drinking became self-punishment, and the band spent years either fleeing or trying to recreate its peak. What surfaces now is gratitude, a renewed love of making music, and a personal faith that is searching rather than performative.

Key Themes
- A traveling-evangelist childhood created an unconventional but formative upbringing, teaching self-reliance and reframing poverty as freedom rather than something to pity.
- Church was the band's musical origin: singing, drums, and participation in revivals built the foundation for a career spent on the road.
- Early insecurity became a lasting chip on the shoulder, a drive to prove worth rather than simple ambition for success.
- The band's breakthrough came through rejection in Nashville, then overwhelming UK attention built partly on a compelling personal narrative.
- Sibling bonds and family harmonies are credited as the intangible reason the band has lasted, while also breeding competition and an us-versus-the-world dynamic.
- Fame is framed as isolating: ego grows like a shadow, employees surround the artist, and the temptation to go solo is described as a dangerous whisper.
- Heavy drinking is described as self-punishment tied to disliking who he was becoming, and sobriety has restored his enjoyment of performing.
- Massive success with Only by the Night brought dark times, and trying to recreate it produces a watered-down version of the work.
- Faith has shifted from spectacle to something personal: prayer, scripture, admitted uncertainty, and the value of recovery meetings.

Detailed Summary
Caleb Followill grew up as the son of a traveling evangelist, living out of a car for much of his childhood and moving town to town for revivals. His father comes across as a charismatic preacher, funny and able to move an audience from laughter to tears. The family traveled between Oklahoma and Louisiana, with summers in Luling, Louisiana, on the West Bank of St. Charles Parish. He was born in Memphis and spent his first years in Millington, Tennessee.

The band's musical start came from church. The boys began singing and playing drums to help with music during revivals, sometimes resisting but often talked into performing. During services they were expected to be good examples, pass the offering plate, and be first to the altar to make others comfortable. Followill contrasts the music-filled Pentecostal services with a Church of Christ service he visited that had no music, where people were falling asleep. Post-service life meant the whole church going out to eat late, often to restaurants with slippery floors and irritated staff.

He frames the constant movement positively, as exciting rather than something to be pitied. A normal childhood of school and relationships felt foreign, yet he chose a career that kept him on the road. Louisiana is treated as culturally singular, its dialect and way of life one of a kind. Childhood summers involved sneaking out, breaking into a swimming pool, and hiding in a drainage ditch from police around two in the morning. He and his cousins took odd jobs like roofing houses in New Orleans.

The religious world he grew up in included speaking in tongues, described as fluid vocalization of syllables and sounds without comprehensible meaning, along with laying on hands and claimed healings. He witnessed healings he describes as real, including a woman with severe cancer whose appearance was described as gray before his father prayed for her. Revivals were most prevalent in the South, with tent revivals common; snake handling was explicitly not part of his tradition, though the practice appeared in American Christianity around 1910 and traces earlier to second-century reports.

Evangelists made little money. One church gave the family tickets to Disney World instead of much cash. He did not grow up with TV, so he did not constantly see what he was missing, and he recalled sewing, doing laundry, and resoling shoes at a young age. His father's recurring message was "You're a survivor," which he says was probably what he needed to hear. His mother said the best thing about being poor is having nothing to lose. Poverty was something people could laugh at, a shared humor that felt freeing.

That upbringing instilled self-reliance and a need to prove his worth. He links childhood insecurity to a lasting chip on the shoulder: walking into a room feeling you do not belong, then resolving that people will know who you are by the time you leave. His mother taught him that once people lose respect for you, you cannot get it back. He initially assumed he would follow his father into preaching, since that was the only model he knew.

The turning point came in Oklahoma while painting houses. He hit a wall, felt there was no future in it, and heard a voice telling him to go home. He returned to Tennessee to try music without knowing what that meant. His older brother Nathan returned from Oklahoma to help, and they began writing simple storybook rhymes inspired by Otis Redding and Sam Cooke. Their stepfather Tom Murphy, after hearing them sing a cappella on a boat, gave them about a thousand dollars to quit their restaurant jobs and try to get a foot in the door in Nashville.

In Nashville, doors were slammed in their faces. With long hair, they would start singing a cappella when doors opened. One person did not close the door, leading to a small publishing deal and songwriting attempts. They met with nine record labels in New York, played a couple of songs, and got seven offers, signing with RCA and returning to Nashville. A lawyer believed in them enough to lend roughly a thousand dollars, which they repaid by month's end after knocking on every door in Nashville. Their mother strongly supported them, including allowing their younger brother to drop out of high school as a freshman to join as bassist.

Their EP became a big hit in the UK before they had broken through in the US. They were far more popular in England than at home, where nobody knew who they were for years. In the UK they were marketed through a compelling personal narrative of southern brothers and a preacher's father, and press even doubted they were really brothers. On stage, their strategy was to play very fast and very country, because their southern sound was what the other bands on the new rock revival bill did not have.

Growing up with brothers in a band meant navigating fame together. It kept them grounded but bred competition and fighting. He credits family connection and sibling harmonies for the band's longevity, something intangible that cannot be replicated by skill or money. Fame brings isolation: artists who get big are often surrounded by people who profit from them, and even friends can become employees. The temptation to go solo is framed as dangerous, a whisper often encouraged by people who would benefit from cutting costs. Having brothers around acted as a check on excess.

He describes needing a drink before going on stage and being unable to have fun without one. There were years he does not remember enjoying a show, and the madder he got on stage, the more the crowd loved it. For ten years he says he never spoke to the crowd, only saying thank you and the band's name. Ego is framed as a shadow that grows, with its goal seeming to be isolation. Heavy drinking was self-punishment tied to disliking the person he was becoming and how others saw him. Songwriting sometimes functioned as a way to get attention and reconnect the band during lonely, tense periods on the road.

Only by the Night is cited as the band's bestselling album: over 6.2 million copies worldwide, over 4.7 billion Spotify streams, a debut at number five on the Billboard 200, and 131 consecutive weeks in the top 75. He calls the success astronomical and says it was when the rough times started. The band did not like that level of success, felt unprepared for it, and spent years either running from it or trying to recreate it. The transcript frames extreme fame as a dangerous environment, with access to anything, ego growth, and isolation. A cited claim holds that rock and pop stars have a mortality rate two to three times higher than the general population.

He now says he enjoys making music and playing shows again. The new album, Oh My Beloved, is framed as gratitude for his life, upbringing, and the band's journey. He says he is finally okay with being himself and would be happy with everything the band has done if this were the end. The band has kept working since its peak, taking only short breaks, but faded into the background without being loud about it.

On faith, he reflects that seeing behind the scenes of religious communities made him bitter for a time, particularly feeling his father was pushed out for having normal human struggles while expected to be perfect. His relationship with God is now personal: he prays, reads the Bible, admits he does not have all the answers, and describes himself as always searching. He emphasizes being raised to be kind and considerate, and that growing up with nothing taught him to love people for who they are rather than what they have. He values recovery meetings and hearing others speak truths he could not articulate himself.

The band remains the same members throughout: two brothers and a cousin, each with a distinct role. Nathan is an elder-statesman figure who watched over and defended them, Jared is funny with a big heart, and Matthew is the cousin who may carry a chip on his shoulder. He speaks fondly of the small churches of his youth, four walls and the smell of the furnace, calling them the best place in town. He is open to a small, humble church revival with his family band backing his father, explicitly rejecting big super-church spectacle. His father no longer evangelizes but still preaches occasionally at his local church in Oklahoma.

text:
Podcast Summary | The Shawn Ryan Show: #354 Reckless Ben - The Internet's Most Controversial Investigative YouTuber

Overview
Reckless Ben built a career on a single strategic insight: the person with nothing to lose can go where institutions and established documentarians cannot. That logic took him from homeless slacklining stunts to undercover infiltrations of Scientology, the Twelve Tribes and the Yellow Deli, and Provo Canyon School, and eventually into an alleged trafficking operation tied to Ideal Living and the JKP religious organization. His method is consistent: verify unbelievable claims, document them from inside, and use a target's own legal and structural loopholes against it. The throughline is a creator who treats investigation as adventure rather than journalism, measures success by audience shock and real-world consequences, and has paid for it in legal exposure that now dwarfs his production budgets.

Key Themes
- Having nothing to lose is the core advantage: Ben entered Scientology while living in his car and made his most aggressive content before he had money, status or a lawyer.
- Unbelievable ideas are the best ideas: if friends call a plan impossible or horrible, he treats that as validation because the payoff will surprise viewers.
- Infiltration works through structure and repetition: love bombing, isolation and constant messaging can affect even people who know they are inside a cult.
- The restaurant is the recruitment funnel: cheap, good food leads to farm invitations, unpaid labor, and payment framed as eternal life.
- Belief systems that reject medicine cause measurable harm: members describe child deaths as God's plan and celebrate rather than mourn.
- Institutions are often money-driven before ideology-driven: Provo Canyon took anyone who paid, hired unqualified staff, and shut down within a day of his video.
- Legal loopholes cut both ways: Ben turns a target's own tactics against it, from state lotteries to small-claims suits to an IRS-approved religion.
- The cost of accountability is real: videos made for under $2,000 have generated roughly a quarter-million dollars in legal fees.

Detailed Summary
Ben's operating philosophy came first. He says his career was defined by never messing with somebody who has nothing to lose, and that this let him take risks others with money or status avoid. Established documentaries struggle to get inside groups like Scientology because their makers have something to lose. Ben entered while living in his car, reasoning he had nothing to lose either.

His content started with slacklining stunts and escalated deliberately. He sought progressively more dangerous setups, reasoning that a fall would only hurt him, so he added risk involving other people, busy bike paths, rocks roughly 20 feet high, mousetraps and tasers, often dressed as Spider-Man. He moved to California to become the world's best slackliner while homeless.

Scientology came from simple curiosity about what happens inside, after finding little information online. A friend, Danny Burke, told him the Yellow Deli was a cult. Ben was skeptical until he visited and saw red flags within about 30 seconds, starting with a waiter saying I love you and inviting them back to the farm.

The Twelve Tribes infiltration was three weeks at the farm, with Danny rotating out under a dogsitting excuse to recharge spy glasses that lasted about 90 minutes per charge. Ben worked roughly 12 hours of manual labor in 100-degree heat and then additional hours at the restaurant. He describes members as overworked and sleep-deprived, performing happiness for recruitment, and notes they are sober and do not use drugs.

The plan was structured as a 12-step guide to joining a cult, beginning with love bombing. Even knowing it was a cult, the pair felt the manipulation working. Repetition and isolation from the outside world caused Ben to begin internalizing the group's messaging about his mission on the farm. Roughly 20 people ran the farm, all living in one large yurt with bunk beds.

The group uses the Christian Bible with an extreme interpretation, including the beliefs that the KKK is good, that America was ideal when slavery existed, and that freeing slaves caused God to turn on America. Members hold rigid gender roles, oppose interracial relationships and homosexuality, and reject medicine.

Ben tested the group with parody TikTok accounts. A pro-womens-suffrage account was criticized as bad, while an account saying women belong in the kitchen was praised as good messages. A fabricated fiancee named Lydia, described as Chinese, drew warnings against race-mixing and claims that mixed-race children would be deformed. In the cover story, Lydia was said to have had a gay thought, then fell ill with pneumonia, which the group framed as divine punishment. When told she died, members reportedly celebrated with a circle dance. They told him not to let her take pneumonia medicine because medicine is a man-made creation and God would heal her if he wished.

The group had about 30 people, with many home births without pain medicine and members saying God wants women to feel childbirth pain. Many in the group had children die and believed medicine could have saved them but that it wasn't God's plan. The operation has locations in the U.S., Costa Rica and possibly Australia, reportedly originated in Tennessee, and Ben was kicked out of California and Colorado locations.

Ben was raised Catholic and attended Catholic school. He describes moving away from certainty about any one religion, using an ant-and-the-internet analogy: complexity doesn't mean something doesn't exist, only that humans may be unable to comprehend it. He still values Catholic teachings as ethical guidance without claiming certainty about religious truth, and argues biblical accounts with differing perspectives may be more trustworthy, since separate witnesses recalling events years later would naturally differ. They were eventually caught when a member asked to see Ben's glasses and pulled out an SD card.

The Provo Canyon School investigation began with a tipster whose extreme claims Ben doubted, including solitary confinement, beatings by staff, no talking and loss of childhood. He found the facility matched the description. The tipster reportedly hoped for jail instead. The school advertised as a high school but allegedly issued fake diplomas.

Ben says the facility prioritized revenue over child welfare, accepting anyone who paid. He called and said take my son; no ID, birth certificate or age verification was required, only a signature. He used the money motive against it, claiming a pending $50,000 transfer and creating urgency with a fake imminent trip, though he had about $2,000 in the bank. Cost was cited at $1,000 per day with a down payment of roughly $50,000 before admittance. Paris Hilton attended the school and had campaigned to shut it down, making the facility skeptical of outside scrutiny.

A fan named Sheldon volunteered to work undercover as a teacher. Ben bought spy cameras, covered travel and Airbnb costs, and Sheldon worked full-time for about a month, producing roughly eight hours of footage per day. Ben entered briefly at the end, posing as a teen sent over a gay thought. The school was reportedly unbothered and did not attempt conversion, which he found inconsistent with its reputation and read as evidence the operation was money-driven rather than focused on helping kids.

Ben says the owner runs several related companies; when one location shuts down it relocates and rebrands under a sister company rather than truly closing. An employee with a criminal history including Grand Theft Auto and prior heroin, meth and fentanyl use was hired despite not being allowed to work with kids, with the only apparent qualification being willingness to physically restrain kids. Lack of background checks was cited as the reason the facility was ultimately shut down.

Rather than staying the planned two days, Ben escaped over a fence, climbing a basketball hoop and jumping a roughly three-foot gap, then doing a parkour roll onto soft grass, to leverage bad PR and pressure the facility. Staff chased him for a couple miles before he got away; he was picked up by a friend after calling from a fast-food restaurant, and described throwing up several times due to cold weather and an asthma-related exercise issue. The facility closed one day after the video posted.

Solitary confinement there was not isolation in a cell but being forced to sit silently at a school desk among about ten other kids, forbidden from looking at or talking to them. Ben calls it worse than normal solitary, since at least normal solitary allows exercise. Kids in a developmental phase where socialization is the drive had interaction dangled in front of them and forbidden, which he describes as psychologically damaging. He says all the kids were suicidal, with no hope, and frames it as childhood being robbed from them.

Staff reportedly bragged in training about physically restraining kids, with restraints lasting up to 45 minutes and stories of kids dying from them. A sister school owned by the same company was shut down after a kid died from a restraint; he reportedly threw a brownie, was restrained, choked, and died, and was a foster kid sent there after his parents died. Education was effectively absent: kids reportedly watched TikTok and YouTube compilations about eight hours a day, and a teacher told Ben class would be a joke to him but had to be done. Ben spent about 30 hours in solitary, reportedly because staff thought he was gay. Population when he arrived was about 300 kids, roughly half boys and half girls.

He considered a mass escape and returning kids to parents but rejected it because parents had signed custody rights to the corporation, making it legally kidnapping. He estimates about half of parents see the place as messed up, while the other half deny it because admitting wrongdoing is too hard to accept. On escaping generally, he emphasizes that the hard part isn't getting out but surviving afterward with no money, phone, food, shelter or safe place to go, since escapees cannot return to their parents without likely being sent back. His own escape was easy because he is a good parkour athlete and rock climber, and he left in 20-degree weather.

Ideal Living began with an email claiming the company was the only reason it exists: to fund the world's biggest human trafficking ring. Ben initially dismissed the whistleblowers as conspiracy theorists, then documented their claims because they provided evidence. Ideal Living makes air purifiers and water purifiers and donated air purifiers during California wildfires. Ben says the whistleblowers were fired after reporting concerns, that the company threatened to call police if he kept asking, and later threatened legal action unless he shared their side, which he did. Their rebuttal essentially denies the allegations, with evidence amounting to the CEO's court testimony.

The two Ideal Living videos have about 37 million combined views, his most-viewed content and least discussed online, with no news pickup. Six or seven former employees out of roughly 30 have come forward. Ben says he has unreleased footage from inside the JKP ashram and temple, where he spoke with high-level executives connected to both organizations, after getting in by saying he was interested in the religion. JKP stands for Jaguru Kpalu Parachot, with Jaguru described as meaning God walking on earth. The group allegedly believes the leader was God in a human body and Jesus; he died a couple years ago around age 90. Followers have a cardboard cutout of the leader they worship and feed cake.

The organization allegedly sought religious status, but the IRS did not grant tax-exempt status because of the abundance of Miracle Blades, viewing it as a company rather than a religion. Former employees allege the leader asked how to fund the operation and the answer was to create companies, with the Miracle Blade created for that purpose. Ben says there were alleged practices of opening businesses and transferring assets to defraud creditors. Roughly six or seven people at the top of Ideal Living are said to also be high-up leaders in JKP, including Peter as CEO of Ideal Living and treasurer of JKP. A trust in India is said to hold billions of dollars. Ben says the alleged billionaire leader is powerful enough to kill news stories, which motivated him to break the story himself.

Ben distinguishes ordinary followers from leadership: most members likely don't know about alleged abuse because it happens behind closed doors, while a small group at the top allegedly runs both the company and the religious organization. The alleged mechanism is spiritual, with sex with the leader presented as a path to greater spirituality, involving minors and non-consenting people. Social stigma in India is described as a major reason victims stay silent. Joe Kelly, formerly high up in both the organization and the company, is described as present when Sarah Swati discussed making it a big religion through infomercial companies; Ben says Ideal Living refused to rebut Joe Kelly's account, which he treats as implicit agreement.

Ben says he was threatened with lawsuits for nearly every video, and Scientology tried suing for about a million dollars. He created an IRS-approved religion called Church of Scientology sucks and says detectives ruled in their favor. The only group that did not sue was 12 Tribes, because they believe God will punish him rather than human law.

He claims nearly every bad company he covers has a legal loophole he can also use against them. He initially avoided hiring lawyers to preserve the image of an ordinary person taking on powerful targets, but public pressure and the Bricks and Minifigs case led him to get legal representation. The Bricks and Minifigs videos cost under $2,000 to produce, while lawyer costs have reached roughly a quarter-million dollars. That dispute centers on a consignment Lego store allegedly keeping a family's collection after new owners took over. The family with the world's largest Lego set allegedly put it in the store to sell, then was told the Legos belonged to the new store owners and threatened with trespassing, with suing framed as costing more than the roughly half-million-dollar collection was worth.

Police allegedly treated the matter as civil. Ben used Oregon law making lottery theft criminal, auctioned a roughly $1,000 Lego set through a state-approved lottery, and had a family win but not receive the prize. He sold the family's debt to 10 friends so each could file small-claims suits, costing about $100 to file and producing faster judgments. Bricks and Minifigs sued him for RICO charges and he filed an anti-SLAPP suit, with a ruling expected by the end of the month. Mediation lasted six days, with lawyers costing almost $1,000 per hour and sessions up to 10 hours a day. Criminal cases mentioned include a GoFundMe, attempted serving of court papers, and an allegation he tried to burn down a building in Provo, which he denies.

The documentary damaged the corporate brand so much that franchisees are suffering, since customers know 6% of every sale goes to corporate. His response is a Reckless Bricks rebrand offer where stores pay him 0%. Two stores have already rebranded, he says he is providing lawyers to franchisees afraid of being sued by corporate, and 30 to 40 stores were reportedly interested before the video's release. He says he would take 0% and claims he may become the first CEO and owner taking 0%, a project that began as a joke and may become real. His core motivation is doing things because they are fun, with YouTube as a side effect of activities he already enjoys. He describes helping people solve problems as the ultimate adventure and says others' happiness strongly determines his own mood. He claims roughly 10 filmed but unedited videos with plans nobody knows about yet, with some content held back pending statute-of-limitations deadlines. The only group that never sued was the one that believes God will handle it.

text:
Nobody asked the birds how they felt about this night.

Start there, because it changes how everything else lands.

Two of the most instinct-driven animals on any farm ended up inside a story they did not choose, could not understand, and had no way to narrate. Whatever they felt, they felt in the only language they have: movement, noise, and a stubborn refusal to leave something behind.

The caption on this clip calls it "a night full of blessings." I can't stop turning that phrase over, because a blessing is only a blessing for someone. Someone has to receive it. And the longer I look at who might be on the receiving end here, the less sure I am that it's who you'd assume.

That's the problem with this video. It looks simple for about two seconds. Then it starts asking questions you didn't know you were carrying.

Who was in trouble? Who was doing the helping? Who was the bravest creature in the frame, and did that creature have any idea?

I'm not going to answer those for you. I don't think I can, honestly, and I don't trust anyone who claims they can after a single viewing. What I can tell you is that this is fifteen seconds long, it was filmed in the dark, and it contains more raw instinct per second than most nature documentaries manage in an hour.

I've watched it more times than I'd like to admit. And each time, I'm watching a different animal.

So before you press play, let me give you the context that made me watch it differently. None of it is in the video. All of it is happening underneath it.

Let's talk about the hen first, because the hen is the part of this story people skip.

A broody hen is one of the strangest commitments in the animal world. When the urge to sit takes hold, her body changes. Her temperature rises in the brooding patch on her belly, where she plucks her own feathers so the eggs touch bare skin. She stops eating the way she used to. She stops caring about the flock. She leaves the nest roughly once a day, for a short break, and is often back before you've finished wondering where she went.

While she sits, she turns the eggs. Not once. Dozens of times a day, shifting each one with her beak and breast so the developing embryo doesn't stick to the shell. Nobody taught her this. No hen has ever read a manual.

She also talks to them. Chicks begin to peep from inside the egg a day or two before hatching, and the hen answers. There is a conversation happening through a shell that is about a third of a millimeter thick, between a mother and a creature that does not technically exist yet.

Think about the arithmetic of that. For about three weeks, one animal puts her own comfort, her own health and her own safety on hold for a clutch of objects that cannot thank her, cannot call for her, and cannot be replaced if they are lost.

Now ask yourself the question the video quietly asks: what does an animal like that do when something threatens the thing she has been guarding?

I'm not going to tell you what this hen did.

I'll tell you only this. When people say "mother's instinct," they usually mean something soft. Warm. A little sentimental. Anyone who has actually watched a hen defend a nest knows it is closer to a force of nature than a feeling. Feathers up. Body low. Absolutely no negotiation.

That's the energy I want you to carry into the next fifteen seconds.

Now the second animal. This is where it gets interesting.

The guinea fowl is the farm's most suspicious resident. It comes from Africa, and it has never fully agreed to be domesticated. Chickens will tolerate a human hand. Ducks will often learn to follow one. Guinea fowl watch you from a distance, calculate the exit, and if you step too close they explode into noise.

That noise is famous. Farmers keep them partly because they function as an alarm system: a harsh, rattling, relentless shriek at anything unfamiliar. A stranger at the gate, a snake in the grass, a hawk overhead. The whole yard learns about it within seconds.

They're also known for nesting in hidden places. Where chickens will accept a box you've prepared, a guinea hen tends to vanish into the undergrowth, tuck eggs into a scrape in the ground and hope nobody notices. Keepers talk about the strange experience of discovering a nest by accident, sometimes with a startling number of eggs already inside.

So here is a bird whose whole survival strategy is distance, concealment and volume. An animal built to avoid being handled.

Hold that thought against the other one, the devoted hen, whose strategy is the opposite: stay close, stay put, guard the eggs with your own body.

Two birds. Two philosophies of staying alive. Hiding versus holding the line.

And one night in which those two philosophies ran into the same problem at the same time.

I want you to notice something about how that feels as a viewer. You are not watching a simple "animal in trouble" clip. You are watching two different kinds of fear and two different kinds of courage share a single patch of dark ground. Neither of them knows the other's plan. Neither of them has any way of coordinating.

That tension is what's underneath the clip. It's also why people who watch it once tend to watch it again, paying attention to a different bird the second time.

Here's the part I find hardest to explain to people who haven't spent time around animals.

For a wary creature, help and harm can feel identical.

A hand reaching toward a frightened bird is, to that bird, a hand reaching toward a predator. The body doesn't have a category for "this one means well." It has heart rate, adrenaline and a set of reflexes older than any farm. Flapping, clawing, screaming, freezing, all of it can be what a grateful animal looks like in the middle of the worst moment of its life.

This is the quiet tragedy of every rescue ever filmed. The rescued almost never know they're being rescued. They experience it as an ambush. The kindness only becomes visible afterwards, if it becomes visible at all, in the form of an animal that is still alive and has no idea why.

Which means anyone who steps in to help a frightened animal is accepting a strange bargain. You will probably be misunderstood. You may be scratched, pecked, shrieked at. You might be the villain in that animal's version of events, permanently, and you'll never get the chance to correct the record.

And you do it anyway.

That's what I mean when I say a small act can carry enormous weight. The person acting gains nothing the animal can acknowledge. There is no applause from the creature, no gratitude, no recognition. If there is a reward, it is entirely internal: the knowledge that something living is still living.

I think that's why the word on this clip's caption keeps catching in my head. Blessing. It's an old word for something given without being earned and without being asked for.

Whether the one being blessed is the hen, the guinea fowl, the eggs, or the people who happened to be standing there, I'll leave to you. Only one thing is certain from the moment you press play: nobody involved is acting for credit.

Then there's the darkness, which deserves its own paragraph.

Poultry are not night animals. Chickens in particular see poorly once the light fades, which is why they roost at dusk and become almost helpless after dark. Their whole evolutionary strategy is to get up high, tuck in and stay silent until morning. A chicken awake and moving at night is a chicken out of its comfort zone, whatever the reason.

Night is also when the things that eat poultry do their best work. Snakes, civets, owls, rats, feral dogs, depending on where in the world you are. The sensible hen stays quiet and stays put.

Which makes it remarkable when an animal chooses to stay exposed.

I don't know why any of the creatures in this video were awake when they were. I won't pretend I do. But I know what it costs a hen to be outside her roost after dark, and I know what it means for a bird that loves silence to be making noise in the middle of the night. Both are signs of something overriding the animal's normal calculations.

That's what instinct looks like when it's strong enough to beat fear. Not calm. Not graceful. Just a very small body deciding that something matters more than its own safety.

There's a reason this kind of footage works best at night, by the way. Darkness narrows the world. It strips out the background and leaves only the essentials: a few bodies, a few sounds, one problem. Everything in the frame is there for a reason, because nothing else can be seen.

So when you watch, give yourself a minute to forget that you're holding a phone. Pretend you came across this scene yourself, walking home late, with a flashlight and no explanation.

What would you have done in the first three seconds? Most of us would have frozen.

I suspect some of the people in this video didn't have that luxury.

Let me be honest about what I don't know, because I think it makes the rest of this more trustworthy.

I don't know the names of the animals. I don't know where this was filmed, or how long the situation had been going on before someone started recording. I don't know what happened in the hour before, or the hour after. I don't know whether the people involved planned any of it or simply walked into the middle of it.

What I know is what a camera could catch in fifteen seconds, plus what's reasonable to say about how these birds behave.

I mention it because the internet is full of animal stories that arrive with a perfectly packaged backstory. A name. A tragic origin. A countdown to disaster. A tidy ending with a bow on it. Most of those details were added later by someone who needed the video to perform. After a while you stop believing any of it, and you stop feeling anything too, which is the real casualty.

This clip doesn't come with any of that packaging. It arrives raw. And I've come to think raw is why it works.

When there's no script, you're forced to supply your own attention. You notice what each animal does with its body. You notice how the whole thing sounds. You notice small things you would never notice if someone were guiding you: where an animal chooses to stand, which bird holds still, which one doesn't.

The absence of an official story is not a flaw in this video. It's the invitation.

So I won't hand you a name or an origin. I'll hand you the same thing the clip hands me, which is a short stretch of real time and a set of creatures who don't know they're being watched.

What you make of it is up to you.

Let me zoom out for a second, because scale is the thing that makes this video so quietly devastating.

A chicken egg takes about 21 days to hatch. A guinea fowl egg takes closer to 26 to 28. Whichever clutch we're talking about, somewhere in this story there is a calendar running. Days of warmth, days of patience, days of a single animal refusing to quit. Weeks of work, held in objects light enough to crack under a careless thumb.

Now compare that to how long a disaster takes. A moment. A shift in the dark. A bad angle, a wrong step, a few seconds when attention drops.

That's the asymmetry at the heart of every story like this. Creation is slow. Loss is fast. A whole season of effort can be undone by something that lasts less time than it takes to read this sentence.

And if you're a hen, you have no way of knowing which of those two clocks is about to win.

I keep thinking about that when I watch the clip. Not the drama, because there's very little drama in the usual sense. No music. No narration. No cinematic angles. Just a short stretch of real time, in which all of those weeks hang in the balance for reasons the animals themselves can't grasp.

It reminds me of something that gets lost in the way we consume rescue content. We tend to focus on the moment of action: the grab, the lift, the relief. But the real story is always the long stretch before. The days nobody filmed. The effort that was already underway before any camera showed up.

By the time a clip like this starts, the most important work has often already been done by someone who will never appear in the credits.

In this case, that someone may be a hen.

Think about that the next time you see a video where the human is the hero. Then ask who built the thing that needed saving.

There's also an old, complicated relationship sitting underneath all of this, and it's worth naming.

Chickens were domesticated somewhere in Southeast Asia from the red junglefowl, thousands of years ago. Estimates on the exact date vary, and researchers still argue about it. What isn't disputed is the shape of the deal. Humans offered protection and food. Birds offered eggs, meat and, eventually, company.

It was never an equal arrangement. It was never meant to be. But it was an arrangement, a kind of long-running promise between species, and every farm that has ever kept a flock is a place where that promise gets tested daily.

Some days the human is the threat. The one who decides, who takes, who ends things. Other days the human is the only thing standing between a bird and the dark.

Animals live inside that contradiction without ever being able to resolve it. A hen that has been fed by the same hand for years will still run from it. A guinea fowl that has lived on the same property all its life will still treat the owner as a potential danger. Trust, for these birds, is never a settled fact. It's a daily decision, made by a nervous system that never fully switches off.

When I look at this clip, I see that old deal being renegotiated in real time. Not in words. Not in policy. In a few seconds of physical decision-making between creatures who share a yard and have never shared a language.

And I think that's why so many people feel something they can't quite name. It's not just "aww, birds." It's recognition. We know how rarely that deal gets honored well. We know how often it's broken. When we see a moment where it's honored, even briefly, even imperfectly, something in us exhales.

I won't tell you whether the deal was honored here.

I'll only say that the question is on the screen the whole time, and that you may find, as I did, that you care about the answer more than you expected to.

There's a harder question hiding in this clip, and I'd rather name it than pretend it isn't there.

What do we owe the animals we depend on?

Most of the world's eggs, and a great deal of its meat, come from birds very much like the ones in this story. Billions of them, alive at any given moment, outnumbering every other bird on the planet by a wide margin. They are so common that we've stopped seeing them as individuals at all. A chicken is a category. An egg is an ingredient.

Then a clip like this arrives and quietly reverses the perspective. One hen. One clutch. One night. Suddenly the category has a face, and the ingredient has a mother.

I'm not here to lecture anyone about what they eat. That's a conversation for people who want to have it, and plenty of thoughtful people land in very different places. But I do think there's something worth noticing in how fast our attention shifts when an animal stops being abstract. The same species we barely register in a supermarket can stop us cold on a phone screen when it's given a few seconds of specific, individual attention.

What does that tell us? Maybe nothing. Maybe that we're easily moved by good filming. Or maybe it tells us that the distance between "a bird" and "this bird" is much shorter than we assume, and that the only thing separating them is whether anyone happens to be looking.

That's an uncomfortable thought, and also a hopeful one. Because attention is something any of us can offer, for free, at any time.

The people in this story offered it, in whatever form. The camera offered it too. Now it's your turn, for fifteen seconds.

It doesn't commit you to anything. It just asks you to look at one animal as though she were the only one in the world.

Because for the length of the clip, she is.

Here's a detail that tends to surprise people: science has started to take the inner lives of chickens seriously.

Researchers have found that chickens can discriminate between quantities, anticipate future events, and show self-control, waiting for a larger food reward rather than grabbing a smaller one right away. Young chicks seem to understand that an object still exists after it disappears behind a screen, something human infants take months to grasp.

Hens use a wide range of calls, with different sounds for different kinds of danger, and different sounds for food, and different sounds for chicks. A mother can send a warning that her chicks respond to before they've seen anything themselves.

One study out of the UK is the one I come back to most. Scientists puffed small bursts of air at chicks to mildly distress them, and watched the mothers. The hens' heart rates went up. Their eye temperature changed. They became more alert and began calling to their young. Their bodies reacted to the chicks' stress even though nothing was happening to the hens themselves.

I want to be careful here. Researchers are cautious about what that means, and so should we be. It doesn't prove a hen feels exactly what you'd feel. It doesn't let us write her thoughts for her. But it does mean the old idea that a hen is a mindless egg machine does not hold up well against the evidence.

So when I tell you the animal in this video is worth watching closely, I'm not being sentimental. I'm being literal. There is a mind in there, or something close enough to one that the distinction stops being useful at three in the morning with a flashlight.

What kind of mind, thinking what, we can never fully know.

But you can watch the behavior. You can see the way an animal moves when the stakes are high, and you can decide for yourself what you're looking at.

That's all I'm asking you to do.

One more angle, and then I'll stop circling and let you go.

We tend to imagine that moments like this belong to professionals. Rescuers with the right gear, vets with the right training, experts who know exactly what to do. And sometimes that's true.

But a startling amount of the world's small mercy is done by ordinary people with no equipment, no training and no plan, who happened to be standing nearby when something needed doing. They use whatever's in reach. They improvise. They make a hundred micro-decisions in a few seconds, none of which they'll be able to explain afterwards.

That kind of help is messy. It isn't elegant. It doesn't look like the version you'd stage for a documentary. It looks like people deciding, in real time, in the dark, that an animal's trouble is worth interrupting their night for.

And I find that more moving than any polished rescue. Not because the polished ones don't matter, but because the improvised ones prove something the polished ones can't: that the impulse to help is not a skill. It's a default setting. We all have it. Most of the time it just sits unused, waiting for a situation that asks for it.

Think about the last time you had that impulse. Did you act on it? Or did you reason your way out, the way most of us do? Too late, too dark, not my business, someone else will.

I ask because I've done the reasoning-out many times. I suspect you have too.

That's part of why this clip stays with me. It's a few seconds of what happens when nobody reasons their way out.

It's not a lecture. It doesn't say you should have acted. It simply shows what it looks like when someone did.

And you may find yourself, afterwards, quietly taking stock of your own defaults.

Why do we share clips like this one?

It's a real question, and I don't think the usual answer is the true one. We say we share them because they're cute, or heartwarming, or funny. But the clips that spread furthest are rarely the cutest. They're the ones that make us feel something slightly harder to categorize: relief mixed with worry, tenderness mixed with awe.

Psychologists have long observed that people respond more strongly to a single identifiable creature in trouble than to a statistic about thousands. One bird, one nest, one night. The smaller and more specific the story, the more of ourselves we're willing to invest in it.

There's a quieter reason too. Compassion is partly a muscle, and most of us don't get to exercise it much. The rest of the day is deadlines, traffic, notifications. A short clip of an animal in need is one of the few places where the instinct to protect something weaker gets switched on without any obligation attached. You don't have to donate. You don't have to sign anything. You just have to feel it for a few seconds, and then decide whether to pass it on.

That small decision is not nothing. Every time someone forwards a moment like this to a friend, they're saying: I want you to feel this too. It is one of the oldest forms of social bonding we have, passing a feeling along in place of a fire.

I'm not claiming a video changes the world. I'm saying it can change the next ten minutes of someone's day, and the next ten minutes is where small kindnesses tend to start.

Here's a test you can run on this one. Watch it, then send it to someone and don't tell them what to look for. Ask what stayed with them afterwards. I'd bet the answers differ: one person will mention a bird, another a sound, another the people who were there at all.

That difference is the whole point. A clip that everyone remembers the same way is just information. A clip that lodges in each person differently is a story.

A note on sound, because it's the most underrated part of this clip.

Most people watch animal videos muted, scrolling in a queue or on a train. If you do that here, you lose half of it.

Birds are acoustic creatures. Hens carry a surprisingly detailed vocabulary: soft clucks for contentment, sharp alarm calls for threats, rapid low sounds for a hen calling her young to food. Guinea fowl communicate in a very different register, a loud, rhythmic, almost mechanical cry that carries across fields and has been used for generations as an early warning.

Put those two sound worlds together in the dark and you get something unusual. A layered soundscape of fear, alertness and urgency, none of it staged, all of it meaningful to the birds producing it.

I can't translate it for you. Nobody can, not completely. But there's a particular kind of attention that opens up when you listen to an animal without trying to decode it. You stop asking "what is it saying" and start asking "what is it like to be saying this."

That second question is harder and much more interesting. It's the one that turns a clip into an experience.

So if you can, use headphones. Close the other tabs. Let the noise of whatever room you're in drop away for a quarter of a minute.

You'll hear things that don't show up in a thumbnail. You'll hear the difference between an animal that's panicking and an animal that's determined. And you'll probably notice, as I did, that the sounds seem to carry more information than the pictures do.

That's the thing about nights like this one. The picture is only part of the story.

The rest is in the air around it.

So here is what I'd suggest before you watch.

Don't look for the obvious thing. Everyone looks for the obvious thing. The obvious thing is loud, and it pulls the eye, and the video knows it.

Instead, give some of your attention to whoever is easiest to overlook. Ask yourself who in this story is paying the highest price for the smallest recognition. Ask who is calm and who is only pretending. Ask which sound belongs to fear and which belongs to something closer to defiance.

Then ask the question that matters most, the one I opened with: whose night was this?

Because a night can belong to more than one creature. A guinea fowl who has spent her life avoiding hands may have had the longest night of her life. A hen who has spent weeks building toward something may have had the most frightening one. And the people who showed up, whatever they came for, may have walked away carrying something they didn't expect to find.

"A night full of blessings" is a generous way to describe it. It might even be accurate. But a blessing and a scare can arrive wrapped in the same hour, and one of the things this clip does better than almost anything I've seen is hold both at once, without choosing, without explaining.

That refusal to explain is its strength. It doesn't tell you how to feel. It simply puts you in the room, in the dark, near creatures who have no idea you're watching.

And it trusts you to work out the rest.

Nobody in this story is performing, and that is rare enough now to deserve your full attention.

Fifteen seconds. Sound on, if you can. Keep your eyes on the animals, not on the humans, at least the first time through. You can watch it again for the people.

I have a feeling you will return to it.

DOJ Sues Penn State Over Tuition Breaks for Illegals Denied to Out-Of-State Americans | Eric Florack, PJ Media

An American family considering Penn State may face a higher tuition rate if they live outside Pennsylvania. The Justice Department now wants the university to explain why its published guidance offers qualifying illegals access to the lower resident rate.

DOJ sued Penn State and its trustees on November 5, alleging that the university’s policy violates federal law. The complaint challenges a benefit based on Pennsylvania residence that isn’t generally available to Americans living elsewhere. For parents calculating college bills, the question reaches well beyond immigration politics.

Universities routinely lecture the country about fairness. Asking whether their own tuition rules comply with federal law shouldn’t require smelling salts and an emergency faculty meeting. American families have every reason to demand a clear explanation of who qualifies for a discount and who gets the larger bill.

Penn State’s admissions guidance says illegal alien students, with or without DACA, can qualify for in-state tuition if they meet residency requirements. The listed conditions include four years at an accredited Pennsylvania high school and graduation from that school or receipt of a Pennsylvania GED. Eligibility carries conditions; the page doesn’t promise every illegal applicant a discount.

Congress addressed residence-based college benefits in 1996. Under 8 U.S.C. 1623, someone unlawfully present can’t receive a postsecondary benefit based on state residence unless Americans can receive an equivalent benefit regardless of their own residence. The wording puts out-of-state American students directly into the legal equation.

The DOJ also raises a separate objection: federal law requires an affirmative state enactment to authorize certain benefits for otherwise ineligible illegal aliens. Prosecutors argue that a university policy can’t substitute for that legislative action. Penn State’s trustees therefore face questions about both the benefit terms and the authority used to offer it.

One complication requires an answer before anyone declares the case finished. A December 2025 FAQ from Penn State Dickinson Law’s immigration clinic says noncitizens seeking resident classification must hold a visa or otherwise be lawfully present. Its description differs from the broader eligibility language on the admissions page the DOJ cites.

From Penn State’s Dickinson Law:

A visa is an official document stamped into someone’s passport that allows a noncitizen to travel to the United States for a specific period and purpose, such as study or work. For tuition purposes at Penn State, holding a visa can satisfy part of the requirement of being classified as a Pennsylvania resident as a noncitizen.

The primary student visas are the F-1 visa, which is issued for full-time study at accredited U.S. schools, including colleges and universities, and the J-1 visa, which is issued for participants in approved exchange programs that involve study, research, or training. While holding a visa can satisfy part of the requirements of being classified as a Pennsylvania resident, Penn State’s residency policy excludes F-1 and J-1 students from Pennsylvania resident classification, even if they hold a valid visa.

Penn State should explain which rule governs, when any change took effect, and whether its public guidance accurately describes eligibility. Conflicting university explanations leave families guessing about expensive decisions. They also require careful scrutiny of the DOJ’s claim about the policy currently in force.

The lawsuit establishes what the government alleges. A court must still determine whether the challenged policy violates federal law, and it will need to treat the distinction between lawful presence, immigration status, and eligibility precisely. The university’s own conflicting materials make that examination necessary, not optional.

Americans shouldn’t need a legal research team to understand the price attached to an education. If Penn State’s operative policy excludes unlawfully present applicants from resident tuition, it should identify that policy and correct contrary guidance. If it offers the benefit the DOJ describes, it should explain how the arrangement satisfies Congress’s requirements.

For a family weighing loans, savings, and another year of work, tuition classifications have lasting consequences. The university should publish one consistent explanation that applicants can use before committing money. Administrators have the resources to clear up their own rules. Families shouldn’t bear the cost of the confusion.

Compassion for young people doesn’t give university administrators legislative authority. Congress wrote a condition protecting Americans from being excluded from residence-based benefits offered to people unlawfully present. Universities can advocate for changes to federal law, but their preferences don’t amend it.

Penn State owes prospective students an accurate policy, and its trustees owe the public an explanation. President Donald Trump’s administration has brought that demand into federal court. American parents who keep hearing that college costs require another sacrifice should welcome a hard look at who gets the lower bill.

Written by Nick Clemons.          
One-Sheet / Pitch Document for a Screenplay
Title: Vaudeville (or The Englishman)
Genre: Historical Western / Biographical Drama
Logline: An English-born Texas gambler and gunfighter rises from Civil War soldier and Mexican mercenary to Austin city marshal—only to walk into a carefully arranged ambush in a San Antonio theater that ends the life of the man Bat Masterson called the deadliest pistol fighter of his era.
Tone: Gritty, character-driven Western in the vein of The Assassination of Jesse James by the Coward Robert Ford or Tombstone, with the refined manners and deadly reputation of a “gentleman killer.”
Three-Act Summary:
Act 1 – Young Ben Thompson arrives in frontier Austin, learns the printer’s trade then the faro table, enlists in the Confederacy, and fights in Mexico for Maximilian. Post-war violence and a prison sentence forge his dual identity as family man and professional gambler.
Act 2 – In the Kansas cow towns he builds a fearsome reputation alongside (and against) Hickok, Masterson, and Hardin. Back in Texas he becomes Austin’s effective city marshal while still dealing cards and settling scores—most notably the killing of Jack Harris.
Act 3 – Acquitted but marked, Thompson and King Fisher walk into the Vaudeville Theater. The ambush ends two of the West’s most dangerous men; the unresolved “who ordered it?” question lingers.
Why It Works: Thompson’s life packs more incident than most fictional gunfighters—English immigrant, Confederate, mercenary, gambler, elected lawman, and public assassination. His gentlemanly code (let the other man shoot first) and flamboyant yet refined style offer a fresh counterpoint to the usual dusty outlaw archetype. The Vaudeville ambush provides a built-in, conspiracy-tinged climax.
This one-sheet can be expanded into a full treatment or screenplay outline. No major recent produced screenplay about him appears to be in active development based on available sources; the 2018 biography and the 2026 podcast are the freshest high-profile treatments of his story

text:
My Fellow Republicans,

Tuesday night was a shocking and, in many ways, a surreal experience. As Chairman, I found myself providing an immediate reaction to the election results on live television, sharing my thoughts with viewers across Wisconsin as the results were still unfolding.

I have taken time to examine the results, review the data, and reflect upon what this election means for our party and movement. Leadership carries a responsibility to offer not only direction, but honesty, especially when events do not unfold as we had hoped.

Tuesday night was, and should be, a wake-up call.

For some time, our movement has sailed aboard a great ship, enjoying favorable winds and relatively calm waters. We have celebrated victories, expanded our reach, and welcomed countless Americans aboard who believed in our destination. But the waters have changed.
The winds are shifting, the horizon is uncertain, and a great tempest lies ahead. We cannot navigate the coming storm by pretending the seas are still calm.

There is no shame in recognizing that a course correction may be necessary. There is, however, great danger in refusing to make one.
That correction must begin with an honest examination of our priorities.

For too long, we’ve let national media fights take up all the oxygen, often ignoring the day-to-day struggles of working families. This doesn't mean abandoning our principles or the cultural issues we care about—our convictions still matter.

But we must return our attention to the kitchen table.

Groceries. Electricity. Housing. Insurance. Transportation. Taxes. The growing cost of simply living in America.

I often think of these challenges as death by a thousand paper cuts. It is rarely one expense that overwhelms a family, but the accumulation of countless financial pressures that make each passing month more difficult.

While Washington debates the controversies of the day, families are asking a much simpler question: How are we going to afford all of this?

Our candidates talked about these problems on the trail. We promised to lower costs and strengthen the economy. But campaign promises don't mean anything if we don't deliver actual results.

Campaign promises cannot simply become campaign slogans. They must become a governing agenda.

I recognize the considerable work undertaken by President Trump and his administration. There have been accomplishments deserving of recognition. But activity in Washington does not always translate into tangible improvements around America's kitchen tables.
We can acknowledge progress while recognizing that more must be done. 

That is not disloyalty. It is accountability.

Congress, in particular, must take a serious look in the mirror. The American people did not elect their representatives merely to occupy offices, engage in political infighting, or prepare for the next election. They elected them to legislate and deliver results.

With the new Congress taking office in January, the opportunity to act under the current Congress is limited. We cannot afford to squander the time that remains.

The time for another round of campaign promises has passed. The time for governing is now.

Our priorities must also reflect the concerns Americans have about our nation's involvement abroad.The war in Iran has renewed frustrations among Americans weary of prolonged conflicts in the Middle East while challenges here at home remain unresolved. 

I recognize the national security threats posed by Iran and the difficult decisions confronting our nation's leadership. But I also recognize the growing desire among Americans to see their government devote greater attention to the problems facing their own communities.

Our government's first responsibility must remain to the American people.

1/2 🧵

text:
[🟢] 🌺Joe O’Cearuill JJ Gabriel’s father on his conversation with Michael Carrick and Jason Wilcox over Manchester United’s contract offer:

🗣️ Joe O’Cearuill: “I had a very honest conversation with Michael Carrick and Jason Wilcox about JJ’s future, and I think some people at Manchester United will be angry when they hear why we said no.

But I’m his father before I’m anybody’s friend at a football club.

JJ is 16 years old.

We are not going to make a decision about his future because of the Manchester United badge alone.

I asked them one simple question.

‘Where exactly do you see JJ playing?’

There was a pause.

And that pause told me a lot.

I said, ‘You want him to stay, but you can’t give me a clear pathway. You can’t tell me when he becomes part of the first team.’

JJ doesn’t want to spend years being told he is one of the best young players at Manchester United while waiting for someone to decide when he is ready.

He wants responsibility.

He wants competition.

Most importantly, he wants a pathway.

The contract discussion became serious.

Our proposal was a £5 million signing package, with performance bonuses taking it beyond £8 million, alongside a clear development pathway.

We also wanted regular first-team training and a defined number of senior appearances once he reached the appropriate age.

Manchester United weren’t prepared to agree to those terms.

Real Madrid were.

And that changed everything for me.

I told Carrick, ‘This isn’t about who pays the most money. It’s about who is prepared to make a commitment to my son’s development.’

‘If you want him to stay, show us where he fits.’

‘Don’t tell me he has potential. Tell me what you’re going to do with it.’

Michael was respectful, but I understood there were limitations.

He has a squad to manage.

Jason has a club to manage.

But I have a 16-year-old whose next decision could shape the next ten years of his career.

Then Real Madrid came into the picture.

Their message was different.

They didn’t say, ‘Come here and wait.’

They said, ‘Come here and compete.’

They were prepared to meet the financial package, accept the bonuses and give us a much clearer pathway toward senior football.

That mattered enormously.

I told United, ‘If you cannot give him what another club is willing to give him, you cannot be surprised when he chooses the other club.’

This isn’t disrespect toward Manchester United.

But Manchester United cannot expect every talented young player to stay forever because of the history of the shirt.

History matters.

Ambition matters too.

JJ wants to play for the biggest clubs in the world.

And when Real Madrid tell my 16-year-old son they believe he can become one of their players, I have to take that seriously.

Some people will say he should have stayed.

Some will say he is too young.

Some United fans will be furious.

I understand that.

But I would rather people be angry with our decision today than JJ wake up at 20 and ask why I didn’t fight harder for his career.

We didn’t reject Manchester United because we don’t respect the club.

We rejected the proposal because we didn’t believe it was the best one for JJ.

Real Madrid showed more ambition.

They showed more clarity.

And they were willing to put their money behind their words.

JJ is only 16.

He has a lot to learn.

But he also has huge ambition.

I’m not going to apologize for protecting that.

Manchester United had the opportunity to convince us.

They didn’t.

Real Madrid did.

So now JJ is going to Madrid to compete.

Not to be Cristiano Ronaldo.

Not to be Jude Bellingham.

Not to be anybody else.

To become JJ Gabriel.

And if Manchester United fans are angry, I understand.

But my responsibility isn’t to make Manchester United fans happy.

My responsibility is to make sure my son gets the best opportunity to become the footballer he believes he can be.”
