text:
Lithuanian MP Dangles Data Centers to Musk After Texas Voters Deliver Clear Message: Democracy Isn't for Sale

Lithuanian parliamentarian Matas Maldeikis took to X on Thursday with a direct pitch to Elon Musk, framing Texas election results as a rebuke and offering his country as the new home for the billionaire’s AI infrastructure.

“Dear Elon Musk, Texas voters have sent you and Donald Trump a rather clear message,” Maldeikis wrote. “And now that Texas may be preparing to show your data centers the exit, Lithuania is ready to offer them a new home in Europe.”

He followed with a personal invitation: “As a member of Lithuania’s Parliament, I would like to personally invite you to consider Lithuania for your next major AI infrastructure investment. We welcome ambitious investments, disruptive ideas and powerful technology. Lithuania may be smaller than Texas, but in ambition, creativity and opportunity, we are second to none. Not even Texas.”

Maldeikis closed with a promise of Texas-style smoked brisket if Musk visits—then added the condition that has drawn the sharpest reaction: “Just one condition: here, democracy isn't for sale.”

The post arrives as Texas Democrats claim victories in key races and signal tighter rules on data centers, citing local impacts on power, water, and communities. Musk had poured significant resources into Republican campaigns in the state. Critics quickly called the European overture smug, noting that an invitation wrapped in a lecture about American democracy is an odd way to court investment.

text:
Recruitment as a state machine, not a spreadsheet

I'm building Nexra HRMS with Recruitment in the same tenant as employees and payroll. A hire should move through clear stages — not live as a loose email thread.

𝗝𝗼𝗯 → open role, clear requirements
𝗔𝗽𝗽𝗹𝘆 → candidate submits once
𝗦𝗰𝗿𝗲𝗲𝗻 → structured review, not inbox chaos
𝗢𝗳𝗳𝗲𝗿 → decision lands in the same system

Same pattern as leave and expense: explicit states, one owner per stage, an audit trail you can defend later.

Takeaway: treat hiring status like any other workflow — named steps beat scattered chat history.

Where does your hiring process break first — screening or offer handoff?

text:
The books and films give us one of the most satisfying character arcs in the entire Harry Potter story, and I genuinely think Neville Longbottom deserves more recognition for it.

When we first meet Neville in Philosopher’s Stone, he’s a nervous, forgetful boy who struggles with confidence. He’s constantly underestimated, occasionally ridiculed, and rarely taken seriously. But there’s something about Neville that people overlook: even when he’s frightened, he has an extraordinary sense of right and wrong.

Remember the end of Philosopher’s Stone? When Harry, Ron and Hermione are about to leave the common room to stop Voldemort from getting the Philosopher’s Stone, Neville stands in their way. He knows they’re his friends, but he also believes they’re breaking the rules and putting Gryffindor in danger. He challenges them anyway.

Hermione has to use the Full Body-Bind Curse to get past him.

That moment is important because Dumbledore later awards Neville ten points for having the courage to stand up to his friends. It establishes something about his character long before he becomes a great wizard: Neville understands that doing the right thing sometimes means standing against people you care about.

Then there’s Order of the Phoenix. During the Department of Mysteries battle, Neville refuses to abandon his injured friends. Even when he’s hurt, struggling and clearly outmatched, he keeps fighting. He also insists on helping Harry carry the unconscious Hermione.

And this is where the prophecy makes Neville’s story even more fascinating.

In Chapter 37 of Order of the Phoenix, Dumbledore reveals that the prophecy concerning the person capable of defeating Voldemort could have referred to Neville just as easily as Harry. Both boys were born at the end of July, and both had parents who had defied Voldemort three times.

Voldemort chose Harry, believing him to be the greater threat. But Neville was another possible answer to the prophecy.

Now consider what happens in Deathly Hallows.

While Harry, Ron and Hermione are hunting Horcruxes, Neville, Ginny and Luna help keep Dumbledore’s Army alive at Hogwarts. Under Snape’s administration and the Carrows’ brutal regime, Neville becomes one of the central figures of the resistance.

He is tortured, punished and threatened, but he refuses to surrender. He helps maintain the resistance, uses the Room of Requirement as a refuge and keeps Dumbledore’s Army alive.

There’s a particularly important detail in the book that the film doesn’t fully explore.

When Harry finally returns to Hogwarts, Neville explains why standing up to the Carrows mattered:

“The thing is, it helps when people stand up to them, it gives everyone hope. I used to notice that when you did it, Harry.”

Think about that. Neville had spent years watching Harry stand up to people who seemed untouchable. Eventually, he became that person for everyone else.

And then comes the Battle of Hogwarts.

In the book, after Voldemort announces Harry’s death, Neville steps forward and refuses to submit. Voldemort offers him a place among the Death Eaters, even acknowledging his bravery and noble family.

Neville’s response?

“I’ll join you when hell freezes over!”

“Dumbledore’s Army!”

Voldemort punishes him by placing the enchanted Sorting Hat on his head and setting it on fire.

But Neville pulls the Sword of Gryffindor from the burning hat and kills Nagini, destroying the final remaining Horcrux.

There’s something particularly beautiful about that moment. The boy who once struggled to perform basic magic becomes the person who destroys the final obstacle standing between Voldemort and defeat.

And let’s not forget his parents.

Frank and Alice Longbottom were tortured into permanent insanity by Death Eaters who wanted information about Voldemort’s disappearance. Neville grew up visiting them at St Mungo’s, knowing they would never recover or properly recognise him..

text:
"Whenever people say they hate Neville Longbottom, I just show them this video.

He started as the kid who said, 'You'll get Gryffindor into trouble again.' The kid everyone laughed at for standing up to his own friends.

Then he said, 'I'll fight you.' With shaky hands. With a broken wand. With no backup. Just heart.

Then the Golden Trio left. Harry Potter, Ron Weasley, and Hermione Granger went Horcrux hunting. Hogwarts was left to the Death Eaters. And Neville Longbottom held it DOWN. He led Dumbledore's Army. He took the beatings. He kept the resistance alive while everyone else was gone.

Mind you, this is the second potential Chosen One. The prophecy could have been about him. Voldemort just picked Harry Potter instead.

And the wildest part? He thought Harry Potter was dead. He watched Voldemort carry his body out. He thought all hope was gone. And he still stood up to Voldemort, in front of everyone, and killed Nagini.

He started as the joke. He ended as the reason Voldemort could die.

So go ahead. Tell me you hate Neville Longbottom again.

Quote this with the exact moment you realised Neville Longbottom was HIM. I'll wait in the comments."

text:
This State Admitted Its Gun Law Violated the Second Amendment. But a Federal Judge Won't Let it Go. | Jeff Charles, Townhall

A federal judge in Tampa has refused to sign off on a deal in which Florida’s own top law enforcement officials agreed that the state’s mandatory three-day waiting period on firearms purchases violates the Second Amendment and refused to defend it in court.

Instead of issuing a ruling, U.S. District Judge Steven Merryday invited other parties, including two anti-gunner organizations, to defend the law in court.

The case stems from a lawsuit filed by four Florida gun buyers, two firearms retailers, and the National Rifle Association (NRA), which sued the state’s Department of Law Enforcement Commissioner Mark Glass, Attorney General James Uthmeier, and 20 state attorneys in August 2025.

The suit challenges the mandatory three-day wait between the purchase and delivery of a firearm prescribed by the Florida Constitution and implemented by Florida Statutes. Florida voters wrote the three-day handgun wait into the state constitution in 1990, and the Legislature expanded it to all firearms in 2018, according to the NRA’s Institute for Legislative Action.

On June 5, 2026, the defendant officials served a Rule 68 offer of judgment, which the plaintiffs accepted the same day, and on June 30, the parties jointly asked the court to enter it. The judgment would have declared the waiting-period provisions unconstitutional to the extent they require retailers to hold a firearm beyond the time required to perform a background check.

The judgment would also have permanently prohibited enforcement of the law, awarded the plaintiffs $10,000 in attorney fees and costs, and awarded no damages. Uthmeier announced the agreement the day it was filed.

Merryday denied the joint motion on Oct. 28, 2026, and directed the clerk not to enter the judgment. He reasoned that a declaration that state law is unconstitutional and a permanent injunction against its enforcement are not available through Rule 68 without full and adversarial presentation of the issues.

“Based on a complaint, an answer, and the acceptance of an offer of judgment but without adversarial briefing or other argument and despite an array of opinion among the circuits on the governing issue in the action, the parties request a summary adjudication on a matter currently the subject of intense debate and litigation around the country, that affects the United States and the Florida constitutions, and that resolves the validity of a Florida statute,” Merryday wrote in his ruling.

The judge’s order invites Gov. Ron DeSantis, the Florida House of Representatives, the Florida Senate, the Brady Center to Prevent Gun Violence, and the Giffords Law Center to Prevent Gun Violence to participate as amici curiae.

The waiting period remains in effect, and no court has ruled on its constitutionality. One defendant, State Attorney Brian Kramer, had already told Alachua County in June that he would not enforce its five-day county waiting period because of the pending agreement.

text:
Donald Trump has the power of the presidency. Barack Obama has something different: the political influence of a former president who remains capable of mobilizing an entire party.

During the 2026 midterm election campaign, Obama stepped back into the political spotlight, raising money for Democratic candidates, appearing at campaign rallies and directly challenging Trump's leadership.

According to NBC News, Obama raised more than $15 million for Democratic candidates. He also campaigned in politically important states, including Ohio, Michigan and Georgia, where Democrats were fighting to strengthen their electoral position.

His involvement was significant because Obama remains one of the Democratic Party's most recognizable figures. 

His appearances attract media attention, his endorsements carry political weight, and his fundraising network gives Democratic candidates access to resources that can make a difference in competitive races.

But Obama was not simply trying to help Democrats win elections. He was also trying to shape how Americans viewed Trump's presidency.

At campaign rallies, he launched a sustained criticism of the administration, attacking its economic decisions, foreign policy and approach to governing.

In Ohio, he described Trump's administration using four particularly forceful words: "chaos, cruelty, corruption, and incompetence."

On the economy, Obama criticized Trump's tariffs and argued that the administration's decisions were contributing to rising costs for ordinary Americans. He also attacked its tax legislation, arguing that its benefits disproportionately favoured wealthy Americans.

His criticism extended beyond America's borders. He questioned Trump's treatment of traditional allies, including Canada, and accused his administration of being too accommodating towards Vladimir Putin while abandoning Ukraine.

These were not isolated disagreements over individual policies. Obama was presenting a broader argument that Trump's leadership was damaging America's international relationships and weakening important democratic institutions.

Trump, naturally, pushed back.

He dismissed Obama's presidential record, called him a lousy president and mocked his campaign appearances. His allies also challenged the former president's criticisms, pointing to economic problems during previous Democratic administrations.

The confrontation revealed something important about the American political system.

A president may control the executive branch, but that does not mean he controls the entire government. Congress has its own constitutional powers, and its composition can determine whether a president's legislative agenda advances or encounters serious resistance.

That is why midterm elections matter. They offer voters an opportunity to change the balance of power in Washington without electing a new president.

For Obama, supporting Democratic candidates was therefore about more than opposing Trump personally. It was also about strengthening the political forces capable of challenging his administration.

This is where Obama's continued influence becomes particularly interesting..

He no longer has the authority to sign legislation, issue executive orders or direct American foreign policy. Yet he can still raise millions of dollars, attract national attention and help shape the political conversation surrounding a sitting president.

Trump has the presidency. Obama has remained an important voice within the opposition.

Their political rivalry is therefore not simply a continuation of the disagreements between two former and current presidents. It represents a wider struggle over the direction of American politics, the limits of presidential power and the future of the Democratic and Republican parties.

The White House has changed hands, but the political battle between the two men has not disappeared.

text:
The night after her first porn scene, an 18-year-old Duke student lay awake staring at her phone, waiting for someone to text “I know what you did.” Months later, it came. And it came from a guy she called a friend.

Her name is Miriam Weeks. In high school she was the nerd who kept to herself, captain of the debate team, the girl guys didn’t look at twice. Then she got into Duke. Secretly, she started flying across the country on school breaks to shoot adult films under a fake name: Belle Knox.

Her first scene was far rougher than she’d been told. That night she couldn’t sleep. She felt guilty and sick, and she was sure that any minute someone would find it and tell everyone.

She kept going anyway. For months, nobody knew.

Then, in early 2014, a close male friend recognized her in a video and outed her on campus. The secret spread through Duke in days. Then she was betrayed a second time: a girl who had acted like her friend turned out to be writing about her for the student paper. Soon the whole country knew her real name. bustle
What came next was a storm. Death threats. People threatening to throw trash on her. Twitter full of strangers calling her worthless. Frat guys mocked her, and she said the girls hated her even more. On CNN she offered her theory why: “maybe they caught their boyfriend watching my porn.” Piers Morgan didn’t let it slide. He told her that wouldn’t be funny for the girl whose boyfriend it was.

He kept pushing. He told her that as the father of a little girl, he’d be devastated if his daughter did this. He asked whether her family had disowned her. Then he found out where her stage name came from: Amanda Knox, the American student accused of murder in Italy. He called it creepy.

Critics went digging to prove she was a liar. They reported she had turned down a full scholarship to Vanderbilt and already had a substantial scholarship from Duke. Half the country called her brave. The other half called her a fraud. thecollegefix

Then the story flipped. The internet turned on the guy who outed her. Now he was the one getting death threats. He apologized publicly. And the girl everyone was attacking did something nobody saw coming: she forgave him and asked her fans to leave him alone.
She was 18. She had been exposed by a friend, sold out by another, and hated by a campus. And she was the one who stopped the pile-on.

Was Belle Knox a victim of a campus witch hunt, or did she know exactly what she was getting into?

text:
Tyrese Boss bends down before every game he plays and writes July 11, 2019 on the grass with his fingers.

That is the day he lost his father. Glen had colon cancer.

He lost his grandmother two years before that, in 2017, right before he started high school. She had helped raise him.

His mother, Linda Scott, raised him by herself. She worked at the California Institution for Men, the state prison in Chino, and the family moved to Chino Hills to be closer to her job. Before that they were in Rialto.

He came out of Chino Hills High School as a two star recruit. Power 4 programs in his own state looked at him and not one of them offered him a scholarship. He was weighing Eastern Washington and Montana State when Wyoming called.

"She thinks it's better for me because in California there's a lot of distractions," he said about his mother. "She thought Wyoming and Laramie was the best place for me to lock into the game and focus on me."

Then he hurt his hand and lost his true freshman season. He did not get on the field until the final game of 2024.

His cornerbacks coach in Laramie was a man named Benny Boyd.

"There was obvious talent on the tape but it's more his personality," Boyd said. "We connected kind of through the tragedy of his dad passing away and my father passed away a lot of years ago now."

"That was a connection, both having hard-working single mothers."

"His mom is a very strong-willed tough woman who has raised him well."

"I was raised in a very similar background, so I think we had an unspoken connection that way."

Boss won the starting job at Wyoming in 2025. He kept writing the date.

"I'm not going to lie; I shed a tear or two on the way to Akron because all those emotions hit me," he said. "I know they're not physically there, but I know they can see."

"They're not here but I've got to make it happen because I promised them."

In February of 2026, Benny Boyd took a job coaching cornerbacks at TCU.

Boss entered the portal and chose Arizona, where the staff spent his visit talking about something other than football.

"It wasn't just football conversations on my visit, it was life talk and family talk," he said. "That's what made me gravitate towards Arizona and make that decision."

Arizona is 6 and 2 and ranked 22nd. Boss starts at cornerback.

FRIDAY NIGHT, TCU comes to Tucson, and Benny Boyd will be standing on the other sideline coaching their corners.

Before the game, Tyrese Boss will bend down and write a date on the grass.

The man across the field is one of the few people in that stadium who already knows what it says.

text:
Trump confirmed he met Kirill Dmitriev, Putin’s envoy and the head of Russia’s direct investment fund. He offered no details of their conversation. He did, however, describe a coming agreement as “great and beautiful.” He said it could extend across all of Europe, beyond the Russia-Ukraine war.

He also said he had not met the Ukrainian delegation, and Washington needs to sit with that. On November 5, Ukraine’s human rights commissioner Dmytro Lubinets and parliamentary faction leader David Arakhamia were at the White House for a meeting with Russian representatives and First Lady Melania Trump. It followed a humanitarian operation in Russian-occupied Oleshky, Kherson region, preceded by a local ceasefire. Humanitarian access matters. So does the question of who gets direct access to the US president while the terms of a wider European deal are being discussed.

The sequence is worth keeping clear:

• November 5: Ukrainian and Russian representatives met at the White House after the Oleshky operation.

• Trump confirmed a separate meeting with Dmitriev, without disclosing its substance.

Trump said he never met Lubinets and Arakhamia.

• Trump framed a potential agreement as extending across Europe.

The White House event also included Melania Trump thanking the Kremlin for its role in the humanitarian effort. The Ukrainian delegation was seated among representatives of the state occupying Oleshky. A local pause in fighting can help civilians. The occupier remains a party with no claim to equal political standing with Ukraine. Diplomatic choreography creates an impression, and the Kremlin knows how to use one.

Dmitriev’s access deserves particular scrutiny. He carries Putin’s message while also heading an investment vehicle. When Trump speaks of an agreement broader than the war, Congress should ask whether economic arrangements with Moscow are being discussed alongside Ukraine’s security. That question belongs to records and testimony, so we should not invent a secret deal. The distinction matters. Serious oversight needs a paper trail.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has already said the Republicans’ midterm losses will not change Trump’s foreign policy. Moscow’s apparent expectation is continuity. Kyiv and Europe have every reason to test that expectation rather than accept a negotiating setup in which Putin’s representative gets a presidential audience and Ukraine’s representatives do not.

CONGRESS HAS A JOB

Zelenskyy has raised the handling of Ukraine aid approved during the Biden administration under the Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative, or USAI. That gives lawmakers a concrete line of inquiry: which approved commitments moved, which stalled, who made the decisions, and what reasons were recorded? They can also examine the administration’s contacts with Dmitriev and the process behind any proposal affecting European security.

Election results alone leave those questions unanswered. Before the new Congress begins work on January 4, members and their staff can put the relevant decisions, dates and officials on an oversight agenda. Democrats should press it. Republicans who support Ukraine should press it too. A request for documents is more useful than another speech about being “concerned.”

EUROPE BELONGS AT THE TABLE

Trump himself widened the scope of the prospective deal to Europe. That makes European participation a practical requirement. European states would live with the security consequences, finance much of Ukraine’s defense and reconstruction, and enforce any sanctions they agree to maintain. A format in which Washington and Moscow settle terms and then present them to Kyiv and European capitals would give the aggressor power over people who must bear the result.

Ukraine can insist that European representatives take part in negotiations touching European security. Kyiv can also insist that humanitarian work in occupied territory remain separate from concessions on sovereignty. A ceasefire that lets people receive help in Oleshky is valuable. It must never become a stage prop for trading away Ukraine’s future.

A wider pressure point exists as well. The reported move by Israeli President Isaac Herzog toward asking opposition politician Gadi Eisenkot to form a government could change the politics around further strikes on Iran. Brent was cited as falling from $114 to $97 over two days as market expectations shifted. Oil prices matter to Russia’s war finances, though a two-day move is no substitute for sustained pressure. Ukraine and its partners should track that opening without building policy on a market forecast.

For now, the immediate task is narrower and firmer: establish what the administration has done with approved aid, establish what Trump discussed with Dmitriev, and put Ukraine and Europe in the room for decisions about their own security. Moscow benefits when all three are left to presidential discretion. Congress has the means to demand answers.

text:
Stephen Kinzer, an award-winning journalist, author and former New York Times foreign correspondent, argues that the war in Ukraine is the culmination of a 75-year American effort to use Ukraine against Russia. Washington repeatedly rejected opportunities to prevent the conflict, prioritising geopolitical dominance over European security and ultimately turning Ukraine into the battleground of a confrontation between great powers.

A War 75 Years in the Making

Describing Russia’s 2022 invasion as “unprovoked” obscures the historical circumstances that produced it. The invasion was the final stage of a much longer process of American intervention in Ukraine.

That process began in 1947, when the newly established CIA sought to destabilise the Soviet Union by supporting armed Ukrainian resistance. American intelligence recruited anti-Soviet operatives through Reinhard Gehlen, the former Nazi intelligence chief responsible for Eastern Europe.

Many of these recruits had collaborated with Nazi Germany, and some had participated in massacres. The American project in Ukraine was therefore built partly upon networks previously employed by the Nazis, establishing connections that continued to influence Ukrainian nationalist movements.
The Origins of America’s Anti-Russian Foreign Policy

American hostility towards Russia did not originate with the Cold War. It inherited a tradition of anti-Russian thinking developed during Britain’s imperial competition with Russia in the nineteenth century.

This hostility subsequently became embedded in American foreign policy through influential officials with personal or family backgrounds in Eastern Europe.

Zbigniew Brzezinski, Madeleine Albright, Victoria Nuland and Antony Blinken exemplify the influence of this political tradition. Their historical experiences and inherited attitudes helped sustain policies directed towards weakening Moscow.

Rather than merely implementing presidential decisions, these officials exercised substantial influence over the formulation of American strategy.

Ukraine became particularly attractive because of its potential to undermine Russia from within its immediate neighbourhood.
NATO Expansion and the Lost Opportunity for Peace

The end of the Cold War offered an extraordinary opportunity to establish a European security architecture accommodating both Western and Russian interests.

Instead, the United States expanded NATO eastward.

Bill Clinton’s decision was heavily influenced by domestic electoral calculations. Polish-American and other Eastern European communities represented important voting constituencies, while the American defence industry anticipated enormous profits from supplying weapons to new NATO members.

Despite warnings from George Kennan and other experienced foreign policy specialists, Clinton proceeded.

Short-term electoral considerations and commercial interests prevailed over long-term European stability.

Washington’s unwillingness to construct an inclusive security system also reflected a deeper psychological obstacle: America’s inability to accept an international order it does not dominate.

text:
The AI trade is facing its most serious repricing yet. Nvidia has broken below $200, Asian semiconductor markets are plunging, and investors are questioning whether unprecedented infrastructure spending will produce the returns promised. The economic boom is real. The investment returns remain uncertain.

The selloff is spreading fast. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index reportedly lost 12.2%, followed by declines of as much as 8.8% in Korea's KOSPI, 7% in Japan's Nikkei and 9% in Taiwan.

These aren't ordinary daily fluctuations. Investors are rapidly reducing exposure to one of the market's most crowded trades.

Nvidia fell as much as 9.3%, breaking below $200 and key moving averages. Concerns over data-center financing, AI regulation and future chip demand are testing valuations that assumed years of exceptional growth.

Yet the underlying investment boom hasn't stopped.

U.S. data-center construction reached a preliminary $96.5B annualized pace in September, nearly 90% above last year. Moody's estimates related investment contributed roughly one percentage point to Q3 GDP growth.

That's real economic activity. But building data centers isn't the same as generating productivity gains or attractive shareholder returns. Electricity, grid connections, utilization and customer monetization still determine the economics.

Geopolitics offers little comfort.

Iran has submitted a nuclear proposal through Qatar, but substantive negotiations depend on seven conditions. With Washington keeping military options open and Hormuz shipping risks unresolved, energy markets remain exposed to renewed disruption.

Financial instability is appearing elsewhere too. Paraguay's reported intervention at Ueno Bank and restrictions on deposit access have raised concerns about financial-system confidence, although the scale of losses and political implications remain uncertain.

The common thread is confidence in future cash flows.

Markets spent years capitalizing AI's enormous potential. Now they're demanding proof that the infrastructure can generate enough revenue to justify its cost.

AI can lift GDP, transform industries and still destroy shareholder value if too much capital is invested at the wrong price.

The distinction between economic growth and investment returns has rarely mattered more.

text:
Qatar’s emir just called Trump as Tehran offers a nuclear paper it refuses to discuss until Washington meets seven demands first.

On 6 November, Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani spoke by phone with President Donald Trump, according to Qatar’s Emiri Diwan. Anadolu Agency and AP both reported the call.

The Diwan said the two reviewed strategic ties and Doha’s mediation toward “a comprehensive agreement that resolves the crisis.” Tamim stressed sustained dialogue, freedom of navigation and the security of energy supplies.

The timing is not accidental. On Thursday, Trump told reporters in the Oval Office the United States may have to “destroy the rest” of Iran, adding people will “know soon enough” if he acts.

Axios quoted a US official saying Central Command is preparing for a possible resumption of major operations and is waiting on orders from Washington. That is a readiness claim, not a launch order.

Tehran answered with paper and conditions. A senior Iranian official told Reuters on Thursday that Iran had sent a nuclear and peace proposal to Washington via Qatar.

The same official said the proposal would be discussed only after the United States meets Tehran’s seven demands. Washington, the official added, is reviewing it.

Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, put the linkage in blunt terms in Moscow on Thursday. “As long as they do not execute our seven conditions, we will neither open the Strait of Hormuz nor have negotiations,” he said, according to Al Jazeera and Reuters.

The published list is incomplete, but Iranian and regional reporting cite lifting US sanctions, unfreezing Iranian assets, war reparations and an end to the US naval blockade of Iranian ports. Washington insists the nuclear file must be in any first round.

Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi spent Thursday working the phones. Iranian state media said he spoke with counterparts in Saudi Arabia, Qatar, the UAE, Turkey, Oman, Kuwait, Pakistan, Jordan, Cyprus and Egypt.

Gulf states want the shooting to stay off their soil. They also want tankers moving. Hormuz normally carries about one-fifth of global oil supply.

At sea, leverage continues. Iran’s Revolutionary Guard claims more tankers hit mines on “unauthorised” routes near Oman this week. UKMTO data, cited by Reuters, still show incidents near a record pace. Maritime organisations have not independently confirmed every IRGC claim.

Markets are pricing hope, not resolution. Reuters reported Brent around $98.60 a barrel by late morning Friday GMT, after an early bounce toward $99.86, yet on track for roughly a 12 to 16 percent weekly drop after Democrats took Congress.

Kpler shipping data, cited by Iran International, say Iran has not loaded oil for export since mid-August under the US blockade. That squeezes Tehran’s budget as hard as Hormuz squeezes everyone else’s nerves.

Russia sits in the room. Rezaei delivered a message from Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei to Vladimir Putin on Thursday. Putin offered help ending what Rezaei called an “unjust war,” while deepening talk of gas pipelines from Russia to Iran.

Scepticism is warranted. Midterm losses raise the political cost of another round for Trump, but hawks remain around him and CENTCOM’s plans are already drawn. Tehran’s seven conditions look closer to a victory schedule than a bridge.

What to watch next: whether Washington answers the Qatari channel with anything concrete on the blockade or frozen funds; whether tanker incidents in Hormuz slow after Friday’s call; and whether Trump’s “soon enough” becomes an order or another Oval Office threat.

text:
Nike pitched Stephen Curry a new contract in 2013. An official called him "Steph-on," like Steve Urkel.

Then a slide came up with Kevin Durant's name still on it.

Curry's father Dell sat in the room and kept a poker face. "I wasn't surprised. I was surprised that I didn't get a correction," he told ESPN.

"I stopped paying attention after that."

Curry was already fed up. He had asked Nike for a youth basketball camp, like other NBA stars had, and never got one.

Under Armour founder Kevin Plank says his company was chasing Curry's locker mate, Kent Bazemore. Curry noticed and started asking about the brand.

Under Armour reportedly offered just under $4 million a year. Nike had the right to match it and didn't. Curry signed with Under Armour.

Nike's former sports marketing director Nico Harrison later said: "In all honesty, if he would have stayed with Nike, his business would be a monster right now."

In 2023 Curry became president of his own Curry Brand and got 8.8 million Under Armour shares worth $75 million at the time. By 2025 the stock had fallen to under $6, from a high of $45.

In November 2025 they split. Curry kept the brand name and logos. He said: "I think it's the right thing for everybody."

The next night, after a win over the Spurs, he said: "I'm a free agent." He had worn Nike Kobe 6s in that game.

In the video below, Curry tells Draymond Green why he left Nike: "that was me betting on myself."

Nike couldn't get his name right. Did Curry make the right call?

text:
⚖️⚖️⚖️When Rehabilitation Reaches Its Limit: Prison Alternatives, Psychopathy, and the Case for Incapacitation

What alternatives have been proposed for punishment, other than classic prison, with it's sometimes inhumane conditions? how could we evolve from this ancient system? what have others suggested? there must be a punishment, but what kind? i know prisons in nordic countries are like a vacation for example

Thinkers and reformers (criminologists studying desistance, public-health approaches like UCSF’s Amend program, and organizations such as the Vera Institute or Sentencing Project) generally argue for reserving incarceration primarily for people who pose ongoing serious risk, while expanding community options and improving conditions and reentry for everyone else. Pure prison abolition is a minority view; most evidence-based proposals retain secure confinement for the most dangerous offenders.Practical evolution and limits

A workable evolution looks like: (1) shorter average sentences and far more community alternatives for non-violent or lower-risk cases; (2) humane, normality-oriented prisons when custody is used; (3) strong reentry supports (housing, employment, licensing reform); and (4) prevention and early intervention outside the justice system. 

Recidivism data and cost analyses generally favor this over mass, harsh incarceration for many offense types.For extreme cases—such as prolonged severe child abuse and starvation—incapacitation remains essential for public safety. Even then, the Nordic evidence suggests that degrading conditions are not required for deterrence or justice and can be counterproductive.

 The loss of freedom, structured accountability, and (where appropriate) restorative processes can constitute the punishment while prioritizing lower future harm. Outcomes depend heavily on the surrounding society: strong social supports make rehabilitation more feasible. Direct transplants of Nordic models into high-inequality, high-violence contexts face real limits, but the core principles (normality, skills, relationships, and proportionality) have been tested in U.S. pilots with measurable benefits.

Nordic-style systems and community-based alternatives offer the clearest evidence-based path away from purely punitive, often harsh imprisonment, while still imposing real restriction and accountability. The core idea is that the primary punishment is the loss of liberty and forced accountability, not additional suffering through inhumane conditions. 

Harsh conditions frequently increase recidivism by damaging people further, whereas systems focused on normality, skills, and reintegration produce better public-safety outcomes.The Nordic approach (especially Norway)Norway deliberately shifted in the 1990s from a more punitive model (then ~60–70% two-year recidivism) to one centered on rehabilitation. 

Key principles include:
Normality: 

Prison life should resemble ordinary life as much as safely possible (own clothes, communal cooking, education, work, private cells).

Staff trained for both security and social support (“dynamic security” and “contact officer” models).
“Import model”: Health, education, and other services come from the regular outside system for better continuity on release.

Heavy use of community sanctions instead of short prison terms: electronic monitoring, community service, suspended sentences, and probation.
Restorative elements such as Norway’s Konfliktråd mediation service.

Results commonly cited include roughly 20% two-year reconviction rates (among the lowest globally) and an incarceration rate around 50–55 per 100,000 people—far below the U.S. Average sentences are much shorter. 

Studies (including work published via CEPR and others) have found that Norwegian imprisonment can reduce reoffending and improve employment for some groups, especially those previously disconnected from the labor market. U.S. pilots inspired by this model (e.g., in Pennsylvania and elsewhere) have shown improvements in internal prison behavior and staff/inmate relations. 

It is not a vacation. Liberty is still restricted, open prisons or progressive freedoms are earned, and serious offenders (including those serving longer terms) face secure settings. 

Pre-trial isolation remains a documented problem in Nordic systems, and the model depends on a strong welfare state, low inequality, and high social trust. Budget pressures have already strained conditions in recent years

Other proposed and used alternativesNordic countries and reformers elsewhere emphasize a tiered system:

Community sanctions as the default for many offenses: Day-fines (income-adjusted), community service, electronic monitoring/house arrest, and supervised probation. These are widely used as substitutes for short prison sentences and show lower recidivism in several studies.

Restorative justice: Victim-offender mediation, circles, or accountability processes focused on repairing harm. Nordic countries have institutionalized versions; U.S. programs (e.g., Common Justice for certain violent felonies with victim consent) report reduced rearrests.

Specialized courts and treatment orders: Drug courts, mental-health courts, and mandated treatment for substance use or psychiatric issues, often combined with supervision.

Diversion and front-end interventions: Pre-arrest or pre-trial diversion into services, violence interruption programs, and addressing root causes (mental health crises, addiction, poverty-related offenses) rather than defaulting to custody.

For youth: Specialized “youth punishment” or follow-up regimes in Norway that keep young people in the community under intensive multi-agency supervision rather than standard prison.
Humane custodial conditions when confinement is necessary: 

Even for longer sentences, the focus is education, vocational training, gradual release (open prisons, work release), and reentry support. The goal is incapacitation plus reduced future offending rather than pure retribution.

What about harsher alternatives to prison?
Explain restorative justice circles
What about other countries with different systems

people like this one here who starved his daugher, may be beyond recover / classic hard conditions prison act as a deterrent also, by fear of prison / but the worst criminals and this type of psychos, don't fear prison, they don't work that way.. so in these severe abusers or criminals, it's complicated ... they should need some type of special treatment, but not sure reahabilitation is possible

These measures accept that full rehabilitation is often unrealistic and treat incapacitation as the primary public-safety response, while still offering structured interventions that can sometimes reduce risk in responsive individuals.Practical implicationFor offenders like the one in the Wisconsin case, the evidence-based response is long-term secure confinement first.

 Any treatment is secondary and focused on risk management rather than “curing” the person. Humane conditions do not preclude this; they mainly reduce unnecessary harm, staff injury, and some criminogenic effects of brutal environments. The hard limit remains: some people will stay high-risk for life, and systems need reliable ways to keep them away from potential victims.

For the most extreme cases—prolonged, deliberate severe child abuse like the starvation example—public safety prioritizes long-term incapacitation over hopes of rehabilitation. These offenders are not a uniform group, but a subset show traits (callousness, lack of empathy, poor behavioral control) that make ordinary deterrence and standard treatment unreliable.

Deterrence and “fear of prison”Research consistently finds that the certainty of being caught and punished deters more reliably than the severity of the punishment (Nagin’s reviews and related work). 

Longer sentences or harsher conditions show only weak, inconsistent effects on general deterrence for most people. For individuals with high psychopathic traits, the effect is weaker still: many have reduced fear responses, limited future-orientation, or simply do not weigh consequences the way others do. 

Harsh conditions can also backfire by increasing institutional violence, strengthening antisocial networks, or worsening post-release outcomes for some. In short, making prison more miserable is a poor lever for the people least responsive to ordinary fear-based deterrence.

Psychopathy, treatability, and severe abusers

Psychopathy (measured by tools like the PCL-R) is one of the stronger predictors of violent and general recidivism. Meta-analyses link it robustly to future dangerousness. Treatment results are mixed and generally modest:High-psychopathy individuals have higher dropout rates and poorer average outcomes.

Some specialized cognitive-behavioral or risk-need-responsivity programs show that a subset who complete treatment and demonstrate measurable change can have reduced reoffending.
Overall, the evidence does not support expecting reliable, deep personality change in the most severe cases. Many remain elevated risk even after interventions.

Not every severe child abuser is a psychopath. Some have other drivers (severe personality disorders, substance issues, trauma histories, skill deficits). Large child-welfare studies still show meaningful re-perpetration rates (often in the 12–15% range for subsequent maltreatment, higher for certain subtypes and extreme cases). Extreme deliberate starvation signals high risk and is treated accordingly by courts.What systems actually do with the highest-risk groupEven rehabilitation-oriented systems retain strong tools for these offenders:

Preventive/indefinite detention (Norway’s forvaring, similar measures in Denmark): Used when a fixed sentence is judged insufficient to protect the public after serious violent or sexual offenses plus an assessed high risk of repetition. It is periodically reviewed. Norway uses it for a small percentage of the prison population (including high-profile cases like Anders Breivik). 
Conditions can still aim for relative normality where security allows, but the priority is containment. These populations show very high rates of mental-health diagnoses.

Long fixed sentences with limited or no early release for the most dangerous.
Secure forensic psychiatric facilities when mental disorder is central.
Specialized high-security units and intensive supervision on any release.

text:
Vasily Tropinin (1776–1857): A renowned Moscow portrait painter who captured Alexander Pushkin, historian Nikolai Karamzin, and Prince Mikhail Obolensky.
He was born into a serf family. Sent to St. Petersburg to learn confectionery, he secretly attended free drawing classes at the Imperial Academy instead. His owner eventually allowed limited study, but later recalled him to the Ukrainian estate to work as a pastry cook, lackey, and house painter.
A card game nearly won him freedom—Prince Dmitriev won a large sum from Morkov and offered to cancel the debt in exchange for Tropinin’s liberty; Morkov simply paid the money instead. A foreign guest who admired Tropinin’s paintings was shocked to see him serving at table in livery; the awkwardness led Morkov to stop using him as a footman, but not to free him. Public pressure finally forced the issue: in 1823 (as an Easter gift, at age 47) he received his freedom and soon became an Academician.

text:
Dennis, I think there's an important lesson here that extends well beyond Democrats or Republicans.

The American dream doesn't belong to a political party. Neither do individual liberty, economic opportunity, personal responsibility, or the pursuit of happiness. Those are American ideals, and both parties should be competing to advance them.

I welcome any movement toward a bigger tent, particularly one that recognizes people as individuals rather than reducing them to political affiliations, demographic categories, or ideological labels.

But I would offer one caution: electoral victories are opportunities, not mandates for ideological certainty. The pendulum swings in part because those entrusted with power too often mistake winning an election for having all the answers.

A durable coalition requires more than welcoming different perspectives when they're politically convenient. It requires genuine intellectual humility, a willingness to challenge one's own assumptions, and the courage to defend individual freedoms even when doing so benefits people with whom we disagree.

And ultimately, results matter. Can people afford homes? Can small businesses thrive? Are families more financially secure? Do Americans feel freer, safer, and more optimistic about their futures?

Those should be measures of success regardless of which party governs.

My hope is that November 3rd represents something larger than a Democratic victory or Republican defeat. Perhaps it can be a reminder that Americans are exhausted by division and increasingly hungry for leadership that puts people ahead of party.

Political power is temporary. The responsibility to serve should be enduring.

The goal shouldn't be to replace one political monopoly on righteousness with another. It should be to build a country where more Americans have the freedom and opportunity to flourish.

🇺🇸 Which way, Republican Party?

Three names lead the early 2028 betting markets, and each one represents a different path for the GOP.

🔴 Ron DeSantis is term-limited, and his next move looks like the White House.

He’s been the most outspoken voice on the right since Tuesday, doing interview after interview.

He appeals to both the establishment and populist wings of the party, with enough Trump in him to keep the base.

He’s also very popular in Florida across generations. If he wins the primary, he could be a tremendous candidate.

🔴 Marco Rubio, the current Secretary of State, is rumored (unconfirmed) to be resigning in order to run.

He’s a pragmatic institutionalist who has adapted to the populist shift, and remains quite popular.

As a Hispanic candidate, he could help win back crucial states like Texas. But being part of the Trump administration cuts both ways.

🔴 JD Vance, the Vice President, may be the purest ideological voice of the new populist right, with real appeal to the post-liberal wing.

But he may have the toughest road, since he’s tied (even moreso than Rubio) to an administration that’s very unpopular right now.

That could change in 2 years, and he did move fast after the midterms to separate himself, blaming the Iran war.

Some voices on the right don’t want any of the three. Tucker Carlson’s name is floating around, too.

And whoever it is faces a brutal question: can ANY Republican win in 2028?

Democrats just took Texas. Republicans aren’t winning California, and the party needs 270 electoral votes.

It’s hard to see how they get there without Texas.

History offers a warning. After Democrats’ big Senate majority in 2009 and 2010, Romney lost in 2012.

Then Trump arrived in 2016, and the party was never the same.

And this time, Democrats may have their own Obama.

Jon Ossoff leads on their side. He’s young, charismatic, from a Southern state, and speaks with that same cadence.

So do the candidates run now, or sit out and hope for better prospects in 2032?

Someone like DeSantis risks fading into irrelevance if he hangs back too long. But run into this headwind, and a loss could end your political career.

The one thing every Republican hopeful has to figure out: is 2028 an opportunity or a trap?

BREAKING 🚨: California fined a Malibu couple $4,185,000 over a beach gate they didn’t even build.

Their “crime”? Keeping a gate that protected the public from a 20-foot drop onto a drainage pipe.

The fine was so brutal they had to SELL their home to help pay it.

When Warren and Henny Lent bought the house in 2002, the deck, the stairs and the gate were already there. Five years later, the California Coastal Commission demanded they rip all three out. 

Why? A previous owner had agreed to public beach access back in 1978, and the gate stood in the way.

The Lents even handed the state a KEY so officials could open the gate any time they wanted.

It wasn’t enough.

Then in 2014, the legislature gave the commission the power to fine property owners up to $11,250 PER DAY. Two years later, it used that power to do the unthinkable:

NARRATOR: “They retroactively fined them for all 744 days that had elapsed since the Lents were informed their violation could expose them to financial penalties. The ultimate fine was a staggering and disproportionate $4.185 million.”

After the hearing, the Lents offered to take the gate down the very next day. The state told them to wait a few months. Why? It needed time to get its OWN gate ready. The moment the old gate came down, the state put a new one up.

Pacific Legal Foundation took the fight all the way to the U.S. Supreme Court. The Court wouldn’t even hear the case.

WARREN LENT: “When you sit down and the dust settles, you say, ‘What did Warren and Henny Lent do?’ They bought a house on the beach to fulfill a lifelong dream. That’s all we did.”

Years later, the 2025 Palisades fire burned the home to the ground. The only thing left standing was that damned gate.

text:
Pancreatic Cancer: The Blood Sugar Clue That Can Appear Up To 3 Years Before Diagnosis | StudyFinds

In A Nutshell

- An Early But Unreliable Signal: In Mayo Clinic records, average fasting blood sugar in people later diagnosed with pancreatic cancer began pulling ahead of matched people without cancer about 30 to 36 months before diagnosis, but those studies tracked group averages and did not produce a test.

- Most New Diabetes Is Not Cancer: In a large prospective study of adults 50 and older with newly detected diabetes, an estimated 0.62 percent, or about 1 in 160, were diagnosed with pancreatic cancer within three years, and a separate analysis found HbA1c alone too weak for widespread screening.

- Patterns Matter, Screening Stays Selective: High or rapidly rising blood sugar, weight loss, older age, pancreatitis, gallstones and family history were linked to higher risk, yet the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force still advises against screening adults without symptoms whose risk comes from factors such as new diabetes or older age.

---

The pancreas helps keep blood sugar in check. So it may not be surprising that when a tumor grows there, blood sugar can start to shift, sometimes long before anyone suspects cancer.

For a disease that usually causes symptoms only after it has spread, according to the National Cancer Institute, that possibility has drawn years of research. The findings point to a real signal, but a messy one. The change can begin early, yet the institute notes that most people who develop diabetes will never get pancreatic cancer. The first question is how early that signal appears.

When Can Blood Sugar Begin To Change?

About three years before diagnosis, on average, in Mayo Clinic records. That does not mean a single lab result can reveal a hidden cancer.

A 2018 case-control study in Gastroenterology pulled five years of fasting blood sugar tests for 219 people in Olmsted County, Minnesota, who were diagnosed with pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, a form of pancreatic cancer. The Mayo Clinic researchers compared them with people of the same age and sex who did not have cancer. Average fasting glucose in the cancer group first rose significantly above the comparison group 30 to 36 months before diagnosis and kept climbing. It crossed the diabetes threshold of 126 milligrams per deciliter roughly six to 12 months before diagnosis. In another group of patients in the same paper, high blood sugar went away after the tumor was surgically removed. That suggests the tumor itself may have been driving the rise.

An earlier Mayo Clinic records study, published in 2009 in The American Journal of Gastroenterology, compared 736 patients with pancreatic cancer and 1,875 people without it. From five to three years before diagnosis, average fasting glucose did not differ meaningfully between the groups. In the cancer group it then rose step by step over the final three years.

Both studies started with people already known to have cancer and looked backward. The 2018 team described the idea that cancer can be found when blood sugar first starts rising as “an unproven but hopeful premise.” Long-standing diabetes is a separate matter. In earlier work, the same Mayo group noted that long-standing diabetes is thought to raise pancreatic cancer risk, while new diabetes may instead be a symptom of the cancer.

Does New-Onset Diabetes Usually Mean Pancreatic Cancer?

Usually not, and the best numbers show how rare the link is.

The clearest estimate of the risk comes from a prospective study in Gastroenterology, published online in 2025 and in the journal’s January 2026 issue. Prospective means the researchers identified people first and then followed them forward. Using real-time monitoring of electronic health records, the team flagged 18,838 adults age 50 or older whose lab results newly met the definition of diabetes. Over a median of 2.3 years, 82 were diagnosed with pancreatic cancer.

After adjusting for the racial makeup of Americans with new diabetes, the estimated three-year risk was 0.62 percent, or about 1 in 160. Risk varied by group, from 0.84 percent among non-Hispanic white patients to 0.22 percent among Asian and Pacific Islander patients. Among people who did develop cancer, diabetes showed up an average of eight months before the diagnosis.

A different blood test tells a similar story. A 2020 analysis in JAMA Network Open examined 851,402 Kaiser Permanente Southern California members ages 50 to 84 who had HbA1c tests, a lab measure of blood sugar. Pancreatic cancer risk rose with higher HbA1c cutoffs and stricter definitions of newly high blood sugar, but the pattern was not consistent across racial and ethnic groups. The authors concluded that screening based on HbA1c alone was unlikely to work. Depending on the cutoff and definition used, doctors would need to evaluate 206 to 600 patients to find one cancer.

Which Patterns Raise More Concern?

A cluster of signs, rather than one lab result.

A 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis in Cancers pooled 22 observational studies covering 576,210 people with new-onset diabetes, 3,560 of whom had pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma. A meta-analysis combines results from many studies to get a more precise estimate. Across four studies, high or rapidly rising blood sugar was tied to more than twice the risk (a pooled estimate of 2.33 that combined risk and odds ratios). Weight loss, older age, pancreatitis, gallstones or gallbladder inflammation, and a family history of pancreatic cancer were also tied to higher risk.

The authors cautioned that most of the studies looked backward, definitions varied from study to study, and results still differed considerably among them.

The National Cancer Institute lists other signs to bring to a doctor: jaundice, which can mean yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, light-colored stools and itching; pain in the upper or middle abdomen and back; weight loss with no known cause; and loss of appetite. It adds that less serious conditions can cause these symptoms too.

What Does The Evidence Actually Support?

Not routine screening for adults at average risk who have no symptoms.

In 2019 the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force reaffirmed its recommendation against screening adults without symptoms for pancreatic cancer. That covers people whose extra risk comes from factors such as new-onset or existing diabetes, older age, smoking, obesity or chronic pancreatitis. It does not apply to people with certain inherited syndromes or a history of familial pancreatic cancer. The task force found no evidence that screening improves outcomes and judged the harms to be at least moderate. Common precursor growths in the pancreas often never progress, so finding them can lead to overtreatment, and pancreatic surgery carries real risks of complications and death.

The best-known blood marker doesn’t solve the problem either. According to Mayo Clinic, a CA 19-9 result can’t confirm pancreatic cancer on its own, and the test is not offered as general-population screening.

Checking out symptoms is different from screening everyone. The National Cancer Institute advises people who develop diabetes without known risk factors for it, such as family history, obesity or heart disease, to ask a doctor about checking for other signs of pancreatic cancer. For concerning symptoms, it says doctors typically begin with an abdominal ultrasound or CT scan. The blood sugar clue is real, but on its own it is a reason to ask a doctor, not a diagnosis.

text:
Breakthrough: FDA Approves First Drug Offering a 'Functional Cure' For Chronic Hepatitis B | David Nield, ScienceAlert

There's new hope for the millions of people affected by chronic hepatitis B (CHB), a liver condition that can lead to cancer, scarring, or organ failure, and which is responsible for over a million deaths worldwide each year.

Following the results of two phase 3 clinical trials, published in the New England Journal of Medicine, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved the drug bepirovirsen for CHB treatment, under the brand name Hibsago.

GSK, the pharmaceutical company behind the drug's development, describes bepirovirsen as the first "functional cure" for CHB, meaning it doesn't just manage the virus causing the infection – as existing treatments do – but suppresses it to undetectable levels in the blood.

What's more, in patients who respond, the infection stays under control even after bepirovirsen treatment is stopped, which is again in contrast to the drugs currently prescribed for CHB.

"This is the start of a new era in treating people living with CHB," says gastroenterologist Norah Terrault, from the Keck Medical Center at the University of Southern California.

"Bepirovirsen offers patients the potential to achieve functional cure after a short period of treatment, a long-standing goal for patients and physicians alike."

The phase 3 trial results showed that a six-month course of bepirovirsen achieved a functional cure response in 233 of 1,220 participants (19 percent), compared to 0 out of 614 participants on a placebo drug.

In those patients, the virus stayed undetectable for at least 24 weeks after all treatment stopped (72 weeks after the trial began).

The drug is administered via weekly injections and was given alongside existing pill treatments, which could then also be stopped for patients given the all-clear.

"For the first time, with Hibsago, US patients have the potential to achieve functional cure after a six-month treatment course, with the added convenience of the option of self-administration after the first dose," says Tony Wood, Chief Scientific Officer at GSK, the pharmaceutical company developing the drug.

It's not all completely positive.

Some patients did experience serious side effects, including liver inflammation, which the FDA says should be monitored for via regular blood tests.

Traces of the virus do stick around, too – it's yet to be proven if the cure holds for years after treatment has ended.

However, the improvements from current treatments are stark enough that the researchers are confident that a significant number of patients are going to benefit, and that's rubber-stamped by the FDA approval.

"For many people living with chronic hepatitis B, treatment can mean taking antiviral medication for years to keep the virus suppressed," says Wendy Carter, the Acting Director at the FDA's Office of Infectious Diseases.

"Hibsago provides a new treatment approach that gives some patients the possibility of maintaining control of the virus after all chronic HBV treatment has ended. This approval represents an important advance for people living with this serious disease."

Some CHB patients responded better to bepirovirsen than others. Lower levels of a key CHB protein at the start of treatment – indicating a less active infection – meant a higher chance of the new drug working. That's something that could be tested for before bepirovirsen is prescribed.

The work doesn't stop here.

The researchers want to see how the new treatment might be combined with other drugs to become even more effective, and GSK wants to make it available to more patients worldwide.

"CHB is a major public health challenge, affecting millions of people in the US and accounting for approximately 56 percent of all global liver cancer cases," says Chari Cohen, the President of the Hepatitis B Foundation.

"Today marks significant progress towards our aim of transforming the way CHB is managed with improvements in screening, diagnosis, and the availability of innovative treatment options for our community."

text:
Two hundred and fifty years ago this week, the Delaware Nation faced a dangerous loss of leadership. Its elderly chief, Netawatwees, had died at Fort Pitt on October 31, leaving Koquethagechton (“White Eyes”) and the Delaware council to maintain peace as the American Revolution threatened to draw their people into war.

Netawatwees and Koquethagechton had worked to keep the Delaware neutral. Netawatwees’ death removed a respected leader who had helped hold that course amid competing pressures from British officials, American representatives, and neighboring Native nations.

For Koquethagechton, known by the British and Americans as White Eyes, the immediate challenge was preserving unity. As a leading spokesman and diplomat, he sought to keep Delaware communities out of the fighting. Some warriors favored the British, while others supported continued neutrality or closer relations with the Americans. No single policy commanded everyone’s allegiance.

The Delaware occupied a strategically important region between American-held Fort Pitt and British-held Detroit. Both sides wanted Native support—or at least assurance that their opponents would receive none. Remaining neutral required constant diplomacy as the struggle spread toward the Ohio Country.

To the south, Cherokee communities were suffering the consequences of armed resistance to expanding settlement. Cherokee attacks that summer had brought devastating American militia campaigns. Troops burned towns, destroyed crops, and left families facing winter without adequate food or shelter. Cherokee leaders who had urged peace could not shield their communities from the destruction. The choices facing Native nations were painfully narrow: resistance risked military devastation, while diplomacy offered no assurance that settlers would stop taking their land.

Koquethagechton sought to protect Delaware land and the nation’s authority to determine its own course. With Netawatwees gone, sustaining that independence became still more difficult. Whether diplomacy could keep the war outside their communities remained uncertain. And that’s the way it was on November 6, 1776.

Seven Kentucky Football Programs Withdraw From KHSAA Playoffs

Seven Kentucky high school football programs have announced playoff forfeitures, ending their seasons ahead of the KHSAA postseason.

Caverna, Frankfort, Fort Knox, Marion County, Morgan County, Berea and Western have all withdrawn from playoff competition. The seven programs finished the regular season with a combined 8-63 record, with school officials largely citing concerns about player health and safety.

For the affected teams, the decisions bring an end to a difficult season. While a postseason appearance offers another opportunity to compete, officials have largely pointed to the well-being of their student-athletes in explaining why their programs will not take the field.

The forfeitures also affect the postseason bracket, allowing the seven programs’ scheduled opponents to advance without playing their opening-round matchups.

The withdrawals put a spotlight on the challenges facing struggling football programs and the difficult decisions school leaders face when weighing postseason participation against player health and safety.
